author: Konner Metz
content:
Garage fire outside Denton causes significant damages

 March 3, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Konner Metz | Section: Local News

 DENTON — A garage fire Sunday morning caused an estimated $700,000 in damages, according to the Office of the State Fire Marshal.Just before 11:30 a.m. Sunday, a fire broke out in a garage on Sennett Road near Hobbs, a community just southeast of Denton.
Firefighters from the Denton Volunteer Fire Company responded and controlled the blaze in around 40 minutes, per the fire marshal. No injuries were reported.
Authorities say the fire started on a work bench in the garage, which had electronic appliances and lithium batteries on it.
"The fire resulted in the total loss of high valued industrial equipment that was being stored in the garage by the occupant," a release from the fire marshal's office stated.
The fire marshal estimated $400,000 in structure damages and $300,000 in content damages.
The preliminary cause is still under investigation.

author: Natalie Jones; njones@chespub.com

 EASTON - Students and staff at Easton Middle School were evacuated Wednesday morning after the school administration received a bomb threat.According to a news release from the Talbot County Sheriff's Office, front desk staff at the middle school received a bomb threat via telephone around 9:25 a.m.Wednesday.The caller said there were numerous explosive devices throughout the building that would detonate at a specified time, police said.Police said all identified calls were made from a New Jersey area code.School officials followed emergency policies and safely evacuated students and staff to St. Marks Methodist Church in Easton.Deputies from the Talbot County Sheriff's Office responded to the school and began investigating. title: Identifying faulty circuit breakers can protect your home
content:
Identifying faulty circuit breakers can protect your home

 August 25, 2023 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Page: A13 | Section: News 
 
 799
 Words 

 Read News Document

 Electricity is at the center of our everyday lives. From computers, cell phones, televisions, and even now our vehicles.We find ourselves in a world where most things are powered by electricity, and we just trust that this electricity is safe.There are a multitude of items that ensure that we are delivered safe electricity throughout our day, and one of the most important items is our circuit breakers.Daniel Morris, Certified Master Inspector with Blackwater Home Inspectors, is a preferred partner with Mid-Shore Board of Realtors and explains circuit breakers and home safety.Circuit breakers are a safety device that is used to protect the electrical wiring running throughout our homes. The wiring in our home is designed to handle a certain amount of electricity that is normal for the fixtures it's attached to. The circuit breaker will detect if more electricity than the wire is rated for is being used, and "trip" to shut off the electrical current to the fixture.What happens if this system fails?The wiring can then become too hot from this increased electrical current and cause a home fire to start. Throughout the development of the electrical safety devices found inside of our homes, there have been some defective products that made their way into some homes. Here are some of those circuit breaker panels, and how to identify if they are installed in your home.Federal Pacific Electric company manufactured a series of panels from 1950-1980 called a "Stab-Lok" panel. The Federal Pacific Electric company purposefully cheated safety testing to ensure that their new "Stab-Lok" panel would pass the testing.When in actuality, these circuit breakers were later found to have a failure rate of about 30 percent. This means that in the case of too much electrical current being sent down the wire to a fixture, the breaker will not trip, and will cause the circuit to become overloaded and potentially cause a fire. These panels and breakers were installed in millions of homes during the production time, and while estimates vary, hundreds of thousands are believed to still be in use. Replacement of both the circuit breakers and panels is recommended.Identifying these panels and breakers is very simple however. Look at your electrical panel and see if the name "Stab-Lok" is identified anywhere on the cover plate, you will not need to remove any screws. Also, look for the red coloring located behind the circuit breaker number rating (15,20,30,50, etc.). When in doubt, always reach out to a licensed electrician for help in identifying.Another common circuit breaker panel with a history of safety defects is the Zinsco/Sylvania electrical panel. This type of electrical panel began production under the Zinsco name, before eventually being bought out by the Sylvania company. Sylvania then continued the production of this circuit breaker panel with no changes made. These panels were installed from the mid-1950s through the mid-1970s. These types of electrical breakers also had a history of failing to trip when overloading occurred. This led to arcs and overloading of the breaker to panel connection.The circuit breakers would often become fused to the electrical panel and be unable to be removed. What's worse, they would also melt the internal components of the breaker and make them unable to be tripped whatsoever.These breakers and panels are also easily identifiable.First, look for the labeling of the panel. The older units will have the "Zinsco" name, while units produced in the '70s will have the "Sylvania" name. Both of these panel names, however, will use the same breaker look. The breakers are skinnier than other electrical breakers seen today.They also had utilized colors, much like the Federal Pacific panel that you do not see. The moveable part of the breaker, that will (hopefully) move in the event of a trip, is colored either red, a light green, or a brighter green color. Identifying if there is damage to these breakers is only possible by having a licensed electrician remove the breaker from the panel.There are more dangers with electricity, however these two common electrical panels are easily identifiable, and can save your home from damage.If you have a home built before the 1990s, it may not hurt to take a minute or so to double check your electrical panel to ensure it is not one of these two defective panels.If you suspect you have one of these panels or are not sure what type of panel you have, reach out to a local electrician or a qualified home inspector to learn more.Morris can be reached at 443-528-1633 or email him at. The company website is Blackwaterhomeinspections.com.The Mid-Shore Board of Realtors is happy to partner with many firms related to the real estate industry. For more news and information check out their website, www.midshoreboardofrealtors.com. 
 
 Caption: Examples of faulty circuit breaker panels to look out for.
 
SUBMITTED 

 © Copyright © 2023 Star Democrat, Chesapeake Publishing Group (Adams Publishing/APGMedia). All rights reserved.

title: Federalsburg Police Department welcomes new officer
author: AHMAD GARNETT agarnett@chespub.com
content:
Federalsburg Police Department welcomes new officer

 June 25, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: AHMAD GARNETT agarnett@chespub.com | Section: News 
 
 337
 Words 

 Read News Document

 FEDERARLSBURG – The Federalsburg Police Department welcomed Officer Chandler Dyott after he graduated from the Eastern Shore Criminal Justice Academy on June 11.Dyott has been with the department since December, participating in ride-alongs while he learned the responsibilities of what he needed to became a full time police officer, the department said.
Dyott, from Easton, worked two years as a correctional officer in Talbot County before heading to the academy, but he said he always wanted to be a police officer.
"Ever since I was little, I wanted to be a cop," Dyott said. "But when I got out of high school, you can't be a cop until you're 21. So, when I got out of high school, I thought, 'I'll join Talbot County Corrections.'
"That way in corrections, it teaches you how to talk to people, interact with the people. Just because they got locked up and you see them in the jail, you realize they're not a bad person. They're just people like us."
Dyott, now 21, is looking forward to being an officer in Federalsburg. So far during his required 240 hours of field training, Dyott has enjoyed introducing himself to the community.
Dyott wants the community to know he will treat them with respect.
"I'm going to be fair, 100%," Dyott said. "I believe in respect goes a long way. You respect me, I'm going to respect you anytime… No matter what, I'm going to be fair, and I'm going to try to step up on community policing."
Lt. Michelle Schuerholz said the police department is happy to have such a young officer on staff.
"We're proud to welcome Officer Dyott to our department," Schuerholz said. "Being so young, he brings a strong commitment to community and public safety, and we're confident he will be a great asset to both our department and the residents we serve. We look forward to seeing the positive impact Officer Dyott will make in our community. He comes from correctional, and he had a good reputation there, and I think he'll do well here."

title: Protecting each other
author: Staff Writer
content:
Protecting each other

 March 24, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Staff Writer | Section: Editors Inbox 
 
 392
 Words 

 Read News Document

 Being a good Catholic does not mean turning one's head to crime committed by priests or anyone else.My six siblings and I were fortunate to attend Catholic School. As adult professionals, we credit the nuns with our integrity.
All the nuns at our school were strong women. They were tough Germans who fled Germany as Adolf Hitler came to power. I stayed in touch with many of the nuns over the years.
Due to their background, they insisted that we look out for one another, for protecting each other, and correcting any aspect of life that would place one in a harmful situation. Sitting down when seeing evil was not an option for them.
It is that teaching that brought me to reporting a priest in our Maryland parish for inappropriate contact with small boys in 1987. Seeing things with my own eyes, I reached out to one of the nuns that I trusted. The parish settled the cases, and the priest was defrocked.
Defrocked. Removed for good. He would have no more Catholic school playgrounds to select his next victim nor another innocent parent to convince that his or her child spend the night with him in the rectory.
Last year at Eastertime, the Maryland Attorney General released a report on the sexual abuse of children within the Baltimore Archdiocese. Due to the stigma of sexual assaults especially for boys, it is impossible to calibrate the exact number of victims.
That report sat poorly with one of the local devout Catholics. She seemed to not understand why the state of Maryland would increase the statute of limitations for child victims. She condemned the amount of money available to the victims and categorically and alarmingly published, while defending the church, false statements: "No new cases have been brought up for over 25 years and most of the clergy who were involved are not even alive today."
That is like stating a crime like drunk driving has been extinguished throughout the country in the last 25 years.
The upset parishioner is considered one of the pillars of the church. Thus, she has a good vantage point to observe. With that comes duty. And one of the duties is to take the blinders off, get educated on child victims and report any inappropriate conduct upon a child. That makes us good Catholics because praying alone does not extinguish pedophilia.
CATHY LINDBERG JAROSZ
Easton

title: Police: Fentanyl overdoses killed Perryville siblings, 10 and 14
author: Carl Hamilton cahamilton@chespub.com
content:
Police: Fentanyl overdoses killed Perryville siblings, 10 and 14

 March 5, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Carl Hamilton cahamilton@chespub.com | Section: State News 
 
 422
 Words 

 Read News Document

 PERRYVILLE — An "accidental overdose" is what killed two children who were found unresponsive in their Perryville home in January — and now investigators are trying to determine how the illegal drug got into the residence, got into the siblings' possession and got into their systems, according to the Maryland State Police."The toxicology report came back positive for fentanyl," reported Elena Russo, an MSP spokeswoman.
MSP detectives and Cecil County Child Protective Services agents are involved in the ongoing investigation, according to Russo, who further reported that the Cecil County State's Attorney's Office "has been apprised of the ongoing investigation and is aware of the progress."
The drug overdoses claimed the lives of Skylar Alice Marie Jones, 14, and her 10-year-old brother, Gaige Marshall Dehaven.
Their 12-year-old sister found Skylar and Gaige unresponsive inside their residence in the 600 block of Cole Street early in the early afternoon of Jan. 16 and called 911, police said. The children lived at that Cole Street residence with their mother, police added. Investigators have not publicly identified their mother.
Troopers assigned to the agency's North East Barrack responded to the Cole Street residence shortly before 1:20 p.m. on Jan. 16 to assist Perryville Police Department officers with what law enforcement officials described at the time as the "cardiac arrest of two juveniles," police reported. Paramedics were attempting emergency medical care on the children when troopers arrived, police said. Paramedics later pronounced the boy and girl dead at the scene, police added.
"The sister reported her brother and sister were suffering from an unknown medical condition. She later told police that she came home and found her siblings unconscious on their bedroom floor. Police believe there was no one else in the home at the time," an MSP spokesperson outlined one day after the deadly incident.
That spokesperson also reported that "there was no indication of violence in the area surrounding the location where the juveniles were found."
Investigators found "drug paraphernalia" and "other items of evidentiary value" while searching the Cole Street residence, after obtaining a warrant to do so, police reported.
On Jan. 17, one day after the children died, MSP officials reported that the cause and manner of their deaths remained unknown after autopsies performed on the bodies of Skylar and Gaige "revealed no abnormalities." They further reported that, at that point, investigators were hopeful that then-pending toxicology results might reveal the cause and manner of the children's deaths.
MSP investigators recently received those toxicology results, which indicate that fentanyl overdoses caused the deaths of Skylar and Gaige, according to police.

title: Trial Begins For Cambridge Man Charged In Fatal Shooting
author: Natalie Jones; Njones@Chespub.Com
content:
Trial Begins For Cambridge Man Charged In Fatal Shooting

 December 13, 2023 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Natalie Jones; Njones@Chespub.Com | Page: 3 | Section: News 
 
 528
 Words 

 Read News Document

 CAMBRIDGE - Testimony began Tuesday in the jury trial for a Cambridge man charged in the shooting death of a 24-year-old man last December.Tramelle Williams, 23, is charged with firstand second-degree murder, armed robbery and firearms offenses in the fatal shooting of Taijay Brian Daniels on Pleasant Street just after 7 p.m.
Dec. 8, 2022.
Wearing a Space Jam jacket and walking down Race Street that night, Daniels was just a normal 24-year-old. He had no idea he was about to be killed "execution-style," said Dorchester County State's Attorney Amanda Leonard, who is prosecuting the case with Senior Assistant State's Attorney Ella Disharoon.
Williams, wearing a mask, approached Daniels with a gun, shooting him in the back. Then, he shot again, striking Daniels in the head twice before taking Daniels' belongings and leaving.
Although a Cambridge resident on his way home that night found Daniels' body lying facedown on Pleasant Street within minutes of the shooting, and police and emergency medical services personnel performed CPR, Daniels was pronounced deceased at the scene.
Daniels' death was ruled a homicide by multiple gunshot wounds, two of which were "rapidly fatal," a state medical examiner testified Tuesday afternoon.
"He didn't stand a chance," Leonard said during her opening statement.
However, Williams didn't count on surveillance cameras from local businesses capturing the shooting, she said.
Williams also didn't count on police arresting him while he was wearing the same backpack from the night of the shooting, or police finding Daniels' phone in his pocket, Leonard added.
Williams was arrested the next evening following a foot pursuit on Lincoln Terrace. After he attempted to flee, a Cambridge police officer fired, shooting Williams in the leg.
But to defense attorneys Michelle Moodispaw and Stephanie DeLang, evidence shown by prosecutors would not prove Williams guilty.
Video surveillance and forensics presented by prosecutors have limited value, Moodispaw said, urging the jury to consider evidence that wasn't being shown.
The only thing to be presented was "maybes and possibilities," she said.
By the end of the day Tuesday, seven witnesses had testified, including Daniels' mother, police officers, crime scene technicians and the medical examiner.
Additional law enforcement witnesses and forensic analysts are expected to testify Wednesday. A verdict is anticipated Friday.
This week's trial is not the only pending case against Williams.
Williams is also accused in a second fatal shooting in Cambridge, which occurred roughly three hours after Daniels was shot.
Around 10 p.m. Dec. 8, 2022, police responded to the 700 block of High Street for a second gunshot victim, who was identified as Lory Eugene Fields, 69, of Cambridge.
Fields was found lying in a yard with a gunshot wound to his head. He was declared deceased at the scene.
Williams is facing additional murder and robbery charges in connection to Fields' death.
Though the shootings happened within hours of each other and all charges appear to be grouped together in Maryland Judiciary court records, Williams is set to stand for a second trial related to Fields' death in mid-January.

title: Anton Black's family settles with state medical examiner
author: Natalie Jones; njones@chespub.com
content:
Anton Black's family settles with state medical examiner

 November 9, 2023 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Natalie Jones; njones@chespub.com | Page: 3 | Section: News 
 
 773
 Words 

 Read News Document

 ANNAPOLIS - A $235,000 settlement approved by the Board of Public Works resolved all claims in a federal lawsuit brought against the state medical examiner by the family of 19-year-old Anton Black, who died in Greensboro in 2018 after being restrained by police.The settlement, which includes a $100,000 payment to Black's family and $135,000 toward attorneys' fees, was approved without discussion during Wednesday's Board of Public Works meeting.The settlement also "makes necessary changes to the Maryland Office of the Chief Medical Examiner's process for autopsies conducted on people killed in law enforcement custody and requires notification to families about the results and their rights to challenge the results," according to a news release from the American Civil Liberties Union.Reforms to the state medical examiner's office include the adoption of a policy addressing how medical examiners handle deaths in custody, which includes those involving law enforcement restraint, according to the ACLU.The policy also incorporates and models guidelines from the National Association of Medical Examiners for determining how such deaths are investigated and how examiners determine causation.The ACLU said the reforms will instill more transparency, impartiality and "independence from improper law enforcement influence." The Office of the Chief Medical Examiner must also provide families with information on their rights to seek correction of an autopsy report and the procedures to seek that correction.In a statement, Richard Potter, the founder of the Coalition for Justice for Anton Black, called the settlement an "excellent first step," adding that community members must stay vigilant to ensure it's effective and increases accountability from within."I hope that with this settlement agencies will begin to recognize their own wrongdoings, catch them and change them before they cause harm," he said in the statement. "What is needed is a sense of shared ownership that can only come through trust and mutual accountability, with police confronting their own biases about mental illness, committing to de-escalation, and truly serving a diverse community." Black died on his mother's front steps on Sept. 15, 2018, after being chased, tased and restrained by three white police officers and a white civilian.That day, Black and a 12-year-old family friend were walking around Greensboro together when Black began pulling and dragging the child, who was calling out for help, garnering attention from onlookers that led to a call to police.The chase ended outside Black's home, where Greensboro Police Officer Thomas Webster IV, offduty Ridgely Police Chief Gary Manos, Centreville Police Officer Dennis Lannon and a civilian attempted to restrain Black, pressing his body against a wooden handicap ramp for six minutes while attempting to handcuff and shackle him.Black later became unresponsive, but continued breathing and had a pulse.Officers rolled Black on his side, then shifted him to a sitting position.After no further response, officers removed the handcuffs and began CPR. Black was later transported to the University of Maryland Shore Medical Center in Easton, where he was pronounced dead that evening.The medical examiner ruled that Black's death was an accident caused by a heart condition, with bipolar disorder as a contributing cause.Unanswered questions surrounding Black's death and excessive use of force spurred the litigation. The family filed a wrongful death lawsuit against multiple police officers, towns and the state medical examiner involved in the case in December 2020.No one was charged in connection to Black's death.In August 2022, the family and coalition reached a settlement that required police departments in Greensboro, Ridgely and Centreville to overhaul use of force policies and the enhancement of resources for police confronting mental health emergencies; officer training in de-escalation, intervention and implicit bias; hiring transparency; and public complaint reporting.The settlement also included a $5 million payment to Black's family from the police and municipal defendants.Black's death caused his family and the coalition to become deeply involved in Maryland's campaign for police reform and accountability.Efforts by the family and the Coalition led to the passage of Anton's Law in 2021, which makes police discipline records available to the community under Maryland's Public Information Act.Sonia Kumar, a senior staff attorney with the ACLU of Maryland, said the "hardfought" settlement is about ensuring the medical examiner is truthful about what happens when people, particularly Black people, are killed by police or corrections officials."We can't prevent such deaths if we aren't honest about what caused them, and this settlement is a crucial step towards that goal in future cases," she said in a statement. "We hope this settlement will make a real, positive impact, but it is truly just the beginning of the reckoning needed to address decades of misrepresentations so we can bring justice to families still waiting for the government to tell the truth." 
 
 Caption: ANTON BLACK

title: St. Michaels approves three new police vehicles
author: AHMAD GARNETT agarnett@chespub.com

St. Michaels approves three new police vehicles

 April 26, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: AHMAD GARNETT agarnett@chespub.com | Section: News

 ST. MICHAELS — The St. Michaels commissioners plan to invest $215,000 from this fiscal year and next fiscal year into three new police vehicles for the St. Michaels Police Department."These guys are always in need for updated equipment," Alfred Mercier, commissioners president, said.
The company that St. Michaels is buying the police vehicles through will allow the commissioners to pay for one vehicle with this year's fbudget and two in next year's budget. The town will receive all three vehicles up front.
"These are all coming out of speed camera funds that are held in a separate account, so unless there's going to be changes in the FY26 budget, this should be something that we can accomplish," Don Richardson, town manager, said.
While the budget for the vehicles is $215,000, the three vehicles will cost $146,820. The rest will be used for graphics, lights and equipment.
Jeffery Oswald, St. Michaels chief of police, credits the St. Michaels commissioners for their help getting the new vehicles.
"I would have to thank to the commissioners because they're always have the support on keeping our equipment up-to-date to match other agencies surrounding us," Oswald said. "We want to keep our emergency vehicles safe and well equipped so we can provide public safety to the town.
"Our fleet is aging, so having the cost and the liabilities of an aging fleet, so not only it will save us money on maintenance, it will provide a better look to attract officers with new equipment and new vehicles."

title: Easton fire department takes home awards from firefighters convention
author: ANDREA GRABENSTEIN agrabenstein@chespub.com
content:
Easton fire department takes home awards from firefighters convention

 June 25, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: ANDREA GRABENSTEIN agrabenstein@chespub.com | Section: Local News 
 
 405
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTERN SHORE — Representing the spirit of Maryland fire departments, Eastern Shore volunteers brought numerous home recognitions from the 133rd Maryland State Firefighters Association annual convention and conference in Ocean City June 18.Each June, the association gathers for its annual convention and conference to conduct business and provide training and educational sessions. In addition to the convention, a parade of apparatus took to the streets of Ocean City.
Easton Volunteer Fire Department was the fire company with the most uniformed fire service personnel attending the event. The department took home awards after the parade, including Best Appearing Fire Service Color Guard, Best Appearing Pumper Tanker, Best Appearing Ambulance, Second Best Appearing Tower and Third Best Appearing Rescue.
Easton volunteers were also awarded the Chief A. Marvin Gibbons Award for the Maryland company with the best appearance overall.
"I am truly honored and proud of the men and women of the Easton Volunteer Fire Department. Preparation for the Maryland State Firemen's Association Parade in Ocean City begins months in advance to ensure that we display our apparatus with pride, professionalism, and a strong representation of our department, the Town of Easton, and Talbot County," said Easton Volunteer Fire Department Chief J.R. Dobson in a statement. "Being presented with the Chief A. Marvin Gibbons Trophy for Best Overall Appearance is an achievement we strive for every year, dating back to 1992, when the award was established in honor of Chief Gibbons. We are proud to announce that this year marks the thirteenth time we have received this prestigious recognition."
Federalsburg firefighters took home the Second Best Appearance Tanker award, and Cordova firefighters won the Fire Prevention Entry Making Best Appearance award.

title: Trial begins for Cambridge man accused of murder, kidnapping of woman
author: Konner Metz
content:
Trial begins for Cambridge man accused of murder, kidnapping of woman

 September 17, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Konner Metz | Section: Local News 
 
 615
 Words 

 Read News Document

 CAMBRIDGE — Witness testimony began Tuesday in the jury trial for a Cambridge man charged with murdering and kidnapping a woman last year.Kenneth Bradley, 43, is charged with first- and second-degree murder and kidnapping, among other counts, in connection to the disappearance and presumed death of Tiyavauna Britt on Feb. 7, 2024, at the Gerry Boyle Park at Great Marsh in Cambridge.
On Tuesday, prosecutors made their first appeal to the jury, asking for first-degree murder and kidnapping convictions. The defense is vying for not-guilty verdicts on those counts, contending that second-degree murder or manslaughter are more appropriate charges.
Bradley and Britt, a 31-year-old mother of three, had been dating, according to multiple accounts provided during trial Tuesday and prior court documents. They were allegedly together in the parking lot of the park on Feb. 7, 2024, before Britt disappeared.
Easton police put out a missing persons report for Britt six days later. Family had found her car abandoned in an Easton parking lot.
Cambridge police, along with state homicide detectives, assumed the investigation from Easton authorities following the review of cell phone location data placing Britt at the park.
Bradley was initially arrested on kidnapping charges in February 2024. Review of camera footage at the park from Feb. 7 revealed "sounds of loud thuds ... consistent with forceful strikes," police wrote in charging documents. Later that night, footage showed a man "carrying and dragging" a woman's body to a vehicle, police wrote.
Bradley was indicted and arrested on murder charges in March 2024. Britt's body was not found.
Dorchester County State's Attorney Amanda Leonard, the lead prosecutor, and public defender Matt Connell, who is representing Bradley, provided opening statements Tuesday.
Leonard told the jury the case is full of "rage, control, domestic violence." Evidence shows Britt's relationship with Bradley was "toxic," she said.
Leonard said Bradley's former employer and a close friend will testify later this week. Bradley confided in them, she said, confessing to the murder and the disposing of Britt's body.
"She vanished," Leonard said. "She was never seen or heard from again. No phone calls or text messages."
Leonard said jurors will see video footage from the park. The audio is "chilling," she said, showing Bradley drag Britt and throw her in the trunk of a car.
Before jurors took their seats to listen to openings, Connell objected to some of the audio evidence, arguing that Bradley could have a "reasonable expectation" for privacy during some of the conversations.
"We are fine acknowledging that that was him in the video," Connell said. " ... 90% of the verbal communication occurred inside the vehicle."
Leonard disagreed with the 90% assessment. Connell said, "it's possible I'm mistaken."
While the full video and accompanying audio wasn't admitted as evidence Tuesday, Judge William Jones sided with the prosecution. It's "quite likely" the court will allow its admission during trial, the judge said, especially if the conversations included yelling.
In Connell's opening statement, he acknowledged Bradley's involvement in Britt's death. But he said prosecutors must show Bradley intended to kill Britt in order for the jury to deliver a guilty verdict on first-degree murder.
"He lost it. He hit her too hard, and she died," Connell said, adding that Bradley tried to resuscitate Britt. "He didn't mean to do it."
"Hold him responsible for what he's really guilty of, not above and beyond that," the defense attorney said.
Thirteen witnesses testified Tuesday, including close family of Britt and police detectives who worked the case.
Linda Harris, Britt's mother, recalled Feb. 12, 2024 during an emotional testimony. It was her other daughter's birthday, and Britt didn't show up.
"She wouldn't miss anything," Harris said of birthday parties and holidays. The mother said she last saw Britt a week before she disappeared.
Trial is scheduled to continue through Friday.

 Thirty-nine people accused of a drug-trafficking ring on the Eastern Shore were indicted following a five-month combined law enforcement investigation.Wicomico Narcotics, a collaborative effort between the Maryland Department of State Police, the Fruitland Police Department, the Office of the State's Attorney for Wicomico County, and the Drug Enforcement Administration, began a covert investigation in spring 2024 that culminated in the indictment of 39 people involved in a large-scale drug trafficking operation in Wicomico County.
Maryland State Police joined more than two dozen local, state and federal law enforcement agencies in dismantling the sale and distribution of illegal drugs, including cocaine and fentanyl, throughout Wicomico, Dorchester and Baltimore counties.

Wicomico Narcotics received funding for this investigation from the Governor's Office of Crime Prevention and Policy and the Organized Crime Drug Enforcement Task Forces. Wicomico Narcotics is a designated Washington/Baltimore HIDTA-funded initiative.
Assisting agencies include the Drug Enforcement Administration, Maryland State Police, Somerset County Sheriff's Office, Worcester Sheriff's Office, Wicomico Sheriff's Office, Dorchester County Sheriff's Office, Talbot County Sheriff's Office, Kent County Sheriff's Office, Caroline County Sheriff's Office, Strike Force 7, Queen Anne's County Sheriff's Office, Eastern Shore Information Center, Homeland Security Investigations, Salisbury Police Department, Ocean City Police Department, and the Maryland Department of Transportation Authority Police.

 EASTON - The card game at American Legion Post 77 ended abruptly on Wednesday evening when a duplex located next door caught fire shortly after 5:30 p.m., pulling players from the table and into the action."We were in there playing cards together, and my father said, 'Come outside and see the smoke.' He said, 'Is that my vehicle on fire?'" said Anthony Wilson, a member of the lodge, who stood across the street as firefighters extinguished dwindling embers. (Some members) ran around here and saw the smoke and said there was a fire Then all of us came out and came over here." "(There were) no injuries. Nothing but the dog. Everyone else was out after that, and it was just a matter of time waiting for the fire company."Dispatchers alerted local fire departments about the blaze at 5:46 p.m. About 60 first responders reported to the scene, according to emergency officials at the scene.An official from the St. Michaels Volunteer Fire Department, who was on the scene, confirmed that there were no injuries reported in the incident and that the fire was contained to a single structure, located at 21 South West St. in Easton.Due to the structure's age, he said, safeguards had not been included in its construction, making the duplex susceptible to the quick-spreading fire.Neighbors who gathered at the scene reported that the duplex, which consists of an upstairs and a downstairs unit, had been engulfed in flames at one point in the evening, with fire visible from both upstairs and downstairs windows.Firefighters on the scene included the Easton Volunteer Fire Department, the Oxford Fire Company, the Trappe Volunteer Fire Company, the St. Michaels Fire Department and the Cordova Volunteer Fire Company.  DENTON - A Preston man pleaded guilty Monday to attempted murder in connection to the February 2022 stabbing of a young woman.After waiving his right to a jury trial two weeks ago, Mark William Thompkins, 25, pleaded guilty to attempted second-degree murder during a hearing in Caroline County Circuit Court.The plea reached Monday comes over a year and a half after the stabbing of a then 25-year-old woman near Holly Park Drive and Gilpin Point Road in Preston shortly before 3 p.m. on Feb. 17, 2022.According to Caroline County State's Attorney Sloane Franklin, trash collection workers near the scene first saw the woman sitting in the driver's seat of her vehicle with a man, later identified as Thompkins, seated behind her. Thompkins began striking the woman with his fists, then brandished a knife to stab her neck.The woman ran from her vehicle and collapsed in the front yard of a nearby house. title: ‘Hang up immediately’: Scam artists impersonating police, targeting nonprofits with big, bogus donations
author: MIKE SUNNUCKS APG Newspapers
content:
‘Hang up immediately’: Scam artists impersonating police, targeting nonprofits with big, bogus donations

 February 17, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: MIKE SUNNUCKS APG Newspapers | Section: National 
 
 915
 Words 

 Read News Document

 Consumers lost a record $10 billion to fraudsters last year across the U.S., driven by crypto currency schemes, and there are fresh warnings from local police as well as scams targeting nonprofits and small businesses.The Maryland State Police issued a warning earlier this month in which the caller used a cloned official number (410-761-5130) claiming to be a law enforcement and tries to intimidate residents into sharing their banking information.
That mirrors some of the scams and warnings being reported across the state by local police.
"The Garrett County Sheriff's Office is aware of a recent scam, where the caller tells individuals they have warrants through the Sheriff's Office and instructs them to withdraw money and take it to the kiosk at Walmart for a deposit," the police agency said in a recent warning. "The numbers displayed by the caller are the Sheriff's Office and/or District Court phone numbers. Citizens are reminded to be aware of scams and know that the Sheriff's Office will never instruct someone to pay in such a manner."
The St. Mary's County Sheriff's Office said in a Feb. 14 advisory that some fraud rings while also impersonate federal agents and will target businesses.
"We urge all residents to be wary of calls or messages demanding immediate payment or threatening legal action. This is a tell-tale sign of a scam," SMCSO said in an announcement, recommending employers talk to workers about potential scammers.
Police across the country have been cautioning of similar schemes snd scams including ones related to supposed missed jury duty.
"The caller claims that the person missed jury duty and that there is a warrant for their arrest, but they can post a fine or bail to take care of it," the Gallatin County Sheriff's Office in Montana said in a community alert issued Feb. 12.
The law enforcement agency tells residents to "hang up immediately" and to not send any payments.
"Scammers want you to act fast. They'll pressure you, threaten you, and even try to keep you on the phone so you can't verify their story. Remember, don't let urgency cloud your judgment," the Washington County Government in western Maryland says in series of tips of how to avoid rip-off schemes.
Consumer protection groups and police say some fraud rings will accept payments via gift cards or crypto currency, which are hard to trace and are additional signs of fraud.
NONPROFITS, SMALL BUSINESSES TARGETED
Nonprofits and small businesses are also being targeted by fraud rings while other associations and charities are being impersonated by schemers.
The Maryland State Bar Association is cautioning members of phishing scams purporting to be from the group's leaders, including executive director Anna Sholl. The effort looks to gain financial and personal information from law firms and attorneys.
Catholic Charities is also warning of imposter scams related to potential financial helping Maryland residents with water bill payments.
Contracting and cleaning businesses are also urged to be leery of bogus insurance providers.
"The Maryland Insurance Administration (MIA) has become aware of an insurance-related scam that predominantly targets small painting, construction, and cleaning businesses," the agency said in scam alert issued Friday, Feb. 16.
The state agency said scammers are approaching small businesses about buying general liability or workers compensation insurance. MIA urges Maryland businesses to verify the legitimacy and licensing of the broker and company offering the insurance.
Across the country, there is another cautionary tale.
Montana Nonprofit Association is also warning organizations of donation schemes that have so far targeted 19 groups statewide and could be used against other groups nationally.
MNA said a nonprofit will receive " an unexpected donation of around $200,000 to honor someone's late mother."
"Multiple (organizations) have said the amount they received was $191,250, and that the email came from Alphonso Blye. The cashier's check looks legitimate so they cash it, " the Helena-based group said in an announcement Monday.
A few days later the same donor will contact the nonprofit and tell them the check should have been for $100,000 and request a refund of the remaining amount.
The check is bogus to begin and will bounce but scam rings hope to bilk groups out of $91,250 in the meantime.
"So far, everyone who has contacted us has managed to catch the scam before falling victim, but with this amount of money, the scammer only needs to convince one," MPA said.
The statewide association recommends confirming the identity of donors before accepting money and asking them to wait 30 days before issuing any refunds.
Major banks statewide and the Montana Bankers Association have also been alerted to the fraud scheme.
RECORD FRAUD LEVELSThe Federal Trade Commission reported Feb. 9 that U.S. consumers lost a record $10 billion to fraud schemes in 2023.
That is a 14% increase from 2022. Some of that jump stems from crypto currency fraud.
"Consumers reported losing more money to investment scams—more than $4.6 billion—than any other category in 2023. That amount represents a 21% increase over 2022. The second highest reported loss amount came from imposter scams, with losses of nearly $2.7 billion reported. In 2023, consumers reported losing more money to bank transfers and cryptocurrency than all other methods combined," FTC which received 2.6 million consumer complaints last year.
The U.S agency received 2.5 million complaints in 2022. The FTC said last year saw an increase in consumer calls involving fraud rings impersonating government officials (including police) as well as businesses.
The FTC received fraud reports from 2.6 million consumers last year, nearly the same amount as 2022. The most commonly reported scam category was imposter scams, which saw significant increases in reports of both business and government impersonators.

title: Dorchester County may need to add to detention center
author: Veronica Fernandez-Alvarado
content:
Dorchester County may need to add to detention center

 October 18, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Veronica Fernandez-Alvarado | Section: Local News 
 
 681
 Words 

 Read News Document

 CAMBRIDGE — The Dorchester County detention center is struggling to keep up with increases in the number of juveniles incarcerated and may ask for money to build a new wing to house the young offenders.During a Tuesday County Council meeting, council members decided to prioritize the topic for the upcoming Maryland General Assembly legislative session.
During a final discussion on priorities for the legislative session, Councilmember Mike Detmer, talked about what he described as his "juvenile crime concern."
In his comments, Detmer said juvenile crime in Dorchester County has been on the rise and the crimes being committed are more than simply jaywalking.
"It's absolutely insane that we have so many people that have had direct and directly affected by this, multiple people in this room directly affected by juvenile crime," Detmer said. "And it's unbelievable that in 2024 that we can be in a place of all the resources and all the talent we have that are wearing badges, that we can be in a place where we're held hostage by ostensibly well intentioned laws."
Detmer pleaded with council to put emphasis on juvenile crime for the Maryland General Assembly legislative session. He reminded the council of stories he shared on juvenile crime during previous meetings including children as young as 10 with guns and speeding cars on U.S. Route 50 and state Route 16 by underage drivers.
"There are kids that are still kids on paper," Detmer said. "(But) they're not acting like children."
Council President George Pfeffer, said the topic is on the list and there's no priority on the list created. Pfeffer described the topics on the list as "equally important to us" and said they will emphasize the importance of those topics once there is a legislator in front of them.
The list will be discussed with the local contingent of state delegates and senators.
Later on in the meeting Councilmember Ricky Travers, added that he agreed with Detmer and said he had issue with the way the juvenile justice system functions and said the system is "setting up a whole group of young kids for failure."
During public comment, detention center Warden Don Satterfield shared that over the last two months the detention center has had seven juveniles waiting for adult status.
Satterfield said because the state of Maryland has passed laws stating that juveniles must be housed separately by "vision and audio," those regulations have created a difficult barrier with the increase of juveniles being sent to adult detention centers.
Satterfield shared that the current detention center is almost 34 years old and is not designed to accommodate increased numbers of juveniles.
"Unfortunately, I'm going to be coming before you to add a wing (to the center)," Satterfield said. "That's where we are with this. We are already in violation of the law because of the audio part, and every other facility in the states is pretty much the same way. But this is where we are with the juvenile situation, and I don't see it concluding. And they are, quite frankly, they're a holy terror."
After hearing comment from Satterfield, Pfeffers suggested in addition to the rise in juvenile crime, that they discuss the restrictions placed on detention centers could possibly force the county to build another wing to the detention facility.
The council unanimously agreed to add the topics to the county's legislative priorities.
Dorchester is not the only county facing questions of outdated detention centers. Earlier this week, Caroline County commissioners discussed plans to join with Queen Anne's and Kent counties to build a new center, in part to deal with the increase in juvenile inmates.
In a March article in The Star Democrat, Cambridge Police Chief Justin Todd talked about the growing challenge of juvenile crime in Dorchester County's largest city.
"Through investigation and statistical analysis, we have determined that the overwhelming suspect profiles for these crimes are male juveniles under the age of 16," according to a Cambridge police report. "But we have detained suspects as young as 11 for stealing vehicles in Cambridge."
According to the report, there is one 12-year-old who has been arrested for vehicle theft 11 times in the past three years.

title: Kent ham radio club tests emergency communications skills
author: WILL BONTRAGER wbontrager@chespub.com
content:
Kent ham radio club tests emergency communications skills

 January 28, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: WILL BONTRAGER wbontrager@chespub.com | Section: News 
 
 557
 Words 

 Read News Document

 WORTON — As wildfire recovery begins in southern California and a lengthy reconstruction effort continues after Hurricane Helene devastated the Appalachian area, emergency preparation is getting attention.In Kent, that conversation and training is happening among amateur radio operators prepared for potential disasters on the Eastern Shore.
Starting at 3 p.m. Saturday, over 24 hours, the Kent Amateur Radio Society club set up satellite and radio equipment in the Kent County High School parking lot. Using emergency power from generators and solar panels, they communicated with 145 stations — 18 were amateur radio satellites.
With a refurbished school bus and a camper, they operated from five stations, classified as mobile, including the emergency trailer EMCOMM 1, which contained equipment from the school's ham radio classes taught by WKHS station manager Chris Singleton, a KARS member for 30 years.
EMCOMM 1 serves as backup when regular emergency dispatch fails.
This was part of the American Radio Relay League's Winter Field Day training exercise. Radio operators set up field operations in remote locations "with the aim to improve their preparedness for disasters, enhancing their operational abilities in adverse conditions."
For KARS members, ham radio is a lifelong passion, but disaster preparation remains the priority.
KARS President Chris Cote cited Hurricane Irma in September 2017, when 7.5 million homes lost electricity. Ham radio could become the only communication mode in such situations.
Inside Cote's bus, three stations operate off a 12-volt battery charging from a solar array — two radio with VHF/UHF capabilities and one satellite communications. They reached operators nationwide without external power all weekend.
The event reached young people when Singleton's KCHS broadcasting students operated the ham radio. Junior, Jordana Capp, in her second year of broadcasting, contacted Washington state over a Russian satellite connection.
Junior, Aidan Maxey, also in his second broadcasting year, made contact with New York. He plans to pursue media studies at Syracuse, impressed with ther program.
Senior, Alayna Brown, featured on Radio World's Jan. 1 cover, contacted Tennessee. Brown, already certified by the Society of Broadcast Engineers, was recently accepted to Belmont in Nashville, where she plans to work with multitrack recording systems, live stage and master tapes.
All three students became interested in ham radio certification after attending the ARRL School Round up on Oct. 21. Brown had communicated with Russia during that event.
Singleton celebrated his students' interest in this vital skill. He had worked for 15 years to engage youth in ham radio, noting that combining broadcasting skills, live audio, music production and SBE certification opens many career paths.
"They are amazed," Singleton said. "They don't get many opportunities to work with this very specialized equipment. It is a rare opportunity."
KARS members continue generating youth interest in ham radio by teaching them radio operating skills and attending the Winter Field Day Contest. They anticipate the ARRL School Club Roundup Contest Feb. 10-14 as well.
On Sunday, as Cote's drone photographed their stations, KARS member Bobby Kelley helped newest member Alberto Larotonda dismantle his homemade antenna built from a ski pole, copper pipes and a drywall mud bucket.
"My little setup just shows anybody can do this with enough imagination," said Larotonda, who joined two months ago.
Cote said while no one wants to think disasters like those in California or North Carolina will strike locally, testing equipment in harsh conditions benefits the county; ensuring first responders that it is battle-tested.
For more information about KARS, visit k3ars.org/kars/.

title: Flashing red lights mean stop - Drivers need to watch, especially when buses stop to load and unload students

 Maryland State Police and the Maryland Center for School Safety remind motorists to stop for school buses as students return to class.Drivers must stop at least 20 feet from a school bus with the stop arm extended and the red lights flashing.Do not pass the bus from any direction until the stop signals are off and the bus is moving again. Motorists in Maryland are not required to stop if the road is separated by a physical median - such as dirt, grass or a barrier.Millions of children ride school buses and are most at risk when they get on or off the bus. There were 1,009 fatal school-transportation-related crashes from 2011 to 2020, according to the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration. The Maryland Center for School Safety encourages Marylanders and visitors to:▪ Pay attention when driving, especially in school zones and during times of day when school buses are typically on routes.▪ Stop when a bus stops. It is illegal to pass a school bus with its red lights flashing.▪ Prepare to stop when the school bus is flashing its yellow lights and be cautious of students beginning to move toward the bus during these times.▪ Students of all ages are unpredictable.Therefore, prepare for the unexpected and maintain a safe distance from school buses at all times.Violators who are stopped by a police officer face a fine of up to $570 and three points on their driver's licenses.Infractions carry a monetary penalty for each violation.For additional school bus safety tips, visit the Maryland Highway Safety Office.

title: 3 suspects arrested in Trappe after multiple vehicle break-ins
author: STAFF REPORT

3 suspects arrested in Trappe after multiple vehicle break-ins

 January 3, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: STAFF REPORT | Section: Crime 
 
 417
 Words 

 Read News Document

 As a result of multiple vehicle break-ins and thefts that occurred on Dec. 30 in the La Trappe Heights community in Trappe Maryland, the Talbot County Sheriff's department made three arrests last week.On Dec. 30, deputies responded to a report of an attempted vehicle break-in on the 3800 block of Seymour Drive in Trappe, according to a release from the Talbot County Sheriff's Office. After further investigation, deputies determined that three male suspects wearing all black clothing and masks attempted to enter multiple vehicles, stealing various items.
At around 5 p.m., deputies were dispatched to Harrison Circle in Trappe for suspicious activity. A resident of the area noticed the three male suspects dressed in black clothing and wearing masks looking into vehicles, police said.
After observation, the suspects fled on foot into a residence on the 3900 block of Main Street and attempted to barricade themselves inside, according to the sheriff's office. Deputies surrounded the residence and made contact with the suspects after a short time, police said.
The suspects were identified as 18 year-old Nihjay T. Greene of Trappe, 18 year-old Aamad A. Turner of Trappe and a juvenile 16 year-old male, who was not named by the sheriff's office.
Police said Greene attempted to resist arrest and assaulted a deputy as he was being detained. No one was injured during the arrests.
Greene has been charged with second degree assault on a police officer, resisting arrest, obstructing and hindering, fourth degree burglary, rogue and vagabond, theft of less than $100 and malicious destruction of property.
Turner has been charged with obstructing and hindering, fourth degree burglary, rogue and vagabond, theft less than $100 and malicious destruction of property less than $1,000.
The 16-year-old juvenile was charged with the same offenses as Turner and referred to the Maryland Department of Juvenile Services, where he was released to a guardian, the sheriff's office said.
Members of the Talbot County Sheriff's Office Criminal Investigations Division arranged and proceeded a search and seizure warrant of the residence the suspects attempted to barricade, which was signed by a judge. During the search deputies found evidence connecting the three suspects to the vehicle break-ins in La Trappe Heights, as well as vehicle break-ins that occurred in Easton early in 2024.
Greene and Turner were transferred to the Talbot County Central Booking Facility for processing and their first appearance before a District Court Commissioner. They are being held without bond at Talbot County Detention Center. Both suspects were released on unsecured bail after bail reviews before a district court judge.

 GREENSBORO — Sgt. Jeff Adams chose the Greensboro Police Department as his next endeavor because of his great relationship with Police Chief Lenox Trams."I was looking at different agencies but I reached out the chief. Chief and I go back to 2005 or 2006," Adams said. "I didn't know if I wanted to come here or not. We just had a brief conversation, then I came and did an interview and instantly fell in love. Ever since talking to him and doing a ride along, I was pretty much sold."
Adams, originally from New Jersey, came to the Eastern Shore in 2004 after his career in the military. Adams served in the Navy and in the Army Reserve.
A friend talked to him about coming down to the Eastern Shore and pursing law enforcement as a career.
Adams started his career in law enforcement in dispatch at Easton Police Department for one year. Then Adams moved to the Federalsburg Police Department, where he served for the past 17 years.
While Adams and Trams' long relationship played a big part in his decision to pick Greensboro as his next stop, Adams' residence in Greensboro played a big part as well.
"I think the people here are very nice," Adams said. "They're genuine, and it just seem like a really good fit after we went for a ride along. Just the environment alone was was good enough."
Adams wants residents to know if they ever cross paths with him, he is a easy officer to work with.
"I'm easy going," Adams said. "So what you see is what you get. I think Chief can attest to that, but I'm just laid back, professional, polite and kind. Hopefully we'll be community-oriented. We're just trying to make our interactions are police-public friendly."
Adams brings a potential coworker with him to the department. His K-9 Mosley has been with him since 2017.
Mosley has experienced cancer, but Adams says she is still able to work as a K-9 dog.
"She's done everything," Adams said. "She's already certified in tracking and narcotics. Now we took off the tracking because she lost her leg to cancer in Halloween of 2023. She went through chemo, radiation, and she's she's still working. She's did awesome with the training last Wednesday, she nailed it."
While Mosley hasn't officially joined the force yet, Trams and Adams expect for her to be apart of the team very soon.
"We're really excited to be able to bring her on," Trams said. "We're going through our budget cycle, and we put the K-9 program in the budget so the Town Council has to approve it. Hopefully we'll get the thumps up and then she can start working because we need one."

title: Officer fights to deter drivers like one who injured him
author: LYDIA HURLEY Capital News Service
content:
Officer fights to deter drivers like one who injured him

 February 20, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: LYDIA HURLEY Capital News Service | Section: State News 
 
 739
 Words 

 Read News Document

 Less than four months after losing his legs in an attempt to stop a reckless highway driver, a Montgomery County police officer is at the forefront of a movement to crack down on negligent driving in Maryland.Sgt. Patrick Kepp plans to testify on two bills in the state capital of Annapolis this session — traveling from Walter Reed National Military Medical Center in Bethesda, where he is still in active recovery from last October's incident.
"When I was brought into the conversation about new laws being created, right away, I knew it was something I wanted to do," Kepp said.
Rehabilitation is his first priority, he said, but treatment won't get in the way of his new mission. "I will be there in Annapolis to make sure these bills happen," Kepp said.
Kepp announced his plans this week in a press briefing alongside Montgomery County Executive Marc Elrich (D) and Montgomery County lawmakers who are taking up the cause with him. Kepp's story has inspired them to craft new legislation that would punish repeat offenders of reckless driving.
"I'm going to call it the Sgt. Pat Kepp Bill on Reckless Driving," Del. Greg Wims (D-Montgomery) said, calling Kepp a "hero."
Reckless driving isn't a new phenomenon in Maryland. Outraged by stories of dangerous driving on the Beltway or the Ocean City Expressway, Maryland lawmakers have in years past have proposed legislation meant to stop these behaviors. This session, two other bills, separate from Kepp's, are making their way through the legislature, specifically aimed at ending the deadly game of drag racing or "exhibition driving."
But Kepp's bill is a personal one, inspired by an officer who patrolled the sponsoring lawmakers' home district. Elrich visited Kepp while he was in recovery to propose the idea of working together on this set of bills, the officer said.
The two bills have not been filed, but the sponsors say they share common goals. The bills would change existing criminal law to widen the definition of what constitutes reckless and negligent driving and increase penalties for those crimes, the sponsors said.
One penalty they will propose is requiring offenders to appear in court for their offenses. "It's way too easy for a driver to just pay a fine and get back on the road and do what they were doing before," Elrich explained.
Kepp, who worked as an officer in the alcohol initiative unit, says these bills will "give a little more teeth to some of our laws." Additionally, he hopes the law will address the "overall frustration" with the difficulty enforcing existing reckless driving laws. The penalties aren't tough enough, he said, and the fines aren't a good enough deterrent.
In the early morning hours of last Oct. 18, Kepp had just finished his shift when he heard a radio report of a speeding driver on Interstate 270. He joined other officers in an attempt to stop the driver. While Kepp was standing outside of his car, the driver struck him and left him critically injured, as Elrich recounted in the press briefing.
The Montgomery County Police officers on duty that night knew the driver "had a history of speeding and taunting police into chasing him," Elrich said. Police say the driver targeted and intentionally hit Kepp, Elrich said, and he is now being charged.
Both of Kepp's legs were amputated due to the injuries he sustained that night. Now he said he spends every day — from 9:45 a.m. to 2:15 p.m. — at Walter Reed National Military Medical Center undergoing rehabilitation. He joined the Zoom call for Elrich's press briefing from the medical center, wearing a blue dry-fit shirt and a short military-style haircut.
It has been four months since the accident, and Kepp said he has had a dozen surgeries since.
Still, he wants to speak on behalf of legislation that "will strengthen our laws and make our roadways safer," Kepp said.
The aim of the bills is "not for everybody to be thrown in jail, have huge fines, or lose their licenses," Kepp said, but rather to end reckless driving, especially by repeat offenders.
Elrich said he hopes the law will stop people from "ignoring lights and sirens from law enforcement, breaking the rules of the road … and performing car tricks like drifting, peeling out, and doing donuts in the middle of a road."
"All it takes is a moment's loss of control over that vehicle," Elrich said. "Instead of being entertaining, it would take little to transform it into a deadly incident."

title: Down to one officer, Greensboro considers closing police department
author: KONNER METZ kmetz@chespub.com
content:
Down to one officer, Greensboro considers closing police department

 September 6, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: KONNER METZ kmetz@chespub.com | Section: Local News 
 
 592
 Words 

 Read News Document

 GREENSBORO — The future of the Greensboro Police Department is up in the air.Mayor David Spencer announced at Thursday evening's Greensboro Town Council meeting that the town will consider closing its police department, which is now down to one officer, Chief Lenox Trams.
Four options were provided to the mayor and commissioners by Town Manager Tammy Kelledes:
Continuing running its own police department.Working "in conjunction with" the Caroline County Sheriff's Office "to fill the spots (it doesn't) have now for (its) own officers."Entering into a "contractual agreement" with the Caroline County Sheriff's Office.Closing the police department, not entering into an agreement and turning "the town over to the sheriff's department and the Maryland State Police."
"The current public safety demands are too much for a one-person police department to handle," Spencer said. "In addition, the mayor and council must consider the increasing costs of retaining a police department and the struggles caused by a shortage of police officers and police applicants throughout the state."
"We will listen to all comments and suggestions and take all of those into consideration," he added. "We will not be making a decision tonight."
The mayor emphasized Thursday was just the beginning of a "fluid" and long-term process.
Greensboro has been receiving assistance from county police in recent weeks to reduce the burden on the town's only officer. Spencer said Greensboro has been paying a $75-per-hour rate for county deputies to cover the town, which will continue "in the meantime."
"When they come in here, they're staying here," Spencer said. "They're not patrolling the county, they're only patrolling the town."
A person recently hired by the town did not complete police academy training, Spencer said in response to a resident question.
Spencer said the town has asked Trams to continue going through officer applications on file in hopes that an applicant who is already certified can be brought on board. Otherwise, certification and training can take up to a full year.
"If you put somebody through the academy, it takes about a year," Trams said. "When you hire them after you do the background, for the nine months that they really aren't much good to you, you are paying their salary and their health insurance."
During his department update, Trams urged those with non-emergencies to call the county at 410-479-2515 since the Greensboro department is limited. "If (we're) working, they will certainly send us. If we're not working, then they will send the next agency that is in rotation," he said.
PUBLIC FEEDBACKAfter Spencer read the four options aloud, resident Paula Turner pushed for more details and asked for the town to host a special meeting.
"Of those options, where is the breakdown of cost, of savings?" Turner asked "If No. 4 is voted in, if that's what the town wants, show us how … (the) money that's budgeted will be allocated back into our town. I want numbers."
Kevin Parks spoke in support of the police department remaining. He referenced the struggle to attract police officers due to Maryland's repeal of the Law Enforcement Officers' Bill of Rights back in 2021.
"I don't want to see the police department closed up," Parks said. "The chief's doing the best he can. If you want to fuss about the police department, call your legislators and your senators for the state of Maryland and tell them to give them their bill of rights back."
Spencer said the town's budget has room for three officers. Public Works Supervisor Brandon Cunningham asked if the town would continue paying for county assistance if it hired a second officer only.
"Those decisions have not yet been made," Spencer said.

title: Dundalk residents view crumpled bridge with shock, dismay
author: MAGGIE TROVATO mtrovato@chespub.com
content:
Dundalk residents view crumpled bridge with shock, dismay

 March 26, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: MAGGIE TROVATO mtrovato@chespub.com | Section: State News 
 
 667
 Words 

 Read News Document

 DUNDALK — A few hours after Teresita Santana and her family drove across the Francis Scott Key Bridge, they felt their house shake."As if something had exploded," Santana said.
Santana and her family, including her children and mother, got back to their home in Dundalk late Monday night after a trip to Washington, D.C., to get their passports and see the cherry blossoms. It was only a few hours after they crossed the Key Bridge on their way home that the bridge collapsed.
A container ship slammed into the iconic bridge just before 1:30 a.m. Tuesday. Within seconds, the bridge crumpled into the chilly waters of the Patapsco River at the entrance to the Baltimore Harbor.
In the hours that followed, authorities began search and rescue efforts for survivors of the collapse. Radar indicated that vehicles had been discovered at the bottom of the river, which is about 50 feet deep.
By Tuesday evening, officials said that six construction workers who had been repairing potholes on the bridge at the time of the collapse had been presumed dead. Two construction workers were rescued in the efforts.
Tuesday morning, Santana looked out on the now collapsed bridge from a hill on Dundalk Avenue, across the street from the Logan Village Shopping Center.
"It was scary because it could have been us," Santana said.
Santana wasn't the only one looking at what's left of the I-695 bridge. People filtered in and out Tuesday morning to see it for themselves. "Shock" was a word repeated often.
"Shock and dismay," were the words Judy Corkhum used to describe the emotions of residents she had talked to.
"Nobody in a million years thought we would wake up this morning to something like that," said Corkhum, who also viewed the collapsed bridge from off Dundalk Avenue. "It brings back emotions from 9/11. ... You saw that and the first thing you think is, 'Oh my god. The people. The workers.'"
Corkhum, who recently moved to Baltimore from Dundalk, said she heard about the bridge collapse via a text from a neighbor at 4 a.m. Tuesday. She said her friend's son, a truck driver, "literally just got over the bridge before it happened."
"She said, 'I was having a heart attack this morning thinking he was out on the road last night,'" Corkhum said.
Corkhum said her friend went into surgery this morning, so she was happy to know her son was OK.
Anthony Meeks, a Dundalk native, said he heard about the collapse as soon as he woke up.
"The Key Bridge is a very iconic piece of Dundalk," he said. "It's something that everybody who's from Dundalk or this city even has at one point in their life crossed."
Meeks remembers being scared to cross the bridge when he was younger. These days, he crosses it every two weeks.
"It (will) make me go out of my way to find a different path to get to where I need to go," he said about the collapse. "It could make my trips be a lot longer."
Meeks called the incident an eye opener.
"Because it's like you don't really expect these kinds of tragedies and stuff to happen and occur in your neighborhood," he said.
Dundalk-Patapsco Neck Historical Society President Jean Walker said this is the first time Dundalk has experienced a large disaster like this.
Historical Society Vice President Joe Stadler called the event "unbelievable."
"It takes a while to fathom it," he said.
For both Walker and Stadler, the bridge has been a big part of Dundalk. They said the founder of the Historical Society, Ben Womer, was "instrumental" in getting the bridge named after Francis Scott Key, the author of the national anthem.
"It's the backdrop for everything around here," Stadler said about the bridge.
Standing on the hill, looking at the wreckage of the bridge, Corkhum said she had to make the trip from her new home in Baltimore to see what had happened with her own eyes.
"I'm so used to seeing that pretty view out there every day," she said. "It's going to be horrible seeing that (there's) no view anymore."

This year, why not resolve to help improve the life of a local child who is under court protection because of abuse or neglect?

Start this New Year with a resolution to learn about how you can make a positive difference in the life of a local abused or neglected child.

title: Fire departments 'charge into safety' for National Fire Prevention Week
author: Lily Tierney
content:
Fire departments 'charge into safety' for National Fire Prevention Week

 October 9, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Lily Tierney | Section: Dorchester 
 
 405

 Read News Document

 Fire companies throughout Mid-Shore made extra efforts to educate the public Oct. 5 to 11, part of National Fire Prevention Week programming.Firefighters visited schools, daycares and even jujutsu studios to teach about fire safety measures.
"In the city of Cambridge, we make a big push to go to all the elementary schools, we get to the preschools, the daycares and just talk a little about fire safety," Cambridge Rescue Fire Company's Chief Brad Walters said.
Easton Volunteer Fire Department Chief J.R. Dobson said they hand out plastic fire hats to the children, and Walters distributes coloring books intended to reach kids' families and reinforce safety messages.
The theme of this year's prevention week is "charge into safety — lithium-ion batteries in your home."
Walters and Dobson said lithium-ion batteries pose a significant fire risk when not handled properly.
The batteries can be found in everyday items like laptops, medical devices such as pacemakers, digital cameras, e-bikes and even some children's toys, according to a press release from the Office of the State Fire Marshal.
According to the press release, in 2023 the fire marshal's office began tracking lithium-ion battery-related fires. So far, 102 incidents have been recorded.
Walters said that in Cambridge, they have had five lithium-ion related incidents within the last six months. Dobson said these incidences in Easton have been "few and far between" but can occur with lithium-ion batteries as small as those that go in hand-held power tools.
The campaign emphasizes three key safety actions when handling lithium-ion batteries: buy safely, charge safely and recycle safely.
The fire marshal's office suggests only purchasing devices and batteries with a safety certification mark, only using manufacturer-approved charging equipment, steering clear of overcharging, and never charging on soft surfaces like couches, beds or pillows.
The office said it is also critical to recycle these batteries at designated recycling centers, which can be found at call2recycle.org.
According to the National Fire Prevention Association, signs there are problems with a lithium-ion battery include an odor, change in color, change in shape, too much heat, odd noises or leaking. If it is safe to do so, the association suggests moving the battery away from anything flammable and calling 911 if necessary.
Walters said beyond lithium-ion safety measures, families should communicate, maintain a home exit plan and practice everyday fire prevention awareness.
"And if you have any questions, reach out to your local fire department, and if you're willing to come volunteer, reach out to your local department," Walters said.

title: House of Delegates hears testimonies for Jamari's Law
author: Sarah Meador somdnewsintern@chespub.com
content:
House of Delegates hears testimonies for Jamari's Law

 February 16, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Sarah Meador somdnewsintern@chespub.com | Section: State News 
 
 520
 Words 

 Read News Document

 Maryland residents on Feb. 7 testified before the state House of Delegates in support of Jamari's Law, which would increase the maximum penalty of manslaughter by vehicle.Jamari Tyrese Duckett, the bill's namesake, was a recent graduate of Great Mills High School and registered for college with plans to study mechanical engineering when a drunk driver killed him on July 9, 2022, in St. Mary's County.
Matthew Mark Mazza was sentenced in October 2023 to the maximum sentence of 10 years in prison. Mazza, 28, of Lexington Park will be eligible for parole after serving only 2 1/2 years, as vehicular manslaughter is considered a non-violent crime in Maryland.
Mazza's braking speed at the time of the collision was between 76 mph and 91 mph in a 40 mph zone at the time of the crash, according to the St. Mary's sheriff's office.
Jamari's Law proposes to increase the maximum penalty for manslaughter by vehicle to 20 years and 15 to 30 years for any subsequent convictions.
"This is reckless and a disregard for life when you get behind the wheel, drunk, driving over the speed limit. That could have been you, me, your kids, parents or grandparents in that car, and to only get 10 years and out a few years later on probation, is a slap to all families that have lost someone to a drunk driver," Shownda Greenwell, Duckett's mother, said at the hearing.
Other families affected by drunk driving testified at the hearing both in person and over Zoom, urging the House Judiciary Committee to increase the maximum penalty to bring justice to their loved ones.
Del. Brian Crosby (D-St. Mary's) is sponsoring House Bill 264, which is cross-filed with Senate Bill 26 sponsored by Sen. Jack Bailey (R-St. Mary's, Calvert). The Senate hearing for the bill occurred on Jan. 24.
"It was very painful for them, but it was very important that the legislators understand what is happening as a result of such a serious crime," Bailey said of the many families who testified at both hearings.
The bill does not propose a minimum sentence, but gives judges further discretion in their sentencing of those who are found guilty of the crime of manslaughter by vehicle, Bailey said.
St. Mary's County State's Attorney Jaymi Sterling (R) also urged both the House and Senate to increase the maximum penalty, stating that the lives lost to vehicular manslaughter are worth more than the 10-year criminal penalty equivalent to passing a bad check.
"We need your help," Sterling said at the Senate hearing last month. "Please consider raising the penalties so that we have more to work with, so that we can rehabilitate, so that we can provide deterrence, but so there is also punishment."
Both the House and Senate bills were referred to the state legislature's committees.
"They're still seeking justice and trying to make sure that no other family should have to endure the same amount of pain that they did and not receive fair justice under the law," Crosby said.
He cited the bravery of all families who testified to bring justice to lives lost to vehicular manslaughter.
If the bill passes, the law would become effective Oct. 1.
