Harris said the appropriations bill to provide funding for the project failed due to negotiations in Congress leading to a continued delay, but she said the project has been reapplied for in the current year's legislation.
"We hope the appropriations process has a better outcome, but then that's not up to us because it involves the minority party as well," he said in an interview with the Star Democrat.
In order to qualify for federal grants, the company must match 25% of the projected project cost of $6 million. The company set a goal of $1,500,000 and set aside $450,000 to begin the efforts.
Fundraising efforts include The Trappe Volunteer Fire Company's upcoming annual fair, held on July 31 through Aug. 2 at the firehouse. The event begins at 6 p.m. and ends at 10 p.m. each day and will include fire truck rides, hay rides, food, games and prizes, and live entertainment, according to the fire company's Facebook page. Saturday's event will open with a parade.
Harris said the outcome of federal funding depends on the successful bipartisan negotiations in Congress to pass this version of the appropriations bill.
"In the end, this is going to depend on the minority party. And you know, if they're not willing to negotiate in good faith, that could end up being a problem," Harris said. "The people in Trappe have to know that their member of Congress was working hard to get that money to the fire company."

title: 'Why can’t they just let people rest in peace?': Dozens of headstones vandalized at Maryland cemetery
author: Jane Bellmyer jbellmyer@chespub.com
content:
'Why can’t they just let people rest in peace?': Dozens of headstones vandalized at Maryland cemetery

 June 7, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Jane Bellmyer jbellmyer@chespub.com | Section: News 
 
 371
 Words 

 Read News Document

 A police investigation is continuing after a vandal or vandals damaged and displaced dozens of headstones at the North East Cemetery earlier this month.According to North East Police Department Chief Stephen Yates, approximately 57 headstones were pushed over June 6 and 7. Most of the headstones were tipped over; however, several were damaged, Yates said. Additionally, some of the commemorative vases placed alongside the headstones were crushed.
"Some people just don't have any respect for things," Yates remarked.
Deidre Taylor came from Charlestown to find the headstones of her siblings tipped over.
"I feel for the families who have lost more today," Taylor said. "I hope they figure out who did this."
Nicholas Grove was angry as he worked with other family members to repair the damage done to stones in their family plot.
"Why can't they just let people rest in peace?" Grove said as he worked to clean the top of the foundation and the bottom of the headstone on one gravesite in preparation for setting it aright. "This is disrespecting everybody."
Like so many others, Karen Haines saw a post of Facebook about the vandalism and came to North East Cemetery to see if her parent's gravestones had been included in the attack. It was.
"I was expecting it to be worse," Haines said. "I was expecting it to be in pieces."
Law enforcement officials reported that they are investigating a number of different leads. To avoid compromising the ongoing investigation, police officials declined to elaborate.
When bystanders asked what would happen if the vandals turn out to be minors, Yates explained that the ages of the vandals would determine the next steps.
Family members spent Friday afternoon cleaning up some of their loved ones' damaged and tipped-over headstones. Yates said the cemetery association has learned its insurance will cover the cost to reset and repair all the headstones.
Michael Kline Jr, whose father, Michael Kline Sr. is among the graves that were vandalized, is offering a reward for information leading to a conviction of the guilty.
"I'm offering a $1,000 cash reward," Kline said Friday. "But I do have a lot of people reaching out to contribute to it."
The investigation is ongoing and anyone with knowledge of the incident is encouraged to reach out to NEPD at 410-287-5996.

 EASTON — After being admitted to Johns Hopkins Hospital a few weeks ago, Fred "Trey" Rider III has been discharged, and a judge has granted his request to be transferred to Avenues Recovery Center at Eastern Shore, an alcohol and drug rehabilitation facility in Cambridge, for 60 days.Rider is accused of setting his house on fire in November 2022.
Through investigation, officials identified the fire as an act of human intervention with an open flame, classifying the cause of fire as incendiary. According to court documents, Rider's reckless conduct in igniting the house on fire "clearly" put emergency services personnel, specifically more than 45 firefighters who responded, in danger as they suppressed the fire.
Rider faces 15 charges for this, including arson, malicious destruction of property and reckless endangerment.
A trial for the case was set to begin March 4, but at a status hearing that morning, Judge Thomas G. Ross stated that Rider had been voluntarily admitted to Johns Hopkins and issued a bench warrant for Rider's failure to appear in court that morning.
According to court documents, Rider was discharged from Johns Hopkins Hospital and placed in the custody of Deputy Fire Marshal Shayne McKinney on Monday.
In court documents, Rider's attorney Stephanie Shipley wrote that Rider and his counsel did not know he was being discharged immediately Monday morning following an endoscopy procedure and recovery from anesthesia.
Following the discharge, Rider, through his defense, requested to be released to Avenues Recovery Center for inpatient treatment "pursuant to the active referral from Johns Hopkins Hospital Psychiatric Department."
According to court documents filed by Rider's defense, Rider's social worker Joseph Antonetti advised over the phone that Rider had obtained long-term placement in Avenues Recovery Center for 60 days.
At a bail review and status hearing on Tuesday, according to court documents, Ross granted Rider a bed-to-bed transfer to Avenues Recovery Center from the Talbot County Detention Center.
The conditions of this transfer, outlined in court documents, are that Rider must be fitted with a GPS tracking device, cannot leave Avenues Recovery Center for any reason and must return to the detention center upon completion of the 60-day inpatient program.
Included in the conditions of this transfer, Rider cannot be given access to internet or any social media accounts. He cannot have contact with any state witnesses, other than his parents, Peggy Rider and Fred Rider Jr.
A hearing for Rider's case is set for April 3. The trial is set to begin Aug. 19.

title: Second fatal crash in three days prompts re-closure of Price Station Road crossover on U.S. 301
author: STAFF REPORT
content:
Second fatal crash in three days prompts re-closure of Price Station Road crossover on U.S. 301

 July 28, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: STAFF REPORT | Section: Local News 
 
 565
 Words 

 Read News Document

 CHURCH HILL — Following two fatal crashes in three days, state transportation officials have ordered the closure of the MD 405 (Price Station Road) median crossover at U.S. Route 301 in Queen Anne's County.The Maryland Department of Transportation State Highway Administration announced Friday, July 25, that the crossover will be closed beginning Saturday, July 26. Emergency vehicle access will be maintained, and alternate crossovers are available at MD 19 (Roberts Station Road), two miles north, and Hayden Clark Road, 1.7 miles south.
"This is a safety-focused decision," said State Highway Administrator Will Pines. "This closure is necessary to save lives and make the corridor safer for the tens of thousands of travelers and residents who use it every day."
The announcement follows two deadly collisions at the intersection this week, resulting in three fatalities.
On Thursday, July 24, a two-vehicle crash occurred around noon, leaving two people dead at the scene.
Just two days earlier, another woman was killed when her vehicle was struck by a southbound car as she attempted to cross Route 301. The impact caused her car to overturn. The other vehicle's two occupants — a 22-year-old man and a 20-year-old woman — were flown to R Adams Cowley Shock Trauma Center in Baltimore in critical condition.
The State Highway Administration had previously closed the crossover in July 2024 due to a high number of crashes. Between January 2019 and December 2023, there were 76 reported crashes at the site — 62 of them in the southbound lanes, most attributed to driver inattention or failure to yield. Despite safety upgrades such as restriping, rumble strips, additional signage, and channelizing devices, collisions have continued at an alarming rate.
Troopers from the Centreville Barrack of the Maryland State Police, Queen Anne's County Sheriff Gary Hofmann, and first responders from the Church Hill Volunteer Fire Company have all voiced strong support for the closure.
The Church Hill Volunteer Fire Company confirmed Friday that it had been notified of the closure and has coordinated with SHA to ensure continued emergency access to communities east of Route 301, including Price and Bridgetown Estates.
"As we did in July of 2024, the department leadership reached out to SHA to ensure emergency access would be available to Fire, EMS, and Police units responding to emergency calls on the east side of Route 301," the fire company said in a statement. "We have been assured by SHA leadership that they intend to use the same process as before and that emergency access will be available.
"While this will create a slight delay in response times, we appreciate the willingness of SHA to work with us to keep those delays as short as possible while long-term solutions for the crossover are worked. The leadership of the Church Hill Volunteer Fire Company is committed to providing the most timely and efficient emergency response possible and will continue to monitor the situation and be a partner with SHA for a permanent solution."
Sen. Steve Hershey (R-Kent, Queen Anne's, Cecil, Caroline) also voiced support for the re-closure, stating, "Given the dangerous track record at this intersection — and now two fatal accidents in just three days — it is clear that further action is urgently needed. While I understand the temporary inconvenience to motorists, public safety must come first."
The Maryland State Police Crash Team is leading both crash investigations. Findings will be submitted to the Queen Anne's County State's Attorney's Office for review.

North East mom, boyfriend charged in murder of toddler

 498

 NORTH EAST — Maryland State Police have charged Darrian Lynelle Randle of North East with first and second degree murder in the death of her 3-year-old daughter, Nola Dinkins.Her boyfriend, Cedrick Antoine Britten, 44, from North East, is charged as an accessory. He's being held in the Cecil County Detention Center on a $75,000 bond.
Dinkins body — described in charging documents released Thursday as "consistent with an emaciated child and were completely wrapped in saran (sic) wrap" — was found in the unit block of Dune Drive in North East inside a blue suitcase.
Randle and Dinkins were living in Britten's home when the alleged crime took place, according to police. The pair shared a room in the home on Elk Nest Road
Charging documents indicate Randle beat the child 15-20 times Monday with a belt. When the child fell to the ground, she noticed the child was no longer breathing.
"Randle stated that Britten attempted CPR ... but eventually realized (Nola Dinkins) was deceased," the documents filed in Cecil County District Court of Maryland read.
Becoming upset, Randle told police that the body was placed in Britten's vehicle — a BMW — and the couple drove around for awhile.
"Randle stated that once they returned to the residence she placed (the body) in a dark blue suitcase belonging to Britten," the court documents read. The suitcase was placed on the third step of the basement stairs overnight. She checked on the suitcase one time, then asked Britten to take it from the house.
Britten told investigators he took the suitcase away, later sending Randle a photo of a park.
On Tuesday, Randle told New Castle County Police the child had been kidnapped from her vehicle at gunpoint; a story later determined to be false. While searching for Dinkins, police questioned Britten, who was described as having "little to no reaction" to word that the child had been reported missing.
At the home, investigators noticed a distinct odor of bleach. Blue nitrile gloves were found during a search; one pair in a downstairs trash can and another pair in the room that Randle and Dinkins shared.
Investigators searched Perryville Community Park in response to the photo of a park, but ultimately located Dinkins' body — still in the suitcase — on a vacant lot near Britten's home.
Randle, being held by New Castle County Police on a $1 million bond for a charge of filing a false police report, is now facing numerous charged in Maryland including first- and second-degree murder, first- and second-degree assault, reckless endangerment, child abuse resulting in death, neglect, failure to report a child death and unauthorized disposal of a body.
Britten is charged with eight counts including accessory after the fact to first- and second-degree murder, neglect of a minor, unauthorized disposal of a body, and failure to report a child's death.
The body has been taken to the Office of the Medical Examiner for an autopsy and positive identification.
Police officials have yet to say when Randle will be extradited from Delaware to Maryland.

title: Cambridge City Council extends juvenile curfew another year
author: MAGGIE TROVATO mtrovato@chespub.com
content:
Cambridge City Council extends juvenile curfew another year

 September 12, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: MAGGIE TROVATO mtrovato@chespub.com | Section: Local News 
 
 445
 Words 

 Read News Document

 CAMBRIDGE — In a four-to-one vote on Sept. 9, the Cambridge City Council extended its temporary juvenile curfew for another 12 months.The curfew — which was originally passed in September 2023 — makes it so that juveniles under 16 cannot be in a public place within the city between the hours of 10 p.m. and 5 a.m. on Sundays through Thursdays and 11 p.m. through 5 a.m. on Fridays and Saturdays.
There are exceptions to this, including when the juvenile is with a parent or when the juvenile is on the way home from work or a school activity.
The extension will keep the curfew in place through Sept. 30, 2025.
At the City Council meeting on Sept. 9, a public hearing was held before the commissioners took a vote. Resident Shay Lewis-Sisco, who is running for Cambridge's Ward 2 commissioner seat, said that during a community visioning session at Mace's Lane Middle School, most of the students involved said they were in favor of the curfew.
Commissioner Sputty Cephas brought up a conversation he had with one young person. He said the curfew made the child think twice about going out at night.
Cephas, who voted to extend the curfew, asked the other commissioners whether they thought the curfew should be reviewed annually or on a longer-term basis.
Commissioners Jameson Harrington, Brian Roche and Laurel Atkiss all said they think the curfew should be reviewed on an annual basis.
Harrington, who voted against the extension, said an annual review allows the council to more easily end the curfew if it isn't working.
In an interview with the Star Democrat, Harrington said he voted against the curfew as a principle. He said he has been against it from the start and data shows it is not effective, but he said he is proud of how it is working in Cambridge.
Roche and Atkiss both spoke about the curfew's effectiveness in allowing Cambridge Police to have conversations with children and employ community policing.
"But definitely an annual reevaluation is great because we hope to make progress and maybe not need such structures at some point in the future," Atkiss said.
Before the vote, Cambridge Police Chief Justin Todd said he thinks the curfew is a good tool. He said there has been less juvenile crime during the hours of the curfew compared to 2023 "when it was a real crisis." He said the curfew has made children think twice about going out at night and has allowed the department to reach more children.
At the end of the meeting, Todd thanked the council.
"I just want to thank everyone for the support of the curfew and the continuation of it for another year," he said. "It's much appreciated."

title: Mid-Shore organization pioneers a 'hub' of resources for victims of domestic violence
author: Veronica Fernandez-Alvarado
content:
Mid-Shore organization pioneers a 'hub' of resources for victims of domestic violence

 December 5, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Veronica Fernandez-Alvarado | Section: News 
 
 557
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — For more than four decades, the Mid-Shore Council on Family Violence has been at the forefront of advocating for victims on the Mid-Shore. With a new program, the organization is now planning to assist far beyond.The nonprofit for victims of domestic violence has taken steps to advance resource access for clients using the Geographic Information System program, a mapping dashboard providing a free one-stop shop for essential resources for victims.
Jeanne Yeager, executive director for Mid-Shore Council on Family Violence, said rural clients face various barriers to receiving care. During the pandemic the barriers to care were more apparent and Mid-Shore Council sought to find alternative solutions to helping their clients.
This initiative, she said, revolutionizes the way domestic violence victims access vital resources.
"I was really mindful of coming out of COVID, because everything we did at Mid-Shore was very one-on-one, personalized — our case management, our meetings, our support groups, everything — and we would say, 'Oh, well, we'll do an online group sometime.' Well, 'that sometime' became tomorrow," Yeager said. "So it normalized using technology, and I think there's no turning back."
The barriers faced by victims in rural communities include limited employment opportunities, spotty cell service, transportation, lack of affordable housing, and social and geographic isolation.
The GIS program operates with a holistic Chesapeake Crisis-to-Self-Sufficiency model, providing comprehensive services and case management from crisis through transition to self-sufficiency.
According to Yeager, the program initially focused on mapping out housing resources in five counties in Maryland. The data team began working with case managers and staff to compile a list of resources that clients frequently inquire about, such as childcare and pet care.
From there it continued to expand.
Kazeem Anifowoshe, GIS senior data analyst, said the project went from the initial five counties to nine counties, and the team decided to create a website as a "hub" for the project. Now, this hub is used by 25 agencies and has expanded resources to include nearby pro bono and legal services across Maryland through a partnership with the Access to Justice organization.
"When people kind of think of victim services, there's kind of like a formula that a lot of people have been doing for 20 to 40 plus years at their organization that works for them," Anifowoshe said. "But again, we're just trying to make things easier the best way we know how, by mapping things."
According to Yeager, the GIS program has been earning notable recognition, such as the prestigious Domestic Shelters Purple Ribbon Award.
The organization's GIS Hub integrates data from various sources, including popular rental property platforms/affordable housing, childcare resources, medical facilities, grocery stores, law enforcement agencies, court houses and local social service organizations.
Pamela Caudill Jordan, program evaluator for the GIS Hub, said she hopes to encourage other organizations to adopt a comprehensive model where the focus is not just on crisis intervention but on helping survivors achieve long-term stability and self-sufficiency. For Caudill Jordan, having access to tools such as the GIS Hub can make the work of advocates for victims easier and more efficient.
According to Yeager and Anifowoshe, the goal is to get the GIS Hub more widely adopted and used by other organizations, going beyond Maryland and, hopefully, one day nationwide.
"We know what victims need," Yeager said. "We ought to work with victims, and we're making this available. Let's see where we're going with it."

title: Man found guilty in death of infant son - Baltimore man sentenced to 35 years by Caroline County judge
author: Natalie Jones; njones@chespub.com
content:
Man found guilty in death of infant son - Baltimore man sentenced to 35 years by Caroline County judge

 November 30, 2023 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Natalie Jones; njones@chespub.com | Page: 3 | Section: News 
 
 465
 Words 

 Read News Document

 DENTON - A Baltimore man was sentenced Wednesday to 35 years in prison after a judge found him guilty of murder in the death of his infant son.Agreeing with joint recommendations from the prosecution and the defense, Caroline Circuit Judge Heather Price handed Sean Casey Pierce the lengthy sentence: 40 years, with all but 25 years suspended, for a second-degree murder charge and 25 years, with all but 10 years suspended, for first-degree assault.The sentences will be served consecutively.Pierce, 50, entered Alford pleas to the two felony charges during Wednesday's court hearing.An Alford plea does not require a defendant to admit guilt, but acknowledges that there was enough evidence for a conviction had the case gone to trial.The sentence comes nearly 18 months after the death of 8-week-old Chance Pierce on May 30, 2022.The case against Pierce stemmed from a 911 call reporting an infant experiencing a medical emergency.Officers from the Federalsburg Police Department responded to a camper on Buena Vista Avenue with emergency medical services personnel for the report.Police said the infant had a weak pulse and was cool to the touch upon their arrival.The child was taken to Nanticoke Memorial Hospital in Seaford before being transported to Nemours Children's Hospital in Wilmington, where he was declared deceased.Pierce told police that he was sleeping in a trailer with Chance and his other young son when he was awoken by the infant choking and vomiting.Pierce and another adult male on the property thought the child was suffering from heat stroke and attempted to cool him off using water and ice pops.However, a medical examiner ruled the child's cause of death as closedhead trauma caused by a blunt force injury.The medical examiner also found the child had several partially healed rib fractures, indicating prior abuse, said Caroline County State's Attorney Sloane Franklin.Pierce was unable to explain his son's injuries, Franklin added. The child's mother said Chance was healthy and had no prior issues.The child's mother was not present in court Wednesday and did not wish to be there, Franklin said."This has been a nightmare for her," he said, adding that he didn't want the child's mother to relive the death of her son.Defense attorney Dana Boston agreed with the prosecution's recommended sentence, calling it and the plea agreement fair."Thirty-five years in prison for a 50-year-old man is not a slap on the wrist," he said.Pierce spoke briefly in court Wednesday, acknowledging the difficulty of the case and some guilt he held, but he ultimately denied criminal involvement in his son's death."I didn't murder my son," he said.As part of the plea agreement, Pierce is not allowed to contact the child's mother.When released from prison, Pierce will be placed on five years of supervised probation.

title: Easton traffic dashboard gives residents detailed look at crash trends
author: KONNER METZ kmetz@chespub.com
content:
Easton traffic dashboard gives residents detailed look at crash trends

 July 17, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: KONNER METZ kmetz@chespub.com | Section: Local News 
 
 537
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — Residents can now easily access traffic statistics online thanks to a new traffic dashboard released by the town last week.The Easton Interactive Traffic Dashboard allows users to view up-to-date vehicle, pedestrian and bicycle data from 2018 to the present.
It includes maps, charts and filters that allow users to see crash information based on time of day, where the crash took place and the weather circumstances. Residents can find specific information on categories such as drunk driving, Route 50 and distracted driving incidents.
Easton Police Chief Alan Lowrey said it will be a valuable resource for the community to better understand where an alarming number of accidents or traffic citations may happen.
"We are focusing on making transportation safety in Easton better," Lowrey said. "We're trying to take a methodical approach, a thoughtful approach to it. … Here is a resource, here's a transparent resource to see what is going on in the town where you live."
Ron Engle, a former town council member, helped spearhead the project, along with the Washington College Geographic Information Systems Program and the Maryland Highway Safety Office. Engle has a background in law enforcement and with the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration.
Sean Lynn, the GIS program manager at Washington College, presented the tool to the Easton Town Council on Monday.
"Hopefully it allows the folks here in the town to be able to get the information quickly," Lynn said.
Ever since the pandemic in 2020, Lowrey said it's been hard to recruit officers. With limited human resources but a need to improve traffic safety, Lowrey began to think about solutions from an "engineering" standpoint.
"An officer sitting at a location, the impact ends soon after the officer leaves," he said. "Engineering (and) other means are more of a 24-hour solution."
Lowrey added that it'll help not just residents, but his team of officers as well. The department will be better-equipped to answer questions such as, "How many of these are left turn-related? How many of these are red light-related?," Lowrey said.
The dashboard is a step in completing a Strategic Highway Safety Plan for the town. Engle, Lowrey and Mayor Megan Cook have been working to develop the plan.
Lowrey said a Strategic Highway Safety Plan will open up the ability for the town to acquire grant funding. He pointed to Salisbury as a local jurisdiction that has embraced the state's "Vision Zero' initiative that was passed by the state legislature in 2019.
"Behind it is the notion that you try to reduce fatalities and serious injury accidents down to zero," Lowrey said. "It's a pretty big goal, a really difficult one."
According to Lowrey, a plan outline for Easton will be completed in about a month. Engle told council members on Monday that a lack of data was perhaps the "biggest problem" for the town in terms of developing a highway safety plan.
Engle said the dashboard will be a "strong compliment" to developing the plan in line with the Vision Zero initiative.
"I would hope by fall that we're at a place where we can present a finalized plan before the council with a pretty good idea that they're going to approve it," Lowrey said.
The interactive traffic dashboard can be accessed by visiting https://eastonmd.gov/196/Police and clicking on the dashboard image.

title: Young driver fatality rates fall sharply in the US
author: Assoclated Press
content:
Young driver fatality rates fall sharply in the US

 October 19, 2023 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Assoclated Press | Page: A2 | Section: News 
 
 286
 Words 

 Read News Document

 Crash and fatality rates among drivers under 21 have fallen dramatically in the U.S. during the past 20 years, a new report says, while noting young drivers are still the riskiest group behind the wheel.Using data from 2002-2021, a non-profit group of state highway safety offices says in the report made public Wednesday that fatal crashes involving a young driver fell by 38%, while deaths ofyoung drivers dropped even more, by about 45%. For drivers 21 and older, fatal crashes rose 8% and deaths rose 11%.The report from the Governors Highway Safety Association acknowledges that young people are driving less than they were 20 years ago, but highlights several other reasons for the improvement, while offering recommendations for building on them.State programs that phase in driving privileges were at the top ofthe list. These programs, called graduated drivers license laws, often restrict or ban certain activities, such as driving at night or with peers, for teens. The GHSA suggests strengthening those programs and even expanding them to cover drivers 18 to 20 years old, like Maryland and New Jersey do.Other recommendations include bolstering adult and parent participation in their child's driving education, more peer-to-peer education programs and making driver training accessible to all."Young drivers are the riskiest age group on the road, and the reasons are straightforward- immaturity and inexperience," said Pam Shadel Fischer, author ofthe GHSA report. "Many young drivers simply don't have the behind-the-wheel experience to recognize risk and take the appropriate corrective action to prevent a crash."According to the National HighwayTraffic Safety Commission, overall traffic fatalities dropped 3.3% in the first halfofthe year compared with the prior-year period and have now fallen in five straight quarters after a pandemic surge.

title: Caroline County meeting sheds light on possible police accountability 'overreach'
author: AHMAD GARNETT agarnett@chespub.com
content:
Caroline County meeting sheds light on possible police accountability 'overreach'

 December 18, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: AHMAD GARNETT agarnett@chespub.com | Section: Local News 
 
 756
 Words 

 Read News Document

 DENTON — Law enforcement officials from multiple counties gathered at the Caroline County Commissioners meeting Tuesday, bringing concerns about an incident involving a Caroline County sheriff's deputy and its implications for police accountability committee practices throughout the state.The officials represented the state's Police Accountability Board, a state agency that oversees administrative charging committees, county organizations intended to provide oversight for police practices.
The charging committees were formed as a result of the Maryland Police Accountability Act of 2021. According to maryland.gov, the committees' job is to "... (review) the findings of each law enforcement agency's investigation of police misconduct complaints forwarded by the agency to the Committee. From information related to the investigation, the Committee makes determinations and recommendations."
"We have a lot of law enforcement representation in the room," Commission President Travis Breeding stated at the beginning of the discussion. "I think this will be a great opportunity to discuss the role of the ACC (Administrative Charging Committee) and the PAB (Police Accountability Board)."
The discussion stemmed from an incident that called into question the county committee's investigation practices.
A Caroline County sheriff's deputy, who was not named, was investigated by the committee about a harassment complaint. Charge committee members invited the deputy to meet with the committee regarding the complaint, a move considered by some sheriff's departments to be "not proper protocol" or an "overreach."
"I understand that," said John Bartlett, a member of the Caroline County Administrative Charging Committee who was involved in the event in question. "I've been called in for incidents happening when I was on the job. That's why I walked to his cruiser, identified myself, asked him if he had talked to a lawyer or if he wanted a lawyer, and he was comfortable with coming in (to meet with the committee) without a lawyer."
A date for the incident was not specified. Charging committee members told The Star Democrat they could not further elaborate on the matter.
Sheriff Donald Barker of the Caroline County Sheriff's Office was very confused as to why his officer was called into the meeting, saying Tuesday that to his knowledge the harassment charge had already been exonerated at the time of the incident.
"But the problem I have is my deputy also told me that John told him that he was not," Baker said. "They'd already exonerated him of harassment. So he's already exonerated the entire complaint. What are you going to ask?"
Police Accountability Board members in attendance voiced that it was unusual for a county charging committee member to approach an officer in this manner.
"I think that the only concern that I've had is it's the first time I've seen an ACC ask an individual to come in and testify," James DeWess, Sheriff of Carrol County, said. "I think if somebody's got to meet a deputy out in the parking lot and ask them if they need an attorney, then they shouldn't be inviting them in. I think that's an extension of an overreach of what they should be doing, and that's really the only thing that concerns me."
The Police Accountability Board and the charging committee members agreed Tuesday that the state legislation establishing the oversight committees needs some work in order to clarify protocols for incidents like this going forward.
Caroline County Attorney Stewart Barroll drafted an agreement that will be sent out to the Police Accountability Board and the charge committee at a later date.
Reading from the draft, Barroll said. "Subpoenas may be issued by the ACC or by the chairman acting on behalf of the ACC. The ACC may not request or compel a police officer to appear before the ACC unless it has first requested the information it seeks from the LEA (law enforcement agency), and if still not satisfied, served written questions upon the officer, together with a notice signed by the chair or presiding officer stating that the ACC is in need of the officer's answers to make its determination of whether an officer is to be administratively charged, a copy of the notice and the questions shall be delivered by the chair or the presiding officer or ACC staff to the head of a law enforcement agency that employs the police officer, who shall deliver same to the officer and notify the ACC of the date of service within 15 days after service, the officer shall provide to the ACC and written the answers and a signed statement that the answers are true to the best of the officers, knowledge, information and belief."
The Caroline County Sheriff's Office could not be reached for comment.

title: Workshop encourages becoming an informed weather spotter
author: WILL BONTRAGER wbontrager@chespub.com
content:
Workshop encourages becoming an informed weather spotter

 April 12, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: WILL BONTRAGER wbontrager@chespub.com | Section: News 
 
 696
 Words 

 Read News Document

 For Warning Coordinator Meteorologist for the National Weather Service, Sarah Johnson, discussing weather's not just typical small talk.She deals in tornados, hail, high winds and severe storms all the time. As Marylanders escape winter weather, hopefully, there's a pause in the storm seasons.
June is considered the beginning of hurricane season and Johnson mentioned some things to stay alert to on the Eastern Shore.
At the Kent County Public Library on March 21, she introduced her audience to their program: SKYWARN.
She's looking for more and more people to become a spotter, who look out for the basics of thunderstorm development, storm structure and severe weather features, then report the information accurately.
"The main mission of the spotter is to be aware of the rapidly changing conditions of the weather," Johnson replied.
And it's sorely needed too.
Johnson said last year they reported the second most severe thunderstorms.
The third most for tornado warnings.
And the fourth most in flash flood warnings.
Unperturbed by the smaller audience in attendance, she was concise and enthusiastic while walking through the process of what to look out for.
For instance, people tend to be on high alert when they get something on their phone saying "tornado warning." Not so much when they get a "severe thunderstorm warning."
"That's a mistake to think one's worse than the other," Johnson commented.
Especially when water can be more harmful than wind in most cases, she said.
"When we look at the fatalities, 75% in the United States are due to water in some way; 50% of those are those are due to storm surge; 25% freshwater heavy rain flooding. Keep that in mind. Don't think, 'Oh, it's just a tropical storm.' No, you still need to pay attention and see what the hazards are."
Severe storms should not be treated much differently than a tornado.
She then pointed out the difference between a storm watch and a storm warning. A watch means to keep an eye on the weather pattern.
A warning means, don't just watch — get prepared.
A severe storm warning means, gather up some candles for light, or buy extra gas for the back-up generator and do things that will prepare your family and yourself for a potential hazard.
As hurricanes emerge from the North Atlantic ocean and the Gulf of Mexico, Johnson reminded her audience how to categorize them and what that exactly means.
Hurricanes, big or small, she indicated, can create problems, such as tornados.
The uninformed, she added, might hear about a category 1 hurricane and think it's not much of a problem. They'll see it as a little rain and wind. Very minimal damage.
The savvy spotter though, will see that even a category 1 hurricane can create big problems, such as a tornado. The spotter will know category 1, simply describes the wind of the hurricane. Nothing else. It does not highlight the possibility of it creating tornados or other adverse weather conditions.
And those who think tornados are only a threat in Kansas are in for a rude awakening.
Tornados hit everywhere, Johnson pointed out. Even in our backyard.
She said Hurricane Ida was a remnant tropical system that produced a lot of tornados in 2020.
Hurricane Isaias was a destructive Category 1 hurricane, producing the longest tracked tornado in Delaware history.
Tornados in Cecil County and Southern Delaware — resulted in fatalities last year.
"That's why we need you all," she said, encouraging her audience to report their observations to their nearest national weather station.
To become a spotter, adults are invited to complete the SKYWARN training.
Those who finish the course join a volunteer program with between 350,000 and 400,000 trained severe weather spotters.
Individuals affiliated with hospitals, schools, churches and nursing homes or who have a responsibility for protecting others are encouraged to become a spotter.
"There can be no finer reward than to know that your efforts have given your family and neighbors the precious gift of time—minutes that can help save lives," as stated by the NWS.
And as the movie "Twisters," the sequel to the original from 1996, comes out in theaters shortly, Johnson jokes that she's preparing to field a lot more questions about tornados.
She discouraged the crowd on becoming storm chasers like sensationalist Hollywood actors and actresses, but rather to become informed citizens who save lives.

title: Banquet honors former commissioner’s dedication to county ALS
author: ANDREA GRABENSTEIN agrabenstein@chespub.com
content:
Banquet honors former commissioner’s dedication to county ALS

 June 26, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: ANDREA GRABENSTEIN agrabenstein@chespub.com | Section: News 
 
 836
 Words 

 Read News Document

 CHESTER — Honoring a lifetime of service, particularly in strengthening local emergency services, a recognition banquet was held in honor of former Queen Anne's County Commissioner and Maryland State Delegate Wheeler R. Baker at Kent Island Volunteer Fire Department June 21.The hall filled with community reunion, reconnecting lives touched by the service of Baker who in addition to a number of attributes, was instrumental in establishing the county's first advanced life support program in the late 1980s.
"We honor a man who has put his service to the public above all his needs, all his life," said Josie Simons, organizer of the recognition banquet and the first woman hired as a paramedic in Queen Anne's County in 1988.
Baker's resume includes a plethora of positions and titles including serving in the United States Air Force 1964-1968; the Queen Anne's County Democratic Central Committee 1974-1978; Queen Anne's County Commissioner from 1986-1990; Maryland House of Delegates from 1995-2003; the Chesapeake Bay Trust from 1995-2001; the Commission to Study Waves to Improve the Financial Viability of the Racing Industry from 1997-1999; the Statewide 800-MHZ Communications System Oversight Committee 1999; the Governor's Task Force on Eastern Shore Economic Development from 1999-2001; the Task Force to Study the Maryland Agricultural Land Preservation Foundation from 2000- 2001; the Mid-Shore Regional Council from 2001- 2003; the Tri-County Council for the Lower Eastern Shore from 2001-2003.
Baker's family also owned Baker's Liquor, a store known for being a community local gathering spot.
Baker has also been recognized as an avid boat racer.
ALS establishedThrough his vision and leadership, Baker was instrumental in educating the public on the need for an advanced life support unit, Simons said.
Establishing an ALS program in the county was by no means an easy road, she said.
"There are two things Eastern Shore folks absolutely dislike: one is beach traffic and the other is change," she quipped.
Laying the groundwork to establish an ALS program in the county and trying to educate the public on the need was often met with community and administrative resistance, including questioning logistical costs, and extensive training, and retention, according to Simons.
That is, until Baker, she said.
Simons recognized Baker, a county commissioner at the time, as the first politician to listen to the needs of the emergency services and ask questions about the proposed program. Even when informed it wasn't in the county budget, Baker saw the betterment of the community and continued to pursue it, she said.
"When the going got tough, we always knew Wheeler was in our corner," Simons said.
Drastically improving the quality of lives for citizens across the county, since its inception the ALS program has not only provided care and saved lives, but inspired a legacy of first responders, according to Simons.
In the 1990s, the ALS program established an intern program allowing high school seniors to learn firsthand from emergency medical professionals.
Reflecting on the impact on the internship, Nathan Powell, Deputy Fire Chief of the City of Annapolis, was one such success story of the inaugural program.
Seeing first hand the lifesaving skills through the internship inspired Powell to pursue a career in emergency services and provided networking and mentorship opportunities that, like many of his peers, set him on a highly successful career trajectory, he said.
Baker fully understood the crucial need for advanced emergency services in the county and was steadfast in his commitment in getting it established, according to Powell.
"His push to have advanced life support paramedics here in Queen Anne's County was innovative and progressive and it was often met with controversy and pushback," Powell said.
AcclamationCounty Commissioners Jim Moran and Patrick McLaughlin presented Baker a citation of recognition for his outstanding service as well as street signs proclaiming Chesterwyne Lane in Grasonville to be eventually renamed a variation of "Wheeler's Way."
State Delegate Steve Arentz (R-36) presented a citation from the Maryland General Assembly congratulating his unrelenting support in establishing Queen Anne's County first ALS system and its immeasurable impact on the health and safety of the community.
An official citation was also received from Gov. Wes Moore.
Baker's dedication to communities serves as an example to follow, not just for government officials or politicians, but for everyone, Simons said.
30 years after Baker's strive to bring forth the county ALS program, "It's never too late to say thank you," she said.
Baker received a standing ovation as he accepted the gratitude of the community he has served lifelong.
Becoming a county commissioner in the 1980s, Baker noted his two main focuses were controlled growth and establishing the ALS program.
Baker noted the recognition was very touching and emphasized the importance of connecting with neighbors and the work done by emergency services.
"This is a great county that helps people," he said.
Bakers reflected on the positive feelings he experiences every time he sees an ALS unit on its way to assist someone in need.
"It makes me feel good. You're supposed to help folks, that's what life is about," Baker said.
The banquet dinner was catered by Chesapeake Celebrations Catering and a dessert table was presented by the Kent Island Volunteer Fire Department Ladies Auxiliary.

 Local and state officials report fire has destroyed a house on Camp Roosevelt Drive in Chesapeake Beach. The blaze was reported Jan. 12 just before 4 a.m.According to Maryland State Fire Marshal's Office spokesman Oliver Alkire, the two adult occupants of the house escaped the structure without injury. Alkire said they are being assisted by family members.
A report from the North Beach Volunteer Fire Department stated crews arrived at the scene "with fire showing from multiple floors and the roof."
Alkire said the smoke alarm that sounded in the house alerted the occupants who fled the home and was also connected to a line that alerted 911.
The Jan. 12 blaze resulted in two alarms.

Both Alkire and the fire department confirmed that crews had a difficult time accessing the burning house.

"Alternative access was located through a neighbor's driveway and crews from other companies deployed hand lines for defensive operations," a report posted by the Huntingtown Volunteer Fire Department stated.
The house was located near Roosevelt Cliffs and the Chesapeake Bay.
The structure and contents sustained an estimated $700,000 in damage.
Despite the arduous conditions, no firefighters were injured and members of the Huntingtown Ladies Auxiliary were at the site providing refreshments and snacks to operating crews throughout the incident, local fire officials reported.
The North Beach VFD reported crews worked at the site for approximately four-and-a-half hours.
The cause of the fire and its area of origin remains under investigation.
North Beach volunteers reminds citizens to "always ensure emergency vehicles can access your house from the driveway. This includes having snow and ice removed from the driveway, trim back any tree limbs and have house numbers visible."

title: Local K-9 units work to overcome retirements from cannabis law
author: Konner Metz
content:
Local K-9 units work to overcome retirements from cannabis law

 May 24, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Konner Metz | Section: Local News 
 
 917
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — In just a handful of months, K-9 Knox is making an impact at the Easton Police Department.The nearly 2-year-old black lab completed training in January. In 2025's first quarter alone, she was deployed 17 times, making six drug arrests alongside her handler, Pfc. Mark Schinault.
"She has that drive for her reward, her toy after she does a good scan," Schinault said. "That means the world to her, so she's very driven to work."
Knox is part of Easton's new guard of K-9s. Last year, three dogs trained in marijuana detection were forced into early retirement due to the legalization of recreational cannabis use legalization in Maryland, which took effect July 2023.
Easton is not the only agency looking to rebuild its K-9 team in the wake of the legislation. Across the state, law enforcement agencies are working to fund and fill their K-9 units, which serve crucial roles not only in deterring crime, but also in connecting with the community.
Police officers largely agree that dogs trained to sniff marijuana can't be used to detect drug offenses any longer, nor does the dogs' expertise hold up in court.
"I really didn't want to go down the road because I didn't want to be challenged in the courtroom," Talbot County Sheriff Joe Gamble said.
Knox joined K-9 Waylon in Easton, and soon two other young dogs not imprinted on marijuana will fill out the town's K-9 unit. Lt. Tim Larrimore said it has been a "complete rebuild" for the unit since the law passed.
Trained dogs can sometimes cost around $14,000, Larrimore said. Younger, untrained pups are significantly less, though they require major time commitments for training and certification.
Across the state, the work of K-9 dogs — depending on their training — often includes drug sniffing, tracking of suspects or missing subjects, and explosives detection. Knox is certified in drug detection and on her way to certification in tracking.
Schinault and Knox completed more than 60 hours of one-on-one training before she was certified in drug detection. Easton opted to go with untrained dogs to save costs and build rapport between K-9s and officers.
While Maryland K-9s are no longer sniffing for marijuana, Larrimore says their work is more important than ever in combating drug offenses.
"This odor of marijuana was enough before 2023 to give us probable cause to search. Now that's out," Larrimore said. "So now you need the ability to smell something that the human nose isn't necessarily good at detecting. It's the dog that gets you there."
PLAYING CATCH UP
Kent County Sgt. Scott Lockerman has a passion for not just his K-9 partner, Khari, but for all police dogs across the state. He is president of the Maryland Police K9 Foundation, a nonprofit that helps police agencies buy, train and protect their four-legged workers. The foundation paid for one of Easton's new dogs.
Lockerman said that after the legalization of cannabis, there was roughly a 60-40 split of agencies that could quickly get their K-9 units back on track versus those that were more affected by unexpected retirements. But he said progress is being made across all departments.
"Most of the agencies were able to replenish the dogs," Lockerman said.
At the Dorchester County Sheriff's Office, one K-9 retired early after the cannabis law was passed, while multiple dogs retired shortly before. The agency worked ahead to bring in replacement dogs not trained to detect marijuana so the state legislation didn't present too many challenges.
"We saw it coming," Sheriff James Phillips said. "It was on the horizon."
Six K-9s currently work for the Dorchester Sheriff's Office. Three can assist in patrols and narcotic detection, two work in narcotics only, and one bloodhound specializes in tracking. Phillips said the office has adequate funding to fill its seventh and final spot for a K-9 trained in detecting explosives.
Funding often comes from grants, local donations, organizations such as the K9 Foundation and county councils. Phillips said it's "mind-boggling" how generous people have been in donating dogs to the Sheriff's Office.
In addition to purchasing the dogs, agencies pay for safety equipment (like bulletproof vests) and health payments. Departments are also on the hook for vet costs incurred by retired dogs, per state law. For a retired K-9, departments could pay up to as much as $2,500 a year, capped at $10,000 per dog.
Larrimore, the Easton lieutenant, says that hasn't yet presented a major funding challenge, though it could down the road.
"It hasn't hit us yet," he said. "These dogs are just retired last year. They're young, they're healthy."
COMMUNITY IMPACT
When the highly-skilled dogs aren't working a case, they're often out in the community showing more of their friendly side.
In Dorchester County, Sgt. Steve Twilley says the K-9 unit bridges the gap between the Sheriff's Office and the community. The dogs especially help police build trust with kids.
"Next thing you know, that kid's come to you for help instead of lashing out or doing something at school," Twilley said.
Schinault and Knox attended a recent Coffee with a Cop event this spring. Schinault said they're very involved with community policing efforts.
Phillips and Twilley say the same is true in Dorchester County. Whatever dollar amount is spent on police dogs, Phillips says, comes back to the Sheriff's Office "10 times over because of the relationships that we build with the kids and the people."
"I think an agency that's trying to do today's police work and doesn't have the K-9 ability out there, I don't think they're a full police agency," Phillips said. "I think it completes the police agency by having the K-9s."

 TAYLORS ISLAND - A Maryland State Police aviation crew helped rescue a 22-yearold man early Thursday morning after the boat he was operating ran aground, stranding him on a small island in Dorchester County.MSP's Trooper 7, which is based at St. Mary's Airport, was dispatched to the area of Taylors Island around 12:40 a.m. Thursday for a report of a missing boater.The request came from the Dorchester County Fire and EMS Department after they had exhausted efforts searching for the subject by boat.Shortly after Trooper 7 arrived in the area, they located the victim in his boat that had run aground in a marshy area. Trooper 7 guided ground rescue crews to the victim location, but conditions proved to be inaccessible by foot or boat.MSP's Trooper 2, which is based at Joint Base Andrews, was dispatched at about 1:20 a.m. to assist with a hoist extraction and take over rescue operations.Once overhead, the pilots on Trooper 2 hovered the Leonardo AW-139 helicopter approximately 50 feet above the marshy terrain while a trooper/paramedic was lowered below to assess the victim.The victim was extracted utilizing the air-lift rescue vest. The trooper/paramedic and victim were hoisted back into the aircraft.Trooper 2 then landed at a landing zone established by the Dorchester County Fire and EMS Department, where the victim was transferred to ground paramedics for a secondary evaluation.The victim ultimately did not require treatment or transport.The Maryland State Police Aviation Command has served Maryland citizens since 1970 and operates a fleet of 10 AW-139 helicopters from seven bases throughout the State. Each aircraft provides coverage 24/7/365 to Maryland residents and visitors.The MSPAC missions include medevac, law enforcement, search and rescue, homeland security and disaster assessment.The success of the missions relies heavily on the cooperative efforts of local fire, rescue, EMS, law enforcement agencies and partners at the U.S. Coast Guard and the U.S. Park Police.

title: Kent County weighs ICE cooperation amid liability concerns
author: WILL BONTRAGER wbontrager@chespub.com
content:
Kent County weighs ICE cooperation amid liability concerns

 March 28, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: WILL BONTRAGER wbontrager@chespub.com | Section: Local News 
 
 626
 Words 

 Read News Document

 CHESTERTOWN — Will Kent County police cooperate with U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement when and if they call? More specifically, will they participate in the 287(g) program, which allows local law enforcement agencies to collaborate with ICE to detain immigrants?Kent County Sheriff Dennis Hickman acknowledges this is a complicated issue, based on recommendations from the Maryland State's Attorney's Office.
A 2018 guidance memorandum states that law enforcement agencies can cooperate, but are not required to do so and could be liable in certain situations.
"As the elected sheriff, I don't want to potentially cause additional liability to me or our county government, but we don't want the same problems that we have seen in other counties," Hickman said in an interview with the Kent County News.
Hickman is referring to the releasing of dangerous criminals back into the community. By refusing to cooperate with ICE, local lawmakers could release a person charged with a minor offense while the federal government has information about a more serious crime.
Although Hickman is aware of liability issues, his first priority is protecting the public.
The issue is politically charged across Maryland and the country. Democratic lawmakers are advocating for eliminating the federal program altogether. On March 17, during the Maryland General Assembly crossover session, Delegate Nicole Williams, D-Prince George's County, advanced a bill that appeared closer to passage.
"We should not be doing the federal government's job for them," Williams told her colleagues during a floor debate.
In the state Senate, Sen. Will Smith, D-Montgomery County, has proposed a "protected spaces" bill that would require guidelines for how ICE carries out actions in sensitive locations like churches and schools.
Several Maryland jurisdictions already have policies limiting cooperation with ICE.
Howard County's Liberty Act prohibits county employees from asking residents about their immigration status and bans discrimination based on citizenship status.
Similarly, in Prince George's County, legislation has been enacted to ban local agencies from cooperating with immigration enforcement.
Despite opposition, sheriffs from Garrett, Allegany and Washington counties agreed to assist ICE, joining Frederick County, which has been assisting for several years.
Hickman acknowledged that this level of cooperation is not feasible in Kent County, not because they oppose the policy, but because it requires additional training and duties without federal compensation.
Most likely, Kent will not enter into a 287(g) agreement but will cooperate while trying to avoid liability and maintain public safety.
On its website, ICE expressed gratitude for the three counties' cooperation in the Secure Communities Program, which helps "identify criminal aliens in state prisons and local jails by running their fingerprints against federal immigration databases when they are locked in the system."
This information-sharing program now includes 21 counties, including Kent.
Matt Elliston, Maryland ICE director, warned that cooperating with the state may put local law enforcement in liability issues, but not cooperating could also create consequences.
In Frederick and Howard counties, Elliston is calling on the U.S. Department of Justice to take action against them for refusing ICE detainers and releasing criminals without notifying ICE.
For Hickman, a balanced approach is best and, most importantly, safest. "Some counties refuse to cooperate with the federal government, resulting in releasing potentially dangerous people back into the community," he said. "Failing to have some measure of cooperation is not in the best interest of our community."
Currently, the county has not been asked to assist ICE beyond notifying the agency before a state release. The Kent County Sheriff's Department has not been asked to hold anyone past their state-release date.
"If ICE has a detainer on someone, we will let them know when they are done with local charges and they are welcome to meet them at the back gate to pick them up," Hickman clarified.
Since the mid-March, there have been no ICE seizures, but one individual completed their local sentence and was then received by ICE.

title: Boyfriend in toddler death case now facing more serious charges
author: Carl Hamilton cahamilton@chespub.com
content:
Boyfriend in toddler death case now facing more serious charges

 July 10, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Carl Hamilton cahamilton@chespub.com | Section: News 
 
 465
 Words 

 Read News Document

 A man accused of disposing of the body of his girlfriend's 3-year-old daughter after the mother allegedly beat the girl to death and falsely claimed she was kidnapped near Newark, Delaware is facing new, more serious charges after a Maryland grand jury handed up an 11-count indictment against him July 3.The defendant — Cedrick Antoine Britten, 44 — is now charged with felony first-degree child abuse resulting in a death of a child under 13 years old and a mirroring conspiracy count, both of which are punishable by up to life in prison if convicted.
Other new charges against Britten include first-degree child abuse resulting in severe injury and an additional conspiracy count relating to that felony offense. Each of those charges carries a maximum 25-year sentence.
Under the original charges filed last month against Britten, the most serious of the eight counts he faced — accessory after the fact relating to first-degree murder — is punishable by up to 10 years in prison.
The indictment retains some of the original charges against Britten, including burying/disposing a body in unauthorized place, neglect of a minor and failure to report a child's death, court records show.
After the additional charges, Britten is being held in the Cecil County Detention Center on no bond.
Britten's co-defendant — his girlfriend, Darrian Lynnelle Randle, 31 — remains in a Delaware jail in lieu of $1 million bond.
She is awaiting extradition to Cecil County, Randle is accused of fatally beating her 3-year-old daughter, Nola Dinkins, inside their shared bedroom at Britten's residence in the 300 block of Elk Nest Road in North East, Md., during the daytime hours on June 9.
She also told investigators that, after picking up Nola, she called for Britten, who also was inside the residence, according to court records. Britten attempted CPR on Nola, but eventually realized that the girl was dead.
Randle told police that she and Britten placed Nola's body in his black 2019 BMW X3 and that they then drove around for a while, before returning to their Elk Nest Road residence.
Then, according to the documented account that Randle gave police, she and Britten placed the girl's body in a dark blue suitcase that belonged to Britten and placed the luggage on the third step of the basement stairs, where it remained overnight. Randle said she checked the suitcase once overnight.
Randle told police that she asked Britten to take the girl's body "somewhere," court records show.
Randle then drove to Delaware and called police to falsely report Nola had been kidnapped at gunpoint on Gender Road.
Randle's abduction complaint triggered an Amber Alert but after further investigation, Randle admitted that she had killed Nola, according to court records.
Police later found Nola's body inside the suitcase on a vacant property near the house where Randle and Britten live in North East.

title: No vote on bill
author: Staff Writer
content:
No vote on bill

 April 7, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Staff Writer | Section: Editors Inbox 
 
 379
 Words 

 Read News Document

 Did you know that in the state of Maryland, you can cause a motor vehicle collision due to reckless or negligent driving that results in the death of another person, and never have to go to court? You can simply prepay a traffic ticket.Again in 2024, a change was proposed with a bill that was cross-filed in both the Senate and House. (SB68/HR1335) Reckless and Negligent Driving — Death of Another — Must Appear Violation (Sherry's and Christian's Law).
"Providing that a person charged with reckless or negligent driving must appear in court and may not prepay the fine if the reckless or negligent driving contributed to an accident that resulted in the death of another person, unless a court for good cause shown waives the requirement to appear."
Sounds like a no-brainer, right?
If you take a life, you must appear in court. For the past two years, a version of this same bill has passed unanimously through the Senate, both in committee and on the Senate floor. But it never made it through the House Judiciary Committee.
This year, the bill was cross-filed and given a hearing in both the Senate Judicial Proceedings Committee and the House Judiciary Committee where it again saw no opposition. But don't assume that it will become law. After countless hours of writing, reading, discussing, and holding hearings in both houses, a bill that is so straightforward it had no opposition, never got a vote on either side this year. To be clear, it wasn't that it didn't pass, it just was never voted on.
In a state with a 90-day legislative session, time is precious. Not only is it a shame that this bill didn't get passed but think of all the wasted time. How many other important bills were never even heard this year while countless hours were spent on bills that never got voted on? To say that this is frustrating is certainly an understatement. To all those that traveled to Annapolis every Monday night to rally support, attended committee hearings, wrote letters and made telephone calls; your dedication and hard work are appreciated.
Del. Luke Clippinger, chair, House Judiciary Committee (Baltimore City) and Sen. William C. Smith Jr., chair, Senate Judicial Proceedings Committee (Montgomery County), you can and must do better.
MARIANNE JACKSON
Queen Anne

title: Easton man killed in hit-and-run crash
author: Konner Metz
content:
Easton man killed in hit-and-run crash

 October 6, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Konner Metz | Section: Crime

 EASTON — A 68-year-old man riding a bike was killed Saturday morning in a hit-and-run crash, according to police.The Easton Police Department said in a press release that a passerby discovered a body next to a bicycle in the area of Route 50 and Woodridge Drive around 7:50 a.m. on Saturday.
Police attempted life-saving measures at the scene, but the man was confirmed dead. On Monday, officials identified the man as Donald Dawson, an Easton resident.
Easton Police Department Deputy Chief Greg Wright said on Monday that police are still searching for the suspect vehicle.
Preliminary investigations by Maryland State Police and Easton police indicated Dawson "was struck by either a tractor trailer or box truck" earlier Saturday morning, according to the press release.
On Monday, Wright said investigators narrowed the timeframe of the hit-and-run to around 2 to 2:30 a.m. that morning. There were no new significant leads as of Monday morning, Wright said.
Police found vehicle debris at the scene, per the press release. The vehicle suspected in the hit-and-run has a missing mirror and damage to the front passenger side.
Woodridge Drive is on the east side of Route 50, south of Easton High School and across the highway and near the Immanuel Lutheran Church. In February, a car struck and killed a 35-year-old man near Route 50 and Woodridge Drive.
Anyone who witnessed the incident or has information is asked to contact the Easton Police Department at 410-822-1111.

title: Juveniles injured after chase ends with car hitting house
author: MARTY MADDEN mmadden@somdnews.com
content:
Juveniles injured after chase ends with car hitting house

 September 15, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: MARTY MADDEN mmadden@somdnews.com | Section: News 
 
 368
 Words 

 Read News Document

 Three juveniles were injured, one critically, after a vehicle slammed into an Owings home over the weekend. The vehicle appears to have been stolen, according to police.Shortly before 6 p.m. Sunday (Sept. 14), deputies from the Calvert County Sheriff's Office were alerted to a stolen vehicle entering Calvert County.
According to a sheriff's office release, the vehicle, a Kia Optima, had been reported stolen out of Prince George's County and was detected traveling on Route 260.
Deputy Justin MacWilliams located the vehicle on Route 260 and investigators reported the driver "accelerated at a high rate of speed, passing vehicles on the shoulder and operating recklessly."
Attempts were made to stop the fleeing vehicle and a pursuit was initiated, with additional units responding to assist. The pursuit continued eastbound on Route 260 to westbound on Mt. Harmony Road.
Stop sticks were deployed in an effort to end the pursuit. However, the driver swerved the vehicle toward officers and continued fleeing.
According to the sheriff's office, the pursuit ended when the vehicle failed to negotiate a turn on Mt. Harmony Road near Alyssa Way, left the roadway, struck a telephone pole, traveled through a yard and ultimately crashed into a residence a residence.
The vehicle was occupied by four individuals. Three occupants sustained injuries, while one fled on foot into a wooded area.
Deputies, along with responders from Dunkirk, Huntingtown and North Beach volunteer fire departments, rendered medical aid at the scene and police established a perimeter.
With the assistance of agency personnel, K9 units, and drone resources, the fleeing suspect was located and detained. That individual was uninjured.
All four occupants were determined to be juveniles. No names will be released in accordance with state law.
The driver was airlifted by Maryland State Police helicopter to an area trauma center in critical condition. Two additional occupants were transported by ground to local hospitals with non-life-threatening injuries.
In accordance with Maryland law, the Office of the Attorney General's Independent Investigations Division was notified of the incident but declined to investigate.
The Calvert County Sheriff's Office Crash Reconstruction Unit responded and has assumed the investigation.
Anyone who may have witnessed the crash or the events leading up to it is asked to contact Deputy Jeffrey Hardesty at Jeffrey.Hardesty@calvertcountymd.gov and reference case number 25-76666.

title: Cambridge man gets 25 years after taking plea deal in murder trial
author: STAFF REPORT
content:
Cambridge man gets 25 years after taking plea deal in murder trial

 September 10, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: STAFF REPORT | Section: Crime 
 
 289
 Words 

 Read News Document

 CAMBRIDGE — A Cambridge teen was sentenced to 25 years in prison on Sept. 6 in connection to the 2021 fatal shooting of Ja'Len Woolford.Daeveon Johnson, 19, faced a first-degree murder charge in the shooting that occurred on Nov. 18, 2021. Johnson entered an Alford plea for the charge in November 2022.
As part of the plea deal, Johnson will serve 25 years at the Patuxent Youthful Offenders Program. Once 50% of the sentence is served, Johnson will be eligible for parole.
Johnson's sentence will begin dating back to Jan. 4, 2022, the day he was arrested by Cambridge police. He will also serve five years probation.
The sentence orders Johnson to have no contact with Key'Marion Ennals. Ennals, 19, was found not guilty on 12 charges relation to the fatal shooting, including first-degree murder, at a trial this August.
Johnson's sentencing was delayed as part of his plea agreement, which included Johnson testifying during Ennals' trial last month.
In his initial interview with police, Johnson admitted to carrying a .40 caliber firearm. An autopsy revealed that Woolford died from a single gunshot wound from a .40 caliber firearm.
Dorchester County State's Attorney Amanda Leonard provided a statement following the sentencing of Johnson.
"The State recommended a sentence of life imprisonment, suspending all but forty years of active incarceration," the statement read. "The Court heard heartfelt victim impact statements from three members of the victim's family, each expressing their choice to forgive Mr. Johnson, and each requesting the Court consider a lesser period of active incarceration for Mr. Johnson given his cooperation and remorse.
"The State continues to offer condolences to all family and loved ones impacted by the loss of Ja'Len Woolford, and thanks the Court for its mindful consideration of all circumstances at sentencing."
