title: Leaving a timeless mark: Remembering lives lost with roadside memorials
author: MARTY MADDEN mmadden@somdnews.com
content:
Leaving a timeless mark: Remembering lives lost with roadside memorials

 February 26, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: MARTY MADDEN mmadden@somdnews.com | Section: News 
 
 1814
 Words 

 Read News Document

 As one drives along Route 210 through Bryans Road in the area of Livingston Road a metal cross can be seen by anyone with an observant eye. It helps to know it's there if you are looking for it, but if you approach it on foot via sidewalk you can better observe its simplicity.The name "Tiffani" in big capital letters using a decorative font is in the middle of the cross, at the top is a red flower and at the bottom is the insignia for the Bryans Road Volunteer Fire Department and Rescue Squad.
According to Deborah Carrington-Smith, the cross commemorates the life of her daughter, Tiffani Carrington, who was killed near the Indian Head Highway intersection on Dec. 21, 1996.
"She was 19 years old," Carrington-Smith told Southern Maryland News. "Her car, a 1987 Nissan 300ZX, was broadsided by a Charles County sheriff's officer."
The deputy driving the sheriff's office patrol car was responding to a call. Tiffani Carrington, according to information posted by the U.S. National Emergency Medical Service Memorial Service, had logged a lot of volunteer hours with the Bryans Road company.
At the time she was killed, Tiffani Carrington was pursuing a career as a Maryland State Police trooper paramedic.
"This is who Tiffani was to our family," her mother said. "She was a child full of spunk, a teenager wise beyond her years and an EMT with aspirations of becoming a flight paramedic. She was a cheerleader, a softball player, a coach and a mentor to other youth. She was the apple of her father's eye and a bit bossy with her younger brothers. She had so much love to give and was never stingy with her affection."
In 1998, the national EMS memorial service honored Tiffani Carrington, declaring her death was in the line of duty.
Carrington-Smith is quoted in the organization's citation saying that her daughter took the career path toward becoming a paramedic "after she saw a lady collapse from a seizure."
Tiffani Carrington, her mother said, was frustrated that she didn't have the expertise to aid the stricken woman. That led to her career path decision.
Carrington-Smith said that over six months after the tragic death, her daughter posthumously earned her flight paramedic wings.
"She spoke her mind unabashedly, valuing authenticity, honesty and courage," Carrington-Smith said of Tiffani. "Material things were not important to her and she judged people by how they treated others."
Marking the spot of a memorialFor those wishing to have a marking to remember a loved one lost in a road tragedy, the rules in Maryland can be ambiguous.
"State Highway Administration does not track memorials that are placed along state highways in memory of crash victims," SHA spokesman Daniel Allman told Southern Maryland News. "However, state law prohibits the unauthorized placement of anything along state highways that are not approved, highway safety-related signs or devices. The placement of roadside memorials could pose safety and maintenance concerns for motorists, pedestrians and highway workers."
A website called "Roadside Tribute" notes in Maryland, the state highway administration "must comply with the law and has an obligation to motorists to keep roads safe, which includes removing distractions and illegal items from state right-of-way. When doing so, crews keep any intact roadside memorials at the nearest shop to be reclaimed within two weeks. If the owners of the memorials are known, SHA tries to contact them."
Those rules don't stop people from placing memorials, though, as evidenced by the many memorials large and small along the region's roadways.
The state website further noted that there are other options in Maryland that can be used to pay tribute to a loved one lost in a road tragedy. Those options include the Adopt-a-Highway program and Partnership Plantings. In some cases, plantings along the highway are done in honor of someone and can be noted with a sign.
Remembered with flowersNearly 18 years after Tiffani Carrington's death, Charles County lost another volunteer responder in a road crash. Autumn Jenkins was 20 years old when her life was claimed in a collision that occurred April 28, 2015, on Route 424 in the area of Tim's Place in Nanjemoy.
Katelyn Shannon remembered her cousin Autumn Jenkins as a consummate volunteer, someone whose passion was to help people and animals. She had worked at the Charles County Humane Society as a technician and was also a manager at a Waldorf swimming pool.
According to a July 2016 Maryland Independent article on the sentencing of the other driver, an Indian Head man in his early 20s, police investigating the crash said the Chevrolet Silverado the at-fault driver was operating crossed the center line and crashed into the Kia Soul that Jenkins was driving.
Crews desperately worked to free her from the wreckage, but Jenkins was pronounced dead at the scene. The driver of the truck, court testimony stated, registered a 0.14 blood alcohol level. He was sentenced to 10 years with all but three years suspended.
Shannon said the memorial to her cousin "sits in front of a telephone pole. We have a stone that was engraved with a drawing of a dog and the fire shield. We also have her helmet shield up and we actively put flowers and solar lights. We actively attend DUI checkpoints conducted by the La Plata Police Department in memory of her."
The Maryland Independent story on the sentencing mentioned that when the defendant's mother made her plea for clemency to the judge, she mentioned that her son went back to the crash site on the anniversary of Jenkins' death and left flowers.
Memories of a 'bright and positive person'Jonna Jones of Lusby remembers her friend, Lauren Pitt, as someone who loved people and life.
"Her enthusiasm for people made me feel like I could do anything," Jones said. "Such a bright, positive person. We lost a bright light when she passed."
Pitt, who lived in St. Mary's County's Hollywood, was 27 when she was killed Sept. 3, 2015, while riding as a passenger on a motorcycle. The operator of the Harley Davidson, Conrado "Chico" Fabricante Jr., 55, of Broomes Island, also died in the crash at the Route 2/4 and Rousby Hall Road intersection in Lusby.
"This year it will be 10 years, that's hard to believe," Jones said.
Fabricante, the father of three, had worked at Calvert Cliffs Nuclear Power Plant for over 30 years. His obituary posted by Rausch Funeral Home said he was an avid motorcyclist and a member of Hells Angels, "who were his second family."
At the time of her death, Pitt was employed at Calvert Orthopedic of Southern Maryland as a radiology technician and part-time by MedStar St. Mary's Hospital.
According to her obituary, Pitt was a 2006 graduate of Leonardtown High, where she played clarinet in the school jazz band. Jones recalled Pitt was in the process of learning to play the mandolin in 2015.
The markers memorializing Pitt and Fabricante — two wooden crosses with their first names — are placed in front of the guardrail on southbound Route 2/4 near the Rousby Hall Road intersection.
Several months after the collision occurred, the Calvert County Sheriff's Office announced that the incident was nobody's fault and no blame would be placed nor charges filed.
Jones said she has never stopped to visit the roadside memorial but has visited Pitt's gravesite in Leonardtown.
"I have done things in her honor," Jones said.
One of the events Jones dedicated to her friend's memory was a half-marathon she trained for and ran in 2016.
"It helped me keep going," Jones said of the 13-mile dash and the inspiration of her late friend. "I finished it with a smile on my face."
'Unknown reasons'It was on a Monday morning, the first day of October 2018, that 24-year-old David Joseph Johnson of Ridge lost his life when his small sedan traveling south of Lexington Park went off Route 235, up a steep embankment, struck a tree and flipped over on its roof.
The Leonardtown High grad was employed as a welder at the time of his passing.
A release from the St. Mary's County Sheriff's Office stated that Johnson's vehicle went out of control "for unknown reasons," before it went off the road and subsequently crashed.
"There's only one person that knows, and that person can't tell us," then-Captain Steve Hall, the county's current sheriff, told The Enterprise the day after the fatality. "There's never any logical explanation."
An array of flowers surrounding a cross with the name "Joseph" in capital letters marks the location of the fatality on Three Notch Road just north of a local bus and car repair shop.
'A gifted swimmer'He was born in a Siberian city in July 1998 and eight months later was adopted by David and Kandia Spain, who brought him to their home in Huntingtown. Zachary David Igor "Zack" Spain attended Plum Point Elementary, Plum Point Middle and Huntingtown High, graduating in 2016.
While he played soccer during his elementary and middle school years, Zack Spain's true passion was swimming, which he did competitively starting at age 5.
"He was a gifted swimmer and swam club team, summer league and for his high school," Kandia Spain told Southern Maryland News. "He was a kind and caring brother, son and friend."
His plan was to study political science with the goal of working for an environmental protection group.
On Thanksgiving Day 2020 — Nov. 26 — Zack Spain was operating a vehicle on Wilson Road in Prince Frederick. He was the lone occupant of the car. According to the Calvert sheriff's office, the vehicle left the road and crashed into two utility poles. Zack Spain was declared dead at the scene. He was 22.
"I keep flowers all year round attached to the utility pole," Kandia Spain told Southern Maryland News.
Remembering 'Lil Bro'It's hard to spot, but somewhere in a sparsely wooded area near the Route 5 and Chingville Road intersection of St. Mary's County a small white cross that had been staked into the earth lays on the ground. Almost one year ago, a horrific, single-vehicle crash occurred there, injuring three — the adult female driver and two small children — and killing a male juvenile who had recently celebrated his 8th birthday.
Brysen McKinley Carter had been a football player for the Pax River Raiders team.
According to the St. Mary's sheriff's office, the three juvenile occupants, including Brysen, "were found to not be correctly restrained."
Brysen was taken to MedStar St. Mary's Hospital and was later pronounced dead.
The crash occurred on March 16, 2024, and more than seven months later the driver, Ashley Nicole Nolan, now 28, of Lexington Park, was served an 18-count indictment, which includes four felony charges for negligent manslaughter and homicide with a motor vehicle while impaired, according to court records. A circuit court jury trial is currently scheduled for early April.
A GoFundMe page in Brysen Carter's honor raised over $19,000 before organizers stopped accepting donations. The Pax River Raiders contributed $500 to the fund.
On a tribute page posted by Briscoe-Tonic Funeral Home, one of Brysen's friends wrote, "I miss you every day, Lil Bro." 

 © Copyright © 2025 Star Democrat, Chesapeake Publishing Group (Adams Publishing/APGMedia). All rights reserved.

title: When all else fails
author: ERIC SYLVIA Special to the Bay Times Record Observer
content:
When all else fails

 June 28, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: ERIC SYLVIA Special to the Bay Times Record Observer | Section: When All Else Fails 
 
 796
 Words 

 Read News Document

 RIDGELY — "There's someone from Ohio — that's 10 contacts so far!", exclaimed Chuck Campbell, an avid HAM radio operator for more than two years. Campbell is in his 70s and took up the hobby late in life. He is an active member of Queen Anne's County RACES (Radio Amateur Civil Emergency Service, pronounced RAY-seas). He is also a part of the QAC Amateur Radio Club (QAARC). The Queen Anne's Amateur Radio Club (QAARC) is a growing group of amateur radio operators who are passionate about the hobby. The club was formed in the spring of 2010 because of a need to support amateur activity and communication in the Queen Anne's County area.Several members of the club endured the heat and set up their kit in a field at Tuckahoe State Park to participate in the 2024 American Radio Relay League Amateur Radio Field Day exercise and contest June 22-23.
This event is the largest on-the-air operation in the amateur radio community and occurs annually on the fourth full weekend of June. It began at 1800 UTC on Saturday and ended at 2059 UTC on Sunday. Field Day is part educational event, part operational contest, and serves as an emergency preparedness exercise. Radio amateurs across the globe set up temporary radio stations in public locations to demonstrate the science, skill, and service that amateur radio provides to the community. It is an opportunity for experienced hams to mentor newcomers and showcase their abilities in operational techniques under emergency conditions or with temporary setups.
According to Corey Ruth, president of QAARC, "This was the hottest Field Day at least in recent memory, but the show must go on. It's actually good practice setting up and operating in adverse conditions like this, since it's highly unlikely to be sunny and 72 degrees in the event we get called upon to assist during an emergency."
Club members ended up making over 400 contacts by the end, using a combination of voice, CW (Morse Code), and digital modes. They hit every corner of the Continental USA, plus Puerto Rico and some up in Canada too. Ruth continued, "It's amazing how far these radios reach with some simple wire and 100 watts or less of power. That's only the equivalent power of a single old incandescent light bulb!" What makes these radios so powerful in an emergency situation — they can be set-up and operated with just a car battery or a simple solar panel for power.
"What most people don't understand is the critical service we provide in an emergency situation — when all the other forms of communications fail due to power loss, widespread outage in the cellular infrastructure, we can still operate and establish comms across a vast distance,"
shared Danielle Wilson of FEMA who was also on hand for the Field Day activities. "When Hurricane Maria, a deadly Category 5 hurricane devastated the northeastern Caribbean in September 2017, particularly the U.S. territory of Puerto Rico, some of the first people FEMA sent were HAM Radio operators who established reliable communications back to the mainland." A critical aspect to getting Puerto Rico back on the way to recovery, she noted.
HAM radio, also known as amateur radio, is a popular hobby and service in which participants use various types of radio equipment to communicate with other radio amateurs across the globe, for the purpose of self-education, civic service, and recreation. HAM operators communicate by transmitting voice, data, and Morse code on designated radio frequencies, which are allocated specifically for amateur use.
One of the primary appeals of HAM radio is its ability to connect people during emergencies or natural disasters when other communication infrastructures are unavailable. Operators often participate in emergency networks and provide critical communications support. To become a HAM radio operator, individuals must pass an examination that tests their knowledge of electronics theory, operating practices, and regulations enforced by national authorities like the Federal Communications Commission (FCC) in the United States.
RACES is an all-volunteer group of licensed amateur radio operators, vetted by the county and authorized to operate under and with the Queen Anne's County Department of Emergency Services (DES). They meet monthly at the county's Emergency Operations Center (EOC — the 911 center) in coordination with Lori Morris, assistant chief of the DES Special Operations Division, and her staff. Emergency Services can call upon the group to activate in an actual or anticipated emergency to deploy to locations across the county, including the EOC, fire stations, medical center, and emergency shelters.
"We provide a backup voice and data communications link between those sites, and to our counterparts in other counties across the state in case regular systems are disrupted. In our capacity as RACES members, we also provide the county DES with backup communications for the annual Bay Bridge Run/Walk," Ruth said.

title: 18-year-old receives maximum sentence for assault on Easton rails to trails
author: Maggie Trovato
content:
18-year-old receives maximum sentence for assault on Easton rails to trails

 July 9, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Maggie Trovato | Section: Crime 
 
 381
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — A teenager was sentenced to 25 years after pleading guilty to first-degree assault for an incident that occurred at the John Ford Park in September.Denilson Mendez-Tomas, 18, will need to serve 20 years in prison, with the last five years of his sentence suspended, according to a news release from the Talbot County State's Attorney's Office. His incarceration will be followed by five years of supervised probation.
Mendez-Tomas was also ordered to pay restitution to the victim, who was represented by Kathleen Callan from the Maryland Crime Victims' Resource Center.
At the sentencing hearing July 2, the victim said the incident made her scared to be alone, prevented her from working and resulted in a permanent scar on her face, among other traumas, according to the news release.
According to previous Star Democrat reporting, police said officers from the Easton Police Department were dispatched to the John Ford Park on the evening of Sept. 21 for an assault. Upon arrival, the officers found a 46-year-old woman who was bleeding heavily from a laceration on her forehead sitting on a bench in the park.
The woman reported that she was walking the Rails to Trails when she saw Mendez-Tomas urinating in the woods. Police said the woman told them she did not pay attention to the teen and continued walking. But as the woman was walking, she heard footsteps coming from behind her. When she turned around, she was repeatedly struck in the head with a rock by Mendez-Tomas, police said.
Police said Mendez-Tomas took the woman to the ground when she started to scream for help. The woman told police that as she screamed, Mendez-Tomas ran down the trail traveling south.
Mendez-Tomas was found later that day by police on the trail at South Street. According to the news release, Mendez-Tomas matched the description of the suspect and had blood on his shirt and hands.
Following the sentencing, Talbot County State's Attorney Joseph Coale said his office is happy with the outcome of the case.

title: Talbot County enacts burn ban
author: KONNER METZ kmetz@chespub.com
content:
Talbot County enacts burn ban

 June 21, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 EASTON – Talbot County Council enacted a burn ban Friday afternoon as a heat wave makes its way through Maryland and local fire departments are seeing increased activity.Council members held a special meeting Friday to discuss the burn ban, which prohibits all "open-air burning." It will last for 30 days, until July 21, unless another resolution is passed to end or extend the ban.
A county press release defined open-air burning as "burning any material in the open or in a receptacle other than a furnace, … including use of fireworks, sparklers, or sparkling devices."
Backyard fire pits are also prohibited. Gas grills and propane stoves are allowed.
Sonny Jones, fire chief for Easton Volunteer Fire Department, has seen increased calls in the county during this spell of hot and dry weather.
"Right now it's so dry, just something as simple as a spark coming from a vehicle … or an ember that flies from someone who has a burn that they're watching, … can spread very, very rapidly," Jones said.
As the Fourth of July holiday approaches, Chris Robertson, state fire supervisor for the Maryland Forest Service, recommends all residents wait for rain before burning. He said county burn bans will help reduce dangerous usage of fireworks and sparklers.
"In Maryland, fireworks are pretty much limited to ground-based fireworks," Robertson said. "So hopefully there won't be too much of that. We do usually have some issues with fireworks, but not a great deal."
Somerset County and Wicomico County both enacted burn bans Thursday. In Talbot, public officers may enter private or public property to put out a fire and confiscate fireworks or sparklers during the ban.

title: Officer fights to deter drivers like one who harmed him
author: LYDIA HURLEY Capital News Service
content:
Officer fights to deter drivers like one who harmed him

 February 12, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: LYDIA HURLEY Capital News Service | Section: General Assembly 
 
 740
 Words 

 Read News Document

 ANNAPOLIS — Less than four months after losing his legs in an attempt to stop a reckless highway driver, a Montgomery County police officer is at the forefront of a movement to crack down on negligent driving in Maryland.Sgt. Patrick Kepp plans to testify on two bills in the state capital of Annapolis this session — traveling from Walter Reed National Military Medical Center in Bethesda, where he is still in active recovery from last October's incident.
"When I was brought into the conversation about new laws being created, right away, I knew it was something I wanted to do," Kepp said.
Rehabilitation is his first priority, he said, but treatment won't get in the way of his new mission. "I will be there in Annapolis to make sure these bills happen," Kepp said.
Kepp announced his plans this week in a press briefing alongside Montgomery County Executive Marc Elrich and Montgomery County lawmakers who are taking up the cause with him. Kepp's story has inspired them to craft new legislation that would punish repeat offenders of reckless driving.
"I'm going to call it the Sergeant Pat Kepp Bill on Reckless Driving," said Delegate Greg Wims (D-Montgomery), calling Kepp a "hero."
Reckless driving isn't a new phenomenon in Maryland. Outraged by stories of dangerous driving on the Beltway or the Ocean City Expressway, Maryland lawmakers in years past have proposed legislation meant to stop these behaviors. This session, two other bills, separate from Kepp's, are making their way through the legislature, specifically aimed at ending the deadly game of drag racing or "exhibition driving."
But Kepp's bill is a personal one, inspired by an officer who patrolled the sponsoring lawmakers' home district. Elrich visited Kepp while he was in recovery to propose the idea of working together on this set of bills, the officer said.
The two bills have not been filed, but the sponsors say they share common goals. The bills would change existing criminal law to widen the definition of what constitutes reckless and negligent driving and increase penalties for those crimes, the sponsors said.
One penalty they will propose is requiring offenders to appear in court for their offenses. "It's way too easy for a driver to just pay a fine and get back on the road and do what they were doing before," Elrich explained.
Sgt. Kepp, who worked as an officer in the alcohol initiative unit, says these bills will "give a little more teeth to some of our laws." Additionally, he hopes the law will address the "overall frustration" with the difficulty enforcing existing reckless driving laws. The penalties aren't tough enough, he said, and the fines aren't a good enough deterrent.
In the early morning hours of last Oct. 18, Kepp had just finished his shift when he heard a radio report of a speeding driver on Interstate 270. He joined other officers in an attempt to stop the driver. While Kepp was standing outside of his car, the driver struck him and left him critically injured, as Elrich recounted in the press briefing.
The Montgomery County Police officers on duty that night knew the driver "had a history of speeding and taunting police into chasing him," Elrich said. Police say the driver targeted and intentionally hit Kepp, Elrich said, and he is now being charged.
Both of Kepp's legs were amputated due to the injuries he sustained that night. Now he said he spends every day — from 9:45 a.m. to 2:15 p.m. — at Walter Reed National Military Medical Center undergoing rehabilitation. He joined the Zoom call for Elrich's press briefing from the medical center, wearing a blue dry-fit shirt and a short military-style haircut.
It has been four months since the accident, and Kepp said he has had a dozen surgeries since.
Still, he wants to speak on behalf of legislation that "will strengthen our laws and make our roadways safer," Kepp said.
The aim of the bills is "not for everybody to be thrown in jail, have huge fines, or lose their licenses," Kepp said, but rather to end reckless driving, especially by repeat offenders.
Elrich said he hopes the law will stop people from "ignoring lights and sirens from law enforcement, breaking the rules of the road … and performing car tricks like drifting, peeling out, and doing donuts in the middle of a road."
"All it takes is a moment's loss of control over that vehicle," Elrich said. "Instead of being entertaining, it would take little to transform it into a deadly incident."

title: Lawmakers battle between cracking down and easing up on prison sentences
author: SASHA ALLEN Capital News Service
content:
Lawmakers battle between cracking down and easing up on prison sentences

 March 13, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: SASHA ALLEN Capital News Service | Section: State News 
 
 745
 Words 

 Read News Document

 ANNAPOLIS — Lawmakers are taking a hard look at prison sentences in Maryland this spring, but from two dramatically different points of view.One measure under consideration would help offenders reduce their sentences for demonstrating good behavior. The other would crack down on violent offenders seeking time off their sentences.
Democrat Del. Cheryl Pasteur is sponsoring the Maryland Second Look Act, which would allow offenders showcasing good behavior to petition the courts for time off after serving at least 20 years.
"They have done every single thing possible to be better folks, better than a lot of the folks that I work with here," Pasteur, who represents Baltimore County said, referring to incarcerated people who demonstrate good behavior. "When do we ever have to spend 20 years to be vetted? Never."
But Republican Sen. William Folden is the sponsor for Real Time for Violent Crimes, a bill that would restrict or prohibit violent offenders from receiving diminution credits, or time off due to good behavior. He disagrees with Pasteur.
"If you commit a violent crime and you prey on our communities, and you're that two percenters that are the worst of the worst, then you should get real time and not allow it to be watered down through dim credits and things of that," said Folden, who represents Frederick County.
Hearings for both bills have elicited contentious and emotional testimony, both from families of murder victims and from formerly incarcerated individuals. But after both bills died during last year's legislative session, proponents of each bill are pushing yet again for passage.
Supporters and opponents alike for the Real Time for Real Crimes Act gathered at a Tuesday bill hearing to provide their testimony. Kurt Wolfgang, the executive director of the Maryland Crime Victims Resource Center, said this bill is "long overdue."
"There are so many ways to already diminish a sentence in Maryland," Wolfgang said. "This is just one more hole in the bucket that needs to be plugged up by taking away or diminishing the use of diminution credits to release violent offenders."
Despite his efforts, Folden told CNS that there isn't a "big appetite" for his bill.
Still, there was some opposition to the Maryland Second Look Act in a nearly three-hour long hearing in February, with some detailing emotional stories of their loved ones who are victims of violence.
Theresa Darvish, whose son was murdered in 2021, opposed the bill. She said it is retroactive, and referred to the procedures in the bill as "rampant and ambiguous at best."
"My son will never return to his home," Darvish testified. "No murderer should be given a free ride home."
This is a sentiment was echoed by many including Folden, who said those accused of rape and murder specifically should not get a second look.
But the bill that could allow review of prison sentences over 20 years was also met with large amounts of support from activists and formerly incarcerated individuals.
Anthony Muhummad was just 15 when he was arrested for two homicide charges in Baltimore City. He served over 29 years and was released under the Juvenile Restoration Act, and was one of the first to testify in support of the bill.
"There are dozens of individuals who are still incarcerated throughout the Maryland prison system who have served 20, 30, 40 and yes, sometimes even 50 years of incarceration who are not juveniles, who have demonstrated their maturity and rehabilitation and we believe are worthy of a second opportunity," Muhummad said.
Muhummad detailed his community engagement since his release, including his current employment at the ACLU. He also spoke about the conversation he had with the families of the two victims in his case, both of whom were in favor of rehabilitation.
And Pasteur, who is a former educator in Baltimore City and Baltimore County schools, believes that all deserve the chance for reevaluation after 20 years, especially those who entered the prison system at a young age. Pasteur said two of her "very favorite" former students have been or are currently incarcerated.
"I am really an educator, not a politician," Pasteur said. "Having always been in schools where things are tough for a lot of the students I have seen students get themselves engaged and involved in things that they know they shouldn't have. So they are in my heart."
And ultimately, Pasteur has high hopes for the bill.
"It's about appreciating and recognizing that some folks under the most horrific circumstances have made themselves better," Pasteur said. "Much better than a whole lot of us on any given day."

title: Butters makes it back home - Missing cat returns to owners 12 years after being lost
author: Isabella Loy; Stanwood Camano News

Butters makes it back home - Missing cat returns to owners 12 years after being lost

 All was calm and it seemed like an average day for Angelo and Shelley Castellino as they recently drove to their Stanwood, Washington, home on their 29th wedding anniversary.They had no idea that a phone call would soon give them the shock of their lives.Shelley Castellino received the mysterious call from an unknown number, and at first, she declined it."We figured was a scam call," Angelo Castellino said.Soon enough, the number called again. This time, they decided to answer."The gentleman said, 'I'm from animal control, and I have your cat, Butters,'" Angelo Castellino said."I go, 'Is this some sort of punk call?'" The Castellinos soon discovered it was not a scam - it was Riverside County Animal Control Officer Dalton Churchwell in California, who had found Butters in his yard late at night on Sunday, Oct. 3, and scanned him for a microchip.The couple had been living in San Diego and reported Butters missing 12 years ago in 2011. They had since moved to Stanwood in 2014 and lost hope of ever seeing the cat again.Luckily, the phone number attached to the microchip is the same one Shelley Castellino has today."I was astonished, it was kind of unbelievable," Angelo Castellino said."We figured that he was a meal for some coyotes." Angelo Castellino said he's unsure how Butters traveled so far, but that he was always trying to explore. The couple had adopted Butters and his brother, Barnacles, from a shelter in San Diego as kittens.After the news was shared, the Castellinos knew they wanted to bring Butters to their new home in Stanwood, but the expenses and logistics of flying a cat from California to Washington made for a tricky situation.The Animal Solutions Konnection Foundation, a California non-profit organization supporting the Department of Animal Services, soon heard the story.The organization decided to fund the cost of a flight to Seattle to see Butters safely return to his family."We were thrilled to work with the Department of Animal Services to make this reunion possible," said Carolyn Badger, president of the ASK Foundation, in a news release from Riverside County Animal Control."It was such a wonderful story, and we are very happy to know that Butters is home and safe with his family," she said.Butters' unlikely reunion finally happened Oct. 7, when Riverside County Department of Animal Services' longtime volunteer Larry Rudolph delivered Butters to the Castellanos in Seattle.Butters is now settled in his Stanwood home, and lives happily beside his brother, Barnacles, and the Castellinos' two dogs, Roscoe and Alita.Riverside Animal Services said Butters' defying of the odds was a testament to dedication and teamwork - but also a reminder to microchip pets to ensure reunification.

title: For All Seasons gives update on human trafficking in Talbot County
author: Konner Metz
content:
For All Seasons gives update on human trafficking in Talbot County

 January 31, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Konner Metz | Section: Local News 
 
 421
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — Representatives from For All Seasons say the problem of human trafficking in Talbot County is persisting, though they are seeing positive gains in awareness and detection.During a Talbot County Council meeting Tuesday, Lauren Weber, the nonprofit's vice president of strategy and development, provided an update to council members regarding human and labor trafficking.
"It is happening and it's happening here. That continues to be the case," Weber said. " … There's a complexity to human trafficking that it doesn't really know county boundaries."
Weber and Katie Theeke, vice president of marketing and communications, each said the organization has a special role given its wide reach. For All Seasons' presence in the five Mid-Shore counties — Caroline, Dorchester, Kent, Queen Anne's and Talbot — is critical to providing victims with essential services.
"We know that human trafficking knows no boundaries and that it affects people of different backgrounds, races, genders," Theeke said. "We have seen several cases come through our doors, and it comes from Talbot County. It comes from neighboring counties. We really aim to be the connector to get those people the help that they need."
Council Member Keasha Haythe asked if For All Seasons is seeing a decline in human trafficking numbers. Weber said it's a "double-edged sword."
"A year ago we sat in front of you and said, when we look at our rape crisis center data, a good fifth of what was coming in was having at least one indicator of human trafficking," Weber said. " … That persists."
The organization has noticed a shift in how many people are recognizing signs of human trafficking and making those reports, Weber says.
"The folks that are self-referring, we're seeing a decline," she said. "But we're seeing a real rapid incline in folks coming to us and saying, 'Hey, I know more and now I've seen something.'"
Weber said that since September, more than 120 people have taken For All Seasons' free, online anti-human trafficking course.
For All Seasons is an official regional navigator for the Mid-Shore area, Theeke said, meaning it works on task forces and serves youth and young adults that are victims of trafficking.
At the end of the discussion, council members thanked the For All Seasons representatives for their work and presented the organization with a proclamation Tuesday declaring January as National Human Trafficking Awareness Month.
"We know that even one victim is too many," council Vice President Pete Lesher said. "We appreciate all that you do both on prevention, but also to develop and take care of those who have been victims."

title: Caroline County leaning towards not going forward with Regional Detention Center
author: AHMAD GARNETT agarnett@chespub.com
content:
Caroline County leaning towards not going forward with Regional Detention Center

 DENTON — At the Caroline County Commissioners' Sept. 2 meeting, County Administrator Kathleen Freeman told the commissioners about a recent conversation she had with Queen Anne's County about whether Caroline County was on board for a potential regional detention center.The commissioners stated that if no new information was made available on the operating budget, they would back out of a drafted agreement that outlines a joint effort on the new 388-bed facility that would house all Caroline, Queen Anne's and Kent county prisoners.
"Unfortunately, because of their schedule and their pay scale, I don't think Caroline County is going to save any money by entering into the agreement," Commissioners President Travis Breeding said. "If we're not going to save any money, why relinquish the autonomy that we have right now to operate as our own facility and better suit the needs of the Caroline County as opposed to a three-county organization.
"I just don't see the the upside at this point," he said. "We did our due diligence, we looked into it, it's just not going to work."
The potential detention center would be located at the former Eastern Pre-Release Unit site at 700 Flat Iron Square Road near Church Hill.
The center aims to address the growing need for modern and efficient detention facilities in the region, where counties are struggling to finance renovations or replacements of their aging detention facilities.
"We appreciate the the time and and the effort that Kent, Queen Anne's and our staff have put into researching this, we did our due diligence, and we just don't feel that it's going to be advantageous for us to enter into the three-county agreement," Breeding said, adding the county spent a lot of time studying the proposal. "We went through the process, and in theory it looked like it should have been a good deal for Caroline County, but it just hasn't worked out that way."
In prior discussions of the detention center, the commissioners' concerns largely dealt with who would manage and staff the new facility, as well as how authority over the facility would be divided among the three participating counties.
The commissioners proposed a regional authority to manage the detention center, which was not mentioned in the original drafted agreement between the three counties.
The majority of the authority over the center would have been in Queen Anne's County hands, according to the draft. All decisions and disagreement must go through Queen Anne's County Commissioners, and if they may have a disagreement it will be mediated.
The Caroline County commissioners expressed concerns about the autonomy and authority of the the new facility's warden. According to the draft agreement, "The Board shall appoint a Warden to operate the Facility with the consent of the County Commissioners of Queen Anne's County."
The draft agreement also stated that "The Warden's contract shall not be terminated without the Board's consent"
The commissioners voiced that they believed under the draft that Queens Anne's county could decide after a certain amount of time to remove Caroline or Kent county from agreement, regardless of the amount of money that was put up. To remove one or both of the other counties from the agreement, according to the draft, Queen Anne's County must give the other county a two-year notice to take its prisoners and house them elsewhere.
The commissioners said they understood Queen Anne's County's decision to conduct the draft agreement this way, but they requested further negotiation and discussion to establish a partnering jurisdiction.
Last week, the commissioners made clear that while Caroline County has not completely abandoned the idea of a regional detention center, the commissioners are leaning toward not participating in the agreement and focusing on upgrades toward the facility within county limits.

title: Moore calls for accountability, rehabilitation
author: KIERSTEN HACKER Capital News Service
content:
Moore calls for accountability, rehabilitation

 January 16, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: KIERSTEN HACKER Capital News Service | Section: State News 
 
 487
 Words 

 Read News Document

 ANNAPOLIS — Gov. Wes Moore said he expects "robust debates" about juvenile justice in coming weeks — and that his administration will be an "active participant" trying to balance rehabilitation with cracking down on crime."The hallmark of what I hope to see in any juvenile justice legislation that's going to make it to my desk can be summarized in one word: accountability," the governor said. "I believe in rehabilitation, but I will not tolerate lawlessness."
Moore's comments came Tuesday, a day before the opening of the 2024 Maryland General Assembly, in a press conference devoted to his legislative priorities regarding public safety. He said he plans to press for three measures aimed at promoting victim's compensation, expanding apprenticeships in law enforcement jobs and preventing firearm violence.
But he also mused aloud on the issue of juvenile justice, at a time when state Republican officials are calling for passage of tougher crime policies — and specifically for reversing recent reforms to the youth legal system. House Republican Leader Jason Buckel, R-Allegany, recently vowed to toughen up what he called Maryland's "soft-on-crime policies."
Moore said Tuesday he will demand accountability for young offenders who are repeatedly violating the law, or who use a handgun to threaten the safety of others.
While Moore acknowledged the coming debate over juvenile crime this session, he stressed the importance of supporting communities and the advocates working at the grassroots level to prevent violence.
He said he supports lengthening probation for juveniles found guilty of certain crimes to allow for more time for rehabilitation programs. He also backs moving more crimes related to illegal guns from misdemeanors to felonies.
"It takes a village to raise a child, and it will take a village to build safer communities," Moore said.
The legislative criminal justice proposals Moore announced do not address the treatment of juveniles, but rather focus on other things.
He proposed establishing a firearm prevention center based on recommendations from the Safer States Initiative launched by Vice President Kamala Harris.
The statewide office would work in partnership with the White House, taking an "all of government" approach to effective prevention and intervention policies or programs, according to Rob Wilcox, deputy director of Biden's Office of Gun Violence Prevention. Maryland would be the first state to establish such a center, said Wilcox, who spoke at Moore's press conference.
"It's a critical step to focus investments and drive the strategies that we know will save lives," Wilcox said.
According to Moore, 75% of homicides in Maryland are committed with a gun. He said he considers it not only a public safety issue but a public health issue. He pledged to get illegal guns "off of our streets."
To help wage that fight, Moore hopes to recruit more people into law enforcement and public safety with a bill to promote apprenticeships.
"We need officers who reflect the diversity of our great state," Secretary of Labor Portia Wu said, "and we need them to come from the neighborhoods they serve."

author: Carl Hamilton cahamilton@chespub.com
content:
11-year-old killed in hit-and-run remembered in Elkton

 December 3, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Carl Hamilton cahamilton@chespub.com | Section: State News 
 
 1038
 Words 

 Read News Document

 ELKTON — Mesiah Lafayette produced a big barrel of cheese puffs recently after the dismissal bell rang at Cherry Hill Middle School and happily shared them with every fellow student who approached him.His display of generosity — one of Mesiah's many endearing qualities — is the last memory that most will have of him.
Mesiah, 11, was killed at approximately 8:30 p.m. on Nov.16, when a motorist struck him as he attempted to pedal his bicycle across Elkton Road from Belle Hill Road and then allegedly drove away. Police arrested the suspect on three days later, after tracking him down in Wilmington, Del., and charged him with involuntary manslaughter and numerous other offenses.
Gauging by the turnouts for two candlelight vigils that were held for Mesiah last week near the intersection where he lost his life, it's quite clear that the smiling boy who loved football, dancing, cool hairstyles, jokes, island music, Skittles and most assuredly his family and friends was adored in his community.
After moving with his family from New Jersey to Elkton in November 2023, Mesiah finished the remaining eight months of his fifth-grade year at Kenmore Elementary School, before starting sixth-grade at Cherry Hill Middle School in September.
Mesiah was here for only a little while, one year, but he made a beautiful, lasting impression on many in that short time.
"He was a kind, loving and gentle child. He spread joy through the school," one Kenmore Elementary School teacher commented Monday night during the first vigil.
An administrator at that school recalled, "He had a bright smile. He hugged people. And he always showed students and teachers affection and gave them attention."
From a much more profound standpoint, Mesiah was here on this earth for only a short time and, yet, he still positively impacted a vast number of people.
"Mesiah was only here 11 years, but he touched a lot of lives — more than most people do in 50 years," emphasized The Rev. Moneira Hawkins of Spirit Life Ministries International in Wilmington, Del. on Tuesday night after praying aloud during the second vigil.
Speaking to the group of children, parents, teachers and others in attendance, Hawkins soothingly said, "His spirit is still alive. He touched every one of you."
One night earlier, some Kenmore Elementary School and Cherry Hill Middle School teachers, administrators and other staff members attended the first vigil and huddled with approximately 20 students.
They shared their fond memories of Mesiah.
"He was a wonderful big brother to his sister. He walked her to her classroom every day," one Kenmore Elementary School administrator said, recalling how fifth-grade Mesiah looked out for his third-grade sibling last school year.
A teacher volunteered, "I remember how friendly and outgoing he was."
The teachers, administrators and staff members spoke words of comfort.
"It's OK to feel sad. It's OK to cry. Take a moment," one of the teachers softly told the students, for whom it was likely that this was the first time most of those children have experienced the death of a peer.
After the circle disbanded, Joanne Carradin, a Cherry Hill Middle School counselor, told the Cecil Whig that crisis intervention counselors were at that school Monday morning to help students deal with their grief.
"They were very busy all morning. They had a lot of questions," Carradin said, adding that some students were sent home.
On Tuesday evening, Mesiah's surviving family members attended the second vigil — and somberness seemed even stronger than it did one night earlier. As supporters standing in a large semi-circle watched silently, Mesiah's relatives gathered in front of a makeshift memorial for Mesiah.
More than 25 candles flickered there. Poster boards covered with decorations and photos of Mesiah smiling and laughing with family members were displayed. Flower bouquets, a football and a bag of McDonald's food were lying there, too. Some helium balloons hovered slightly above the memorial.
The boy's relatives hugged, stood, crouched, sat and cried while gazing at the memorial for several moments amid the hush. Mesiah's stepfather made a couple of comments to the reverently quiet onlookers, expressing the family's gratitude for the show of support and love.
Mesiah's surviving family members include his mom, dad, stepdad, younger sister, 8; older brother, 15; and older sisters, ages 16 and 20.
Attendees of the two vigils fondly remembered Mesiah, who played wide receiver on a boys league football team. Mesiah rooted for the Philadelphia Eagles, probably because he and his family lived in Philly at one point. Without hesitation, one of his school buddies answered, "Professional NFL player," when asked what Mesiah wanted to be when he grew up.
Mesiah had flair.
"I remember his fancy hairstyles," one of the teachers shared during Monday night's vigil. Another teacher referred to them as "adorable hairstyles."
As it turns out, Mesiah's 16-year-old sister was the person responsible for keeping his hairstyles sharp and different. "I do his hair. I do it in different ways about once a month. He likes braids, straight backs — I guess you'd call them cornrows," his sister said Tuesday night, still speaking of Mesiah in the present tense.
Mesiah had a special spot in his heart for island music, which includes reggae, calypso and other genres. His favorite song was "I Am A Bajan," a festive recording by an artist known as Rupee.
He loved to dance — unabashedly. His stepdad smiled when he recalled the times he saw Mesiah dancing with his mom in the kitchen.
Mesiah's stepdad and dad, both of whom write and record music, agree that Mesiah had a gift for composition. His stepdad recalled how Mesiah, after hearing one of his beats, sat down and wrote lyrics. Mesiah titled the song, "I Wish I Had You," a tribute to his twin sister who died before birth. Mesiah then seamlessly rapped that fresh new song to the beat.
"He's a natural. He has a way with words," his stepdad marveled, before shifting into past-tense and declaring, "That kid was special."
Mesiah had a winning, charismatic personality and the football, the hairstyles, the dancing, the music and all of the other things that he loved were just some of the countless manifestations of it.
"He was a bright light. When he walked into a room, he lit it up," his dad summarized while walking away from the memorial site at the conclusion of Tuesday night's vigil.

title: Kent Samaritan Group nears goal to open emergency shelter in December
author: WILL BONTRAGER wbontrager@chespub.com
content:
Kent Samaritan Group nears goal to open emergency shelter in December

 October 16, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: WILL BONTRAGER wbontrager@chespub.com | Section: News 
 
 649
 Words 

 Read News Document

 CHESTERTOWN — On Sunday afternoon, the day of its fundraising rally at Presbyterian Church of Chestertown, the Samaritan Group of Kent County had $1,400 toward its goal of $14,000 needed to open the Emergency Winter Shelter, in operation since 2003.Because of Christ First United Methodist Church's $5,000 donation, along with other donations, at the end of the event that afternoon, the group had $12,000.
Shelter Director the Rev. James Diggs said they need donations and are optimistic to reach the goal, but they also need volunteers for the shelter: some cooks, but more importantly they need hosts and sleepers. The host, Diggs explained, meets and greets the guests, ensures they are comfortable and safe while the sleepers stay the whole night.
Diggs announced this year they are aiming to open the shelter in December, a first.
That is up to the amount of volunteers that sign up. Diggs said that they have to have 85% of December filled to accomplish this, with volunteers especially needed Christmas Eve, Christmas, New Year's Eve and New Year's.
"Let's make this month a recruiting month. Help us do it because I think we certainly can. We're excited to be able to add December and maybe next year, add another month."
As winter approaches, the need increases to care for Kent County's homeless population he stated.
As their mission describes, the Samaritan Group of Kent County work with local agencies, churches, businesses and organizations and individuals to keep them warm and also providing financial assistance.
During the rally with refreshments and ice cream served by Marcia Stoltzfus and family, Diggs listed the shelter's accomplishments and gave out certificates and awards to the hardworking, caring volunteers which make it possible each year, adding a fun family event along the fundraising.
In the early winter months of 2025, they served 21 clients, seven women, two children and 12 men, 661 bed nights total. In 2018 they served 21 people as well, 1,033 bed nights and that next year, 28 people and 921 bed nights.
"The number of people we serve is unpredictable. We just don't know from year to year. The point is to be ready and all of you volunteers make that possible."
He thanked some of the volunteers that helped get the shelter ready.
Receiving the Laverne and Shirley Award was dynamic duo Annie Woodall and Andrea Nieman. Top Chef, and also supplying that tasty soft serve ice cream was Marcia Stoltzfus and family. The Host with the Most was Allison Brieske and Volunteer of the Year, who dedicated time cooking/ inspiring her whole church to cook, and hosting, was Anne-Marie Walters.
Many other certificates given as well, some of whom were not in attendance.
"They may not be here, but they were when it counted," joked Diggs.
Giving her testimony about the rewards of volunteering was Melanie Keller, who was recruited by Woodall and Nieman years back and was the volunteer coordinator for a time.
Keller said that after her third child, part of what kept her volunteering was her two children who also volunteer. They play hide-and-seek with guests and see other people's experiences, their suffering and joys and practice reaching out with compassion.
"We are a community and I hope to see some of you as hosts," she told attendees.
Diggs said hosts have a very important role, stay from 5:30-10 p.m. and are in pairs. Diggs personally greets the hosts each night and briefs them on what they need to know, ensuring they are comfortable.
Sleepers stay into the night and see guests off in the morning.
Diggs encouraged the audience to not only sign up but to become recruits, sharing the joys of volunteering at the shelter where Mid-Shore Community Foundation, United Way of Kent County, the Good Neighbor Fund and Kent County Department of Social Services partner in this important mission.
"We need your help," Diggs said to the community. "With it we can open up in December...one month at a time."
To contact them go to: info@samaritangroupofkentcounty.org.

title: After-school activities canceled, some Wednesday delays in place due to strong storm
author: Natalie Jones
content:
After-school activities canceled, some Wednesday delays in place due to strong storm

 January 8, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Natalie Jones | Section: Local News 
 
 574
 Words 

 Read News Document

 UPDATE 1:30 p.m. Tuesday: Impending heavy rains, gusty winds and flooding from the powerful storm system moving across the region have prompted local school districts to cancel after-school activities Tuesday, with delays and closures possible Wednesday.Dorchester County Public Schools are operating on a half-day dismissal schedule Tuesday, with all after-school activities canceled. All of the county's schools will be operating on a two-hour delay schedule Wednesday, Jan. 10, for evaluation of overnight flooding and storm damage, according to the school system.
Queen Anne's County Public Schools were also dismissed early Tuesday due to the storm. As of Tuesday afternoon, all of the county's schools are set to run on a 90-minute delayed opening Wednesday, with reevaluation and modifications possible in the morning.
Schools in Talbot and Caroline counties canceled all after-school activities Tuesday. Both districts are monitoring conditions to determine if delays or closures will be necessary Wednesday.
The Caroline County Board of Education meeting will be held as scheduled at 6 p.m. Tuesday.
Gov. Wes Moore enacted a State of Preparedness declaration Tuesday morning, directing the state's department of emergency management to coordinate responses to the storm's impacts.
Rainfall of 1 to 3 inches is possible across the region Tuesday, with the heaviest rain expected Tuesday night before tapering off Wednesday morning, according to the National Weather Service.
The main concern is the potential for coastal flooding in Talbot and Queen Anne's counties, said Mike Lee, a meteorologist with the National Weather Service's Philadelphia/Mount Holly office. Dorchester County is also expected to experience significant flooding.
A coastal flood warning is in effect from 7 p.m. Tuesday to 7 p.m. Wednesday for areas along the lower Chesapeake Bay, including Cambridge, which will see major impact from flooding early Wednesday morning, according to the Weather Service. Water is expected be two to three feet above ground level in some low-lying areas.
A coastal flood warning and a flood watch are in effect for Talbot, Caroline, Queen Anne's and Kent counties from Tuesday afternoon through Wednesday morning.
Moderate coastal flooding is possible Tuesday with the high tide cycle. Water levels are expected to continue rising Tuesday night from strong southerly winds. The rising water levels could lead to potentially significant flooding.
The highest tides will be early Wednesday morning and again in the afternoon.
Widespread roadway flooding is expected across the region's bayside communities and along tidal waterways. Dorchester County could see road closures.
Strong, gusty winds are also expected to build across the region throughout the day Tuesday.
Dorchester County is under a high wind warning from 4 p.m. Tuesday to 4 a.m. Wednesday, with south to southeast winds of 30 to 40 mph with gusts up to 60 mph possible. Fallen trees, downed power lines and widespread power outages are expected.
Talbot, Caroline, Kent and Queen Anne's counties are under a wind advisory from 5 p.m. Tuesday to 3 a.m. Wednesday. Sustained winds of 25 to 35 mph are expected, with gusts up to 55 mph.
The already-saturated ground in the region has also made trees more vulnerable to becoming uprooted with strong winds.
The Talbot County Department of Emergency Services urged residents to make sure loose items are secured ahead of time and reminded residents to not drive through or stand in flooded roadways.
The region will dry out some on Thursday, but a second storm is likely to roll through the region again Friday night into Saturday, the Weather Service said.
This story has been updated to include information on school delays and closures. This story may be updated.

title: Man handed life sentence for Federalsburg murder
author: Maggie Trovato
content:
Man handed life sentence for Federalsburg murder

 September 13, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Maggie Trovato | Section: Crime 
 
 549
 Words 

 Read News Document

 DENTON — Quandre Winder, 27, was handed a life sentence on Wednesday for the September 2023 murder of 27-year-old Caryn Faye Brown in Federalsburg.Judge Brett Wilson handed Winder a life sentence with all but 50 years suspended for first-degree murder and a consecutive 20-year sentence for firearm use in a violent crime with eligibility for parole after five years.
Winder's incarceration will be followed by five years of supervised probation.
In July, Winder pleaded guilty to first-degree murder and using a firearm in a violent crime. Although Winder received 10 charges relating to Brown's death, the remaining eight charges — including manslaughter, assault and additional firearm charges — were abandoned by the state.
Shortly after midnight on Sept. 4, 2023, Brown was found dead in front of an apartment complex in the 700 block of Gardens Court in Federalsburg. Officers from the Federalsburg Police Department were called to the scene and found her lying in the grass with apparent gunshot wounds to the head and chest.
At a plea hearing on July 8, Caroline County State's Attorney Sloane Franklin said Winder, who had a handgun on him and had been arguing with Brown before she was killed, was seen shooting Brown multiple times. Franklin said the two were in a "volatile relationship," which Brown had ended due to domestic violence.
During the sentencing hearing on Wednesday, Franklin said the system had failed Brown, who had cases against Winder for domestic violence.
Brown's siblings, mother and eight-year-old son all provided statements at the sentencing hearing. Brown's son Dominic's statement read, "My mommy was a beautiful person, and you took her away from me."
Brown's mother, Nancy Geeslin, recounted the night she got the call that her daughter had been killed. She spoke about how Brown's death has affected each of Brown's children.
Brown's younger sister, Tyrah Banks, said she didn't know if Winder would every fully grasp what he did to their families.
"This will never not hurt," she said.
Banks said she has found peace in the fact that her sister can't be hurt again and peace in the fact that Brown lives on through her children.
Winder's attorney Dana Boston, who is with the Maryland Office of the Public Defender, said Winder committed a terrible act that shouldn't have happened. Boston said Winder had a rough upbringing and developed a drug addiction. He said Winder was on Percocet and Xanax the night of Brown's death.
Boston said Winder expressed "heartfelt remorse" for his actions and is dealing with the psychological repercussions of those actions.
Before handing down Winder's sentence, Wilson said it wasn't the system, but the nature of law that failed Brown. He said when it comes to domestic violence, peace orders are just pieces of paper.
"They're not bullet-proof vests," he said.
Wilson said Winder's criminal history, including firearm and assault charges, show a pattern of disregard for law, authority and others.
Wilson said he is sorry anybody has to grow up in imperfect conditions. But he said this "senseless" act should not have happened.
After the hearing, Jennifer Roberts, Brown's aunt, said in an interview with the Star Democrat that their family is happy to have closure after this has hung over their heads for a year. She said they have no choice but to be satisfied with the outcome, and they have to put their faith in the court system.

title: Meet the bikers who try – and fail – each year to erode Maryland’s helmet law
author: SAPNA BANSIL Capital News Service
content:
Meet the bikers who try – and fail – each year to erode Maryland’s helmet law

 March 19, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: SAPNA BANSIL Capital News Service | Section: State News 
 
 945
 Words 

 Read News Document

 A group of bikers in leather vests and wispy beards greets lawmakers here each Monday of the legislative session, hoping this is the year they'll succeed in their galvanizing cause: gutting a Maryland law that requires them to wear helmets.The group, which calls itself A Brotherhood Against Totalitarian Enactments, has experienced decades of setbacks on the helmet issue. Its vociferous critics say ABATE's position is at a minimum, eccentric and at worst, dangerous.
But driven by a burning belief in personal freedom and a joy for riding, ABATE has used persistent, grassroots activism to keep the helmet issue alive in Maryland. It's why in nearly every legislative session since the state's mandatory helmet law took effect in 1992, the Maryland General Assembly has at least considered a bill that would make wearing a helmet optional for most riders.
"It's been 32 years this year to no avail," Bob Spanburgh, Maryland ABATE's board chairman, said. "But we keep introducing it. We have some pretty ardent supporters. We have a lot of people who think we're nuts, probably."
Like many of its previous incarnations over the last three decades, this year's bill would make wearing a helmet optional if a motorcyclist is at least 21 years old, has been licensed for a minimum of two years and has completed a safety course. It is named in honor of Gary "Pappy" Boward, a former ABATE executive director and motorcycle rights advocate who died in 2020 of health issues.
ABATE and other supporters insist that they aren't opposed to riders wearing helmets if they so choose. But they feel the current mandate abridges freedom of choice and represents government overreach.
"I firmly believe that we as government do better when we educate people, [rather] than legislating something," said Sen. Mike McKay (R-Allegany, Garrett, Washington), the bill's primary Senate sponsor and a friend of Boward's. "There are people that would like to have the choice [to not wear a helmet.] And I tend to believe that we should give people the choice but 100% support educating them about it."
Established in 1974, ABATE will mark 50 years of advocacy for motorcyclists' rights this June. Its animating issue has been eroding Maryland's helmet law, different iterations of which have been in place since 1968. Today, Maryland joins 16 other states and the District of Columbia in requiring all riders to wear protective headgear.
Spanburgh, a 66-year-old retired carpenter, only casually followed politics when he joined ABATE in the mid-1980s. Initially, he saw the group as a community of like-minded individuals, who shared his enthusiasm for bikes, firearms, the outdoors and rock and roll. But right away, ABATE turned Spanburgh into an unlikely activist.
"At the first meeting I went to, the thing they told me [was,] 'You got to register to vote. It's very important in this organization,'" Spanburgh recalled. "That was actually the first time I ever registered to vote in my life. I was 27 at the time."
Each legislative session, the helmet bill faces cockeyed glances and prodigious odds. Contending with a wealth of scientific evidence, which shows crashes involving non-helmeted motorcyclists are much more likely to result in severe head trauma and death, the measure almost always dies in committee.
But ABATE ensures the issue is revived and relitigated, year after year, by finding ways to get in front of elected officials, despite limited financial resources and dwindling numbers. In the past, the group used a tactic involving following lawmakers into the bathroom to gain an audience and get its message heard.
"They're diehards for what they believe in," Del. Jay Jacobs (R-Caroline, Cecil, Kent, Queen Anne's) said. "Thank God they do. They don't let go of this stuff. It's a tough fight over here to get that kind of legislation passed."
While Republicans are the most likely to sympathize with ABATE's cause, the group engages lawmakers on both sides of the aisle. This year's bill, cross-filed as HB639 and SB503, has bipartisan sponsors in both chambers.
"I don't agree with them that they shouldn't wear a helmet, but I do agree about the civil liberty issue," said Sen. Jill Carter (D-Baltimore city), one of the bill's Senate co-sponsors.
"They are adamant as dedicated motorcyclists that this is not something they want mandated to them," she added.
In a recent hearing of the House Environment and Transportation Committee, opponents included highway safety groups, medical associations and public health officials. They argued that a weaker helmet law would increase motorcyclists' risk of injury and death, impose an avoidable burden on taxpayers and encumber the healthcare system.
"A lot of people might say, 'Well, it's my free will to do whatever I want to do, no matter how stupid it is,'" Gene Ransom, CEO of MedChi, the Maryland State Medical Society, said in an interview. "The problem is, when it comes to healthcare … your decision then ends up costing the entire system a whole lot of money.
"Not only is it the right thing to do and the smart thing to do — logical people wear helmets when they ride a motorcycle or a bike or other things — it also is appropriate from a common good and cost point of view," Ransom added.
The bill is scheduled for a hearing before the Senate Judicial Proceedings Committee later this week. Spanburgh hopes to see the measure make it out of committee and get a vote on the House or Senate floor. If unsuccessful, proponents vow they won't stop trying.
"If I don't do it, who else is going to do it?" said Ken Eaton, Maryland ABATE's executive director. "We try to get other people to help us as much as possible. But if I don't do it, how can I convince other people to do it?"

title: Court docs: Delaware middle school teacher spent months grooming student online with sexual messages
author: Josh Shannon jshannon@chespub.com
content:
Court docs: Delaware middle school teacher spent months grooming student online with sexual messages

 March 4, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Josh Shannon jshannon@chespub.com | Section: State News 
 
 681
 Words 

 Read News Document

 Delaware court documents released Tuesday shed new light on how a Kirk Middle School teacher allegedly spent months grooming one of his students by sending her sexual messages and fantasies through an online chat application.Ultimately, the inappropriate behavior expanded to school grounds, where David DiFilippo would spend time alone with the 13-year-old girl in his classroom, making sexual comments to her and, on one occasion, touching her legs, court records allege.
DiFilippo's actions "are clearly and reasonably indicative of an adult grooming and enticing a minor for the purpose of sexual contact and/or a sexual experience," Detective Marc Conway, of the Delaware State Police, wrote in court documents, adding that DiFilippo was trying to build up trust with the girl to "ultimately entice and arouse her sexually."
DiFilippo's alleged behavior took place between September 2023 and February 2024, when DiFilippo was 43 and 44 years old.
During that six-month period, DiFilippo and the girl chatted nearly every day over Discord, a messaging app. The messages were "flirtatious and sexual in nature," and DiFilippo suggested sexual acts with the girl, made comments about her body and clothing and referred to her as "babe" and "baby," court records show.
He sent her several stories detailing explicit sexual fantasies involving her engaging in sexual intercourse, masturbation and oral sex. He would then ask the girl "if the writings were good enough that she could picture them in her mind and if reading them made her feel a certain way," court documents allege.
One story involved a teacher and a student having sexual relations on a school bus during a field trip, and DiFilippo then told the girl he was planing a field trip and asked if she would like to sit with him on the bus, court records indicate.
DiFilippo would delete the messages after the girl read them, but she kept screenshots of the messages on her phone.
DiFilippo's behavior eventually extended into in-person encounters, and he would allow the girl to skip class to hang out with him alone in his classroom during his planning period when he did not have a class to teach. Other times, she would stay in his classroom after class ended and the other students left.
On one occasion, DiFilippo told the girl he liked her "milky white thighs" and said seeing them made him feel "like an animal ready to attack his prey," court documents allege. Another time, he suggested they go into a closet to kiss, but the girl refused. On a different day, the girl brought DiFilippo an assortment of snack food and asked him which he liked best, to which he replied he liked "the snack in the dress," presumably referring to her.
Court records describe one incident in which DiFilippo's behavior turned physical. The girl was sitting on a counter near his desk, and DiFilippo allegedly knelt down and rubbed her legs. The girl told him to stop, which he did.
It's not clear why DiFilippo's behavior ended in February 2024. Court records indicate that the girl told her therapist about it in August 2024, sparking a police investigation.
The girl provided police with screenshots of DiFilippo's Discord messages, and detectives later subpoenaed Discord for a transcript of the messages sent from his account. Investigators interviewed the girl with help from the Child Advocacy Center in Wilmington.
DiFilippo turned himself in to police in February after the months-long investigation.
He was charged with sexual solicitation of a child, enticement for purposes of sexual conduct, dangerous crime against a minor, promoting sexual solicitation of a child, providing obscenity material to a child, sexual abuse of a child by a person of trust and offensive touching. He was released after posting $65,500 secured bond.
Police asked anyone with information or who may be a victim to contact Conway at 302-365-8411.
According to a brief biography posted on Kirk's website, DiFilippo taught in the gifted and talented program and has been a teacher for approximately 15 years. He wrote that his favorite part of the job is "forming strong bonds and relationships with my students."
A spokesperson for the Christina School District did not respond to a request for comment.

title: Construction advances for first responder training campus
author: Konner Metz
content:
Construction advances for first responder training campus

 May 7, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Konner Metz | Section: Local News 
 
 461
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — Construction on the A. James Clark Emergency Services Training Campus is well underway — and project leaders even had the chance to show Gov. Wes Moore around the construction site last week.Brett Whitehead, president of Friends of the Easton Volunteer Fire Department, has spearheaded fundraising efforts for the state-of-the-art training campus, which will be used by firefighters, police officers and EMS workers when it opens.
Whitehead said construction teams have made "unbelievable progress."
The 7,200-square-foot campus is located on Mistletoe Drive. Once complete, Easton Volunteer Fire Department Assistant Chief Daryl Caldwell said it will include a 4,200-square-foot classroom building, a burn building for search-and-rescue and active shooter simulations, and two pads for car fire and extrication training.
The burn building won't be damaged, project leaders say, since it's going to be a metal building with concrete floors and stairs. It will have movable walls to provide a variety of room configurations during trainings.
Caldwell said the training campus will keep on-duty first responders centrally located. The campus also will reduce long travel times that local first responders often incur when going to Salisbury or the western shore for necessary training.
Ground was broken in December on the project. As of Monday, significant work had been done to both the classroom and burn buildings. Whitehead said the goal of opening by the end of the year still remains.
"If weather holds up, permits get approved," he said.
Whitehead said more than $4 million has been raised, which leaves less than $1 million remaining of the project's $5 million fundraising goal.
As the name indicates, the A. James & Alice B. Clark Foundation was fundamental in fundraising efforts. Last September, the foundation donated $1 million to the training campus. Overall, the foundation has contributed $1.9 million to the project.
The project also has received $300,000 in state grant funding.
On April 29, Moore toured the training campus as part of a private visit in Easton.
Caldwell said Moore was "very attentive" and asked many questions. Caldwell, Whitehead and other members of the department, along with town leaders, were present for the governor's visit.
"Governor Moore's visit to the A. James Clark Emergency Services Training Campus site in Easton highlights his continued commitment to public safety, and ensuring Maryland is providing our law enforcement and first responder personnel with the best resources available," Moore's office said in a statement. "The governor is proud to work alongside so many local electeds and community leaders in supporting this project."
Whitehead believes the Easton training campus will be a model for future first responder training facilities where personnel can train separately or together.
"This is the only one of its kind in the Mid-Shore period," Whitehead said. "Where you have real-time training opportunities. You have all first responders training together. No other site does that in the Mid-Shore."

title: Cambridge man found guilty of child abuse, assault
author: Maggie Trovato

Cambridge man found guilty of child abuse, assault

 December 28, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Maggie Trovato | Section: Crime
