 CAMBRIDGE — A Cambridge man has been found guilty of first-degree assault and first-degree child abuse relating to an incident with his infant.Marcus Peak, 28, was arrested in April 2023 after his five-week-old child was seriously injured with a traumatic brain injury. He was charged with attempted first- and second-degree murder, first- and second-degree assault, first- and second-degree child abuse, neglect of a minor and reckless endangerment.
The state later decided it would not prosecute for the murder charges. Peak was found guilty by Dorchester County Circuit Court Judge William Jones of the other six counts.
The charges against Peak stem from an incident on April 21, 2023, when Cambridge Police officers responded to assist Dorchester County Emergency Medical Services with an infant who was unconscious and not breathing. EMS treated the infant and transported her to the University of Maryland Shore Medical Center at Cambridge. The baby was then transported to Johns Hopkins Hospital in Baltimore.
According to police, Peak told detectives he had just fed the baby a bottle and placed her in a bassinet for a nap. He said the baby was asleep. He said that when he returned to check on the her later, he noticed the baby's head was tilted to the side with fluid coming from her nose and mouth. He said the baby's eyes were partially opened.
At that time, Peak denied any traumatic event that could have caused injury to the baby.
Detectives were told Peak had lied and did not inform them that the baby had fallen to the floor striking her head. Peak allegedly then picked the baby up and shook the baby to wake it, according to a report from the Cambridge Police Department.
During the trial, Jones heard a variety of testimony, including testimony from doctors and the child's mother.
The mother, Paris Keene, testified that she had left the house that day to pick up their older child from daycare. She said Peak had stayed with the their five-week-old. She said that when she came back, Peak told her the infant had choked on her spit up.
When Keene took the baby from Peak, she realized that the baby's eyes were rolling back, and Peak called 911.
Dr. Eric Klotz, an emergency medicine physician who treated the child that day, said her injuries were consistent with a high mechanism of injury. He said it was one of the more severe head injuries he's seen in his career.
Dr. Joseph Scheller, a pediatric neurologist who was asked by Peak's defense to testify, said it is possible the child's injuries were caused by an accidental fall. He said that while it is rare, short falls can sometimes cause serious injury.
"I am thankful for the judge's consideration," Dorchester County State's Attorney Amanda Leonard told the Star Democrat. "He gave a very well thought out explanation citing case law and it was obvious that he took significant time to consider the evidence put forth by the state, including expert testimony and other evidence."
Leonard said that a "long form" pre-sentence investigation will be conducted, which may take multiple months. As of Friday afternoon, no sentencing date for Peak was scheduled.

title: Tilghman man sentenced to five years for sexual abuse of a child
author: Natalie Jones
content:
Tilghman man sentenced to five years for sexual abuse of a child

 February 18, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Natalie Jones | Section: Crime 
 
 680
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — A Tilghman man was sentenced Friday to five years in prison for sexually abusing a child last February.After nearly an hour-long recess following statements from the child's family and the defense, Talbot County Circuit Judge Stephen Kehoe sentenced Eric Werner, 62, to five years of active incarceration.
"This is a very awful situation," Kehoe said prior to handing down the term.
Werner received nearly a year of credit for time already served. He will be required to serve at least half of his sentence before being eligible for parole.
State sentencing guidelines for the case recommended 15 to 30 years, according to Deputy State's Attorney Chelsea Endzel, who prosecuted the case and recommended 30 years of active prison time.
The sentence comes over three months after a jury found Werner guilty of 16 counts, including sexual abuse of a minor, third- and fourth-degree sex offenses, second-degree assault and displaying obscene matter to a minor.
Detectives from the Talbot County Sheriff's Office began investigating Werner last February after learning of multiple child sexual abuse incidents that occurred at a home in Tilghman that month.
Police investigation revealed that Werner sexually assaulted a preteen girl through inappropriately touching her on three different occasions that February.
Werner also showed the child pornographic videos, which the child remembered in detail during the trial.
At Friday's sentencing, Endzel emphasized Werner's "calculated effort to groom and abuse the child" over several months.
Werner inserted himself into the child's life as a "pseudo family member," learning what made her especially vulnerable, she said. And once the girl felt comfortable spending time with him, he began making sexual comments, increasing her self-consciousness, Endzel added.
Things escalated further when Werner inappropriately touched the child.
Werner always told the child not to tell anyone else about his actions, threatening the possibility of her going to jail, Endzel said, but in a show of "astonishing strength and courage," the girl told a friend.
For the child's mother, whom the Star Democrat is not naming to protect the victim's privacy, it was difficult to see her child referred to as a victim and just as hard to put the impact into words.
"I have no way to measure what this has cost my daughter and … my family," she said.
The impacts were wide-ranging, she explained. Invoices added up with homeschooling and therapy. Hours of sleep were lost and anxiety built up. The child struggled "every hour of every day."
"She — the victim, my daughter, my child — will never be the same," the child's mother said.
Defense attorney Philip Cronan said it was easy for the prosecution to suspect "nefarious intent" with Werner's community activities involving direct contact with children, but Werner had never displayed similar behaviors, he said.
Psychiatric evaluations deemed Werner to be a low risk for repeating similar crimes and determined he would have a high chance of success in returning to the community, he added.
Though Cronan did not make a specific sentencing recommendation, he argued that Endzel had effectively asked for a life sentence, given Werner's age.
When given a chance to speak, Werner acknowledged his actions as wrong, saying he lost his "moral compass."
"I have no excuses and no explanations," he said.
When released, Werner will be required to register as a Tier III sex offender — a lifetime registry in Maryland.
He will be under supervised probation for five years, is barred from contacting the child and must stay away from the child's home. He will also be required to complete mental health treatment.
Cronan did not give a comment following the sentencing.
Endzel highlighted the "huge team effort" with the Talbot County Sheriff's Office in investigating and prosecuting the case, along with providing support to the family.
But above all, she commended the child for her "bravery and strength" throughout the process.
"The child victim stood up to her abuser in front of a courtroom full of strangers and found the courage to recount her abuse and withstand a grueling cross-examination," she said. "This showing of tenacity and strength gives me hope that this remarkable child will one day recover from the abuse inflicted upon her and will find a way to move forward."

title: Natural Resources Police use thermal imaging to rescue lost kayaker in Talbot County
author: Konner Metz
content:
Natural Resources Police use thermal imaging to rescue lost kayaker in Talbot County

 July 9, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Konner Metz | Section: Local News 
 
 344
 Words 

 Read News Document

 BROAD CREEK — Police and firefighters teamed to locate a lost juvenile kayaker last weekend in Talbot County.On July 4 around 10 p.m., Maryland Natural Resources Police were informed of a lost kayaker in the Broad Creek area, which is on the west side of the county south of St. Michaels. Officials said he was on the water for "several hours" and around three miles from home.
Using thermal imaging cameras, a Natural Resource Police aviation unit quickly found the lost person — in around five minutes, according to Sgt. John Buchanan, chief pilot for NRP. Buchanan was in the aircraft with tactical flight officer Christian Helwig.
Buchanan said the kayaker left out of Grace Creek.
"I think it got dark on him, and he didn't know where he was," Buchanan said.
Once located, police used a spotlight to direct a rescue boat from the Tilghman Island Volunteer Fire Company toward the juvenile.
A video posted to Facebook by Natural Resource Police shows the aircraft hone in on the kayaker and direct the fire boat to retrieve the juvenile.
Buchanan said such a rescue isn't too common, but it become somewhat prominent during boating season.
"(The) Chesapeake Bay and the tributaries are very large," Buchanan said. "When you start thinking about the different rivers and creeks and stuff off the Chesapeake Bay, we go out on different search missions like that probably a few times a month."
The pilot emphasized Helwig's expertise is crucial to such rescues. Helwig handles the thermal imaging camera, which can expose subjects in dark conditions, as well as a mapping system to pull up addresses and latitudes and longitudes.
"He's gotten really good with it, he's worked really hard at it," Buchanan said. "He's made us as a team very successful going out and doing these search missions."
Buchanan advises those going out on the water, especially alone, to be prepared with a charged cell phone and other equipment in case of emergency.
"Have a life jacket if you're out at night," he said. "Obviously have some kind of flashlight. And know the area, that's probably the biggest thing."

title: Talbot County Sheriff's Office to place cameras in patrol cars
author: Konner Metz
content:
Talbot County Sheriff's Office to place cameras in patrol cars

 July 11, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Konner Metz | Section: Local News 
 
 465
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — The Talbot County Sheriff's Office is planning to add cameras to its patrol vehicles, a move that Sheriff Joe Gamble said will increase transparency with the public.Earlier this month, Talbot County council members approved the purchase of 30 in-car cameras for $415,000, spread across a five-year period. Body-worn cameras have their limits, Gamble said, only showing the steering wheel during situations like police chases.
The sheriff said the in-car cameras have two main benefits.
"One, it's another level of transparency with the public," Gamble said. "And the other is evidence gathering."
But Gamble noted that a state investigation into a fatal police-involved chase last year factored into the decision.
"It definitely played a role in it," he said.
In July 2024, Talbot County deputies and an Easton police officer engaged in a pursuit of a vehicle on U.S. Route 50 in Easton after the driver failed to pull over for a traffic stop. Police reached speeds over 100 mph, and the chase ended with the vehicle crashing into a tree on Black Dog Alley. An 18-year-old passenger died.
The Independent Investigations Division of the Maryland Attorney General's Office reviewed the incident, as it does for all fatal police-involved chases statewide. Body-worn camera footage was eventually released in September. It wasn't until January when state investigators determined they wouldn't seek charges against any of the involved officers.
At the time, Gamble said it shouldn't have taken that long for the state to complete its investigation and clear his deputies. Now, the in-car cameras will better show the actions taken by vehicles being pursued by police, he argues.
"You couldn't see the egregious disregard for public safety by the driver in that car," Gamble said in an interview this week, referencing the limited view of the chase provided by body-worn cameras.
"It protects our deputies in the sense that, this is what they did," he added. "And if there's allegations they did something else, it's on footage."
Other sheriffs on the Eastern Shore concur with the effectiveness of the cameras.
Queen Anne's Sheriff Gary Hofmann said most patrol vehicles have had the in-car cameras for a few years. Complaints are down, and it's increased trust with the community, Hofmann says.
"It's been extremely beneficial for us to avoid any type of complaints or allegations," he said.
Dorchester Sheriff James Phillips said he would love for his agency to buy them, although cost is a problem — the in-car cameras are more expensive than body-worn ones.
In Caroline County, the vehicle cameras were purchased under a former sheriff, current Sheriff Donnie Baker noted. They are key in providing a better perspective for traffic stops and other incident, he said.
"I think that they make a good cop better," Baker said, "and they limit false reports."
Gamble said the Talbot County Sheriff's Office hopes to install all 30 in-car cameras by 2026.

 CENTREVILLE — The Queen Anne's County Sheriff's Office has arrested 19-year-old Kamryn Andrews, 20-year-old James Lawson and 27-year-old Travis Lissau in connection with the June 2025 shooting death of 19-year-old Christopher Parsley of Centreville.On June 1, at approximately 1:15 a.m., deputies from the Queen Anne's County Sheriff's Office, along with allied emergency services, responded to the 1500 block of Centreville Road in Queenstown for a report of shots fired involving multiple victims.
Responding units discovered Parsley, who had been attending a bonfire with friends, fatally shot. Life-saving measures were initiated; however, Parsley was pronounced dead at the scene.
In a statement issued by the Sheriff's Office Wednesday, Oct. 8, police said detectives from the Sheriff's Office Criminal Investigation Unit immediately launched an investigation, working closely with multiple federal, state and local partners. The investigation was conducted with the collaborative support of the Federal Bureau of Investigation's Baltimore-Annapolis Field Office, the Chesapeake Bay Safe Streets Task Force, Homeland Security Investigations' Baltimore Eastern Shore Field Office, the Maryland State Police Centreville Barrack, Centreville Police Department, Delaware State Police, Delaware Information and Analysis Center, Delaware State Police Governor's Task Force, Delaware Probation and Parole, Seaford Police Department and the Queen Anne's County State's Attorney's Office.
After an extensive investigation, the case was brought before a Queen Anne's County grand jury. The grand jury returned indictments, and on Oct. 6, arrest warrants were issued.
Andrews, of Seaford, Delaware, is charged with attempted second-degree murder (two counts), manslaughter, first-degree assault (four counts), second-degree assault (four counts), reckless endangerment (four counts), firearm used in the commission of a crime of violence (four counts), handgun on person (two counts), handgun in vehicle, loaded handgun in vehicle, and possession of a firearm as a minor.
Lawson, of Queenstown, is charged with attempted second-degree murder (four counts), manslaughter, first-degree assault (five counts), second-degree assault (five counts), reckless endangerment (five counts), firearm used in the commission of a crime of violence (five counts), conspiracy to alter physical evidence to avoid criminal prosecution, handgun on person (two counts), loaded handgun on person, possession of a firearm as a minor, and possession of a firearm without a serial number.
Lissau, of Centreville, is charged with attempted second-degree murder (four counts), manslaughter, first-degree assault (five counts), second-degree assault (five counts), reckless endangerment (five counts), firearm used in the commission of a crime of violence (five counts), conspiracy to alter physical evidence to avoid criminal prosecution, loaded handgun on person (two counts), and possession of a firearm without a serial number.
All three were taken into custody and held without bond.
Sheriff Gary Hofmann said, "This has been an incredibly difficult time for Chris' family and for our entire community. The effects of this tragedy have been deeply felt, and our thoughts remain with those who continue to grieve. This investigation reflects the strength of collaboration between our community and our law enforcement partners.
"As the investigation continues, every tip, video, and witness account remains vital to bringing closure for Chris's family and our community. We have zero tolerance for crime in Queen Anne's County and will always stand up for victims who no longer have a voice."
The investigation into the death of Parsley remains ongoing. Investigators continue to seek information from the public and encourage anyone who may have details related to this case to contact the Anonymous Tip Line at 410-758-6666 or email Sheriff-Info@qac.org.

title: Bradford House resident wants to feel safe at home after multiple assaults
author: MAGGIE TROVATO mtrovato@chespub.com
content:
Bradford House resident wants to feel safe at home after multiple assaults

 May 12, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: MAGGIE TROVATO mtrovato@chespub.com | Section: Local News 
 
 581
 Words 

 Read News Document

 CAMBRIDGE — Tena Cheaton looked forward to moving into the Bradford House Apartments about five years ago.At that time, Cheaton, now 59, was homeless.
She was receiving temporary disability assistance and waiting to be approved for supplemental security income, which is financial assistance for people who have little or no income and resources and have a disability, blindness or are 65 years of age or older.
"So I wanted to come," she said about Bradford House. "I didn't realize it was this bad."
Since moving in, Cheaton — who has PTSD, ADHD, bipolar disorder, fibromyalgia and back problems that include degenerative disc disease and spinal stenosis — said she has been assaulted, threatened and had her belongings stolen on the property.
Cheaton said that about two years ago, she was raped by a man who was staying with another tenant at Bradford House.
Cheaton said it happened in her apartment. She knew the man. He drugged her before raping her, she said.
After a few weeks of "throwing up constantly" and "crying uncontrollably," Cheaton went to rehab to get treatment.
She said it was her therapist that told her she didn't have to face her assaulter in the Bradford House halls everyday, and there were resources that could keep him out of the building.
Although Cheaton said she didn't call the police after she was raped, she did get restraining order against her rapist later on.
But despite the restraining order, Cheaton said she would still see her rapist in the halls at Bradford House.
Under the Violence Against Women Act, a housing provider may evict or terminate the assistance of a perpetrator of domestic violence, dating violence, sexual assault or stalking, according to the U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development's Notice of Occupancy Rights under the Violence Against Women Act.
According to the notice, those who have experienced domestic violence, dating violence, sexual assault or stalking must have the option to stay in their subsidized housing and can request an emergency transfer from the housing provider for safety reasons.
In a statement to the Star Democrat, Millennia Housing Management — which manages Bradford House — said the Bradford House property management team sends violations to anyone residing at the property that is the cause of an assault or theft.
Cheaton said she is not the only tenant that has been raped in the building. And this is not the only time Cheaton said she has been put in danger at Bradford House. She said she has also been held at knifepoint, threatened and assaulted on the property.
In one instance, Cheaton remembers taking her dog outside a few hours after midnight.
"I had just shut that door," she said. "And somebody standing way down there at the end of the building was hollering at me."
Cheaton, who said she doesn't leave the door to the building open for anyone, said the person was telling her to leave the door open.
She said the man got in her face and threatened to shoot her. By the time police arrived, he was gone, Cheaton said.
According to a Cambridge Police Department calls for service report requested by the Star Democrat, of the 1,099 calls for service to Bradford House made between Aug. 1, 2021, and Feb. 21, 2024, 18 were for reports of threats.
After being threatened outside the building, Cheaton — who has had experiences with substance abuse — said she moved out of Bradford House for about a month to live with her daughter.
"To stay sober in a building like this is very, very difficult," she said.

title: National Night Out connects cops with community
author: Tom McCall
content:
National Night Out connects cops with community

 August 7, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Tom McCall | Section: Local News 
 
 576
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — A crowd in Moton Park joined communities all over the country in celebrating the 40th annual National Night Out Tuesday.National Night Out connects different branches of law enforcement with the community. The goal is to prevent crime and have people know the officers and emergency services personnel who serve their area.
Megan Coxon, a sergeant with the Easton Police Department, has been a primary force in organizing the event.
"We are here for First Night Out, which is a nationwide event. It happens the first Tuesday in August. I probably know half the folks here just because we interact on a daily anyway," Coxon said. "It is like a mini reunion. We get to hang out for a night, and of course you get to meet new people. If I don't know you, I will come talk to you and if I have seen you before, we will reconnect."
She said she got a lot of help from Jill Garvey, an EPD management assistant, and Lorraine Gould, director of Easton Parks and Recreation.
Coxon pointed out the law enforcement representatives in attendance.
"We have at least ten from EPD. We have sheriff's office, fire marshall's office, Natural Resources Police, Talbot Sheriff's office and MSP. There are about 40 people," she said.
Over a smoking hot grill with about 50 burgers were members of the Easton Volunteer Fire Department.
"We are cooking some good burgers. We got some good hot dogs. We got a decent crowd of people, it is its a good time," Aiden Lowery, a firefighter and EMT said.
Mayor Megan Cook was also present, immersed in community.
"Talking to people? That is the best part of my job," Cook said. "The sense of community is what is important tonight. I think to see the police department as partners and to get them visible in the community so our neighbors know that they are a resource and they are there to help."
John Grothe of the state's fire marshal office had a full kevlar and ballistic shield bomb squad suit and special helmet on display. He is a bomb tech and said the suit weighs 100 pounds.
"In the event that there is a device or suspicious package, we try to stay as remote as possible. We try to utilize our bomb robot, but every once in a while, we have to put on the suit and go downrange in person. Night Out is a great opportunity to meet people and have them come up and touch the equipment. We get to explain what we do. It puts a face to the agency," Grothe said.
There were over 100 community members wandering around, getting food, visiting with friends and getting information from the community service booths.
Jessica Carter, who was sharing an shaved ice with her daughter, said the National Night Out event gives her family an opportunity to see what resources are available to them.
"We come every year. The resources. Giving back to the community. Some people may not know what resources are available to them. So it is good. I like the health department and Chesapeake Voyagers," Carter said.
Garvey said she has been working on this event for over a month. She had two massive sheet cakes from Cordova Bakery in her air conditioned vehicle.
"It falls into place. I have been planning these for 18 years. It is a free fun family event. The pool is open. Come out and enjoy. There is free food. It is a good community event," she said.

title: Caroline Police Accountability Board reports progress
author: Connie Connolly
content:
Caroline Police Accountability Board reports progress

 February 14, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Connie Connolly | Section: Local News 
 
 1030
 Words 

 Read News Document

 DENTON — The Caroline County Police Accountability Board shared its second annual report with the County Commissioners at their Feb. 6 meeting.The bottom line: Of the thousands of contacts people had with county and town law enforcement officers, a handful of complaints were made, and a fraction of those resulted in disciplinary action.
Presenting the report were Police Accountability Board Chairman John Bartlett and Board Administrator Kimberly Raeder.
Bartlett said he wanted to make one "very important" point: The Caroline County Sheriff's Office had over 26,000 calls for service in 2023, which generated only six complaints, he said.
"Five of those six were exonerated, meaning unfounded, and one was a very minor infraction, which led to a written reprimand," he said. "I think that speaks volumes with law enforcement here in Caroline County."
A state mandate
Raeder explained the purpose and scope of the three police oversight boards mandated by the Maryland Police Accountability Act of 2021, which became effective July 1, 2022.
The role of the county's Police Accountability Board "is to receive police complaints, recommend policy changes and identify any trends," Raeder said.
"The second board is the five-member Administrative Charging Committee, and their role is to look over and review completed complaint investigations and recommend discipline," she said. If the Charging Committee decides to administratively charge, they use the statewide police disciplinary matrix to "decide what kind of discipline would be necessary based on the complaint."
The five members of the Charging Committee were appointed and trained in April 2023 at the Fretterd Center by the Maryland Police Training and Standards Commission.
The third board is the Trial Board comprised of retired Maryland Circuit Court Judge Owen Wise, a citizen and a police officer of the same rank, Raeder said. No complaints have been referred to this board.
"I'm proud to say that Caroline County is leading the way for other counties on the Eastern Shore who have reached out to us regarding using Judge Wise, if they need a judge for a trial board," she said.
Few complaints filed
Among the county's municipalities, 15 complaints were filed, including a pending complaint related to an April 7, 2023, incident in Denton that prompted millions of views on YouTube, Bartlett said.
A video of the incident shows Christopher Morgan threatening the residents and breaking the window of the storm door of a home while two Denton Police officers stand on the sidewalk watching.
The way the officers handled the call for service prompted Denton Police Chief George Bacorn to request the Talbot County Sheriff's Office to investigate the handling of the incident. Their findings were turned over to the Administrative Charging Committee.
There were no complaints from Ridgely or Greensboro. One was brought to the Police Accountability Board from Federalsburg, which was exonerated, Bartlett said.
The report breaks down the 15 complaints by percentages; numerically, four complaints are pending investigation, three were administratively charged, two were withdrawn by the complainant, four were exonerated and two were "not in the purview of the ACC (Administrative Charging Committee)."
The Accountability Board identified trends in the disciplinary process and didn't "recommend any changes at this time."
"A common identified trend, however, has been the lack of activation of body cameras when officers interact with the public," the report stated. "The ACC discovered this trend when reviewing completed complaint investigations which had no body camera footage for the ACC to review. The Board advised the municipal Police Departments and the Sheriff's Office to remind Officers to adhere to department policy and activate their cameras when encountering the public. The policy protects both the Officer and the Citizen if a complaint were to arise from the interaction."
Cost to the county
Bartlett thanked the commissioners for their "financial support of the committee for legal decisions when needed."
The boards' complying with the state mandates has incurred expenses for the county, although some have been covered by the Police Accountability, Community, and Transparency Grant program.
Of the $105,272 in grant funds received, the Accountability Board has spent $49,545, which includes the purchase of IAPro software for filing complaints, annual computer licensing for all board members, and pay for the Board's administrator.
The Police Accountability Board is asking the state to continue offering these grants, as well as other police-oriented grant programs for local police departments to be able to purchase "the required technology, resources, and tools to comply with the law," including software and a change in the vendor for body cameras, so that every law enforcement agency in the county has the same system.
Other costs included outside legal counsel, with expenses the County Commissioners agreed to fund to the tune of nearly $8,000.
Questions arose requiring legal clarification for both the Police Accountability Board and Administrative Charging Committee, and the county commissioners "agreed to bear the expense of hiring outside legal counsel" to represent both. "Legal Counsel attends each quarterly meeting and provides interpretation of the Maryland Police Accountability Act of 2021 as needed," the report stated.
The legal expenses for the Police Accountability Board were $3,650, while those of the Administrative Charging Committee amounted to $4,300.
PAB recommendations
The Accountability Board recommends "changing ACC training from all in-person training to online meeting based or pre-recorded online training. With one member of our ACC board resigning this past July, we have firsthand knowledge of the burden imposed on the newly appointed volunteer Board member. As terms end or resignations occur, the pool of applicants will continue to shrink when advised that members must undergo uncompensated training prior to serving."
Another unanticipated result of the law has been the withdrawing of multiple complaints, which created a legal conundrum for the Accountability Board and is currently being resolved with the Office of the Attorney General.
The report also suggested amending the law by mandating only complaints of "matters of public concern," that is, "police misconduct, such as abuse of power, false arrest, police brutality, or criminal activity" be referred to the Charging Committee, thus alleviating pressure on municipal police departments. "Rude and discourteous" behavior towards a citizen would be handled at the department or agency level, as suggested by the Accountability Board.
To read the full report, which includes rosters of members of the PAB and ACC boards, visit carolinemd.org/DocumentCenter/View/8606/2023-Annual-Report-PAB?bidId=. The last page provides links to other documents and resources provided by the PAB.

title: Human remains found on farm during Cherrywood Solar construction
author: AHMAD GARNETT agarnett@chespub.com
content:
Human remains found on farm during Cherrywood Solar construction

 Author/Byline: AHMAD GARNETT agarnett@chespub.com | Section: News

 Words

 GREENSBORO — On May 20, while Cherrywood Solar workers were at Ronald Spearing Farm, human remains were found."They found that while they were conducting grading activities at the Spearing Farm on Bridgetown Road, and they immediately stopped work, secured the area and went to their plan," said Crystal Dadds, Caroline County director of planning and codes.
"Cherrywood has a plan when anytime they come across what's called an 'unanticipated discovery,' they made all the proper notifications contacting Public Service Commission, the Maryland Historical Trust, the sheriff's office, the state's attorney, the planning and code, the health officer, roped off the area, covered the area with tarps to protect it because we did have bad weather."
Cherrywood then brought in Search, an organization that has an archeological team to do a preliminary assessment of the area where they presumed remains were found.
The Search team then made a determination that there were human remains at the site. Five burial plots were discovered.
Cherrywood Solar brought the team back to do an ground-penetrating radar to see if there were any more potential burial sights. Once the final report from that test comes back, the Burial Sites Preservation Board in Caroline County will review that data and make a recommendation of what area needs to be protected.
Cherrywood Solar, produced by NextEra Energy Resources LLC, is a 145-megawatt project in Caroline County.
NextEra Energy Resources sent a press release to the Star Democrat Wednesday stating, "We are cooperating with Caroline County and other pertinent agencies on the investigation. Once we receive clearance from the relevant authorities, we will resume construction activities."
All parties involved believe that there was no foul play involved. They are believed to be human remains of family members from previous property owners.
"Given the fact that the house on this farm is a late 1800s house, most likely it was a family burial plot that could date back that far," Dadds said.

title: ‘Hang up immediately’: Scam artists impersonating police, targeting nonprofits with big, bogus donations
author: MIKE SUNNUCKS Belgrade News
content:
‘Hang up immediately’: Scam artists impersonating police, targeting nonprofits with big, bogus donations

 February 14, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: MIKE SUNNUCKS Belgrade News | Section: News 
 
 664
 Words 

 Read News Document

 Consumers lost a record $10 billion to fraudsters last year across the U.S. and there are fresh scam warnings from local police as well a scheme targeting Montana nonprofits.The Gallatin County Sheriff's Office is warning local residents of telephone scams involving fraudsters impersonating law enforcement officers.
On Monday, Feb. 12, the Sheriff's Office issued a scam alert saying it "has dozens of reports in recent weeks of a jury duty phone scam making the rounds."
"The caller claims that the person missed jury duty and that there is a warrant for their arrest, but they can post a fine or bail to take care of it," GCSO said in its announcement.
The law enforcement agency tells residents to "hang up immediately" and to not send any payments.
Like with other police-related scams across the state and country, the Sheriff's Office said it would not request monetary payments over the phone.
The latest alert follows one issued by GCSO on Jan. 26.
This scam also involves someone impersonating law enforcement and telling residents they missed jury duty, a court date or have unpaid parking tickets or criminal warrants.
"They will tell you to get gift cards and/or money to send over the phone in order to avoid arrest. Please know that while we may contact you to serve you various documents, we will never request money or gift cards. Any payments related to law enforcement or the jail are processed through the courts, never our office," GCSO said.
The scam artists might also use cloned police telephone numbers and actual deputy names. Again, police recommend hanging up immediately on the bogus callers.
"Scammers will be insistent that you stay on the line, which prevents you from thinking through their demands or calling someone else," GCSO said.
Other police agencies across the state and country have also seen imposters posing as officers as part of various phone scams.
NONPROFITS TARGETED
The Montana Nonprofit Association is also warning organizations of donation schemes that have so far targeted 19 groups statewide.
MNA said a nonprofit will receive " an unexpected donation of around $200,000 to honor someone's late mother."
"Multiple (organizations) have said the amount they received was $191,250, and that the email came from Alphonso Blye. The cashier's check looks legitimate so they cash it, " the Helena-based group said in an announcement Monday.
A few days later the same donor will contact the nonprofit and tell them the check should have been for $100,000 and request a refund of the remaining amount.
The check is bogus to begin and will bounce but scam rings hope to bilk groups out of $91,250 in the meantime.
"So far, everyone who has contacted us has managed to catch the scam before falling victim, but with this amount of money, the scammer only needs to convince one," MPA said.
The statewide association recommends confirming the identity of donors before accepting money and asking them to wait 30 days before issuing any refunds.
Major banks statewide and the Montana Bankers Association have also been alerted to the fraud scheme.
RECORD FRAUD LEVELS
The Federal Trade Commission reported Feb. 9 that U.S. consumers lost a record $10 billion to fraud schemes in 2023.
That is a 14% increase from 2022. Some of that jump stems from crypto currency fraud.
"Consumers reported losing more money to investment scams—more than $4.6 billion—than any other category in 2023. That amount represents a 21% increase over 2022. The second highest reported loss amount came from imposter scams, with losses of nearly $2.7 billion reported. In 2023, consumers reported losing more money to bank transfers and cryptocurrency than all other methods combined," FTC which received 2.6 million consumer complaints last year.
The U.S agency received 2.5 million complaints in 2022. The FTC said last year saw an increase in consumer calls involving fraud rings impersonating government officials (including police) as well as businesses.
The FTC received fraud reports from 2.6 million consumers last year, nearly the same amount as 2022. The most commonly reported scam category was imposter scams, which saw significant increases in reports of both business and government impersonators.

title: Greensboro adds security measures, hears resident feedback after water system 'sabotage'
author: KONNER METZ kmetz@chespub.com
content:
Greensboro adds security measures, hears resident feedback after water system 'sabotage'

 August 3, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: KONNER METZ kmetz@chespub.com | Section: Local News 
 
 549
 Words 

 Read News Document

 GREENSBORO — Town employees discussed an apparent "sabotage" of Greensboro's water system and heard feedback from residents during a Thursday evening Town Council meeting.On July 29, the town announced that the its water and wastewater contract operator, Susquehanna Operational Services, conducted tests throughout town, finding higher than normal chlorine levels. It came after a bevy of complaints from concerned residents, who said the water had a chlorine-like taste and smell the weekend prior.
The town concluded that "one of the chlorine regulators had been tampered with" in the tower wells. In a press release, it was deemed "deliberate sabotage," and the town stated the Caroline County Sheriff's Office would conduct an investigation.
Brandon Cunningham, the town's public works supervisor, provided an update Thursday on security measures put in place in days since. Cunningham said "the locks have all been changed to all the well houses."
Keys were given to members of Susquehanna Operational Services, and himself and the town manager in case of emergency, he said.
He also said he's been in contact with SafeHouse, a security system company, to potentially procure security cameras and keypads. Cunningham said SafeHouse security measures, including adding cameras, would cost $15,865.54.
Councilmember Joe Noon said he'd "like a couple more bids" for the cameras and security additions. Carly Landolfi, assistant to the town attorney, told councilmembers they could vote on a "contingent" motion to purchase the SafeHouse services, depending on whether she finds the town must legally seek out other bids or not.
Mayor David Spencer said he's visited the wells and vouched for security services to be adopted as soon as possible.
"I really don't want to push this off," Spencer said. Councilmember Pete Breila made a motion to pass the "contingent" motion, which was seconded by Councilmember Bob Harrison.
PUBLIC COMMENTMultiple residents expressed concerns about the water quality and the town's response to councilmembers Thursday.
"The word sabotage, that's a pretty extensive word," resident Chris Mason said. "It means a lot, and it puts fear in the community."
Mason continued, questioning why the investigation is being conducted by Caroline County Sheriff's Office and not the Greensboro Police Department. He added that he wished the town had passed out water to residents during the days in which the chlorine-like taste and smell was apparent.
"Who has access to sabotage?" resident Melissa Knight asked. "Where'd that information come from? We're not getting any forthcoming information."
Knight said that "the entire bedroom (smelled) like chlorine" after flushing the toilet in her house last weekend. She also asked about the process of testing the chlorine levels.
George Smith, president of Susquehanna Operational Services, said his team tested multiple locations when notified by the town of the complaints. Smith and a Susquehanna employee confirmed there were readings of 2.2, 0.6 and 0.54 milligrams per liter. The Environmental Protection Agency's standard is that anything above the 4.0 milligram per liter mark is not healthy to drink and could pose long-term health effects such as eye irritation and stomach problems.
Smith declined to comment on the investigation since it's active. Spencer also declined.
"There's a lot that we'd all like to say," Spencer said. "But since there is an investigation ongoing, when that is concluded, then we will try to give you as much information as we possibly can."
The Caroline County Sheriff's Office declined to comment on the investigation for this article.

 EASTON — Inside the Bradley Meeting Room of the Talbot County Courthouse, high schoolers bring court into session.It's not mock trial, but instead, a program called Talbot Teen Court. First-time youth misdemeanor offenders of crimes such as second-degree assault or possession of cannabis stand before a jury of their peers awaiting a disposition.
Teen Court is a restorative justice pathway for youth offenders as much as it is a volunteer opportunity for students interested in the judicial process, organizers say.
"Kids can get a really bad rap these days. The kids that we have are amazing," Teen Court Coordinator Kelley Callaghan said. "They are passionate about it, they are prepared, they are super into it."
Around once every month, student volunteers handle three cases, agreeing on sanctions for the offender such as community service or conflict management. Students assume the roles of attorneys, bailiffs, clerks, jurors and judges, all taking an oath of confidentiality.
The program is an alternative to going to the Department of Juvenile Services for youth offenders ages 13 through 17. Offenders, called "respondents," must admit involvement in the crime and follow through with their sanctions.
Callaghan says the aspect of guilt or innocence isn't the program's focus, but rather affording respondents a chance for a "clean slate."
"By the time they come to us, this is kind of a pivotal moment for a lot of them," Callaghan said. "You could go this way or you could go this way. We're going to give you every resource possibly to help you get back on track."
Teen Court volunteer Allegra West, a senior at Chesapeake Christian School, believes the program helps youth offenders feel like they're being heard.
"At this level, I think that everybody deserves some forgiveness," West said. "And it's harder for us when we hear things from adults, because we maybe feel like they don't necessarily appeal to us or understand our struggles and our problems."
'REAL GAME-CHANGER'
Last month, Easton High School senior Skylar Blades sat in the courthouse diligently preparing notes to be the defense attorney for the night's first case. Across from her was Easton High junior Matthew Bravo, the prosecutor.
Blades and Bravo both were respondents in the Teen Court program at one point in time. Now, they're committed volunteers who enjoy learning about law and helping their peers.
Callaghan said respondent-to-volunteer turnarounds illustrate that Teen Court is succeeding. And students like Bravo notice it as well.
"It was a real game-changer because when I was the defendant, it was like, 'This is what it's like to be on the other side,'" Bravo said.
Blades said she knows the nerves that respondents experience, part of the reason she now enjoys talking to respondents and making sure they feel at ease.
For Blades, she sees a future in therapy, a career she thinks her Teen Court experience will help with. Other volunteers like Bravo and Easton High freshman Rhys Campbell want to pursue law, making the program a perfect fit.
"Ever since the seventh grade, I really wanted to be a lawyer," said Campbell, who was the defense attorney for a case later that night. "I bought the textbooks and everything."
Thirteen student volunteers sat in the courthouse room on Feb. 26, catching up with one another despite age and grade differences and being enrolled at different schools.
Teen Court has become a mini-community of its own, as well as a school club at Easton High.
"There are some people that are nervous just because it's their first time being here," Blades said, "but we all try to make each other feel comfortable."
LONG HISTORY
Teen Court has been a pillar of the community since 1999, when then-Spotlight on Schools probation officer Cory Fink organized Talbot County Teen Court's inception and its first hearings.
Fink, now chief operating officer at the Maryland Department of Juvenile Services, stayed involved until 2006. But in the last decade, he's watched Teen Court persist and evolve.
His daughter Caroline Fink, a sophomore at Easton High, began volunteering this school year as a juror and a clerk.
"I like dealing with their punishments because I like that they can understand what they did is wrong," Caroline Fink said. "And it's not serious punishment, but it's enough for them to know that they shouldn't do it again."
"The fact that Talbot County was the first one (on the Eastern Shore) and it's still here — it's weathered the storms of budget, of personnel changes, of oversight and lead agency changes," Cory Fink said.
In 2021, the Talbot County Sheriff's Office took Teen Court under its wing, providing the main chunk of funding needed to save the program after the previous agency closed. Maj. Steve Elliott leads the Sheriff's Office efforts.
As the decades have passed, typical youth crimes have changed. Elliott noted that right now, the busy time for Teen Court is during the school year. Fights and cannabis use are two of the leading referrals.
While the most common offenses have changed over time, Elliott and Fink both say that youth still deserve the same room to learn as kids of years past.
"You can't demonize a kid because he makes one mistake," Elliott said. "And that's kind of what society has gone to."
"Kids are still kids," Fink said. "Kids still make impulsive decisions. Kids don't necessarily think about the consequences of their actions given their brain development."
Callaghan, the program coordinator, said it's impressive seeing the commitment from community and law enforcement partners to divert kids from the juvenile system and make a real difference in their lives.
Elliott says as long as the program is helping someone, it has a place in Talbot County.
"If you change the path of one kid, it's 100% worth it," he said.

title: Videos of Easton High School assault circulate online
author: Veronica Fernandez-Alvarado
content:
Videos of Easton High School assault circulate online

 September 12, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Veronica Fernandez-Alvarado | Section: Crime 
 
 406
 Words

 EASTON — Videos showing the Tuesday assault at Easton High School have been circulating online. The incident involved three students and one staff member and ended with a student being transported to a hospital for non-life-threatening injuries.According to a press release released by the Talbot County Sheriff's Office, the assault happened on Tuesday afternoon. The videos paint a picture of the incident, though no further official statement has been released by law enforcement on the assault.
In the videos, a group of students are circling around the three students involved in the assault. Seconds into the video, one student in a black hoodie moves toward a student in a red hoodie and assaults him. The student in red falls to the floor. Immediately following, an additional student in a gray hoodie proceeds to join in the assault.
In the video, a male staff member in a white shirt attempts to protect the student that is being assaulted and physically puts his body on top of the student, seemingly to act as a barrier between the students.
The other two students seemingly continue to assault the student in red and begin to also assault the staff member. Soon after, other staff members intervene and separate the students and defuse the situation. The incident lasted around 30 seconds.
Deputies were able to identify two victims of the assault, one was an Easton High School staff member and the second was a student of the school. No identities have been released, and the incident is currently under investigation.
The assault resulted in one student being transported to the University of Maryland Shore Medical Center at Easton via Talbot County Department of Emergency Services to be treated for non-life-threatening injuries, police said.
The two other students in the video were identified and arrested in relation to the assault.
According to a statement from Debbie Gardner, director of communications for Talbot County Public Schools, the event is being evaluated and those involved will face appropriate disciplinary action.
"The safety of our students and staff is always our top priority. We are grateful for our partnership with the Talbot County Sheriff's Office and the presence of School Resource Officers in our schools," the statement said. "Deputy Horseman, along with several other Sheriff's deputies and members of the Easton High staff responded quickly to contain the incident. The students involved will face appropriate disciplinary action, and we are continuously evaluating safety measures to prevent or mitigate incidents of this nature."

Dorchester County Circuit Court Welcomes New Casa Volunteers

 New Court Appointed Special Advocates for CASA of the Mid-Shore were sworn in by Clerk of the Court Amy Craig at a ceremony in Dorchester County Circuit Court on December 6.CASA staff and board members were present as the new advocates took an oath promising to advocate for the best interest of children who are under court protection because of maltreatment.
Court Appointed Special Advocates are officers of the court and, as such, are provide assessments and recommendations to judges regarding the best interest of the children to whom they are appointed.
Presiding over the swearing-in ceremony in Dorchester County Circuit Court were the Honorable William H. Jones and the Honorable Mary O'Donnell.
The judge and magistrate thanked the new CASA volunteers for their time and talents on behalf of children and commended the organization for the important information contained in their insightful reports to the court.
"Our program strives to ensure that all children under court protection due to maltreatment receive needed services and a safe, permanent home. We could not accomplish our work without the dedication and commitment of our amazing staff and volunteers.
They work passionately to help improve the lives of maltreated children to assist them in growing to their full potential and giving them hope," said Robin Davenport, executive director of the CASA of the Mid-Shore.
CASA of the Mid-Shore is a private nonprofit created to advocate for every child who is under the protection of the circuit court because of abuse, neglect or abandonment.
CASAs attempt to identify specific needs of each child for the court, advocate for service provision to meet those needs and assist in seeking a permanent resolution for each child's life as quickly and safely as possible.
Most importantly, the CASAs get to know the child and frequently become one of the most consistent adults in the child's life.
CASA of the Mid-Shore is currently accepting applications from adults from Talbot, Dorchester, Queen Anne's and Kent Counties who are interested in becoming CASA volunteers. An organization valuing diversity and equity, CASA seeks volunteers from all walks of life, varied experiences, backgrounds and professions, and who are at least 21 years of age. After completing the application and screening process, prospective volunteers participate in pre-service training before being sworn in as officers of the court.
To learn more about becoming a Court Appointed Special Advocate visit casamidshore.org

title: Students warned of 'imposters' with offers of 'DoorDash-style' marijuana deliveries
author: Josh Shannon jshannon@chespub.com
content:
Students warned of 'imposters' with offers of 'DoorDash-style' marijuana deliveries

 October 16, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Josh Shannon jshannon@chespub.com | Section: News 
 
 283
 Words 

 Read News Document

 A fraudulent marijuana operation is targeting University of Delaware students and Newark residents by illegally offering marijuana deliveries, according to state officials.The Delaware Division of Alcohol & Tobacco Enforcement issued an alert to the public on Thursday indicating that the agency is investigating reports of flyers and business cards that are being distributed around Newark. The ads falsely claim to be associated with Fresh Cannabis, the licensed medical and recreational marijuana dispensary on Ogletown Road.
"The impostors are attempting to mislead potential customers into purchasing marijuana products illegally," said Jon Peterson, a spokesman for DATE.
One of the ads includes a cartoon of a marijuana leaf character holding a joint and targeting UD students with the words "UDEL-iver? Yes we do!"
"Quick delivery for on-campus students only! (DoorDash/Uber Eats Style!)," reads the ad, which includes the Fresh Cannabis logo and a promise of a free sample of marijuana for students who sign up.
Another ad also includes the Fresh Cannabis logo and shows a menu of offerings. It notes that the business delivers 24/7.
Peterson emphasized that no licensed marijuana dispensary in Delaware is permitted to deliver marijuana or marijuana products.
"Any business claiming to offer delivery services is operating illegally," he said. "Delaware's adult-use marijuana marketplace includes strict regulations and testing standards designed to ensure consumer safety. Products sold through illegal channels bypass these safeguards and may contain dangerous contaminants such as mold, pesticides or heavy metals."
Though Delaware legalized recreational marijuana, it remains illegal to sell it outside of licensed dispensaries.
Tips about this or similar cases can be sent to Cpl. Tristin Burris at tristin.b.burris@delaware.gov.
"DATE's Marijuana Enforcement Unit is actively investigating this matter and encourages anyone with information about these fraudulent materials to come forward," Peterson said.

Off-duty Prince George's officer faces attempted murder charge

 A Prince George's County police officer was arrested and charged with attempted murder and first-degree assault after firing his service weapon at a man in Charles County while off-duty.On Feb. 23, the Charles County Sheriff's Office responded to the area of Crain Highway and Budds Creek Road in Newburg for reports of shots being fired at a moving vehicle, charging documents say.
Charles County emergency communications received ongoing updates from the caller, who said that he was following the shooter in his vehicle on Budds Creek Road. A detective was able to locate both of the vehicles, and they came to a stop on Ryceville Road in Mechanicsville.
The alleged shooter, David Hardester, 42, of Mechanicsville, cooperated with responding officers and was detained after a felony stop was conducted, according to charging documents.
The document says an officer asked Hardester where he was coming from and he said, "Down there at the Aqualand neighborhood. I was just going to talk with him."
Hardester was asked how he knew the man he allegedly shot at, to which he told officers that his wife knew him, the document says.
Officers talked to the other man who said Hardester was going to meet him at his house and that he was expecting a fight with him because Hardester was aware that the man was talking to his estranged wife, according to charging documents.
The man told officers that he believed they would have a fist fight and "get it over with as men," charging documents say.
The two met in a parking area by the man's residence and began arguing when the man began to walk away. When his back was turned, he heard a loud gunshot, felt a "whiz" allegedly from a bullet go past him and ran from Hardester, the document says.
Upon taking Hardester into custody, police allegedly located live ammunition and Hardester's 9 mm handgun, which was later determined to be his service weapon.
According to the charging documents, Hardester's driver's door had damage consistent with a gunshot entering the door panel from inside the truck and exiting out the door.
Officers were able to obtain video footage that was consistent with the victim's story.
Hardester's estranged wife came to the scene at Ryceville Road and informed officers that before the alleged shooting Hardester had assaulted her at her home in St. Mary's County after finding out about her new relationship, charging documents say.
Hardester informed her that he was going to go to the man's house and allegedly grabbed her, slammed her into a wall and left the residence. Hardester's estranged wife took the opportunity to warn the man that Hardester was coming, the document says.
Currently, Hardester is suspended without pay, according to the Prince George's County Police Department.

title: Demolition of remaining Key Bridge structures beginning around July 7
author: Matt Wynn mwynn@chespub.com
content:
Demolition of remaining Key Bridge structures beginning around July 7

 June 26, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Matt Wynn mwynn@chespub.com | Section: News 
 
 457
 Words 

 Read News Document

 Demolition of the remaining Key Bridge structures will begin on or about July 7, the Maryland Transportation Authority announced on June 26.The work is expected to take several months to complete and will involve the use of heavy machinery to dismantle what is left of the bridge.
The process will begin with the removal of the bridge deck over the river, followed by demolition of sections over Hawkins Point and then Sollers Point, the Maryland Transportation Authority said in a release.
This phase of work focuses on removing portions of the existing structure that interfere with the alignment of the new bridge.
No controlled detonations will occur.
The general demolition sequence will include the removal of deck, barriers and parapets over the river from both Hawkins Point and Sollers Point, followed by the removal of deck, barriers, parapets, girders and piers on the landside approaches, down to just below ground level.
Finally, the original north and south abutments will be removed.
Nearby communities should expect to see active tug and barge operations on the river, with heavy equipment and trucks visible on the existing bridge structure.
Barges will serve as protective shielding during demolition and must be avoided by waterway users. Machinery used may include excavators, concrete saws, vacuums, cranes and trucks.
An on-site concrete crusher will recycle materials for haul roads and staging areas, reducing truck trips and cost.
Typical large construction project noise is expected from 7 a.m. to 7 p.m.
Equipment is being installed in nearby communities to capture baseline noise and vibration data before the start of demolition and upcoming construction activities.
Buoys will mark a safety zone, no entry area around active work areas.
Notices will be issued to designate speed restrictions and safety zones to ensure the safe passage of vessels near the construction area.
The Maryland Transportation Authority said that it will continue to provide updates and advance notice of any work that may affect nearby communities, roads or waterways.
Based on months of field investigations and engineering analysis, the bridge alignment is slightly east or downriver of the original structure, remaining entirely within the Maryland Transportation Authority's existing right-of-way. To proceed with construction, the Maryland Transportation Authority is requesting modifications to permits that have been issued by the Maryland Board of Public Works, Maryland Department of the Environment, U.S. Army Corps of Engineers and the U.S. Coast Guard in support of the Key Bridge Rebuild, according to the release.
The permit modification requests will reflect updates to the bridge pier foundation design, pier protection elements, and trestle configuration. They also include a decrease in authorized impacts to tidal waters and some additional impacts to non-tidal wetlands and waterways.
A reevaluation of the project's categorical exclusion will also be submitted to the Federal Highway Administration.
No significant increase in environmental impacts is expected, the release said.

title: Greet the military in your city with flowers
author: ARNOLD J. OLIVER
content:
Greet the military in your city with flowers

 October 3, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: ARNOLD J. OLIVER | Section: Columns 
 
 643
 Words 

 Read News Document

 During some of the large anti-war demonstrations during the 1960s some of the protesters gave flowers to the troops faced off against them. In the 1967 March on the Pentagon, it was the 503rd Military Police Battalion, and elsewhere the National Guard was deployed. An iconic photo from 1967 shows a young man placing a flower into a soldier's gun barrel during the protest.Let's bring that custom back when the U.S. military occupies your town in 2025, but this time let's include a note along with the flower.
Allow me to explain.
The demonstrators of the 1960s understood that the soldiers faced off against him were not the enemy. Nearly all of the soldiers were young and patriotic and trying to do the right thing. Many of them were under economic hardship and wanted help paying for their education. The flower symbolized the protesters' belief that the soldiers were not their enemies, and they did not wish to be theirs. And in fact, as the almost entirely peaceful protests grew, many soldiers came to sympathize and began to actively oppose the war as well.
Now we have federalized Guard troops being called out by President Trump in Washington, D.C., Los Angeles, Portland with other cities soon to follow. Chicago is likely next. The authority for this is said to be Title 10 of the U.S. Code that says that the president may federalize the National Guard if the U.S. "is invaded or is in danger of invasion by a foreign nation; there is a rebellion or danger of a rebellion ... or the president is unable with the regular forces to execute the laws of the United States."
Legitimate grounds for a military or National Guard deployment do not exist. The claim that crime is spiraling out of control is false, and those pushing for the deployments know it. There is zero credible proof that crime is increasing. According to a recent FBI report (August 2025) robbery, assault, rape and murder all continued a decline that began post-COVID. We are not being invaded, there is no rebellion, and the laws are being enforced about as well as ever.
A second reason against deploying the military on our streets is that the Posse Comitatus Act of 1878 forbids the use of military forces within the country for active law enforcement except in exceptional circumstances such as insurrection, and then must be explicitly approved by Congress. The military is forbidden from making arrests, conducting searches, issuing warrants or interfering with local law enforcement. The law also applies to National Guard forces unless approved by state governors. No governors this year have made any requests for federalized National Guard troops.
And it is worth noting that Trump's military forays into cities are only being used in Democrat-run areas. High crime in red state cities is ignored. And the Trump administration refuses to realize the obvious danger of political violence and threats from MAGA and the American right which are much higher than those from the left, according to the Anti-Defamation League, the Center for Strategic and International Studies and others. Antifa is officially (and improperly) designated as domestic terrorists while violent right-wing groups get a pass from the administration.
And the president's rhetoric seems aimed at inflaming and dividing. The "enemy from within," "full force," "thugs," "vermin" and much more. And there is hardly a peep of protest from the Republican party.
So this time around, how about if we give the troops a note along with the flower? You could use wording such as this:
Dear U.S. soldier:
Your service oath included a pledge to uphold the U.S. Constitution, and your training taught you to disobey illegal orders. The orders sending you here (insert name of your city or town) are unlawful and unjust. You have a legal obligation to disobey.
We encourage you to go home, and we will support you in that decision.

title: Glen Burnie man sentenced for role in Eastern Shore Hospital Center escape
author: MAGGIE TROVATO mtrovato@chespub.com
content:
Glen Burnie man sentenced for role in Eastern Shore Hospital Center escape

 December 6, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: MAGGIE TROVATO mtrovato@chespub.com | Section: Crime 
 
 633
 Words 

 Read News Document

 CAMBRIDGE — A Glen Burnie man will serve 12 years for helping a patient escape the Eastern Shore Hospital Center in August 2023.Israel Labastida Jr., 20, was sentenced Friday to 25 years, with all but eight years suspended, for first-degree assault, followed by 10 years, with all but five years suspended, for use of a firearm during a felony or violent crime. Labastida was also sentenced to five years for first-degree conspiracy to escape, with all of those years suspended.
Labastida will get credit for one year of time served.
He will serve five years of supervised probation following his release from prison. Conditions of probation include that he must receive a mental health evaluation and seek treatment, receive a substance abuse and alcohol evaluation and seek related treatment, abstain from alcohol and illegal drugs, stay away from the Eastern Shore Hospital Center, and not contact Darrin Jeter, 20, who was also involved in the incident.
Before Dean handed down the sentence, Leonard recommended Labastida be sentenced to five years without parole followed by five years of probation. Dean said she was "taken aback" by the state's "lenient" sentencing recommendation.
She said that although she feels for Labastida's family and the pain they have been going through, she also feels for the people that were at the psychiatric facility on the day of the escape.
In June, Labastida pleaded guilty to the three charges. The charges stem from Jeter's escape from the psychiatric facility located on Woods Road in Cambridge last year. At that time, Jeter, who has schizophrenia, had been committed to the hospital center.
At the June plea hearings for both Labastida and Jeter, Dorchester County State's Attorney Amanda Leonard said Labastida approached the facility on Aug. 1, 2023 and shot into a window several times. She said Labastida and Jeter kicked out the broken window so Jeter could exit the building. The two fled the area in a black vehicle.
Jeter was located by the Montgomery County Sheriff's Office the following day. Leonard said Labastida was identified as a suspect through investigation. Evidence of an escape plan between the two was discovered through investigation, Leonard said at Jeter's hearing.
Jeter was sentenced to 10 years in prison for first-degree escape with eight of those years suspended.
During Labastida's sentencing hearing Friday, defense attorney Marvin Ochoa said Labastida is sorry for his actions and is ashamed and embarrassed. He said when Labastida was in middle school, he withdrew from his family and started hanging out with the "wrong" crew, making bad decisions.
Ochoa said that when Labastida helped with the escape, his brain wasn't fully developed and didn't realize the consequences of his actions, including the "pain and suffering" it would cause his family.
Before showing the certificates Labastida was awarded for classes he took in jail, Ochoa said Labastida has "a lot to give to this world" and he just needs guidance and support.
Labastida told Judge Karen Dean that there was no reason for him to do what he did on Aug. 1 2023, but there is also no reason for his life to be "stunted." He said he believes he can be a productive member of society.
Labastida's family also spoke at the hearing Friday, sharing the toll this incident has taken on their family. His mother Patricia Sanchez said her son "has learned a lesson." She said that she never imagined she would see one of her children standing in front of a judge like this.
"We should (have been) getting ready to go to a graduation or something else," Sanchez said, "not to this."
Labastida's older brother, Nicholas Sanchez, said that Labastida is a hard worker and that with the right guidance, he can become a productive member of society.
The victim of Labastida's assault charge was not present at the hearing and did not wish to make an impact statement.

title: Cambridge man pleads guilty for altering evidence in fatal Easton shooting
author: Maggie Trovato
content:
Cambridge man pleads guilty for altering evidence in fatal Easton shooting

 March 13, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Maggie Trovato | Section: Crime 
 
 559
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — A Cambridge man pleaded guilty Monday to altering evidence in an August 2023 fatal shooting in Easton.Raheem Green, 28, was handed a suspended 18-month sentence with credit for time served and three years of probation — the first year supervised — after entering an Alford plea Monday morning.
An Alford plea allows a person to maintain their innocence while acknowledging the state had enough evidence to obtain a conviction.
The Aug. 7 shooting took place in the 100 block of Blake Street and resulted in the death of Ty Brooks, 55, of Easton.
In late February, 22-year-old Deseir Cornish, of Denton, pleaded guilty to manslaughter and possession of a handgun in the death of Brooks. Cornish was sentenced to 10 years in prison and five years of supervised probation upon his release.
Green had initially been charged with acting as an accessory after the fact of murder for allegedly helping Cornish flee from the scene and discard evidence. The charge was amended to altering physical evidence.
At the plea hearing Monday, Talbot County Circuit Judge Broughton Earnest read the conditions of the plea agreement. He said that per the agreement, the state and defense would agree to dropping an additional charge of accessory after the fact, and Green would receive a fully suspended sentence with a 25-day credit for time served and probation.
At the hearing, Talbot County State's Attorney Joseph Coale detailed what happened the day Brooks was found unresponsive in the grass with three gunshot wounds.
Coale said Brooks had gotten into an argument with a group of young men around a white Range Rover parked on Blake Street that day. He said Brooks left Blake Street and returned with a shotgun, operating an ATV. When Brooks approached the passenger side front window of the Range Rover on the ATV and held up the shotgun, Cornish shot Brooks with a handgun.
Coale said Green was outside the driver's side of the Range Rover at the time and got into a Hyundai to leave the area. He said Cornish, who was in the Range Rover with other individuals, followed Green.
Green told police that he drove to a gas station. At the gas station Cornish asked to use Green's cellphone. After Cornish returned the cellphone to Green, a passenger in the Range Rover told Green where to meet them so they could abandon the Range Rover.
Upon abandoning the vehicle, Green gave the individuals that had been in the Range Rover a ride, Coale said.
After Coale spoke, Green's attorney, Stephanie Shipley, said Green was not a part of the group of young men, adding that Green is in his late 20s. She said Green left the scene in his car when he heard gunshots, and the Range Rover followed him without him telling them to do so.
Shipley later said Green was simply "in the wrong place at the wrong time," and the only mistake he made was lending Cornish his cell phone and giving the individuals in the Range Rover — including Cornish — a ride. She said Green didn't know Brooks had been killed when he gave them the ride.
After accepting the plea, Earnest said that although he did not want to ignore the emotional trauma Brooks' family has faced, he didn't think Green was directly involved in the shooting and accepted the sentencing recommendations made by the State's Attorney's Office and the defense.
