title: OFFICERS WANTED: Mid-Shore law enforcement grapples with recruitment, retention
author: Konner Metz
content:
OFFICERS WANTED: Mid-Shore law enforcement grapples with recruitment, retention

 January 18, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Konner Metz | Section: Local News 
 
 1400
 Words 

 Read News Document

 In his 48 years with the department, Dorchester County Sheriff James Phillips says the current landscape of law enforcement recruiting is the "absolute worst" he's ever seen.His department historically had applications on file at all times, but in recent years, the number of applicants has severely dwindled.
Phillips said while he loves his career, he understands why many are hesitant to become police officers.
"If it were me today, and I was starting over again, I'd probably go and try to be a paid firefighter somewhere," Phillips said, "because their schedules are better, they make good money and they're not under the scrutinization that we are."
For Phillips, increased state oversight on police officer conduct and a social shift in how the career is viewed by the general public have both negatively impacted the recruitment and retention of officers on the Eastern Shore.
Other sheriffs and police chiefs have cited those same state oversight actions, along with growing competition between agencies and a decline in quality applicants as reasons why smaller departments are struggling to staff at 100%.
Easton Police Department Deputy Chief Greg Wright says "police officers that were once held on the pedestal as being heroes are now villains."
"I think that all the negative talk that's broadcasted across the nation does affect these small agencies," Wright said. "There's larger agencies that we've talked to that talk about their struggles, because they're a thousand short of officers. But when you scale that down to a 48-man agency, 10 is a quarter of your agency."
STATE ACTIONSMaryland's Police Accountability Act of 2021 ushered in a new era of police reform, requiring counties to have police accountability boards and repealing the Law Enforcement Officers' Bill of Rights. It came the year after George Floyd's murder by a Minneapolis police officer and calls for reform to prevent police brutality.
Wright believes the enacted reform has positive aspects, but he worries that officers feel the waning trust from the public.
"You feel like you can't be trusted," he said. "They don't trust us to do the job."
In Easton, the police department has 43 of 48 slots full. Wright says the town has always been supportive of its police, and in his 37 years in Easton, he's never felt that community support evaporate.
Wright and Talbot County Sheriff Joe Gamble each mentioned local support is critical to the success of small departments. The Talbot County Sheriff's Office is at 47 of 48 slots, and Gamble says some of that is due to "lateral" transfers — officers choosing Talbot over other nearby departments.
However, multiple sheriffs and chiefs on the Eastern Shore separately raised concerns about the Maryland attorney general's Independent Investigations Division, which investigates all police-involved deaths such as high-speed chases.
Since its inception in 2021, the division has investigated 65 police-related deaths, according to data on its website. A fatal vehicle pursuit in Easton last July — which involved both county deputies and Easton officers — is still under investigation.
Wright says there's no doubt that it's in the back of officers' minds when conducting chases and "could delay their response." Phillips said it not only affects how many applicants Dorchester receives, but also how long current law enforcement employees remain.
"I've had several officers that could've worked longer, but as soon as they got their time then were able to retire, they retired just to get away from it," Phillips said.
Cambridge-Dorchester Fraternal Order of Police Lodge 27 President Thomas Hurley believes the state's actions are hurting recruitment and retention.
"You have to get them in the door, you have to keep them, and when they get old like me, you have to get rid of them," Hurley said. "The only thing that's working right now is retirement."
Hurley — a retired Cambridge officer of 30 years — said he sees officers leaving "all the time now" and that some "feel like they can't be cops."
"Absolutely it affects their job performance," Gamble said of the investigations. "Proactive policing in Maryland is dying. Proactive policing is traffic enforcement, it's DWI enforcement, it's drug enforcement. It's dying. People don't want to go into those units in some of these larger departments."
"Cops are going to shut down," Gamble later said. "They're going to do what they do in the metro areas. They answer the 911 calls and no more."
Last month, Attorney General Anthony Brown announced the indictment of two Anne Arundel County police officers in connection to a fatal 2023 chase. It was the division's first time charging an officer since the state passed a bill in 2023 giving the attorney general prosecutorial power in the investigations instead of local state's attorneys.
The attorney general's office declined a request for comment. In 2023, Brown voiced his support for that bill, noting that the Independent Investigations Division has "a team of experienced criminal prosecutors and investigators" and the measure to ensure independence and transparency "would fall in line with police accountability in many other states."
"The public should have confidence that prosecution decisions are made in an impartial manner, by people who do not work together or rely on each other professionally or personally," Brown wrote in a letter addressed to Maryland House Judiciary Committee Chair Luke Clippinger.
{h3 style="text-align: center "}PATH FORWARD{/h3}
While legislative decisions have drawn worries that police recruiting may only become more difficult, law enforcement leaders are also aware of challenges such as applicant quality, salaries and tight competition.
In Caroline County, Sheriff Donnie Baker noted that agencies in Delaware create serious competition in terms of hiring.
Sgt. Timothy Maloney of the Milford Police Department, around 20 miles from the Maryland border, said his department sees a "consistent" one to two Maryland officers apply during each hiring cycle.
The Caroline County Sheriff's Office has 46 of 48 positions staffed. Baker said many officers are working overtime to provide coverage in the towns of Ridgely and Greensboro.
Ridgely has been without a police department since it was suspended by the town last March, while Greensboro is down to Chief Lenox Trams as its lone officer.
Cambridge Police Department Chief Justin Todd said the hiring process remains "strict," and that many applicants fail background checks or the police academy.
Todd, though, has seen improvement in the last few years. Currently, 36 of 40 positions are filled in Cambridge, compared to 29 in the summer of 2022, despite the department's $56,000 starting salary for officers in the academy being slightly below Dorchester County ($57,458) and other agencies.
"The competition per agency is so strong," Todd said. "You have different agencies that make more money, say, than us. So it's a challenge for us to recruit the good officers."
This year, the Cambridge chief says the goal is to increase recruitment at job fairs, colleges and universities. He already feels the City of Cambridge and its council has been supportive of the police department's efforts.
"We know there's qualified applicants and great people out there that want to be officers," Todd said. "I think that we just need to promote ourselves better."
Maryland State Police leaders are similarly focusing on recruitment. Lt. Col. Scott Keyser, chief of MSP's Support Services Bureau, said the department is "incredibly aggressive," noting it went to 558 events and contacted more than 19,000 applicants last year.
MSP is authorized to have 1,564 troopers and there are currently 155 vacancies, Keyser said. He said the department's unique task is recruiting amid what is a "rigorous" and "daunting" hiring process.
"We're casting a wide net, just as far as we can go to get anybody that might be pursuing a career in law enforcement," Keyser said. "We want to bring them to the Maryland State Police."
In Easton, Wright said it's difficult to compete with MSP, though the town focuses on an appealing pension plan and other perks to recruit. State troopers start at a $68,000 salary upon training graduation, which is around $5,000 to $10,000 more than many departments on the Mid-Shore.
In terms of a path forward for recruiting, Wright sees it as a "reset button." Since George Floyd's death, Wright believes all officers have been viewed in "the same light," which has affected both public perception and desire to become an officer.
"We have to gain the trust, and we probably have to start young again," Wright said. "As they grow up, let them see that we're not the monsters that the news or the parents or society's making us look to be."
"We have no choice. We have to regain our fanbase," he continued. "And make people interested and excited about doing the job."

title: American Legion Post 77 looking to jumpstart Hometown Heroes banner project
author: KONNER METZ kmetz@chespub.com
content:
American Legion Post 77 looking to jumpstart Hometown Heroes banner project

 August 22, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: KONNER METZ kmetz@chespub.com | Section: Local News 
 
 428
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — An effort to honor past and present veterans, firefighters and police officers gained momentum at the Easton Town Council on Monday evening.Joan Harris-Brooks, speaking on behalf of Blake-Blackston American Legion Post 77, asked the council to partner with the group in creating a banner program so that families of Talbot County veterans, firefighters and officers can honor their loved ones.
Harris-Brooks said the banners would be placed on Ward 4 roads such as Glenwood Avenue, Port Street and West Street. Her father, John Harris Jr., and her uncle were members of Post 77, which operates on Glenwood Avenue.
With members of Post 77 in attendance, council members expressed nothing but support for the project.
"I think that this is a great endeavor," Ward 4 Council Member the Rev. Elmer Davis said. "(It's important) that we don't lose the memory of those persons who fought for our country. I believe it's our responsibility to help out with this project. Secondly, it doesn't cost the town a dime."
The Hometown Heroes Banner program began in 2006 in Harrisburg, Pennsylvania. Today, Mid-Shore towns including Federalsburg, Hurlock and Preston showcase banners honoring past and present veterans.
Harris-Brooks said the banners would cost $200 each. There will be no ask of the council to provide any money for the project.
She asked that the town office hold blank applications for interested families, in addition to applications being advertised on social media and at Post 77.
"It will instill a sense of pride and unity in Easton and for our country," Harris-Brooks told the council. "It is our goal that you grant us approval. And we believe that if you grant us an approval, this will make a landmark for you as our councilmen."
Council members unanimously approved the request. Prior to voting, the council expressed hopes that the banner project could extend to the entire town.
Harris-Brooks said that Post 77 will accept donations from the community that can help families who cannot afford the cost of a banner. She added that Post 77 will work with American Legion Talbot Post 70, Easton Utilities and the town as the project comes to life.
"I think our children need to be aware," Harris-Brooks said. "We still have young people still enlisted in the service. I will just very passionately say my uncle was a member of Post 77 … He gave his ultimate self serving."
Commander Victor Middleton thanked the council for their support following the approval.
"When people say thank you for your service, it really lifted me up just now to a higher level," Middleton said. "And I thank you all."

title: Easton's new fire chief has plans for equipment, recruitment
author: Konner Metz
content:
Easton's new fire chief has plans for equipment, recruitment

 January 18, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Konner Metz | Section: Local News 
 
 626
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — J.R. Dobson grew up around the fire house, always knowing he wanted to be a firefighter.In his teenage years, Dobson joined the Trappe Volunteer Fire Company as a junior cadet, and by 16 he began riding the fire trucks. He fondly recalls the "everybody knew everybody" aspect of the tight-knit community.
Dobson eventually moved to Easton, beginning his journey with the Easton Volunteer Fire Department in 2003. Over time, he's served in a number of roles, including most recently, assistant chief.
Now he's taking on the department's top role for the first time. Dobson was elected the department's chief in December.
With a wife and two daughters, timing was everything for Dobson when considering the commitment to assume a role as demanding as Easton fire chief. The timing is right, he said, and he's looking forward to leading and making a difference.
"There's a lot of tradition here," Dobson said. "It's certainly the biggest department in the county. It's got probably the most going on out of all the departments in the county. I think just being here, seeing how this department operates versus a small department. It's a business. And we're all here for free, none of us get paid."
Dobson officially began as chief this month. Sonny Jones just wrapped up his third two-year term leading the department.
Dobson, who volunteers at the fire department as all the firefighters do, is a patrol and operations commander at the Talbot County Sheriff's Office. He believes his experience leading around 35 deputies across multiple divisions will translate to his duties in the fire house.
"I think that I bring a lot of management skills, leadership skills," Dobson said. "Just from my experience there, I think it helps you here."
Thus far, Dobson says the support he's received has been "overwhelming."
Past fire chiefs have reached out, and he hopes to pick up one thing from each of them to set himself up for success. For instance, Jones' ability as an incident commander is something Dobson admires.
"If there were ever a bad day anybody was having, he's who you would want there," Dobson said of Jones. "Just the way he kind of rolls through an incident scene. He's been there and done that kind of thing."
Similarly, Jones — who is remaining involved with the department — spoke highly of Dobson.
"I've known J.R. the entire time that I've been a member of the Easton fire department," Jones said. "J.R. is a first-rate guy. He's a terrific leader. He has many, many qualities which will bode well for him as the chief of the department."
Some of the ongoing projects the new fire chief has his eye on include purchasing a utility vehicle to use for Rails to Trails and woods fires, buying a new engine and updating box alarm assignments. He also wants to implement some new standard operating procedures.
Dobson said he hopes to nail down a handful of tasks for the year and keep circling back to see what progress is being made. At the top of his list is recruitment and retention of volunteers.
"I think it all starts with recruiting. I think it all starts with retention," Dobson said. "Those are things that we've done well in the past, although the last year or so we haven't gotten as many members as we would like. And sometimes we'll get members in and they don't realize the commitment."
While acknowledging the town's consistent support of the department over the years, Dobson believes Easton Fire can do better in attracting more volunteers amid struggles statewide and nationwide to fill volunteer fire departments.
"We got to get people in here," Dobson said. "We've got to get these trucks out. And I think that the way the town's growing, if we don't grow with it, then we're failing ourselves."

title: Man sentenced to life without parole for 2023 murder of Jasmine Hicks
author: Matt Wynn mwynn@somdnews.com
content:
Man sentenced to life without parole for 2023 murder of Jasmine Hicks

 August 6, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Matt Wynn mwynn@somdnews.com | Section: News 
 
 579
 Words 

 Read News Document

 On Aug. 6, Deanthony Lamont Warrick, 35, was sentenced to life without parole for the April 2023 murder of Jasmine Hicks.Hicks was stabbed to death in the overnight hours of April 12, 2023 after an argument with Warrick. She was 29 at the time.
A video captured by a security camera system on a nearby house was presented during the trial.
The video depicted Hicks and Warrick leaving a red Chrysler vehicle in the 2300 block of Woodberry Drive in Bryans Road, when Warrick realized that PCP, a handgun and an assault rifle were missing from the vehicle, according to testimony.
Warrick argued with Hicks and got progressively louder until Warrick grabbed a knife and repeatedly stabbed Hicks. Police said lacerations were found on her head, neck, hands and upper arms.
Hicks could be heard on tape, from across the street, saying, "You've already killed me. I'm already dead."
Warrick tried to move Hicks, who was still alive at the time, into his car. He gave up and fled the scene.
Hicks' family attended en masse for the sentencing, with Assistant State's Attorney Laura Caspar presenting the case to give Warrick life without parole.
Caspar told Judge William R. Greer that the State's Attorney's Office does not seek this sentence in every case, but that the murder of Jasmine Hicks was "vile, malicious and vengeful."
Warrick claimed at one point that Hicks had a gun and that the killing was in self-defense, but the footage from the camera that caught the murder showed otherwise.
"Where's my s—," Warrick could be heard screaming on the footage, looking for PCP and a firearm that Hicks' brother took in fear that he would use the firearm on his sister after he had pointed the firearm at a vehicle Hicks was in.
"There was no fear there," Caspar said. "There was no gun and he knew it."
After the argument escalated, Warrick stabbed Hicks a number of times before saying, "Don't make me kill you."
Hicks replied, "You already did."
Caspar could only speculate the horror that Hicks had to endure after Warrick left the scene of the murder, where Hicks was alive for another hour and a half.
Members of Hicks' family came forward to ask that Greer impose the maximum sentence.
Arthur Lancaster, Hicks' uncle, told the judge that Hicks was the type of person that would "brighten your day" and that she was a loving mother to her three children.
"Today, your honor, we are looking for closure," Lancaster said. "Deanthony Warrick is an atrocious, cruel, heinous, cold-blooded murderer."
Lancaster called Warrick a "wild animal" before saying, "Wild animals need to be caged."
Mary Lawson — Hicks' mother — fought tears to say, "She went too soon."
Lawson recalled how Hicks' children came home from school and were looking for their mother, but she had to tell them that she would not be there.
"I'll be there every time," Lawson said.
Andre Mahasa, Warrick's attorney, said that while he and Warrick respected the jury's verdict, they still believed that there was no premeditation in the murder and that it should have been second-degree murder at most.
Warrick had nothing to say to the judge after being informed of his right to speak.
During the sentencing, Greer dismissed Warrick's claim that Hicks had a firearm, saying that at some point during the stabbing, he had to realize that there was no gun.
Greer said that Warrick's actions after the attack showed a lack of empathy.
"Jasmine Hicks died alone in the night on the cold ground," Greer said before imposing a life sentence on Warrick.

 CAMBRIDGE — Two students from Cambridge-South Dorchester High School were arrested on the second day of school after multiple fights broke out, Dorchester County Sheriff Jimmy Phillips said.The school resource deputy alerted the Sheriff's Office that a student was assaulting the school safety monitor. title: 2 more charged with murder of man in Cambridge
author: Konner Metz
content:
2 more charged with murder of man in Cambridge

 August 1, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Konner Metz | Section: News 
 
 426
 Words 

 Read News Document

 CAMBRIDGE — Police have arrested two more Cambridge men on murder charges in connection to a fatal shooting in June, bringing the total of murder arrests on the case to four.Jasire Kane, 20, and Kah'Zion Johnson, 18, were arrested on July 25 and July 29, respectively, on first-degree murder charges. Police identified them as suspects in the June 8 shooting of 23-year-old Alyson Elien of Seaford, Delaware.
Just after 8:30 p.m. the night of the shooting, officers responded to the 900 block of Camelia Street in Cambridge. They found Elien lying outside of a vehicle in a driveway with a gunshot wound to his head. He was pronounced dead at a hospital.
Per court records, police allege Kane and Johnson acted as two of the "co-conspirators" in a five-person operation to rob and kill Elien.
Court records identify 15-year-old Jakai Wilson as the alleged shooter. Police say Wilson, followed by four others, walked up to Elien's car, opened the driver side door and shot him, the victim falling out of his vehicle. The five people then fled, court records say.
Charging documents for Kane allege he returned to Elien's body shortly after Elien was shot.
"After Elien was shot and lying on the driveway with life threatening injuries," Kane allegedly took "something off Elien" and ran away, per court records.
Later, a crowd formed near the scene, and two other subjects — not any of the five main suspects — allegedly stole a bag from Elien's vehicle, police wrote.
Charging documents show police identified Kane and Johnson through video footage. Johnson was also identified during witness interviews, court records state.
Kane faces 12 total counts, including first- and second-degree murder, first- and second-degree assault, robbery, firearm use and more. He's being held without bond. A preliminary hearing is set for Aug. 25.
Johnson, meanwhile, faces 13 counts, including first- and second-degree murder, first- and second-degree assault, robbery, firearm use and more. He's being held without bond. A preliminary hearing is set for Aug. 28.
Wilson was arrested June 10, two days after the murder. He was charged with first- and second-degree murder, first- and second-degree assault, and other firearm and armed robbery counts. Wilson is being charged as an adult and held without bond; however, court dates for Wilson are not publicly available since he is a minor.
18-year-old Nisiah Fletcher, of Cambridge, was arrested on July 6. Fletcher faces similar murder, firearm and robbery charges to Wilson. Fletcher is being held without bond. A preliminary hearing is set for Aug. 5.
Police have not announced an arrest of the fifth suspect in connection to the shooting.

title: Santa On The Shore: St. Nick, Mrs. Claus Visit Local Firehouse

Santa On The Shore: St. Nick, Mrs. Claus Visit Local Firehouse

 Once they entered the firehouse door, the lucky local children who attended this year's Lunch with Santa on Dec. 3, were mesmerized by only one thing in the room. There, sitting in his big chair, was Santa.And it wasn't just any Santa, it was the real Santa.
Even parents were loving the magic.
"I am very happy I got to come to Chestertown today," Santa said. "We've been so busy at the North Pole. And then we had this fog- lucky thing I had Rudolph to guide the way." This year for the first time the fire company was able to welcome Mrs. Claus as well.
"I am usually so busy monitoring the elves who are getting ready for Christmas," she explained.
"But I managed to get away this afternoon." This family-friendly annual event is sponsored by the Chestertown Volunteer Fire Company, whose members are committed to making the holiday memorable for local families.
Along with the choice of pizza or hot dogs, families were offered an enormous display of a variety of cookies, lovingly prepared by company members.
The most popular? "Definitely the s'mores," longtime fire company family member Megan Darling said, "but chocolate chip is a close second." Numerous tables were set up in the firehall, with different crafts at each.
Kids were busily traveling to new spots, making ornaments and snowmen throughout the day.
But the purpose of their visit was to meet Santa and let him know what they were looking for on Christmas morning.
A Barbie Dreamhouse and her pink corvette was one of the most popular requests.
"Do you know that the elves made one for themselves?" Santa asked a little one. "They have the best time driving it around in the snow." Ken Young, a member of the company and professional photographer, was there to catch the moment when children shared some time with Old St. Nick.
"This is my third year doing it," said Young. "I bring my special equipment, including a printer where I can print the photo out for the parents before they leave." Cindy Morris, who organizes the event, said the day wasn't about the funds raised. "This is us supporting our community."

State Police arrest man in connection to 2021 homicide

 October 23, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: STAFF REPORT | Section: Crime 
 
 329

 Read News Document

 Maryland State Police homicide investigators arrested a wanted fugitive in connection with a Trappe homicide that took place nearly three years ago.Ibarra Juarez, 32, is charged with first and second-degree murder, along with other related criminal charges in relation to the killing of Marta Merina, 33, on Christmas Eve in 2021.
That morning, police responded to the 2900 block of Howell Point Road for an apparent shooting. Upon their arrival, they found Merina outside of her home with a gunshot wound. According to prior reporting in the Star Democrat, Merina was located inside a vehicle with multiple bullet holes. She was pronounced dead on the scene.
Following an investigation by the Maryland State Police Homicide Unit and consultation with the Talbot County State's Attorney's Office, a felony arrest warrant was issued for Juarez a few days later.
Juarez was located by Mexican authorities for an unrelated crime in Oaxaca, Mexico on March 24, 2022. The U.S. Department of Justice's Office of International Affairs worked with Mexican prosecutors to request Juarez's provisional arrest in April 2022. Extradition was granted on Oct. 5, 2022, but was deferred pending completion of Juarez's sentence in Mexico.
Juarez was extradited to Maryland Tuesday and processed at the Maryland State Police Easton Barracks. He is currently being held at the Talbot County Detention Center without bond.
Investigators from the Maryland State Police Homicide Unit led the investigation. Assistance was provided by troopers from the Easton Barrack, the Maryland State Police Criminal Intelligence Section, crime scene technicians from the Forensic Sciences Division, troopers from the Maryland State Apprehension Team, Talbot County Sheriff's Office, Talbot County State's Attorney's Office, the Maryland Coordination and Analysis Center, Salisbury City Police Department and the Fruitland Police Department.
Federal law enforcement assistance was provided by the United States Marshals Service Baltimore Field Office and the Capital Area Regional Fugitive Task Force, and the United States Department of Justice's Office of International Affairs, who worked with law enforcement partners in Mexico to secure Juarez's arrest and extradition.

title: Police: Man, 63, took inappropriate photos of girls at volleyball games
author: Carl Hamilton cahamilton@chespub.com
content:
Police: Man, 63, took inappropriate photos of girls at volleyball games

 October 9, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Carl Hamilton cahamilton@chespub.com | Section: News 
 
 840
 Words 

 Read News Document

 CHESAPEAKE CITY — A 63-year-old man is charged with disturbing school operation and disorderly conduct after he allegedly took numerous inappropriate photos and videos of girls playing volleyball matches inside the Bohemia Manor High School gymnasium, according to Cecil County District Court records.Investigators identified the suspect as Michael Cornell Griffin of Townsend, Del.
Maryland State Police Master Trooper Jason Proctor conducted an on-scene investigation during the incident, which occurred shortly before 8 p.m. on Thursday, and he was able to view the photographic content of the suspect's cell phone after Griffin had given verbal consent to do so, police reported.
"I reviewed the photo album and observed that it contained several photographs and videos of the junior varsity teams and varsity teams from both schools: Bohemia Manor High School and Perryville High School . . . The photographs observed in the photo album were of the buttock areas of the juvenile aged female players," Proctor summarized in his written statement of probable cause.
The investigator noted, "The uniform shorts that are worn by all the volleyball players are tight in nature; however, the photographs that were taken were zoomed in by Griffin revealing inappropriate detail, as certain curvature of the female players body parts could be clearly observed."
Court records indicate that the investigation leading to the two criminal charges against Griffin started after spectators noticed the suspect acting suspiciously in the bleachers during the volleyball game, police said. The initial complainant was a 41-year-old woman, court records show. (It is not clear if Griffin had direct ties to the volleyball competition, such as a relative who was one of the players.)
The complainants had seen the suspect "deliberately zoom in on the players' buttock areas" while he was taking digital photos with his cell phone, court records allege.
Griffin's alleged actions caused nearby parents and other spectators to ask him why he was taking pictures, creating a scene that diverted some of the spectators' attention away from the volleyball game, according to the charging document.
"This was actively causing disturbance within the stands," court records allege.
After spectators complained and pointed to the suspect, the trooper escorted Griffin from the gymnasium into the lobby, police said. Bohemia Manor Middle School Assistant Principal Stacy Rahnama was in the lobby and was present during the on-scene investigation, police added.
Proctor informed Griffin that he had been accused of taking inappropriate photos of female volleyball players, court records show. Griffin denied taking pictures of the players and started opening and closing the photo album on his phone, according to court records.
"It appeared as if he was trying to hide the photographs. Griffin appeared to be extremely nervous while speaking with me. I observed his right hand and fingers shake multiple times as he was scrolling through his phone," Proctor outlined in court records.
At that point, the trooper asked Griffin if he would be willing to show him the photos that he had taken and Griffin gave verbal consent, court records show. During that viewing of the photographic content of Griffin's cell phone, Proctor and Rahnama saw numerous inappropriate photos and videos of the female volleyball players, court records allege.
"While reviewing the photo albums, the initial complainant entered the lobby and made inquiries as to whether or not her daughter's photograph was on his phone and was making comments that she wanted the photographs deleted," according to the charging document.
Proctor then escorted Griffin out of the building and into the breezeway, where — with the suspect's consent — he and Rahnama deleted all of the questionable pictures and videos found in the phone's photo library and then from the phone's trash bin file, court records show.
"While this was taking place, a group of patrons had gathered in the lobby and were actively observing my interactions with Griffin. Another patron had to tell that group of people to remain inside and not to interfere, as they were making threats to assault Griffin due to his actions," according to the charging document, which indicates that the group obeyed and returned to the gymnasium.
After the deletion of the photos and videos, Rahnama requested that Griffin leave the school property, police said. The trooper then escorted Griffin to his 2014 Chrysler 200 that was parked in the school lot and ordered him to leave the premises, which Griffin did, police added.
At the end of his written statement of probable cause, Proctor summarized, "Griffin's direct actions of being visible while he was taking inappropriate and offensive photographs (by way of zooming in) caused direct disturbance within the stands of the sporting event which is also disruption of school activities."
Griffin was not arrested but, instead, was charged through a criminal summons that was issued on Monday, court records show. Griffin is charged with disturbing school operation, a misdemeanor that carries a maximum six-month penalty and a $2,500 fine if convicted; and disorderly conduct, which is punishable by up to 60 days in jail and a $500 fine if convicted, according to court records.
Griffin is scheduled to appear for a preliminary inquiry on Nov. 25, court records show.

title: 'Just grateful no one was home' - Resident reflects on Wednesday evening house fire
author: Tom Mccall; tmccall@chespub.com
content:
'Just grateful no one was home' - Resident reflects on Wednesday evening house fire

 October 27, 2023 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Tom Mccall; tmccall@chespub.com | Page: 3 | Section: News

 EASTON - Clara Dorsey was sitting in a red beach chair with neighbors, family and friends on the curb in front of the melted yellow siding and charred timbers of her home on Thursday, Oct. 26.Red caution tape blew in the breeze and even the metal house number, 21, is seared.The evening before, a structure fire tore through the duplex where Dorsey has rented her apartment for 20 years."I am just glad it wasn't in the night time," she said."We were sitting on the porch, and I left for a few minutes. When I came back it was all on fire." According to the fire marshal, there were no injuries or fatalities reported in the blaze, but all of the residents' belongings were lost.Dorsey's beloved terrier, Peanut, has been missing since the event. She said she thought about looking for the remains in the charred rubble, but she is pretty sure there is nothing left.The fire, which broke out at 21 South West Street in Easton shortly after 5:30 p.m. on Wednesday, drew the attention of passersby, who alerted emergency officials to the blaze."It was some of them from the American Legion (which is next door) that were sitting there playing cards. They looked out the window," Dorsey said.The fire marshal estimates that $50,000 worth of damage was done to the building.They could not determine the smoke alarm status, and there was no sprinkler action."The building consisted of two apartments with the fire originating in the kitchen area of the downstairs apartment," the fire marshal wrote in a report about the incident."The families in both apartments were displaced due to the fire." Investigations into the preliminary cause of the blaze are still ongoing.Dorsey said her next step is to find a new place to live.She said she is being taken care of and has a place to sleep in the meantime."If everybody could say a prayer and thanks to everybody.This is different than yesterday when it happened.It was chaotic," Dorsey said.60 emergency personnel responded to the fire, according to the fire marshal's report, representing five volunteer fire departments, along with law enforcement and EMS personnel.Dorsey said in the aftermath of the event, she leans on gratitude that no one was hurt. She is also grateful she had renter's insurance."I've got to wait for the insurance adjuster to call me.They want to come and take pictures," she said.A GoFundMe has been established by Dorsey's grandson, De'Andre Dorsey.In the description on the page, De'Andre wrote "Unfortunately my grandma's house caught on fire today (10/25), and she lost everything. Her dog, Peanut, who was by her side for 14 years, clothes, family photos, important letters and documents, several sentimental items, and, unfortunately, her savings were in her house." He continued, "My grandmother has given her heart to the community of Easton, and today she is in desperate need of yours." More details can be found at https://www.gofundme.com/f/7u4cy-my-grandma.

The fire is said to have originated in the kitchen of the duplex's downstairs unit.

title: Poultry property outside Denton suffers 2nd fire in as many days

Poultry property outside Denton suffers 2nd fire in as many days

 July 2, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Konner Metz | Section: Local News

 DENTON — A poultry property outside Denton was the site of a fire Wednesday morning, marking the second consecutive day crews battled a blaze at the property's chicken houses.The two fires occurred at two different chicken houses located southwest of Denton on the 8600 block of Tuckahoe Road. Terry Tribbett's family owns the chicken houses. She said the first fire was at Tuckahoe River Farm Poultry LLC and the second at L&B Farms LLC.
The Denton Volunteer Fire Company, along with other agencies, responded to both incidents. Denton Fire Chief Doug Higgs said both were second-alarm fires, each taking around three hours to control.
Both chicken houses involved were housing around 35,000 chickens each, Higgs added.
"(Crews) arrived, they had over 50% of the chicken house was involved in fire, and then today was roughly the same," Higgs said on Wednesday after returning to the Denton fire house.
In a statement Wednesday, Tribbett expressed deep appreciation for the volunteer firefighters.
"It doesn't matter if it's day or night, rain or shine, hot or cold, they are called and they come," Tribbett wrote. "We certainly appreciate all their efforts and dedication."
After Tuesday's fire, which began around 3:20 a.m., one firefighter received heat exhaustion treatment at a local hospital. No other injuries were reported. Higgs said no injuries occurred as a result of Wednesday's blaze.
On Tuesday, the Office of the State Fire Marshal released an investigation report on the first fire, estimating $525,000 in damages.
The fire marshal said the first fire's cause was still under investigation. On Wednesday, Higgs said both fires were likely due to electrical issues, though he noted that's not yet official.
"I think it's just unlucky," Higgs said. "Chicken houses are dirty because of the feathers and dust."
Tribbett said the family is thankful for all of the community members who have reached out with prayers and support in the last two days.
"We too are truly blessed even through this trying time," she wrote.
Ahmad Garnett contributed to this report.

title: It's time to confront ongoing youth violence
author: Armstrong Williams
content:
It's time to confront ongoing youth violence

 September 15, 2023 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Armstrong Williams | Page: 7 | Section: News 
 
 689
 Words 

 Read News Document

 If you go to Google and type "heinous crimes up with young people," you'll see over 2 billion results.It's a stark reminder that the alarming trend of young people committing gruesome acts isn't a new phenomenon, but the sheer proliferation and frequency of these acts most certainly is. Our society is grappling with a disconcerting reality - a reality born out of the convergence of various factors.From the messages embedded in our music to the desensitizing violence prevalent in our culture, and even the erosion of moral and ethical values, each contributes to the emergence of a more violent society.It's a society where individuals no longer temper their darkest impulses, and regrettably, it's our youth who often find themselves on the frontline, manifesting behaviors at an unacceptable rate. This is a phenomenon that should deeply trouble us all and lead us to pause in concern for the direction in which our society is headed.These young individuals, driven by a cocktail of influences, often react impulsively or, in the gravest of cases, meticulously plan calculated crimes that result in the loss of innocent lives. We've witnessed stories like that of Mackenzie Shirilla, a name etched into the annals of a society grappling with the aftermath of senseless violence.Shirilla was recently found guilty of the murder of her boyfriend, Dominic Russo, and her friend, Davion Flanagan. Their tragic deaths underscore the gravity of the situation we're facing - a situation where young people are becoming entangled in webs of aggression and desperation. In Shirilla's case, she purposely sped up her car to 100 mph and drove straight into a wall, instantly killing her boyfriend and friend.The breakdown of morality in our society is contributing to this disturbing trend. Traditional values that once served as guiding principles seem to be waning, leaving a moral vacuum in which right and wrong are increasingly ambiguous. The erosion of moral foundations means that young people are less equipped to distinguish between ethical choices and destructive actions.The deterioration of ethics further compounds the issue. Ethical conduct is the cornerstone of a civilized society, fostering a sense of responsibility and accountability. Yet, as we witness these disturbing trends among our youth, it becomes evident that the concept of ethics is losing its grip. The pursuit of personal gain, even at the expense of others, has become alarmingly normalized.As we reflect on these developments, the implications for our future are profoundly concerning. A society that permits the erosion of morality and ethics in its younger generation is sowing the seeds of its own demise. The actions of today's youth foreshadow the trajectory of tomorrow's adults. If we fail to address these concerning trends, we risk a future marked by increased violence, social fragmentation and a dearth of empathy.It's time for us to confront these unsettling truths and take meaningful action. By reemphasizing morality and ethics in our families, communities and institutions, we can recalibrate the moral compass of our youth. This requires an unwavering commitment to fostering values that prioritize human dignity, compassion and respect for one another. Only through concerted efforts to restore these foundational principles can we hope to guide our society toward a more harmonious and promising future.This alarming trend of young people exhibiting violence and aggression should serve as an urgent wake-up call for our educational institutions. We must prioritize emotional education alongside academic excellence. By equipping our youth with the tools to manage their emotions, resolve conflicts constructively and communicate effectively, we can help curb the escalation of anger and violence.It's imperative that our schools become places not only of intellectual growth but also of emotional well-being and character development.The rising wave of heinous acts committed by young people underscores the pressing need for a comprehensive societal response. We must address the erosion of morality and ethics, and we must prioritize emotional education within our education system. This is a challenge that requires the collective effort of families, communities, educators and cultural influencers. By refocusing on our shared values, investing in the emotional well-being of our youth and fostering a renewed sense of empathy, we can shape a society that rejects violence and paves the way for a brighter and more harmonious future.COPYRIGHT 2023 CREATORS.COM

 DENTON - CASA of Caroline welcomed veterans of the armed forces to its annual Veterans Day Heroes Breakfast Friday, Nov. 10, at the Denton Diner.From a former corporal to a retired lieutenant colonel, local veterans enjoyed the free breakfast hosted by the nonprofit organization that "advocates for the best interest of all abused and neglected children who are in the Caroline County court system through no fault of their own," according to carolinecasa.org.Executive Director Amy Horne welcomed about two dozen veterans. "Anybody who has had the courage to put on the uniform is a hero in my mind," she said.The 7:30 a.m. gathering began with a prayer led by Pastor Don Reynolds of Calvary Baptist Church in Denton. He is also a retired lieutenant colonel with the Maryland Army National Guard.Horne read a lengthy statement from U.S. Sen.Ben Cardin, who expressed his "profound admiration for the unwavering service and sacrifices of our veterans," particularly recognizing Maryland veterans who have served in every armed conflict since the Revolutionary War.Following a moving short video that depicted a military veteran, who is a court-appointed special advocate (CASA) volunteer, helping a young child. A few veterans wiped tears from their eyes."At CASA, we really want to honor and recognize our veterans because veterans are people who protect our freedoms, just like our advocates are the people who protect the rights of the children we serve," Horne said.She said her late father, Talbot County Circuit Court Judge William S.Horne, who was an Army veteran, helped bring the CASA program to the Eastern Shore in 1990.Denton Town Councilman and former Marine Keith Johnson is also president of CASA of Caroline.After some good-natured ribbing of the other service branches, Johnson asked veterans to consider becoming CASA volunteers."Why is CASA, a child advocacy group, hosting a Veterans Day (event)?" he asked, answering the question by listing traits that correlate between veterans and CASA volunteers."Discipline, fighting spirit, leadership, resiliency. We see our veterans as difference-makers in the world.They're mission-ready," said Johnson, whose wife is CASA volunteer Stephanie Johnson."Being married to an advocate, I know that those traits overlap," he said. "Our advocates make a difference every day, our staff makes a difference every day." "As a (Maryland State) trooper, I served about three years as the primary investigator for Caroline County for the Maryland State Police, dealing with child abuse, child neglect," Johnson said. "There's a need in our county for advocates because our children are underserved and our children live as victims of abuse and victims of neglect every day." Johnson appealed to the gathered veterans to consider becoming a CASA volunteer."If you're not an advocate, think about what you can do different this year," he said. "The military focuses on protecting our country, while at CASA we want to protect tomorrow's future - our children."

 QUEEN ANNE - A Queen Anne man is facing multiple charges in connection to two assaults earlier this year, police said.Travis N. Lynch, 33, is charged with first-and second-degree assault and reckless endangerment stemming from incidents in September and October.

Investigators with the Talbot County Sheriff's Office responded to the University of Maryland Shore Emergency Center at Queenstown on Friday, Dec. 22, and interviewed a woman who said she was the victim of two separate assaults in the 13000 block of Cannery Road in Queen Anne.

title: Easton police chief: Traffic stops bill would have 'drastic' impacts on police work
author: Konner Metz
content:
Easton police chief: Traffic stops bill would have 'drastic' impacts on police work

 February 20, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Konner Metz | Section: Local News 
 
 478
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — Police Chief Alan Lowrey raised concerns over a proposed bill in the state legislature that would limit police officers' abilities to make traffic stops for certain violations.Senate Bill 292, cross-filed in the House of Delegates, would shift many primary offenses to secondary offenses, including improper use of headlights and taillights, failing to use turn signals, missing or improper license plates, and excessive noise.
That change would mean police officers can only cite a driver for those offenses if they pull over the driver for a different, primary offense.
During an Easton Town Council meeting Monday, Lowrey, also serving as the interim town manager, said the bill's proposed changes would be "drastic" and negatively impact police in detecting crime.
"There's a number of concerns on my part as the chief of police, and I've spoken with my staff about this," Lowrey said.
Lowrey said offenses such as driving without headlights are common signs indicating potential impaired driving. He said all of the offenses that would be reclassified are safety issues.
"I personally have arrested a number of people, based upon traffic stops, for serious crimes," Lowrey said.
As written, the bill seeks to make evidence gathered during traffic stops inadmissible if an officer fails to state their name, identification number, agency and reason for the stop. Lowrey called that measure "drastic" as well.
Sen. Charles Sydnor III (D-Baltimore County) is the bill's sponsor. At a Jan. 28 Senate Judicial Proceedings hearing, Sydnor noted Baltimore County statistics that indicated Black and Hispanic drivers face inequities in the rate of citations issued.
"It is these disparities that spurred me to seek and introduce a legislative remedy," Sydnor said.
Sydnor said he worked with the Maryland Office of the Public Defender on the drafted bill. Moving primary violations to fall under secondary violations make way for technologies such as cameras to detect traffic violations, the senator said.
"Technology that can be modified to do what people do today," Sydnor said. "So really, this bill kicks off a conversation about, I would say, a reimagining of how we deal with traffic offenses on the highways."
At the hearing, though, some legislators and law enforcement officials from around the state spoke unfavorably of the legislation.
Those conversations around Maryland have continued in the weeks since. Last month, the Caroline County Commissioners discussed the bill at a meeting and expressed intent to write a letter in opposition.
Monday in Easton, Ward 2 Councilmember Don Abbatiello said the job of being a police officer is "tough enough as it is."
"We don't need to make it any tougher," Abbatiello said. "So I would support anything that the town would like to do in order to try to prevent this from passing."
Town Council President Frank Gunsallus asked Lowrey how the town could express its concerns regarding the bill. Lowrey suggested drafting a letter.
Following discussion, Easton councilmembers voted unanimously to send correspondence to committees in Annapolis opposing the bill.

title: Indictment returned for man who allegedly killed girlfriend, buried her in forest

Indictment returned for man who allegedly killed girlfriend, buried her in forest

 Words

 A man charged with murdering his girlfriend is back in Charles County after being returned from U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement custody.The state's attorney for Charles County advised that on Friday, April 25, a grand jury returned an indictment for Keycy Robinson Alexi Barrera-Rosa, 24, of Waldorf for the murder of Lesbia Mileth Ramirez Guerra.
The indictment charges Barrera-Rosa with first-degree murder, second-degree murder and making a false report, a release from the state's attorney's office said.
On April 2, Barrera-Rosa contacted the Charles County Sheriff's Office to report that his girlfriend, Guerra, was missing from their Waldorf residence. During the investigation, detectives reviewed video surveillance showing the victim entering their residence on March 31 but never exiting, the release said.
Witnesses reported that during the early morning hours of April 1 Barrera-Rosa and Guerra were allegedly in a violent argument.
During the afternoon of April 1, video surveillance allegedly captured Barrera-Rosa grabbing a large plastic bin from a shed in his backyard and carrying it to the back of the house, the state's attorney's office said.
Barrera-Rosa then drove his truck to the back of the house.
Cellular tower data records indicate that Barrera-Rosa traveled to Prince George's County to meet with his uncle, Rolvin Eduardo Barerra-Barerra, at a construction worksite, according to the release.
Further cellular records indicate that Barrera-Rosa and his uncle traveled to a secluded, densely wooded intersection in the area of Cedarville State Park.
Barerra-Barerra was interviewed by detectives and reported that on April 1 his nephew told him that he had killed his girlfriend by strangulation and asked for help with hiding the body, the release said.
He further stated that when Barrera-Rosa allegedly traveled to his work site in Prince George's County, the woman was already deceased and in a plastic bin in the back of Barrera-Rosa's vehicle.
The uncle, Barerra-Barerra, allegedly told detectives that he and Barrera-Rosa disposed of the Guerra's body by burying her in a wooded area near Cedarville State Park, the release said.
On April 18, Charles sheriff's officers located Guerra's body in a plastic bin buried at a location described by Barerra-Barerra and in proximity to where phone records indicated Barrera-Rosa and his uncle parked their vehicles on April 1.
On April 5, Barrera-Rosa was arrested and detained by U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement for unrelated charges.
On April 22, he was transported by ICE agents and turned over to the Charles County Sheriff's Office. He is being held without bond at the Charles County Detention Center.
Barerra-Barerra has been charged as an accessory after the fact to murder in Prince George's County and is also being held without bond in that jurisdiction.

title: Our roads need to be safe for all
author: Staff Writer
content:
Our roads need to be safe for all

 October 11, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Staff Writer | Section: Editors Inbox 
 
 234
 Words 

 Read News Document

 We are deeply saddened to learn of the tragic loss of life that occurred on Saturday morning, Oct. 4, when a person riding a bicycle was struck and killed on a westbound lane of Route 50 in Easton. Our hearts go out to the victim's family, friends and all those affected by this horrific incident.Every life lost on our roads is one too many. This tragedy is a stark reminder of the vulnerability of those who travel by foot, bicycle or wheelchair in our community — and of the urgent need to make Talbot County's roads safer and more connected for everyone, not just for those in cars.
At Talbot Thrive, we advocate for a future where people can move safely and efficiently — whether they drive, walk, bike or take transit. We believe that investing in complete, connected neighborhoods and better infrastructure for people without cars is essential to building a community that is equitable, healthy and resilient.
This moment underscores the importance of thoughtful implementation of the Town of Easton's Complete Streets Plan and the county's Safety Action Plan, including expanding transit options and designing streets that prioritize safety for all users. These efforts need to be, at their core, about saving lives.
We extend our condolences once again to the victim's loved ones. May this loss strengthen our shared resolve to make Easton and Talbot County safer and more accessible for everyone.
HEATHER GRANT
Easton

title: State on pace for record traffic deaths
author: Lucy Hubbard; Capital News Service
content:
State on pace for record traffic deaths

 October 5, 2023 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Lucy Hubbard; Capital News Service | Page: 3 | Section: News 
 
 995
 Words 

 Read News Document

 ANNAPOLIS - Maryland is on track to see the highest number of roadway fatalities since 2007, according to Motor Vehicle Administrator Christine Nizer, with Prince George's County leading the state in fatal crashes.As of Oct. 4, Maryland has seen 456 roadway fatalities this year, according to Maryland Department of Transportation's Crash Data Dashboard. Last year, 564 people died on Maryland roadways, while in 2007, 615 people were killed on state roads."We are on track at this point, if the numbers stay consistent, to go over 600 fatalities," Nizer said during the Transportation Revenue and Infrastructure Needs meeting last month. "We have not seen that kind of numbers since 2007 and so we are sounding the alarm." More traffic around the fall and winter holidays often increases the toll."We see a lot of fatal crashes during holiday weekends and especially during those highly traveled holidays," Elena Russo, a spokesperson for the Maryland State Police, said. "We see a higher volume of traffic and with a higher volume of traffic, as you can guess, we see a lot more violations of the rules of the road." The number of roadway fatalities in Maryland rose in 2020. Despite the COVID-19 pandemic decreasing travel across the state, Maryland saw 574 roadway fatalities in 2020, 39 more deaths than the year prior. Traffic deaths continued higher than typical pre-pandemic numbers into this year.On Sept. 12, Gov. Wes Moore announced more than $11.5 million in funding for 85 organizations, agencies and programs working to improve roadway safety in Maryland. The money is destined for measures such as overtime traffic enforcement, to prevent distracted or impaired driving and to promote use of seat belts and child seats.Changes in driving behaviors since 2020 are at least partly responsible for the increase in roadway fatalities, said Ragina Ali, public and government affairs manager for the American Automobile Association - Mid Atlantic."We know there were less people on the roadways, at least in our area and across most of the country, but it seemed like those who were driving were engaging in more dangerous and risky behaviors," Ali said. "That they kind of thought the roadways were open and raceways and we did definitely see an alarming increase in dangerous driving behaviors." The unsafe and reckless driving habits that proliferated during 2020 have continued into 2023, she said."Any increase in the fatalities on our highways is alarming," said Russo. "And when we see our numbers increasing, it should be a wake-up call to motorists to sort of revisit the rules of the road." The leading causes of roadway fatalities have been consistent in the years since 2020. Over the last four years, distracted driving has been involved in the most crashes, followed by speed. Often, though, several things contribute to a crash."In some instances, a crash may have multiple factors," Ali said. "In other words, somebody may be impaired and be distracted.They may be distracted and speeding." According to John Seng, founder of the Maryland Coalition for Roadway Safety, a shortage of police officers monitoring roadways and, ironically, an increase in speed cameras encourages speeding."(When) you get to drive 11 to 12 miles over the speed limit and still not get a ticket for speeding through electronic speed enforcement," Seng said, "you are tacitly saying, 'It's OK if you speed eight miles over the speed limit.'" According to Russo, law enforcement agencies across the country have faced difficulties recruiting officers."Like every law enforcement agency in this nation right now, we're having a tough time recruiting individuals who are qualified for the job," Russo said. "One of the primary reasons may be public perception at this time of law enforcement.In the media, you've seen a lot of high-profile incidents that include police misconduct and therefore our citizens may have lost trust in their law enforcement agency." While the number of crashes has decreased every year since 2018, the number of fatal crashes continues to rise, according to MDOT. In 2018, one in every 243 crashes was fatal. Comparatively, in 2022, one in every 203 crashes was fatal.Prince George's County has led the state every year at least since 2016 with more fatal crashes than any other county, according to MDOT's Crash Data Dashboard. In 2022, 121 roadway fatalities were reported in Prince George's County, 21% of the statewide total.Just a few days ago, on Sept. 29, four people died in a crash in Prince George's County after their car ran into a tree on Woodmore Road.Commuters' reliance on Prince George's roadways is one reason the county sees higher rates of fatal accidents than any other county in Maryland, according to Ron Weiss, a member of the MD Route 210 Traffic Safety Committee."A lot of people travel through Prince George's County to get to the District to work," Weiss said."A lot of the traffic on our roads is commuting back and forth from the Beltway and I think that plays a part (in) it." One area of concern for drivers in Prince George's County is Maryland Route 210, known colloquially as Indian Head Highway.According to Rev. Robert L. Screen, founder of MD Route 210 Traffic Safety Committee, in 2022 10 people died on the 14-mile segment of MD 210 in Prince George's County."People are scared, they're nervous, they're anxious," Screen said. "I can't tell you the number of people that avoid 210, they go on other roads to avoid going on Indian Head Highway. The reputation precedes itself in the mindset of a lot of people that live in this community." According to Screen, Route 210, sees higher volumes of traffic than other highways because it offers access to Washington, D.C., which when combined with increasing populations in Charles County and St.Mary's County from infrastructure improvements has meant more wrecks."It's got a reputation in the area and it's not a good reputation," Weiss said. "It reflects not just on Fort Washington or Accokeek or Oxon Hill; it reflects poorly on all of Prince George's County and Maryland."

title: Jury acquits woman who stabbed two women in neighborhood fight
author: Carl Hamilton cahamilton@chespub.com
content:
Jury acquits woman who stabbed two women in neighborhood fight

 March 8, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Carl Hamilton cahamilton@chespub.com | Section: News 
 
 1193
 Words 

 Read News Document

 A woman maintained that she stabbed two women in self-defense during a dispute that turned physical on the street of a neighborhood near North East in August and a Cecil County Circuit Court jury apparently believed her or concluded that prosecutors fell short of proving otherwise, acquitting the defendant of attempted second-degree murder, first-degree assault and all other charges on Thursday.Jurors deliberated approximately two hours at the conclusion of a three-day-long trial before finding the defendant — Lacey N. Siple, 31 — not guilty across the board. Assistant State's Attorney Ellis Rollins prosecuted the case. Siple was represented by Assistant Public Defender Denise Winston. Cecil County Circuit Court Judge William W. Davis Jr. presided at trial.
Testimony showed that an ongoing dispute between Siple and other people in the Cedar Hill neighborhood, including the two women who suffered stab wounds, cropped up a few times over several days. The disharmony purportedly related to one of Siple's children shooting other kids in the neighborhood with a toy gun that is typically used to fire gel balls. The dispute came to a head in the unit block of Cedar Hill Circle at approximately 9:30 p.m. of Aug. 30 when, according to state witnesses, Siple and the two women got into an argument that turned physical.
Testifying as state witnesses, the two woman who suffered stab wounds admitted to macing Siple during the altercation — but qualified that they did so after she became aggressive, lunging at them.
One woman testified that Siple stabbed her near the shoulder, causing blood to squirt out from the gash, and then stabbed her in the back as she retreated. She suffered a total of four stab wounds, according to state testimony.
The other woman suffered knife wounds, including on her arm and hand. Ambulance crews drove the wounded women to a Delaware hospital for treatment. One law enforcement officer testified that first responders applied a tourniquet to the arm of one of women because her wound was so severe. The ground was covered in blood where the incident occurred and there was at least one blood trial leading to a nearby residence, according to testimony.
Siple testified on her own behalf, giving an account that was similar to another defense witness, a female friend of hers..
They testified that the two women who suffered stab wounds were part of a mob that descended upon them on the street in front of Siple's residence and threatened them, as they were walking to Siple's home to pick up pizza that Siple had forgotten. Siple testified that she had forgotten the pizza because moments earlier, before the mob showed up, four masked men got out of of vehicle and ran toward her children while making threats, prompting them to run into their friend's residence, where they had planned to eat dinner. Siple's friend testified that she volunteered to accompany Siple back to her place to retrieve the forgotten pizza, because it was clear that Siple was terrified.
Siple testified that a man punched her in the face, as the mob behind him started closing in. "I thought I was going to die. I thought they would stomp me," Siple testified.
After Siple had been pepper-sprayed by one of the women, Siple grabbed her knife and started flailing her arms blindly, Siple told jurors. "I was just trying to get home, trying to get home with my kids. I didn't mean to hurt anybody," Siple sobbed on the witness stand, maintaining that she didn't realize that she had stabbed anyone.
Her friend testified that she pulled out her own pepper-spray container and squirted it toward the mob surrounding Siple, causing people to back away and giving her an opening to grab Siple and lead her away. During her testimony, that woman emphasized a few times that the events were frenzied and unfolded swiftly. Once home, Siple tossed the blood-covered knife on her couch, which is where investigators later confiscated the weapon, and dead-bolted the door, according to defense testimony. She did not unlock that door until police arrived.
During his cross examination, Rollins asked Siple why she didn't call police when the four masked men chased and threatened her and her children. He also asked why she didn't do likewise when the mob descended upon her. Siple explained that if she were viewed as a "snitch" in that neighborhood it would put her life and the lives of her four children in jeopardy. In addition, she testified that she was wise enough not to pull out a cell phone in front of a group of aggressors, revealing that she even possessed one, because someone simply would snatch it from her.
Rollins reminded the jury during his closing argument on Wednesday afternoon that Siple had been convicted of theft, which is a crime that involves deceit and, therefore, is one of the convictions that can be used to impeach the credibility of a trial witness. "There was no mob," Rollins asserted.
The prosecutor told jurors that Siple was the "initial aggressor" and spurred an altercation with the two women, whom he opined were forthright in their testimonies. After that altercation with the two women grew into a "more significant fight," Siple grabbed a knife she had in her waistband and lunged toward them with the weapon, according the scenario proffered by Rollins during his closing argument.
"She (Siple) was the aggressor. She started it and she was going to end it," Rollins told jurors before contending, "She raised it to a deadly force level. She upped the ante. She brought a knife to a fistfight."
Along those lines, Rollins maintained that the cuts on hands of one of the women who testified for the state were "defensive wounds" and also told jurors that the women pepper-sprayed Siple to fend her off.
In addition, Rollins told jurors that the women didn't suffer only cuts, but also puncture wounds — calling into question Siple's account of waving the knife blindly. "She didn't just slash the victims; she stabbed them," Rollins stressed.
But Winston emphasized in her closing argument, "My client acted in self-defense."
Winston reminded jurors of where the Aug. 30 confrontation between Siple and the neighbors occurred, as well as the ones that happened during the days leading up to it. "Every time there was an interaction, it happened outside of her house. They went to her; she didn't come to them," Winston told jurors.
Addressing the one woman's stab wound to her back, in context of the state's assertion that she was trying to retreat, Winston told jurors, "If you're twisting and turning, you can get stabbed all over the place."
Winston also told jurors to recall the police body-cam audio that, according to the defense lawyer, captured the terror in Siple's voice when, unbeknownst to her, responding law enforcement officers knocked on her door after the incident. 'She screamed, 'Who is that?'," Winston said. Then that recording reflects a calmness in Siple's voice when she learns that it is police officers knocking on her door, according to Winston. "She says, 'OK, OK, let me unlock the door'," Winston told the jurors.
Summarizing toward the end of closing argument, Winston commented, "They brought the fight to her. She just wanted to go home."

title: Chester woman sentenced in 2024 multi-vehicle crash on Bay Bridge
author: STAFF REPORT
content:
Chester woman sentenced in 2024 multi-vehicle crash on Bay Bridge

 July 11, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: STAFF REPORT | Section: Local News 
 
 558
 Words 

 Read News Document

 CENTREVILLE — The woman responsible for a 20-plus vehicle crash on the Bay Bridge has been sentenced in Queen Anne's County Circuit Court.On July 8, Gwendolyn Persina, 49, of Chester, was sentenced to three years of jail time with all but 315 days suspended, which is the time Persina has served in jail from the time of her arrest.
According to the Office of the State's Attorney, Persina was sentenced for causing a life-threatening injury to another while operating a motor vehicle while under the influence of alcohol. This was the most serious charge that Persina was charged with and the maximum penalty for the offense is three years in jail and a $5,000 fine.
Persina was also sentenced to five years of supervised probation, ordered to have a mental health evaluation and complete any recommended treatment, to abstain from alcohol and drugs, to get an alcohol evaluation and complete any recommended treatment.
Persina pleaded guilty by way of an Alford guilty plea, by not admitting guilt but by acknowledging that the state had sufficient evidence that she could be found guilty of the charge.
The case was prosecuted by Lance G. Richardson, state's attorney for Queen Anne's County, assisted by Carolynn Grammas, assistant state's attorney from Anne Arundel County, appointed as a special prosecutor for the case.
The state said the sentence fell within the recommended sentence range as calculated by the Maryland Sentencing Guidelines, which recommended a sentence ranging from six months to three years of active incarceration.
Persina's conviction was based on a Jan. 27, 2024, incident when at approximately 7:46 a.m. she was operating a Honda Civic passenger vehicle at a high rate of speed in heavy fog traveling westbound on the Bay Bridge on the Queen Anne's County portion of the Chesapeake Bay Bridge. Persina rear-ended another vehicle, which disabled her vehicle in the travel portion of the bridge, resulting in a 23-vehicle chain reaction collision.
The collision resulted in a victim having his arm severed from his body. The man's arm was unable to be reattached. Persina suffered serious injuries in the collision and was transported to the hospital.
Through the course of their investigation, police determined at the time of the collision, Persina's blood alcohol content was between 0.24 and 0.27 — three times greater than the legal limit.
Although the accident occurred on Jan. 27, 2024, Persina wasn't criminally charged until August 2024. The state reported the delay in formally charging Persina was due to the incredible amount of vehicle data that had to be reviewed for the more than 20 vehicles involved.
According to State's Attorney Lance Richardson's chief of staff, Rob Penny, medical records had to be obtained and then the large volume of records had to be reviewed.
Additionally, a large volume of other evidence, and information from witnesses, had to be reviewed and analyzed. All of this investigative information took months to be collected and examined, Penny said.
Once Persina was formally charged, she was arrested and held without bail. Her attorneys ultimately filed a notice of incompetency to stand trial due to her inability to assist in her defense or an inability to understand the nature of the proceedings.
Experts from both the state and the defense examined Persina. After many delays, the state doctor from the Maryland Department of Health deemed Persina competent to stand trial on July 2.
The Office of the Public Defender represented Persina.

title: Man pleads guilty to 2021 murder of Trappe woman
author: Konner Metz

Man pleads guilty to 2021 murder of Trappe woman

 302

 A man has pleaded guilty to the murder of a Trappe woman that took place on Christmas Eve in 2021.Mauricio Ibarra Juarez, 33, entered an Alford plea on May 23 for a first-degree murder charge in connection to the killing of Marta Merina over three years ago.
Judge Philip Cronan handed down a life sentence with all but 75 years suspended.
"I am confident that Mr. Juarez will spend the rest of his life in prison for this heinous crime," said Talbot County State's Attorney Joseph Coale in a press release.
An Alford plea allows a person to maintain their innocence while acknowledging the state had enough evidence to obtain a conviction. Five other counts levied against Juarez — including second-degree murder and first-degree assault charges — will not be prosecuted.
The morning of the murder, police responded to Howell Point Road in Trappe for a reported shooting. Merina, 33, was found outside her home and pronounced dead on the scene.
A few days later, following an investigation, Maryland State Police issued a warrant for Juarez in connection to the murder.
Per the recent state's attorney's office press release, investigators traced a phone found at the scene to Juarez. They also worked with police in Virginia — where Juarez lived at the time — to match a vehicle driven by Juarez to what was found on nearby security footage the night of the murder, according to court documents.
Juarez was located by Mexican authorities for an unrelated crime in Oaxaca, Mexico in 2022. The U.S. Department of Justice's Office of International Affairs worked with Mexican prosecutors to request Juarez's provisional arrest. Extradition was granted later that year, but was deferred pending completion of Juarez's sentence in Mexico.
Last October, Juarez was extradited to Maryland. His 75-year sentence will credit back to February 2023. Juarez is being held without bond.
