title: Man gets three life sentences for double murder
author: Carl Hamilton cahamilton@chespub.com
content:
Man gets three life sentences for double murder

 July 1, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Carl Hamilton cahamilton@chespub.com | Section: News 
 
 1084
 Words 

 Read News Document

 A man who gunned down a woman and her boyfriend inside an abandoned house near North East in July 2023 before stealing their cell phones received three consecutive life sentences — plus 35 additional years — on Monday, one day before the second anniversary of the double murder.The defendant — Richard L. Stone, 46, of Aberdeen — fatally shot Christopher Blaine Thomas, 46, in his chest and Thomas' cohabiting girlfriend, Ashley Dove Brown, five times on July 1, 2023 inside the bedroom of an abandoned house in the 100 block of Bethel Church Road.
Shot in the chest, abdomen, thigh, arm and wrist, Brown was murdered on her 34th birthday.
Stone's co-defendant — Jordan Patrick Perry, 28, of Elkton — is scheduled to be sentenced on July 14. Perry is facing three life sentences and a significant humber of additional years after a jury convicted him of two counts of first-degree murder and 31 related charges on May 1 at the conclusion of a four-day-long trial, after deliberating about 90 minutes.
"I hope you both rot in Hades and that God . . . not . . . have . . . mercy . . . on . . . your . . . souls," Jerry Brown, the father of Ashley Brown, remarked Monday during his victim impact statement while standing at a courtroom podium a few feet away from Stone, seated at the defense table in a jail uniform.
Brown purposely left pregnant pauses between the last few words of his comment for emphasis. Brown told the judge that he still cries frequently over the senseless taking of his daughter's life. "They murdered a big part of me," he said.
Moments earlier, his 64-year-old wife, Bonnie Brown, who discovered the bodies of her daughter and Thomas, commented, "I have a life sentence of PTSD, and they have shown no remorse," during her victim-impact statement in the courtroom. (The Browns have been married for 38 years.)
Thomas' surviving family members also read victim-impact statements with similar sentiments aloud in the courtroom, including his mother and son, who listed his high school graduation and his senior walk off the football field as some of the milestones that his murdered father missed. Thomas' daughter submitted a written victim-impact statement to the judge and appeared on courtroom screen via Zoom.
Assistant State's Attorney Scott Lewis described the murders of Brown and Thomas as a "very senseless crime" while making his sentence recommendation. Lewis also told the judge that he is still taken aback by the "brutality of it," noting that bullets lethally damaged the hearts of both victims and that the fatal gunshot for Brown was fired while she was prone on the floor, already wounded.
"What compassion was shown? Where is the sense of humanity?" Lewis asked rhetorically.
Cecil County Circuit Court Judge William W. Davis Jr. imposed sentences on Stone that matched Lewis' recommendation.
Davis imposed a life sentence on Stone for first-degree murder relating to Brown; a consecutive life sentence for first-degree murder relating to Thomas; and a consecutive life sentence for conspiracy to commit first-degree murder.
In addition, the judge imposed a consecutive 25-year sentence on Stone for home invasion and then suspended 15 years of the penalty, leaving Stone with an additional 10 years of incarceration.
Davis also imposed two consecutive 20-year sentences on Stone for armed robbery and use of a handgun in the commission of a felony or a crime of violence, before suspending 10 years of each of those penalties. The judge noted that the use-of-a-handgun conviction carries a mandatory five-year sentence.
On April 4, at the conclusion of a four-day-long trial, a jury deliberated approximately five hours before convicting Stone of all 45 charges against him. The majority of those convictions merged into other convictions during Monday's sentencing.
Stone maintained his innocence at sentencing and, through his defense lawyer, Michael J. Halter, he indicated that he planned to file an appeal.
Prefacing that Stone does not lack "sympathy and empathy," Halter told the judge, "He had nothing to do with this crime. He has been adamant since Day One that he did not participate in these crimes."
Halter noted that Stone's convicted co-defendant, Perry, had "a grudge with Thomas over a drug sale" and that Stone had had no interactions with Thomas.
The defense lawyer stressed that, on the morning of the double murder, Stone unwittingly accompanied Perry and one other man in a convoy from their Aberdeen residence to the abandoned house where Brown and Thomas were living.
(Brown and Thomas were recovering drug addicts, and they had been squatting in that abandoned house with boarded-up windows and no electricity for approximately eight months, according to trial testimony, which indicated that Thomas sometimes borrowed a generator to power the place.)
"He (Stone) was with them, but he did not know what they were going to do. He was at the wrong place at the wrong time with the wrong people," Halter assertively summarized.
Halter asked the judge to run the sentences concurrently, opining that, otherwise, Stone would have "no possibility to see the light of day."
Stone stood at the defense table and maintained his innocence during his allocution, telling the judge, "The events that happened, I had no part in it. No life should be (taken)."
From the bench, Davis reminded Stone that the jury had spoken.
The judge reviewed that the evidence that Cecil County Sheriff's Office detectives, deputies and crime-scene technicians collected included Stone's registered handgun — one of firearms used in the double murder — and that it had Stone's DNA on it. (Investigators recovered the stolen cell phones belonging to Brown and Thomas inside Perry's bedroom, in the same Aberdeen house were Stone was living.) Incriminating text messages also were gathered.
Collected evidence also included distinctive masks matching those described by an eyewitness who saw an unmasked Perry accompanied by masked men on that Bethel Church Road property on the morning of July 1, 2023. Moments after that group arrived on a motorcycle and in a car, the eyewitness heard someone kick in the front door of the abandoned house, a scream and then a gunshot, which prompted him to run into the wood in fear.
In addition, the judge reviewed that CCSO investigators had tracked down several videos gleaned from security-cameras between Aberdeen and North East and that those videos showed Stone traveling in that caravan to that Bethel Church Road property on the morning of the double murder and directly after it occurred.
"It's hard not to listen to the jury and to what the (surviving) family (members) said," Davis told Stone from the bench.

title: Easton, other Eastern Shore towns host vigils for Charlie Kirk
author: Konner Metz
content:
Easton, other Eastern Shore towns host vigils for Charlie Kirk

 September 16, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Konner Metz | Section: Local News 
 
 657
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — Communities on the Eastern Shore have been hosting vigils for political activist Charlie Kirk after last week's shooting, including in Easton, where Republican officials organized a gathering in front of the Talbot County Courthouse.Talbot County Sheriff Joe Gamble, council member Dave Stepp and state Sen. Johnny Mautz (R-Caroline, Dorchester, Talbot, Wicomico), among other Republican officials, joined with around 200 people for a vigil late Sunday afternoon.
Gamble said the idea for the vigil came from a conversation he, Stepp and Mautz had on Sept. 11, the day after Kirk was shot and killed while speaking at an event at Utah Valley University.
Gamble and Stepp said Sunday's event drew people from "all walks" of life. Gamble said he saw people attend with "all types of political backgrounds."
"Call for a time of prayer, a time of reflection, a time to try to come together as a community and lower the temperature," Gamble said of the vigil's purpose.
Kirk, founder of the youth conservative organization Turning Point USA and a close ally to President Donald Trump, spoke at the Utah college on Sept. 10. Police have since arrested suspect Tyler Robinson, 22, who is accused of fatally shooting Kirk from a rooftop.
The Kent County Republican Central Committee hosted a vigil earlier Sunday for Kirk in Chestertown. In Denton, the Caroline County Republican Central Committee is hosting a vigil on Thursday at 6:30 p.m. on the courthouse steps, according to the group's Facebook.
Stepp said the recent trend of political violence seen nationwide is "unacceptable." Kirk's death came less than three months after Minnesota Rep. Melissa Hortman, a Democrat, and her husband were assassinated in their home on June 14.
In a statement, Talbot County Democratic Central Committee Chair Phil Jackson said the killings of Kirk and Hortman and her husband "are not only assaults on individuals but on the democratic principles we all share."
"This moment demands that we show it's possible to disagree fiercely without resorting to violence," Jackson wrote. "When leaders exploit and weaponize a tragedy like this, they dishonor the victims, deepen the divide, and fail to solve the problem of political violence. At the same time, gun violence — in our schools, our neighborhoods and in our politics — is a scourge on our nation, that we must confront with honesty, courage and a shared commitment to do better."
Sunday's vigil included a lot of prayer, Stepp said. He said it was successful in bringing people together and that the large gathering was "God's work."
"We are so thankful for the hundreds of Talbot County and other Maryland residents of all ages who, with very short notice, filled the courthouse lawn for the emotional and moving prayer vigil for Charlie Kirk and other victims of violent crime," wrote Shari Wilcoxon, chair of the Talbot County Republican Central Committee, in a statement.
Gamble said the discourse on social media since the shooting has been intense. He released a statement on the Sheriff's Office Facebook page the night of the shooting stating he was "saddened and angry."
In an interview Monday, Gamble said he's a taken "a lot of phone calls" from residents in regard to social media harassment and threats made in recent days. Sunday's vigil had no disruptions, he said, but he's hoping the online chatter tones down.
"We need to lower the temperature. We need to talk more," Gamble said. "We have a history here of hashing out our differences through public debate."
In Ridgely, an employee at The Benedictine School was seemingly fired after making a social media post about the shooting, though the school provided only some details. In a press release Monday morning, the school said the employee "referenced the murder of Charlie Kirk in a repulsive manner."
"This matter has been addressed in accordance with the organization's policies and the employee is no longer associated with Benedictine," the release stated. "No further information be provided."
This story has been updated to include a statement from the Talbot County Democratic Central Committee.

title: Easton police seek permits for future protests
author: Konner Metz
content:
Easton police seek permits for future protests

 October 21, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Konner Metz | Section: Local News 
 
 620
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — While police said Saturday's No Kings protest in Easton remained civil, they're asking the town to consider requiring public assembly permits for similar future protests.Easton Police Chief Alan Lowrey raised the concern at a Town Council meeting Monday. He said Saturday's protest — during which hundreds lined sidewalks on Dover Road — was a challenge for police.
"As with any big event, my concern with police coverage is the unexpected, the person who does not appreciate that (protest)," Lowrey said. "We've seen it all across our country. It's a little frustrating when these events are not going through the public assembly event process, to allow us to plan."
Easton's No Kings rally was just one of thousands nationwide, where people gathered in opposition of the Trump administration. Lowrey said one counter-protester remained civil, though police did get a call from a business concerned about people crowding parking lots.
Talbot County Democratic Central Committee Chair Phil Jackson said in an interview that the committee and the Talbot County Democratic Forum were in "regular contact" with the mayor and police in advance of Saturday's rally to ensure safety.
Also on Saturday in Easton, police and emergency officials held a mass casualty simulation, designed to train first responders in an active shooter scenario. The training ran from 11:30 a.m. to 5 p.m. at the Temple B'nai Israel and surrounding areas.
Lowrey said the Easton Police Department had a "great deal of resources committed" to that simulation. Combined with the large protest, the agency's patrol division was "essentially wiped out."
"We were able to respond to a call here or there, but if something happened, at that point, it comes at the expense of all the other citizens in the town because we have no officers available to respond to other emergencies," he said.
Saturday's No Kings protest didn't obtain a public assembly permit, nor did the first No Kings gathering in June. Lowrey said the town should look at rewording its public assembly permit rules to explicitly require such protests obtain a permit beforehand.
The police chief said the permits allow the department to adequately staff both the event and day-of calls or emergencies.
According to town code, permits must be obtained for "any open air public meeting, rally, conference, assembly or similar gathering upon any public property." The word "protest" is not included in the code.
Permit applications cost $100, though some events require additional costs depending on the equipment and police officers needed. Permits are first reviewed by police and then either approved or denied by the Town Council. Rarely does the council reject a permit request after a positive police recommendation, though some requests in the past have garnered debate and slim majorities, such as the Delmarva Pride Festival.
Jackson noted that the No Kings Day protests are nationally coordinated and then organized at a local level in the days and weeks leading up. Local organizers, he said, are open to following any new or adjusted permit requirements brought by the town.
"We are very interested in ensuring that these events comply with local policy," Jackson said. "Should the Town of Easton move forward with changes to their public gathering permits, we will look to comply with those and follow the process."
Lowrey added that Easton police typically provide as much coverage as possible for public assemblies at no cost by using on-duty officers. Feedback from Saturday, he said, was that officers were helpful. But he hopes the department can better prepare for future protests.
"But when you have 800 to 1,200 people lining streets and stuff, things can go wrong very quickly," he said. "And that's always my biggest fear. It takes a car driving through 30 people, and we have a mass casualty, actually, incident, and not an exercise."

title: Teens charged in armed carjacking at car wash
author: WHIG STAFF REPORT
content:
Teens charged in armed carjacking at car wash

 August 25, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: WHIG STAFF REPORT | Section: News 
 
 705
 Words

 Two teens allegedly attempted to carjack a man at gunpoint at an Elkton carwash — a crime that was captured on video by a business security camera, according to the Elkton Police Department.Investigators identified the suspects as Landon Shane Diebold and Aiden Anthony Meadows, both of whom are 18 and both of whom are Elkton residents who reside at the same address.
The investigation leading to their arrests and the charges against them started at approximately 3 a.m. on Friday, when EPD officers rushed to the Elkton Car Wash in the 500 block of North Bridge Street after receiving a dispatch regarding an attempted armed robbery, police reported.
According to Cecil County District Court records, the victim told investigators that three males dressed in all-black clothing approached him on foot as he was seated in his car a short distance outside Bay 3, where he was cleaning his interior windshield.
The video, which lacks audio, shows one of the masked suspects pulling a handgun out of a tan bag that is on his waist and then pointing the weapon at the victim for a few seconds, before putting the firearm back into the pouch and running away, court records indicate.
Police reported that the victim told investigators that he did not respond to the threat made at gunpoint and that his resistance caused the suspects to flee.
In addition to the all-black clothing, two of the suspects wore ski masks to conceal their facial features, police said. The third — later identified as Meadows — was not wearing a ski mask, and that helped EPD investigators identify him, court records show.
"While walking away from the (victim) and nearer to the camera, the unmasked male with long brown curly hair is clearly identifiable as Aiden Meadows," according to the charging document.
The lead investigator, EPD Detective J. Jollie, notes in his written statement of probable cause that he is familiar with Meadows because of his "prior encounters and interactions" with him during his law enforcement career, court records show.
In that court document, Jollie also reports that he is familiar with Diebold.
"I am familiar with Aiden and his associates because of prior investigations regarding the theft of firearms and the theft of vehicles. One of the associates Aiden is known to commit these types of crimes with in the past is Landon Diebold. Diebold has a thin build and tall frame, similar to that of the perpetrator in the video that retrieves, displays and points the firearm toward (the victim)," court records allege.
In addition, according to the charging document, Diebold's distinctive tattoos, which could be seen on the security-camera footage, helped investigators identify him as a suspect — despite him wearing a ski mask.
"Diebold has tattoos on his hands. I then accessed Diebold's Instagram account . . . and reviewed his profile picture. Within this picture, Diebold's hand tattoos are visible and tattooed on his left hand is red lettering, directly next to a dark arch, which also is close in proximity to a dark round figure," Jollie explains in the written charging document.
EPD officers and detectives worked throughout the better part of Friday to identify, locate and arrest Diebold and Meadows, according to police. During a court-approved search, investigators found and confiscated two guns, police reported.
As of Tuesday, investigators still were trying to identify the third suspect. Anyone with information that might help in this investigation is asked to email EPD Detective Jollie at jjollie@elktonpd.org. EPD officials posted a press release about the alleged attempted carjacking on the agency's Facebook page on Monday morning, along with mugshots of Diebold and Meadows.
Diebold is facing 11 criminal charges, including first-degree assault, armed robbery, use of a handgun in the commission of a felony or a crime of violence, handgun on person and attempted carjacking, according to Cecil County District Court records.
Meadows is facing 10 criminal charges — all of them the same as those filed against Diebold, court records show. Meadows, however, is not charged with handgun on person — the additional charge that Diebold is facing, according to court records.
Both remained in the Cecil County Detention Center on no bond Tuesday, one day after their bail review hearings in front of Cecil County District Court Judge Clara E. Campbell, court records show.

title: Never plug these into power strip

Never plug these into power strip

 For safety's sake, never plug the following items into a power strip.HAIRDRESSING APPLIANCES You need 'em hot and ready to go, which makes a power strip on the bathroom counter pretty much a godsend when you have only that one outlet. Here's the problem with that: Hairdryers, curling wands and flat irons are required to produce heat, which means they pull large amounts of amperage to get them good and hot. Plugging them into a power strip is just asking for trouble. These types of hairdressing appliances must be plugged directly into a wall outlet - preferably one with a ground-fault circuit interrupter breaker to avoid danger should those tools accidentally be exposed to water.REFRIGERATOR AND FREEZER.These appliances pull too much current for a power strip because they are continuously cycling on and off.That will quickly overload a power strip. These items need to be plugged directly into a wall outlet dedicated solely to that appliance.TOASTER.Here's the clue: It has exposed wires inside those slots that heat up to become red-hot. It takes a lot of current to fire up those wires, which can easily overload a power strip. So, no, do not plug your toaster into an extension cord or power strip.Ditto for your toaster oven.MICROWAVE.I still think of my microwave oven as a miracle for food preparation, thawing, cooking and reheating in a fraction of the time it takes a conventional oven. However, such incredible activity demands more energy than what a power strip can deliver.SPACE HEATER.Most portable heaters consume 1,500 watts of energy on their high settings. Connect one to a power strip and it becomes potentially hazardous due to allowing them to run for an extended period.

Cambridge man faces murder charges for 2024 shooting

 CAMBRIDGE — A Cambridge man is facing charges including first-degree murder in connection to the fatal shooting of 26-year-old Virgil Simms last year.Jahmere Bryan, 19, is charged with first- and second-degree murder, first- and second-degree assault, use of a firearm while committing a felony, and three other firearm and handgun charges.
Bryan is one of two shooters police allege are responsible for the death of Simms on Oct. 20, 2024, in the area of Pine Street. Nineteen rounds were fired and Simms sustained a fatal gunshot wound to the chest.
On Thursday, though, a jury acquitted the other main suspect, 18-year-old Jo'Mir Norman, of all charges in relation to the case. Prosecutors relied heavily on video evidence and clothing in trial, but dealt with challenges during witness testimony and the fact that the murder investigation started off with a significant mistake.
Bryan was arrested by police last November, but it came after police misidentified 15-year-old Brian Wongus Jr. as one of the two suspects. Maryland State Police wrongly arrested Wongus and charged him with first-degree murder, among other offenses. Charges were dropped in late October or early November, according to an MSP spokesperson.
The misidentification of Wongus as one of the two shooters came up in Norman's trial this week. Attorneys on both sides acknowledged the error, though offered different opinions on how the evidence leading to the misidentification compared to the evidence presented against Norman.
As for Bryan, a jury trial previously slated for mid-July was postponed. A future trial date has not yet been released.
Charging documents allege Bryan fled from the shooting scene just after 7 p.m. on Oct. 20, 2024. Investigators reviewed surveillance video and allege clothing worn by Bryan earlier that day was found in a house on Camelia Street where the suspects allegedly fled to after the shooting.
According to court documents, investigators interviewed a witness who identified Bryan and provided his street name, "Krunch." The witness saw Bryan on Camelia Street before the murder, per court documents.
Bryan is being held without bond at the Dorchester County Department of Corrections.

title: Delaware park closed due to safety concerns, hazardous conditions
author: Josh Shannon jshannon@chespub.com

Delaware park closed due to safety concerns, hazardous conditions

 June 5, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Josh Shannon jshannon@chespub.com | Section: News 
 
 262

 Read News Document

 A Newark park will be closed for the foreseeable future after a recent inspection found "significant safety concerns and hazardous conditions," city officials said.One of the city's lesser-known parks, Coleman Park is located near the Maryland border, bounded by Valley Road and the Country Hills and Briarcreek neighborhoods. The main entrance is in Country Hills.
The 8.5-acre park contains walking trails but otherwise is preserved in its natural state.
The inspection found that the tree canopy near the entrance to the park consists of many black locust trees that are structurally compromised by fungal decay and pose a significant risk of falling.
The walking paths are eroded and surrounded by dense thickets of greenbrier, multiflora rose and poison ivy.
"These thorny species have overgrown the area and become entangled with large woody debris from fallen trees and limbs," City Manager Tom Coleman wrote in a memo to city council. "Significant land clearing and tree removal must be completed before we can reopen the park."
The city does not have funding for such work in the 2025 budget, according to Coleman, who did not provide any indication as to when the park might reopen.
The city's five-year capital improvement plan includes plans for broader improvements to Coleman Park, such as building a turf/meadow area, planting new trees and possibly paving the trails. However that $50,000 in funding, which is dependent on a state grant, is not budgeted until 2027.
Coleman Park was created in 1993 when Newark purchased the land for $180,000 and annexed it into the city. It is named for the family that previously owned the property.

title: Serving, protecting for 250 years - The Caroline County Sheriff's Office celebrates its sesquicentennial
author: Connie Connolly; cconnolly@chespub.com
content:
Serving, protecting for 250 years - The Caroline County Sheriff's Office celebrates its sesquicentennial

 November 15, 2023 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Connie Connolly; cconnolly@chespub.com | Page: 1A | Section: News 
 
 979
 Words 

 Read News Document

 DENTON - To mark the 250th anniversary of the Caroline County Sheriff's Office, a new badge has been struck, containing symbols of its history dating to colonial Maryland.But the badge itself is a symbol of the long line of sheriffs who have held the office since 1773, when Thomas Hughlett of Greensboro was appointed by the British governor after the county was formed from parts of Dorchester and Queen Anne's counties.Bookending the long blue line is Sheriff Donnie Baker, who, like Hughlett, is also a Greensboro native. He's the county's 77th sheriff.Caroline County Deputy Lt. Jacob Andrew is the unofficial historian of the sheriff's office. And because he's the fifth generation of the Andrew family to serve the office during the past century, he's well-qualified for the job."Jake was just teaching me something," Baker said. "I didn't know that the first sheriff was buried up there (in Greensboro)." According to Andrew's research, Hughlett was a plantation owner appointed to a one-year term by the governor to be in charge of weights and scales because he was deemed trustworthy.Ironically, the next year he became captain of the Caroline County Militia Fifth Company, which encompassed Greensboro, Goldsboro and Bridgetown during the American Revolution.Hughlett later became a judge. He is buried in a crypt in a tiny, privately-owned graveyard in a Greensboro subdivision, the site of the Hughlett family farm.During the Civil War, John Wilson Saulsbury served a two-year term from 1861 to 1863 and was required to swear allegiance to the Union.Andrew said Sheriff James Temple, who served from 1923 to 1926 "was actually a pretty cool guy." A veteran of the Spanish-American War, Temple was known as the walking sheriff."He had the first Buick in Caroline County. He always told everybody that," Andrew said. However, "he hated driving it.So, if he had to go serve a warrant on somebody, he'd walk from Denton to Ridgely, lock them up and walk them back." "The original sheriff's office was pretty much a shed on the courthouse green, and it was very easy to break out of," Andrew said. The lynching on the green of Federalsburg blacksmith Marshall Price following accusations of murder in 1895 prompted the government to build a new jail across Gay Street on the Choptank River, where it stands today.In 1921, William Curtis Andrew, Jacob Andrew's great-great grandfather, became sheriff and served a two-year term. His son, William E. Andrew served from 1938 to 1946 and, following a four-year term by Saulsbury Sparks, served again from 1950 to 1961, dying of a heart attack in his office.William's son Louis C. Andrew served from 1961 to 1994, retiring when he was 70. His son, then-Deputy Charles Andrew, served as acting sheriff until Phil Brown was elected sheriff the following year.Back then, the sheriff and his family lived in the center section of what is now the Caroline County jail. Two wings were added to the large brick structure, but Charles Andrew remembers when the original section was home."I got to know a lot of inmates," he said.He recalls the night his "mother had a fit" when a naked woman was brought in by the state police."They had to come in the front door and walk down the hall which separated the living room and dining room directly back to that one-room office" at the back of the house, he said."I would have been seven or eight" years old, Charles Andrew said. "So, she made my father go to the commissioners, and that's when they put stairs on the side of the building to come in the outside door." "Back then, when my father started, he was only making $2,600 a year," he said. "They had to supply their own vehicle. The only thing the county gave them was a radio that went into their own private car." That center section of the current jail is called the Andrew Building today.Until 1994, both the sheriff's office and jail were under the jurisdiction of the sheriff, according to Charles Andrew. When Brown became sheriff, the county Department of Corrections was formed as a separate agency, and Charles Andrew served as the superintendent for 13 years, after serving in the sheriff's office for 20 years.Charles's son Jacob, now the fifth generation to serve in the sheriff's office, serves the county with almost 50 fellow deputies. After serving in the Air Force, Jacob Andrew joined the sheriff's office and has been on the job for 19 years. "I love it. I love my job," he said.The commemorative badge symbolizes not only his family's history of serving county citizens in the sheriff's office, but a long legacy of the office's commitment to public safety stretching back to the nation's founding.At the five points of the badge's star are a Revolutionary War soldier, the Caroline County Circuit Court building, the original courthouse before the renovations, the original sheriff's office on Gay Street, and the current office, completed in 2021 on Double Hills Road."One of the things that former Sheriff Randy Bounds wanted to do was have a wall of sheriff's (pictures)," Baker said."So I told him that Jake is going to fulfill that dream of his." The sheriff's office is seeking memorabilia from the public for a future museum or showcase. If you have any artifacts, photos or clippings you'd like to share, contact Lt. Jacob Andrew at 410-479-4124 or jandrew@carolinemd.org. 
 
 Caption: CONNIE CONNOLLY/STAR DEMOCRAT
 
Sheriff Donnie Baker commissioned this commemorative badge for the 250th anniversary of the Caroline County Sheriff's Office
 
COURTESY OF CCSO
 
Joining current Caroline County Sheriff Donnie Baker, center, are former Sheriff Phil Brown, left, and Sheriff Randy Bounds.
 
COURTESY OF CCSO
 
H. Saulsbury Sparks served as Caroline County Sheriff from 1934 to 1938, and again from 1942 to 1946. Note the handcuffs on his desktop.
 
COURTESY OF CCSO
 
Charles Andrew, left, served as acting sheriff and was a deputy for 20 years with the Caroline County Sheriff's Office.

title: Bill could improve police awareness of unseen disabilities
author: SOfIA APPOLONIO Capital News Service
content:
Bill could improve police awareness of unseen disabilities

 February 18, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: SOfIA APPOLONIO Capital News Service | Section: State News 
 
 466
 Words 

 Read News Document

 ANNAPOLIS — Lawmakers are considering a bill that would make it easier for first responders in Maryland to know when they're dealing with a person who has invisible disabilities.The measure would allow Maryland residents to request a notation on their driver's license or state ID card that identifies their unseen disability, such as autism or hearing impairment.
If adopted, the bill would mandate training for law enforcement on how to improve interactions with people who have hidden disabilities. It would also require the Maryland Motor Vehicle Administration to work on awareness programs.
The changes are meant to help protect people with invisible disabilities during encounters with first responders — a special concern for parents of Black children who may be at higher risk during conflict with police.
"The reality of these encounters presents differently when your Black son transitions to adulthood and becomes a legally independent Black man," said bill co-sponsor Del. Kym Taylor, a Democrat representing Prince George's County, who said her son has a hidden disability. "There are no visible signs nor immediate indicators to help first responders understand potential reactions."
The bill, known as Eric's ID Law, is named for Maryland native Eric Blessed Carpenter Grantham, 20, a Black man who lives with autism.
Following the 2020 death of George Floyd — a Black man who died at the hands of Minneapolis police officers — Grantham and his mother Linda worried about Grantham potentially encountering police and failing to respond as expected because of his disability. The two met with Sen. William Smith Jr., a Democrat representing Montgomery County, Senate sponsor of the bill.
Grantham says that he designed special logos that easily identify hidden disabilities to law enforcement.
"Eric's ID Law was created to help save lives for people who cannot use their own voice," he said.
Prince George's County Sheriff John Carr said he supports the proposal, adding that increased resources to aid people with invisible disabilities during encounters with law enforcement are a "must."
"From a law enforcement perspective, we want you to know that we are here to serve you and we want this bill to pass," Carr said. "Any time that we're able to put a citizen at ease during a traffic stop, that is something that helps us interact and keep our community safe."
Similar initiatives exist in Maryland already, such as the MVA "blue card" that people can present to identify their disability. Additionally, the Ethan Saylor Alliance was established in 2015 to "provide increased training for law enforcement and other public service entities" to address situations with people with invisible disabilities.
Its formation follows the death of Saylor, a 26-year-old man with Down syndrome, following a police altercation at a Frederick movie theatre.
The passage of this law would mean Maryland joins 11 other states allowing people with disabilities to identify themselves on their identification cards.

title: After deadly work zone crashes, a push for change
author: SAPNA BANSIL Capital News Service
content:
After deadly work zone crashes, a push for change

 April 18, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: SAPNA BANSIL Capital News Service | Section: News 
 
 631
 Words 

 Read News Document

 ANNAPOLIS — After a pair of deadly work zone incidents cast attention on the dangers of road work, Maryland Gov. Wes Moore enacted a set of protections for workers and their families that his administration describes as "a moral imperative."Hours after the state's legislature adjourned, a bill increasing fines for work zone speed violations and another covering educational costs for families of fallen workers were among the first measures from the 2024 session that Moore signed into law.
At a bill signing ceremony, Lt. Gov. Aruna Miller, a former transportation engineer, invoked two fatal crashes that inspired the new legislation. In March 2023, six highway workers died when a car careened into a work zone on Interstate 695. Nearly a year later, six construction workers repairing potholes atop the Francis Scott Key Bridge were killed when a container ship struck the bridge, causing it to collapse.
"The men and women in the construction industry place themselves in harm's way every day on the frontline of service," Miller said. "We saw it happen on March 22, 2023. And we saw it happen again on March 26, 2024. It's a moral imperative that we protect workers who provide critical service, public service for all of us."
Among the measures to receive Moore's signature was the Maryland Road Worker Protection Act, which Miller championed throughout the legislative session and touted Tuesday, during an event overlooking the site of the I-695 crash to mark National Work Zone Awareness Week.
Effective June 1, the new law permits the installation of multiple speed cameras within a single work zone and raises the fine for speed camera violations to $80. The current penalty in Maryland is $40, among the lowest such fines in the country.
Beginning January 2025, fines shift to a tiered system ranging from $60 to $500 depending on the driver's speed. Fines will double if workers are present at the time of the violation.
The new law is part of a larger effort to change driver behavior in work zones by strengthening enforcement methods and increasing education. Distracted driving, aggressive driving and speeding are the leading causes of work zone crashes, according to the State Highway Administration.
"Most crashes are not accidents," State Highway Administrator William Pines told Capital News Service. "In reality, they're very preventable. The majority of crashes that occur happen because of behaviors with drivers. So if we want to stop the root cause of most crashes, we've got to deal with driver behavior."
But the law offers no safety solutions for incidents like the collapse of the Key Bridge, which was unrelated to driver behavior. Maryland Transportation Secretary Paul Wiedefeld told Capital News Service on Tuesday that officials may consider structural solutions to bolster bridge safety but are awaiting the results of an investigation by the National Transportation Safety Board before making any specific policy proposals.
Instead, lawmakers responded to the bridge collapse by recognizing the toll that work zone crashes leave on workers' families.
In the final hours of the legislative session, the General Assembly passed the Protecting Opportunities and Regional Trade (PORT) Act, primarily aimed at providing emergency aid to workers and businesses affected by the closure of the Port of Baltimore.
Moore's administration offered a successful amendment to the bill creating the Fallen Transportation Workers Scholarship Program, providing tuition assistance for five years of full-time study or eight-years of part-time study to children and spouses of workers who have died on the job since 2022.
"What happened on the bridge is horrifically traumatic, and I think one of the things that we wanted to do is protect others who are in a similarly dangerous situation," said Maryland Senate President Bill Ferguson (D-Baltimore City), who co-sponsored the PORT Act.
"Certainly, we wish there were no one participating in that fund, but sadly, we know how dangerous this work is," he continued.

title: Easton officials weigh in on Complete Streets study, pedestrian safety
author: Konner Metz
content:
Easton officials weigh in on Complete Streets study, pedestrian safety

 October 22, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Konner Metz | Section: Local News 
 
 640
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — Town officials on Monday discussed ongoing efforts to shore up pedestrian and bike safety, including a comprehensive study on the town's roads and streets.In a workshop, Town Engineer Rick Van Emburgh updated the Town Council on an ongoing study into street safety conducted by the engineering firm Wallace Montgomery.
The study, known as Complete Streets, aims to create a manual for Easton outlining which types of roads and streets prioritize certain modes of transportation, such as walking, biking and driving. The study itself will not make road safety improvements, though officials see it as a guide to initiating those upgrades.
Those leading the study are in the process of meeting with local businesses and safety stakeholders to gather feedback on how best to define and classify different streets. Larry Marcus, an associate for Wallace Montgomery, said some classifications include residential, collector, commercial urban and commercial industrial streets.
Roads are further defined by land use: downtown, residential, commercial and industrial, Marcus said. The categories roads fall into will determine the study's recommendation on which sidewalk, bike lane or vehicular improvements should be taken.
Van Emburgh added that the manual will make it easier for the town to require certain road safety steps be taken when residential or commercial developers apply for site plan approval. Moving forward, the town will be less likely to give developers breaks or reliefs from ensuring private roads are up to town standards, he said.
"It's a very practical document that I can think of a lot of different ways it will be used," Van Emburgh said of the Complete Streets study. Guidelines will be drafted and applied to a map of town roads in November.
During the nearly hourlong workshop, many specific pressure points in town were raised, including Port Street and North Washington Street.
Council President Don Abbatiello said telephone poles in the middle of sidewalks on Port Street make it difficult for people to walk safely. Council members Maureen Curry and the Rev. Elmer Davis echoed the concern about the street.
"It's gonna (be) awfully difficult to make Port Street pedestrian friendly unless we make some serious improvements," Curry said.
On North Washington Street, sidewalks are expected to be added. Van Emburgh said the town has funds in its budget already for survey and design work for North Washington Street from Easton Hardware (near the Creamery Lane intersection) to Gay's Seafood (close to the stoplight at the Easton Parkway, or Route 322).
The Complete Streets guidance will help determine the specific bike, pedestrian and vehicular safety measures taken for the North Washington Street project.
Pedestrian and bike safety has been an ongoing discussion among town leaders, residents and local advocates. Earlier this month, worries about safety on Route 50 — a state-operated highway — were raised after a man on a bike was struck and killed.
Ward 3 Councilmember David Montgomery shared concerns that the town would sacrifice the efficient flow of vehicular traffic in order to prioritize walking and biking. He said many of the older residents in his ward — including the west side of Easton Parkway — aren't "interested in bicycling to downtown."
"Automobile transportation is pretty much what everybody uses in order to get into the center of town," Montgomery said. "So I'm very concerned about our sacrificing the flow of single-occupancy vehicles, sacrificing it to other things, that for my ward, don't do any good at all by way of mobility."
Heather Grant, executive director of Talbot Thrive, a local nonprofit that advocates for pedestrian and bike safety, refuted Montgomery's stance. In a statement, she said residents who "don't want to drive everywhere" deserve "equal access to safe infrastructure."
"Some council members who mention the difficulties in traveling by car during school drop off and pick up should consider that if we make our streets safer for kids to walk and bike to school, we can reduce vehicle congestion," Grant wrote.

UPDATE: Cambridge man killed in shooting on Wednesday

 June 26, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Konner Metz | Section: Crime 
 
 201

 CAMBRIDGE — Police are investigating a shooting that killed a Cambridge man on Wednesday night.Steven Lee Dennis, 45, was identified as the victim by the Cambridge Police Department on Thursday. Police are actively conducting a homicide investigation.
Just after 8:30 p.m. on Wednesday, police responded to a shooting in the area of Hudson Road (Route 343) and the Westside Bypass. Officers found Dennis lying in the roadway with a gunshot wound to the chest, according to a press release.
A civilian and off-duty officer attempted CPR, later joined by the responding officers, police said. EMS, upon arrival, declared Dennis dead at the scene.
Investigators say a car was seen leaving the area on Route 343, but no other details about the investigation were provided as of Thursday afternoon.
Wednesday's homicide is the second in Cambridge this year — matching marks set in both 2023 and 2024. Both of this year's homicides occurred this month. On June 8, a Delaware man was killed in a shooting on Camelia Street. A 15-year-old was later arrested on murder charges in connection to that shooting.

title: Eastern Shore officials shocked by Trump rally shooting
author: STAFF REPORT
content:
Eastern Shore officials shocked by Trump rally shooting

 July 13, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: STAFF REPORT | Section: Local News 
 
 593
 Words 

 Read News Document

 Eastern Shore leaders reacted with shock after a Saturday shooting at Donald Trump's campaign rally in Butler, Pennsylvania, resulted in the death of at least one attendee and left the former president with a minor injury.Wicomico County Executive Julie Giordano, a member of the Wicomico County Republican Central Committee, is attending this week's Republican National Convention in Milwaukee. She is one of three delegates from the Eastern Shore who will be attending the convention.
Giordano will be flying to Wisconsin Sunday.
"I know that I'll be safe, I know that there's a lot of police presence at the RNC," Giordano said in an interview with The Star Democrat. "But yeah, it does make you sort of hesitate.
"I'm getting ready to hop on a plane and go to a place where you know there's going to be protests, you know there's going to be people that aren't in favor of President Trump and the RNC," she continued. "It does make you think, and you just have to be cautious."
Giordano said Saturday's events will likely raise her vigilance and caution at the convention.
"I think everything becomes so much more real," Giordano said. "When somebody says, 'Hey we got to look out for protesters,' or you need to make sure that you're paying attention and that you're staying with the group. ... I think today made it really real on how important and imperative that is."
Easton Mayor Megan Cook was shocked and saddened by the news of political violence in Pennsylvania against Donald Trump.
"The headline came across on my watch. It's horrible. It is very sad. No one should be (a victim) of political violence. It is not worth it," Cook said.
Giordano described her initial feelings as "shock and horror" when she learned of the news. She provided a similar sentiment to Cook, saying that "political violence is never acceptable," and offered prayers for Trump and those affected at the rally.
"It's obviously inexcusable, no reason for it at all," Giordano said. "And today, someone who traveled to the rally to support President Trump has lost their life."
U.S. Rep. Andy Harris (R-Md.), who represents the Eastern Shore, also offered prayers for the former president in a press statement issued Saturday night.
"Tonight, I am praying for President Trump, his family, the victims and those injured at the rally, and for the future of our country," Harris said. "President Trump showed incredible bravery in the face of evil today, and his courage deserves the utmost respect. May God bless America."
The Dorchester County Republican Central Committee released a statement on Facebook Saturday night signed by Michael Dodd, its chairman.
"Rest assured, this incident will not diminish President Trump's resolve to save America from the evil that seeks to destroy us," the statement read, in part. "To the contrary, this cowardly act will serve to further strengthen President Trump's fight to restore America."
The Maryland Republican Party shared support for Trump in wake of the shooting.
"The Maryland Republican Party stands with President Trump and pray for his quick recovery and safety," Chairwoman Nicole Beus Harris said in a statement. "We trust that the Secret Service and all law enforcement involved will do a thorough job and provide answers when they can. We support them and thank them for the difficult job they do."
Gov. Moore also weighed in on political violence in a statement released Saturday night.
"Political violence is unacceptable and against what our country stands for," Moore's statement read. "This kind of cowardice must be roundly condemned by all Americans. What happened today to President Trump is abhorrent and should never be tolerated. Ever."

title: Talbot Police Accountability Board releases inaugural report
author: Natalie Jones
content:
Talbot Police Accountability Board releases inaugural report

 January 7, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Natalie Jones | Section: Crime 
 
 749
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — The Talbot County Police Accountability Board's first year was marked by challenges in adjusting to citizen oversight in policing, but "reluctant confidence" from law enforcement is believed to be growing, the board said in its inaugural report.The annual report, submitted to the Talbot County Council on Dec. 20, 2023, outlined the board's yearlong struggle in establishing a rapport with the county's four law enforcement agencies, which voiced concerns with the state-mandated legislation that created the board and a committee to review complaints of police misconduct.
Trends in call volume, arrests, struggles with recruitment and retention, use of force and police-community relations within each of the county's law enforcement agencies were analyzed in the report.
The board also asked the County Council to consider a number of recommendations to improve police accountability in Talbot County.
However, the board said most of the concerns from local police agencies centered on the Administrative Charging Committee, which is tasked with determining if officers should face administrative charges following a police agency's own investigation into the allegations. The committee also recommends appropriate discipline.
The committee is composed of five county residents and is helmed by Mitchell Ettinger, who also serves as the chairman of the Police Accountability Board.
Gaining the confidence of the county's law enforcement agencies proved to be the Administrative Charging Committee's great challenge last year, the report said.
Police questioned the wisdom of citizen oversight, the breadth of the committee's role and a lack of experience in law enforcement, which could translate to a gap in understanding the tasks and competing interests police officers face daily, according to the report.
In 2023, 15 complaints were submitted to the Administrative Charging Committee for review: 10 from the Sheriff's Office and five from the Easton Police Department.
Twelve complaints resulted in officer exonerations or were ruled as unfounded charges. Three complaints ended with varying disciplinary actions — two of which involved disagreements on recommended dispositions between the Administrative Charging Committee and the officers' respective agencies, the report said.
In one case, a Sheriff's Office deputy was administratively charged for undue use of force. According to the report, the deputy deployed pepper spray in an attempt to stop a juvenile who was improperly operating a mini-bike on the road.
The Administrative Charging Committee found it was unreasonable for the deputy to do so and imposed charges. The committee recommended two days' loss of pay, which the deputy accepted, according to the report.
The Sheriff's Office also revised its policy to clarify that deploying pepper spray on a moving motorist is inappropriate.
Use of force reports were a particular focus of the Police Accountability Board in 2023, according to its report. Law enforcement agencies now submit those reports quarterly.
The board's report said given the extensive interaction between police and the public, it was "remarkable" that officers only resorted to use of force on 10 occasions — six times by the sheriff's office, three times by the Easton Police Department and once by the St. Michaels Police Department.
Another case was heard against an Easton officer for unbecoming conduct off-duty, along with administrative failures to report conduct and a subpoena to testify. The allegations in that case were sustained, with the committee recommending two days' loss of pay or leave and a letter of reprimand.
The committee heard a third complaint against a sheriff's office deputy for speeding, which the deputy acknowledged. The deputy received a letter of reprimand.
Despite a year of building relationships, some distrust still lingers between the Administrative Charging Committee and local law enforcement.
"...The LEAs most certainly will maintain that they did not (and do not) need citizen oversight to exercise proper review and disposition of citizen complaints," the report said.
Though work remains to be done, the board believes the Administrative Charging Committee has established credibility with police through its "well-reasoned and supported" opinions on each of the complaints.
Easton Police Chief Alan Lowrey acknowledged the lack of consensus between law enforcement and the committee on some case dispositions, but he said there was space for those disagreements.
"I think that we all want to be going in the same direction, and that is to have professional law enforcement in Talbot County," he said. "I've never gotten a sense from either entity, the PAB or the ACC, that they're looking to do in law enforcement like has been the narrative nationally for a few years of some groups — not all groups."
"We understand that it's important to have a rule of law in our community, and we just want it to be done well," Lowrey continued.

title: Jury acquits man of all charges in fatal shooting
author: Carl Hamilton and Lilly Howard cahamilton@chespub.com
content:
Jury acquits man of all charges in fatal shooting

 December 6, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Carl Hamilton and Lilly Howard cahamilton@chespub.com | Section: News 
 
 978
 Words 

 Read News Document

 Donald Raymond Snyder Jr. pulled a 9mm handgun from his waistband in the driveway of his Elkton-area residence at approximately 9:20 p.m. on June 17 and, from close range, he fired two shots into the upper torso of his friend, Christopher Cimorose, who was in the driver's seat of a red Nissan Versa.Snyder, 41, and his defense lawyers maintained during the two-day-long trial this week that he shot Cimorose — killing him — in self-defense because Cimorose, 55, had threatened, "I'm going to kill you, (expletive)," while a "metal pipe" was resting on his lap.
The prosecution, however, contended that Snyder gunned down Cimorose "in cold blood" because Snyder's 41-year-old girlfriend, Michelle McCarthy, was ending their relationship and that Cimorose — her former boyfriend — had come to Snyder's residence to pick her up at McCarthy's request.
On Thursday morning, the jury acquitted Snyder of first-degree murder, second-degree murder, voluntary manslaughter and the eight related charges after about four hours of deliberations.
As the forelady announced the not guilty verdicts, Snyder lowered his head and appeared emotional while standing beside his Timonium-based lawyer, Joshua Insley, at the defense table. Then they embraced for several seconds. Bruce Saller, who wasn't present, served as Insley's co-counsel at trial.
Snyder, who reiterated his self-defense account on the witness stand, was released from the Cecil County Detention Center on Thursday after his acquittal, court records indicate. Snyder had been incarcerated on no bond since his June 20 arrest.
Maryland State Police investigators elected not to charge Snyder after interviewing him in the hours after the shooting because they lacked probable cause and they let him go home.
But on June 20, after viewing security-camera footage of the incident in the drivefway of Snyder's Locust Point Road residence, south of Elkton, and re-interviewing the sole eyewitness, McCarthy, detectives charged him with murder and other offenses.
The pertinent part of that video was played for jurors.
"Thirteen seconds, in real time, you are going to see the intentional, premeditated killing of Mr. Cimorose," Cecil County State's Attorney James Dellmyer told jurors Wednesday during his closing argument. "This is evidence of first-degree murder. Chris (Cimorose) didn't stand a chance. That gun was on him before he got out of the car."
The footage starts with Snyder "briskly walking up" to the driver's side door and punching Cimorose in the face, according to Dellmyer, who prosecuted the case with Deputy State's Attorney Patricia Fitzgerald. State evidence included a photo of Snyder's right hand, which showed bruising on his knuckles, and a picture of an abrasion on Cimorose's forehead.
After the car lurches forward a few feet, Snyder pulls the handgun as he walks forward to the driver's side door, gets into a shooting stance and rapidly fires three shots at Cimorose, including one errant round, Dellmyer reviewed.
A person cannot be the aggressor and then claim self-defense, Dellmyer said. The video doesn't show Cimorose swinging the object or advancing, nor does it show Snyder retreating because of a perceived threat, he added.
"You cannot start a fistfight and then shoot someone to death," Dellmyer stressed, before asking, "Is it reasonable to use deadly force?"
McCarthy testified that Snyder hurled her cell phone, cracking the front, during a heated argument between the two shortly earlier that day and then alleged that Snyder, in anger, had broken five other cell phones of hers that year.
McCarthy told Snyder that she was leaving him during that dispute.
"I said, 'That's it. I'm done with you . . . I packed all my stuff in the car," McCarthy said.
But McCarthy could not legally drive her packed car because it lacked valid license plates — so she called Cimorose for a ride.
McCarthy testified that she was in the front passenger's seat of Cimorose's car when Snyder wordlessly sucker-punched Cimorose in the face and swiftly fired three shots. "I saw the punch. I saw everything," she said.
Insley, however, maintained that McCarthy wasn't a credible witness.
The defense lawyer proffered that the footage shows McCarthy outside Cimorose's car during the incident. Seconds earlier, McCarthy and Snyder had been inside her vehicle waiting for Cimorose to arrive.
Insley also reminded jurors that McCarthy admittedly never mentioned Snyder throwing a punch during her first interview with investigators. "I was covering a little bit for my boyfriend," McCarthy confessed on the witness stand.
Guilt prompted McCarthy to contact police on June 19 and set up a second interview, in which she told investigators that Snyder punched Cimorose without provocation before the shooting, she testified. McCarthy testified that she and Cimorose were no longer romantically involved.
When Insley asked McCarthy if she had asked the prosecution to dismiss two drug cases against her in exchange for her cooperation, she combatively responded, "Drugs has nothing to to do with this case."
Also during Insley's cross-examination, McCarthy confirmed that Cimorose was on probation in a criminal case for strangling her.
Insley reminded the jury during his closing argument Thursday that the autopsy report showed that Cimorose had methadone, cocaine and fentanyl and other drugs in his system at the time of his death.
"Ever smoke crack before," Ingsley rhetorically asked the jury, before remarking, "I heard it makes you pretty wacky."
The defense also took exception to the state's interpretation of what the shadowy footage showed. The state contended that Snyder lunged forward and punched Cimorose, but Insley insisted that a thrown punch is not visible in the video.
As for the object Cimorose purportedly possessed, Insley accused investigators of "sugar-coating" by using words like stick, pole and a table leg to describe it, so it wouldn't be associated with a weapon. Insley referred to the object as a club. It looked like a wooden cane with a section of metal where the handle should have been.
Snyder called 911; identified himself as the shooter; told the dispatcher he acted in self-defense and turned himself in after learning about the charges against him — all actions of an innocent man, according to Insley.

title: Emergency officials offer safety tips for frying turkey
author: Tom McCall
content:
Emergency officials offer safety tips for frying turkey

 November 21, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Tom McCall | Section: Local News 
 
 656
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — There are a few ways to cook a turkey. Deep frying has become a popular, though sometimes treacherous, way to get the job done.Many people like the crispy results deep frying can provide, including Easton Volunteer Fire Department Assistant Chief JR Dobson.
"I love deep fried turkey. It is like eating fried chicken. It is always moist in the middle. It tastes pretty good, especially if you season it right," Dobson said.
But when frying a turkey, especially for the first time, Dobson and other emergency officials warn it's important to research proper safety protocols.
"I think they can be dangerous if you don't do your research first," Dobson said. "You don't want to overfill that pot with grease and then the grease comes out of the pot and gets in the flame. We recommend that people who have never done it before, do your research."
Grease fires can happen quickly and are difficult to extinguish, as water cannot be used to put them out.
According to the National Fire Protection Association, Thanksgiving Day is the peak day for fires caused by cooking. About 1,000 home fires occur on that day nationwide.
On top of keeping an eye out for splashing grease, those frying turkeys are encouraged to ensure cooking oil doesn't get too hot, fryers are used in outdoor settings away from any structures and turkeys are fully thawed before being dropped in the oil.
"Make sure your turkey is thawed out. Make sure not deep frying a turkey inside of your house or inside a shed. Make sure you are outside away from any structure. If there was an event, make sure you are far enough away not to catch your building on fire," Dobson said.
Though it's not his favorite way to cook the bird, Jordon Lloyd, the chef at the Robert Morris Inn, offered some tips for frying turkey.
"You have a nice big pot. You want to keep it self-contained like out in a yard. You have kind of a jet propulsion burner is what you need, like what you would steam crabs with. It has a basket inside that you can lift up out of it. It takes about 45 minutes. You don't want the oil to be ripping hot like at 400 degrees. 325 is good. Fry it kind of slow and low," Lloyd said.
"You can't put stuffing in. It just falls out. Maybe I am not doing it right. Everyone seems to like it, but it just tastes weird to me," Lloyd said.
He offered his favorite way to cook a turkey.
"The best way is to brine it. The classic brine is one gallon of water, one cup of salt, half a cup of sugar. That is your brine. You boil that, and then chill it, and then you let your turkey soak in that," Lloyd said. "... A 12 pound turkey, you leave it overnight for 24 hours. Then I roast in an oven, no basting necessary. The brine is absorbed in the meat, keeps it nice and tender. The sugar you put in the brine activates that gorgeous brown turkey crust. Say 375 for three hours."
Those looking to give frying a turkey a try can find everything they need at local hardware stores.
"I sell it all. I have the pot, I have the burner, I have the oil, gloves. We have peanut oil. We sell propane and injectors if you want to put your own seasoning into them. Most of the people that buy know what they are doing and have done it before. But there are some that don't," said Mason of Easton Hardware, who did not share his last name.
"The bucket of oil pretty much explains it. So many minutes per pound and at such and such a temperature, and you roll on. It is easier than sitting in an oven. Just don't let there be any moisture on the bird before you put it in there. Happy Thanksgiving," Mason said.

title: St. Michaels VFD places new engine into service
author: Mike Detmer; mdetmer@chespub.com
content:
St. Michaels VFD places new engine into service

 August 3, 2023 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Mike Detmer; mdetmer@chespub.com | Page: A3 | Section: News 
 
 740
 Words 

 Read News Document

 ST. MICHAELS - A brand new piece of fire equipment is in service for the residents of St. Michaels and Talbot County.St. Michaels Volunteer Fire Department's Engine 45, an engine tanker, was put into service on July 27 and has already run calls, including pumping water for the response to an attic fire in town last week.Engine 45 is a 2023 E-One Cyclone, featuring a 1,035-gallon water tank, Cummins L9 engine, Hale QMAX pump, Harrison Hydraulic Generator, Whelen and Firetech lighting, and an Arkon Electric Monitor.St. Michaels VFD President Chris Thomas said the new engine has a larger water tank, a necessity in the rural environs of St. Michaels and elsewhere the engine will serve in the area, often not near hydrants.The new engine carries 1,000 feet of 5-inch supply hose, 500 feet of 3-inch hose, five attack lines, a Blitzfire Monitor, a battery powered fan and work lights, and a full complement of firefighting tools.Engine 45 replaced Engine 49, a 2009 engine, in the top of SMVFD's rotation as the "first due" engine. Engine 45 was purchased to replace Engine 48, a 1990 engine that served the department for 33 years, and was placed in reserve in the department's fleet.Thomas said the older engine had exceeded the expected 30-year service window, and that while it is still serviceable, parts for repairs are getting harder to find and the apparatus lacks updated safety features.Typically, the department would sell the engine, Thomas said, but it is being retained as a precaution due to the lengthy lead time to fill orders that has become the norm in the fire apparatus manufacturing industry.Engine 45 was designed by the SMFD Engine committee and purchased through Patriot Fire in Grasonville. The engine cost $718,850 and carries well over $200,000 of tools, hose, radios and breathing apparatus.The RFP for the new engine was put out in 2021, and the committee moved swiftly to finalize the purchase, and the efficient of the process led to the relatively rapid acquisition and placement into service, Thomas said.The funding for the fire apparatus came from a variety of sources. "It's a combination of fundraising efforts and money that we get from the county, town and state," Thomas said."The department thanks the generous residents and businesses who helped make this purchase happen through their donations and support over the past few years," the fire department said in a statement about the new engine.Thomas, who is in his third year as the department's president, said the department's board does a good job of strategic budgeting for future equipment replacements and maintenance of the fire station.Fundraising efforts include barbecue chicken dinners, a fund drive and a rotation of other types of campaigns, but he said the department's pit beef and pit turkey offerings were particularly tasty. "I think that it is off the charts it's phenomenal," he said.SMVFD has around 70 members, and of those about half are fire and EMS personnel.Just like fire companies across the country, paid and volunteer alike, SMVFD faces a manpower crunch.Thomas said the nature of the demographics of the St. Michaels area poses a challenge for the department, as many residents are retirees, although the talent pool of retirees helps ensure the administrative part of the community organization is well staffed.As far as fire and EMS personnel, Thomas said, "We're hurting just like everyone else." Still, the department forges on as the status quo of consistent calls for emergency response continues, and the department continues to plan and save for future acquisitions.Thomas said the brush truck and tanker truck are both in the latter stages of their service, and the department continues its work on that front too, continuing to raise and secure funds and being prepared for what is now a three-to five-year wait time on new equipment.The newest member of the SMVFD fleet isn't the first with the title of "Engine 45" - the previous 45 was an engine with an open cab and tailboards that volunteers ride on, braving the heat and cold depending on the season, before carrying out their emergency response.The equipment has changed, but the fundamental aspects of the job have not. Engine 45 sits in the right hand of the middle bay of the firehouse, waiting to carry to the volunteers to the next call.

title: State could improve juvenile justice system
author: STEPHEN RIDEOUT
content:
State could improve juvenile justice system

 January 25, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: STEPHEN RIDEOUT | Section: Columns 
 
 759
 Words 

 Read News Document

 The first juvenile court was founded in 1899 in Chicago. Since then, the states have passed laws that created their own juvenile court systems. These are broad systems that function differently within each state. That impacts similar cases in different ways.So, in one state a child of a certain age automatically can be treated as an adult depending on the crime charged while in another state that same child would go through a hearing in the juvenile court to determine probable cause and if a judicial officer felt the case should remain in juvenile court or go to adult court for trial and treatment as an adult.
After I retired from the bench in 2004, I began consulting in states to help them improve how their systems worked for children and families with a focus on local collaboration efforts among courts, child welfare agencies, lawyers and service agencies to help improve outcomes.
From my experience as a judge in Virginia and my consulting work around the country, some states have confusing and sometimes counterproductive laws for the treatment of juveniles tried for delinquent offenses or crimes. Maryland is one of them.
To that end, what follows is an explanation of just one way that Maryland could improve its juvenile justice system. It is not, however, intended to say that the proposed legislation that the General Assembly is considering is the right answer. It is meant to offer an alternative that might work better for everyone.
In Virginia, where I was a juvenile and domestic relations district court judge, the decision for treating a youth as an adult was left to the juvenile court judge after he or she made a determination of probable cause that the child committed the offense, reviewed a report prepared by the juvenile justice agency on the child's background and court history and heard other evidence that the parties wanted to present.
The judge then decided if the evidence supported the removal of the case to adult court or not. No matter what the decision was, either the commonwealth attorney or the defense attorney could appeal that decision to the Circuit Court for a new hearing by a different judge.
The Virginia process worked well and efficiently, and those cases that were removed to Circuit Court were done with a more complete understanding of what happened and who may have done what. It also allowed the juvenile court judge to detain the youth in a juvenile detention facility where services were available rather than in an adult jail, where he or she should have been held separate from the adult population.
The concern that I have about the Maryland process is that the state's attorney can have limited information about the crime and alleged perpetrator and his or her background. The decision can be made based on public outrage that may not be founded on facts but rather, nowadays, on social media.
I recall cases that I heard that would have met the Maryland standard for trial as an adult that did not, in my opinion, warrant removal to Circuit Court. One involved a youth with no prior court involvement who was handed a gun while riding in a car with four other youth, one of whom was his cousin, who was sitting in the front seat of the car. The defendant was holding the gun when it discharged accidentally and killed his cousin.
In Maryland, given his age, from my understanding of Maryland law, it would have gone to Circuit Court for trial as an adult; and he would have been held in jail rather than a juvenile detention facility.
Another case involved what would have been a school yard fistfight. The commonwealth attorney sought to remove that case involving several youths to Circuit Court. While there was probable cause for the removal of most of them, there was no probable cause as to one and the cause of death was a blow to the back of deceased youth's head when his head hit on some steps after he was hit one time with a fist.
Some of the youth had prior records with the court and so their cases went to Circuit Court for trial as adults while I kept some in juvenile court and found no probable cause as to one youth. Appeals were allowed for all those cases for new determinations by our Circuit Court.
Despite opposition by state's attorneys to a change in the law, I would urge the members of the General Assembly to work to improve the current law by supporting reasonable changes such as the process in Virginia.

title: Vote 'yes' on Question A — support public safety
author: PETE LESHER
content:
Vote 'yes' on Question A — support public safety

 October 5, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: PETE LESHER | Section: Columns 
 
 478
 Words 

 Read News Document

 Four years ago, Talbot County voters overwhelmingly approved a temporary increase in the property tax revenue cap by an "extra penny." Our public safety operations were facing a recruitment and retention crisis because of low pay and inferior benefits compared to surrounding jurisdictions.Talbot County has made enormous progress with the "extra penny" on the property tax since 2022. Sheriff's deputies' pay is competitive and sheriff's deputies now are on the state-sponsored LEOPS retirement program, allowing them to retire after 25 years. These benefits, in conjunction with solid leadership, means the Sheriff's Office can fill open positions. Deputies now retire from the department – a once-rare circumstance – rather than leaving to work in other jurisdictions.
Likewise, our Emergency Services compensation has increased.
Pay for paramedics, emergency medical technicians and 911 dispatchers is more competitive than in 2020 — though we need to monitor this against surrounding counties, and paramedics are now eligible for the LEOPS retirement program, a popular benefit. The county has stepped its sixth advanced life aupport ambulance crew to a seven-day, round-the-clock unit, helping us keep response times within the critical 8-minute standard.
The county is planning a new ambulance station near the Chapel District Elementary School, which will help reduce response times in the northeast corner of Talbot County, where we have struggled to meet the 8-minute standard.
Our County Detention Center has faced staffing shortages, forcing mandatory overtime to operate the facility safely. The County has responded by boosting correctional officer salaries and budgeted to convert their retirement plan to the more robust state-sponsored CORS program.
The state of Maryland mandates what we spend on our court system and the minimum that we must spend on public schools. While the state allows the county to exceed its property tax cap to fund schools, there is no state mandate to fund the sheriff's department or ambulance services or road repairs. And so these critical county services may suffer if the property tax cap restricts revenues and forces cuts.
All of the funds raised by the "extra penny" on the property tax since 2022 — and more — has gone to boosting public safety. The "extra penny" runs out in 2026. The Talbot County Council unanimously authorized a ballot question to renew the "extra penny" for seven more years, out of concern public safety costs will continue to rise faster than the 2% property tax cap.
Voting for Question A allows the County Council the option to levy the "extra penny" for seven more years — through fiscal year 2033. Even with this "extra penny," over the last four years or for the next seven years, Talbot County maintains the lowest property tax rate in the state of Maryland.
If you support public safety and emergency services, vote for Question A. Do it for your family's safety. Do it for your neighbors. Do it for your own good. Vote for Question A.
