 EASTON — Fourth of July is right around the corner, and many residents and towns will began setting off fireworks to celebrate.Fireworks come with risks from starting fires to injuries of an individual, safety officials say. Residents are advised to follow certain protocols to keep celebrations safe.
Master Deputy State Fire Marshal Oliver Alkire recommends residents to go to public fireworks shows. For those who are dead-set on setting fireworks off themselves, Alkire doesn't recommend going over state lines to purchase fireworks.
"If you are going to be using any fireworks, just to keep in mind that you should only be purchasing and using fireworks that you are buying within your county or your area," he said. "... Anything that you can purchase at a roadside stand, I can assure you, has been inspected, or anywhere in any retail stores."
The most important thing Alkire emphasizes is only adults should handle fireworks.
"If you're going to light fireworks, only allow the adults to light the fireworks, only light one firework at a time, and also keep all children and pets away from fireworks," he said.
For those handling fireworks at home, Easton Volunteer Fire Department Chief J.R. Dobson recommends to have a water hose nearby and ready in case of a fire.
For fireworks that light and don't work, Alkire recommends putting the fireworks in a bucket of water for 24 hours, then disposing of them properly.
The state fire marshal's office recommend not putting fireworks anywhere on the body. In 2023, there were two deaths in Maryland resulting from people holding fireworks to their chest or head.
In the event of an emergency, people are advised to call 911 for assistance.

title: A 'crisis' on the shore — animal intake on the rise
author: Veronica Fernandez-Alvarado
content:
A 'crisis' on the shore — animal intake on the rise

 June 28, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Veronica Fernandez-Alvarado | Section: Local News 
 
 462
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — Animal shelters across the Eastern Shore are facing higher levels of dog and cat intake than seen in years past.Patty Crankshaw-Quimby, executive director of Talbot Humane, said that just in the first six months of this calendar year, the shelter has seen a significant increase in the number of animals entering its care.
There has been a 35% increase in dog intake and a 25% increase in cat intake this year over 2023, she said. Crankshaw-Quimby noted that the shelter has yet to reach its busiest time of the year for kitten, which is in the later summer months and early fall.
"This is a trend we are seeing across the country," Crankshaw-Quimby said. "I am the president of Professional Animal Workers of Maryland, the state association of shelters and animal control agencies, and we are seeing crisis level intake in our larger municipalities."
A similar trend is being seen in Caroline County.
Karen Culotta, director of the Caroline County Humane Society, said the number of dogs at the animal shelter has increased significantly over the past four years.
The shelter is currently at 95% capacity. Though Culotta said they spend all their efforts caring for all the animals they can, the influx has overwhelmed the shelter.
Culotta acknowledged that it is difficult to determine the exact reason for the influx. She said it seems to go beyond issues of pets going without being spayed or neutered. She speculates that it could be economically driven.
"For some people, with the cost of vet care going up, with the cost of everything going up, or, since the pandemic, sometimes (people) can't afford to feed their animals or can't afford to get vaccinations, which is required of every cat and dog in the state of Maryland," Culotta said. "It's very challenging for everybody here."
Crankshaw-Quimby said that the Talbot County Shelter has embedded essential programs to help address the large number of animals the shelter is facing.
"We work very hard to keep animals out of the shelter with our robust assortment of programs; however, being an open admission shelter that turns no county resident in need of surrendering their pet away, as well as performing the role of animal control, one large animal control seizure or a wave of animal surrenders could put us over the top," Crankshaw-Quimby said. "This is why the foster, spay/neuter and intervention programs are so very important."
Culotta said she has contacted directors of other local shelters, and they have noted the "odd" rise in intake.
"It's definitely a crisis here on the Eastern Shore," Culotta said.
Culotta and Crankshaw-Quimby encouraged residents to partake in spray/neuter programs and to sign-up to take in foster animals, particularly dogs, at a local shelter. Participating in these programs can assist shelters as they go through high animal intake, they said.

title: Following lockdown, lawmakers express worry over Capitol’s emergency alert system
author: ANGELIQUE GINGRAS Capital News Service
content:
Following lockdown, lawmakers express worry over Capitol’s emergency alert system

 March 2, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: ANGELIQUE GINGRAS Capital News Service | Section: State News 
 
 449
 Words

 ANNAPOLIS — A day after a threat to the state capitol prompted a near two-hour lockdown, lawmakers applauded the quick work of law enforcement, but raised concerns about efficient communication.Sen. Antonio Hayes (D-Baltimore City) said he was voting in a Finance Committee meeting when a member of the press texted him about a security threat to the State House. A few minutes later, a state trooper in the room notified committee members to shelter in place, before they were escorted out of the building.
"I wish I would have gotten a text message internally before I got one externally, but I think just given the series of events, it is what it is," Hayes said.
The incident occurred around 5 p.m. Thursday when an anonymous call was made to the Annapolis City Police Department threatening to target the state capitol. After nearly two hours of lockdown, the Maryland Capitol Police determined there was no evidence of a potential threat.
The Senate and House of Delegates convened Friday, each opening their floor sessions with a standing ovation for the law enforcement officers who sprang into action.
"Yesterday was certainly a very scary moment for many, a very intense moment, but a moment when our first responders did everything that they were supposed to do and kept everyone safe, followed protocol and really responded to a very intense situation appropriately," Senate President Bill Ferguson (D-Baltimore County) told reporters Friday.
Capital News Service reached out to a spokesperson for the Department of General Services, which oversees the Maryland Capitol Police, who provided no comment on the communication efforts by law enforcement.
"The one thing you can't have happen is, you don't want to over alert or over alarm the people you're trying to protect," said Sen. Will Folden (R-Frederick), who also serves as an active duty police officer in the city of Frederick. "It's a necessary element to only provide absolutely necessary information to not create panic."
The incident occurred just days after the General Assembly signed a contract with Motorola to incorporate a text message alert system for state officials in the State House complex, according to Ferguson. That system is still being built, he said, and was not in use at the time of the threat.
"Within the structure we have right now, (state troopers) did an amazing job. I think we all would like a world in which we had a text service to keep us informed." said Sen. Sarah Elfreth (D-Anne Arundel).
Hayes added, "I didn't even realize that we were in the middle of negotiating a text messaging contract, which I think would have been helpful."
While it isn't clear when the alert system will be up and running, lawmakers expressed gratitude for police efforts yesterday.

 CAMBRIDGE - The sunny, warm afternoon of Sept. 20, 2022, was a perfect day for a family birthday barbecue in Cambridge. Around 3 p.m., everything changed.Numerous officers from the Cambridge Police Department responded to the area of Rigby Avenue and Fairmount Avenue for a report of shots fired around 3:05 p.m. Police spread out, canvassing the area nearby for any witnesses.Minutes later, officers found the body of20 year-old Kevin Raeford laying in a wooded area near the 600 block of Edgewood Avenue. Police officers would later testify that Raeford's body was covered by a blanket.About 20 minutes after police were dispatched, Raeford was pronounced dead by medics. A medical examiner ruled his death a homicide by gunshot wound.Only one person is responsible for Raeford's death, and it wasn't a random shooter - it was Raeford's cousin, Geett Cornish, said Dorchester County State's Attorney Amanda Leonard, pointing toward Cornish across the courtroom at the outset of his trial Tuesday.Cornish, 31, of Cambridge, faces first-and second-degree murder, assault, reckless endangerment and handgun charges in connection to the shooting that left Raeford dead.Family members who were present that day would be called to testify against Cornish, sharing emotions they'd struggled with for the past year, Leonard said. The family would provide the 'who' of the case, while others, including law enforcement, would fill in the 'what' and the 'where' of the shooting.But to Baltimore-based defense attorney Brad MacFee, testimony from three other civilian witnesses, along with Raeford's affiliation with a local gang, would be key for the jurors deciding the case.In his opening statement, MacFee asserted that Cambridge has a gang problem - a "significant, substantial" one. title: Ridgely police vehicles, equipment were sold, transferred this summer
author: KONNER METZ kmetz@chespub.com
content:
Ridgely police vehicles, equipment were sold, transferred this summer

 RIDGELY — The town of Ridgely has sold seven vehicles and three firearms once belonging to the Ridgely Police Department since the police department was disbanded, according to records obtained by the Star Democrat.The vehicles and firearms were sold to the the Caroline County sheriff and other Eastern Shore municipalities.
Residents in Ridgely have been without the service of the Ridgely Police Department since a state investigation into the town's police chief was opened in March. Ridgely's commissioners suspended Eckrich and the entire department on March 12.
The town entered into a short-term agreement with the Caroline County Sheriff's Office to provide police coverage in place of the suspended officers. When the Ridgely officers were officially laid off at the start of the fiscal year on July 1, the town entered into a new memorandum of understanding with the county sheriff's office for fiscal year 2025.
Caroline County Sheriff Donnie Baker says he is committed to ensuring his office provides Ridgely residents with adequate police coverage.
"We have had positive feedback from a large number of residents who are happy with the service," Baker said. "I am absolutely here for the citizens of the Town of Ridgely and the citizens of Caroline County."
A July report said state investigators found no "sufficient evidence of criminal activity" looking into "suspected" perjury and misconduct by Ridgely Police Chief Jeff Eckrich.
Transaction records from Ridgely show the town began to sell and transfer vehicles and equipment in the weeks before the release of the investigation's report and before officers were officially laid off.
In June, the town transferred three pistols and three radios to the Caroline County Sheriff's Office with no charge associated.
Three police vehicles — two 2022 Ford Interceptors and one 2020 Ford Interceptor — were sold to the Sheriff's Office for $1 apiece on June 18, transaction records show.
On July 12, the town sold a 2023 Chevy Tahoe to the Town of Denton for just over $44,000. On July 27, Ridgely sold three vehicles to the City of Salisbury — a 2014 stripped K-9 Ford Interceptor for $1,000, a 2015 Ford Interceptor for $4,000 and a 2017 Ford Interceptor for $8,000.
Ridgely Town Commissioners did not respond to questions from the Star Democrat regarding the vehicle and equipment sales. Commissioners have maintained that a statement provided at a Sept. 9 town meeting, which did not address the vehicles and equipment, will be the town's final statement regarding the police department.
COUNTY COVERAGEBaker said the vehicles and equipment acquired by the county are being used by the deputies providing coverage to the town. The vehicles and equipment those deputies previously had will go back to the Sheriff's Office inventory to be used by county officers.
The current memorandum of understanding between the town and county outlines that the Sheriff's Office provides 480 hours of coverage per month.
Baker said the end goal is to have three full-time deputies providing coverage in Ridgely. At this time, there are only two full-time deputies, with a third in the police academy.
Sgt. Keith Collison, a former Ridgely officer, is overseeing daily operations in the town. The second full-time deputy is Cpl. Tracy Ferguson, who has more than seven years of law enforcement experience.
When the deputies stationed in Ridgely are not working, the Sheriff's Office and Maryland State Police are supplementing that temporary gap with patrol checks, Baker said.
Baker added that at one point during the current agreement, there were two officers training in the academy that were planned to be stationed in Ridgely. During that time, the county brought an "experienced" officer to serve as the second full-time deputy and assumed the cost of one of those officers in training at the academy.
By February or early March, Baker says he plans to transfer a third full-time deputy to Ridgely, which he says will "more than fulfill the agreement set out in the MOU."
The Ridgely Police Department office within the town hall building is serving as a substation for the Sheriff's Office deputies, Baker said. It is "up and functional" with fiber optics, computer systems and phone lines.

 CHESTERTOWN — On Tuesday afternoon, Nov. 19, ground was broken for the future site of the Robert B. Rust Jr. Kent County Emergency Medical Services headquarters at 104 Vickers Drive. The site was dedicated to the public servant for his vision almost 30 years ago.Rust, as well as Director of Emergency Services Pete Landon, Chief of Emergency Services Logan Quinn, Kent County Commission President Ron Fithian, Commissioners John Price and Albert Nickerson and County Administrator Shelley Heller tossed out the first shovelfuls of dirt as community members applauded.
Rust reflected on the past, his son, Danny, at his side. Rust said he would have never imagined this building being named after him when he first proposed an idea for a 24-7 Advanced Life System (ALS) to then, Sheriff John Price.
Fithian pointed out that in 1994, Rust approached the County with an idea to pay EMT's to assist with the volunteers.
At the time, the County only had one paramedic, part time, and that was deputy John Longest, Fithian said.
Price added, "It was Mr. Rust who started the conversation and the reason the program has grown to this degree."
Rust was director of emergency services management in Kent from Oct. 24, 1983 to April 12, 2005, a county employee, a dedicated volunteer and Chief of Kent and Queen Anne's Rescue Squad for 11 consecutive years.
According to Director of Public Works Dan Mattson, they can expect the building project to be finished late spring of next year and will begin moving dirt shortly.
Heller noted how fast the project has moved since it was introduced at the commissioners meeting in early September.
"It has defied the laws of government," she said, crediting the Department of Public Works and the Department of Emergency Services on an effective collaborative effort.
Quinn noted the importance of the site. He said the property is not just a headquarters, but a second home for his crew. Quinn expressed gratitude for all the repairs the County made to preserve the current headquarters in Lynch, but stated it was clear they could not stay in that place longterm.
The new site will enable them to expand their programs, Quinn remarked. A place where ideas will be posed and where they can grow as a community.
Landon told the audience consisting of policemen, EMT's, county employees and concerned citizens, that this is not as much of a groundbreaking ceremony as it is a gathering, of past, present and future.
The new building will be designed and constructed by Industrial Engineering Incorporated and will roughly cost $628,000.
Quinn honored Rust as well as those who followed him.
"They were trailblazers of the past, and with this building, myself and others can be trailblazers of the future."

 CAMBRIDGE - After more than three hours of deliberation, a jury found Jonathan Diaz-Santiago, 36, of Cambridge, not guilty of first-and second-degree assault. The jury could not come to an agreement on a reckless endangerment charge, resulting in a mistrial on that count.Thursday, Dorchester County State's Attorney Amanda Leonard said the state had not yet made a decision on whether they will retry the reckless endangerment charge.The charges stemmed from a report made by two of Diaz-Santiago's family members that Santiago attempted to hit, choke and stab his stepfather, Jose Sierra, during an argument on Decoursey Bridge Road in Cambridge on May 6.Diaz-Santiago was originally charged with attempted first-and second-degree murder, as well.Leonard said it was a prosecutorial choice, based on the evidence in the case, to drop those charges before the trial.During opening statements of the trial, Leonard said that a family fishing expedition on May 6 ended in violence and bloodshed. She said Sierra was "battered, bruised and in need of medical treatment," following the altercation.Worse than the physical injuries, Leonard said, are the long term effects Sierra is facing from the incident.Defense Attorney Michelle Moodispaw, from the Dorchester County Public Defender's Office, said that the state's case was based around the victim's claims."Because he said so," Moodispaw said in her opening statement, adding that law enforcement didn't talk with others in the area in which the fight took place.Moodispaw said that the case was not simple and straightforward, and said the jury would have just as many questions at the end of the trial as they did at the beginning of the trial.Moodispaw said Sierra was drinking that day, angry with Diaz-Santiago, and said Sierra hit Diaz-Santiago with a liquor bottle "several times."According to police, following the incident, Sierra reported that Diaz-Santiago grabbed his throat, attempting to choke him, while on the fishing trip. According to charging documents, the victim told police that Diaz-Santiago put a knife to his throat and verbally threatened him.Sierra told police he exited the car and was followed by Diaz-Santiago, who then attempted to stab him in the upper chest area.  CHESTERTOWN — A day-long law enforcement operation on Flatland Road ended peacefully Friday when a man experiencing a mental health crisis surrendered after firing multiple gunshots and prompting widespread community response.The incident began around 5:45 a.m. March 28, when Chestertown Police Department and Kent County Sheriff's Office responded to shots fired in the 100 block of Flatland Road. Witnesses, including neighbor Todd Hughes, reported hearing gunshots around 5 a.m., followed by someone knocking on a nearby door.
Police vehicles were first spotted in the area around 5:30 a.m., with tactical response escalating throughout the morning. At approximately 8:30 a.m., a SWAT-type vehicle with a large ram approached the house, officers repeatedly calling for the individual to come out, saying they wanted to "check on him" and were "not there to hurt him."
The extensive operation disrupted community activities. Shortly before 1 p.m., parents were notified that students on bus routes near Flatland Road and Hilltop Drive would need to be picked up from school due to safety concerns. Radcliffe Creek School, the closest school to the incident, advised keeping students indoors.
Residents in surrounding areas, including a trailer park near Sunny's Mart, were advised to stay inside.
Law enforcement personnel were observed in nearby woods, and a helicopter and drone were part of the operation.
At approximately 1:30 p.m., the subject voluntarily exited the residence and surrendered without incident. He was taken into custody and transported to a local medical facility for a mental health evaluation. Criminal charges are pending, Chestertown Police Chief Ron Dixon, lead agency on the incident, said.
Flatland Road remained closed throughout the day, with motorists advised to avoid the area. Authorities used the Everbridge alert system to notify nearby residents of the ongoing situation.
While initial police statements suggested no immediate public risk, neighbors expressed concerns about the incident's severity. The precise circumstances leading to the standoff remain under investigation.

 CHESTERTOWN — Every first and third Wednesday, the Kent County Sheriff's Office K-9 unit, cooperating with law enforcement in Talbot, Dorchester and Caroline counties, train their dogs.On Wednesday, Sept. 18, they trained at Geno's Automotive in Kent County. After that, the K-9 units were invited to the Kent County Middle School to receive something special.
In a gesture of police support, the Kent Puppy Pals 4-H Dog Club donated a Line of fire Defense Street Fighter vest to Addy, a German Shepherd, handled by Dfc. Craig Lewis of the Dorchester County Sheriff's Office.
Going through Kent County Sheriff's Office Sgt. Scott Lockerman's organization, the Maryland Police K9 Foundation, the Puppy Pals donated a check for $300 in June.
Club Leader of Puppy Pals Kim Montooth explained each year they do a service project. Last year, for instance, they raised money for the Humane Society. This year was exciting for the kids and something different, Montooth said.
Molly's Place also donated $1,000 in a vest for Waylon, a K-9 black lab handled by Pfc. Nick Lang of the Easton Police Department.
In front of about 20 people, the dogs modeled the vests, which are lightweight enough yet specially designed to protect their vital organs.
Then the Puppy Pals kids and their families gathered around to pet the dogs.
After the children met with the dogs and 4-H mom Karri Bryant had a playful tug of war with Addy, they were invited into the school where they witnessed a live demonstration of how Addy sniffs out controlled substances.
Controlled substances were stashed in two classrooms. Led by Lewis, sniffing desks and drawers, Addy alerted to the controlled substance in both rooms in about 30 seconds.
Trainer Mark Carr of Tidewater Strategic Services said the dog doesn't go right to the spot because of the nature of scent itself. The K-9 moves around the perimeter of the room, getting the entire scent. Once she gets a complete picture, she can hone in.
President of the club Trenton Montooth was impressed. At 14 years of age, he has decided he wants to be a K-9 officer.
Lockerman thanked the Puppy Pals and Molly's Place, expressing the importance of their giving by showing the positive impact K-9 dogs make.

title: Cambridge PD provides holiday cheer with Shop with a Cop
author: Veronica Fernandez-Alvarado
content:
Cambridge PD provides holiday cheer with Shop with a Cop

 December 16, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Veronica Fernandez-Alvarado | Section: Local News

 Words

 CAMBRIDGE — On Saturday afternoon, police sirens rang as dozens of children were escorted by Cambridge police to Walmart for the annual Shop with a Cop event.The children were met with warm welcomes from police officers before they raced inside for this holiday tradition.
Shop with a Cop provides the opportunity for underprivileged children in the community to spend quality time with local police officers and purchase Christmas presents.
Sergeant Antoine Patton from the Cambridge Police Department, said this event began in 2015 in an effort to help families throughout the area during the holiday season.
"We realized that in today's economy that everyone doesn't have the funds, and we as a police department here, wanted to make sure that we could help as many families as possible," Patton said. "We wanted to see as many smiling kids on Christmas as we possibly could."
Through a live raffle system, families and loved ones of local children apply to have the children participate. Each drawing is broadcast on Facebook Live.
After names are picked, Patton calls the families to let them know their child has won. Then, a small group leaves the station to pick the children up from their homes and take them to Walmart.
Each child then gets to spend $100 on "anything of their choosing." This year 30 children were chosen during the raffle.
According to Patton, this is the first year that all funds for the event were entirely made available through donations. Patton said several organizations, including Paul Davis Restoration of Delmarva, The Lions Club, the Friendship Methodist Church of Aireys, and private donations provided funds for gifts.
On Saturday, the children were split into small groups and assigned a police officer, who guided them through the toy aisles. With the help of the officers, children choose toys from Nerf guns to pink tea sets.
Lydia Travers, a parent of a Shop with a Cop winner, said her mother sent her son Zyonn's name into the Shop with a Cop raffle and they were lucky enough to be chosen.
According to Travers, this event allows the community to come together and help each other.
Patton said the children aren't the only ones benefitting from Shop with a Cop. Police officers have shared positive experiences with the children outside of the event.
"It helps us out tremendously, because the children get to see us doing something fun and positive," Patton said. "And these children don't forget. I have children that we took maybe three or four years ago, and they still remember me, say, 'Hey Mom, that's the guy took us Christmas shopping.'"

title: Eastern Shore legislators prioritizing health care, public safety this session
author: Maggie Trovato
content:
Eastern Shore legislators prioritizing health care, public safety this session

 January 10, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Maggie Trovato | Section: General Assembly 
 
 909
 Words 

 Read News Document

 ANNAPOLIS — As the 446th session of the Maryland General Assembly kicks off, Eastern Shore legislators are focused on health care, public safety and the implications of the budget shortfall.Sen. Johnny Mautz, Sen. Stephen Hershey and Del. Tom Hutchinson all said the University of Maryland Shore Regional Health's new regional medical center in Easton is a top priority for Eastern Shore legislators this session.
"Making sure all the pieces are in place for that project to move forward," Mautz said. "It's long overdue to be replaced and upgraded."
Mautz (R-Caroline, Dorchester, Talbot, Wicomico) said there are multiple hurdles to achieving this, including state regulatory approvals and other "loose ends." He said the University of Maryland Medical System has made it clear that a new medical center in Easton is also their top priority.
"Which is a huge help," Mautz said. "However, making sure that everything else is in place ... it's a huge undertaking."
Hershey (R-Kent, Queen Anne's, Cecil, and Caroline) said that in creating an Aging & Wellness Center in Kent County and a freestanding medical facility in Dorchester County, the "spokes" are being put in place when it comes to health care on the Eastern Shore.
"But now we need the hub," he said. "And so what we are advocating for down here in Annapolis — and I've spoken with the governor about it — is we need to finalize that final piece on how we deliver health care services in the Mid-Shore region."
Hutchinson (R-Dorchester, Talbot, Wicomico), who is on the Maryland House Health and Government Operations Committee, said he is sponsoring a number of bills that will make sure health care facilities have additional resources. He said he also plans to support bills related to better access to mental health care on the Shore.
Del. Chris Adams (R-Dorchester, Talbot, Wicomico), who is the chair of the Eastern Shore Delegation, called public safety a "top-line issue" for this session.
On the Eastern Shore, Adams said that it has become more difficult to hire and retain law enforcement officers.
"I think it's because we've made this career path so difficult and so unclear about what the role is and what the responsibilities are," he said, adding that the job of law enforcers are to serve and protect.
In 2022, state legislators passed bills to limit what charges children under the age of 13 face. Adams said this legislation is a piece of this public safety issue.
"(Juvenile justice) has been an incremental step that has been, shall I say, just anti-police," he said.
Mautz said there are different approaches to amending the juvenile justice legislation. He said one approach is to look at enforcement and another is to look at services that can prevent children from engaging in criminal activity.
"You can have all the services in the world, but if you don't have the deterring enforcement, the services aren't going to do any good," he said. "You've got to have both, and you really need to start with enforcement. I mean there's got to be a rule of law."
Hutchinson, who said he thinks the existing juvenile reform laws need to be modified, has spearheaded a group of different stakeholders in Dorchester and Wicomico counties to discuss the the juvenile reform laws and its effects.
"I got to the point that I invited the Secretary of Juvenile Services to come, where we could express our frustrations," he said.
Hutchinson said it will be interesting to see what the pushback will be on these laws. He said that some members of the General Assembly feel that the laws haven't been in place for long enough to amend them.
"Me, along with many, many other members of the delegation, completely disagree with that," he said. "We need to address it now."
When it comes to finances, the state is facing a projected $761 million budget shortfall for FY2025.
Adams said he fears that tax increases are coming. He said that in his nearly 10 years as a legislator, this might be the first year he votes against the budget.
Hershey said dealing with the budget is a priority this session.
"We're going to have to find some ways that we can cut spending and pass a budget that doesn't include increasing taxes," he said.
Del. Jay Jacobs (R-Kent, Queen Anne's, Cecil, and Caroline) said the legislature needs to be careful how it spends money.
"I like to prioritize the necessities first," he said. "If you've got extra money after your primary duties are taken care of, then you can address some of that."
Jacobs said he has concerns with funding for the Blueprint for Maryland's Future, a statewide plan to increase public education funding, improve student outcomes and improve the quality of public education.
He said meeting the Blueprint requirements will be especially hard on his home county, Kent County, adding that a one-size-fits-all approach is not going to work.
"I am not at all in favor of one-size-fits-all anything," he said. "Because we are so diverse in this state."
Jacobs said that counties should not have to face raising taxes "to a ridiculous level" or cutting services in order to fund the Blueprint.
"And some of that is potentially on the line right now," he said. "That's what's very concerning."
Del. Sheree Sample-Hughes (D-Dorchester, Wicomico) said she understands that some jurisdictions are struggling to fund the Blueprint.
"I know what that looks like," she said. "Because they can't get any more property taxes out of the citizens, because in areas such as Crisfield, they don't have anymore property to sell. It's flooded. So, it's a struggle."

title: Easton minister detained by ICE
author: Lily Tierney
content:
Easton minister detained by ICE

 July 22, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Lily Tierney | Section: Local News 
 
 507
 Words

 EASTON — A beloved Easton minister was detained by U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement agents, taken to Salisbury and is now at the Baltimore ICE detention center where he is awaiting his next transfer, according to his daughter.Honduran born Daniel Fuentes Espinal has lived in the United States since 2001 and has served as the minister of Iglesia del Nazareno Jesús Te Ama since 2015. According to his daughter, Clarissa Fuentes Diaz, Espinal was arrested by ICE agents early Monday morning after stopping by Lowe's to pick up material for a job site.
"He didn't see anything suspicious. He put the material in the car, but then when he went to McDonald's to get something for breakfast, he saw a car behind him that looked kind of weird," Cordero said.
ICE agents followed Espinal to the Easton pool, ultimately arresting him on Route 322. He was taken to the Salisbury holding center. "He preached to them all the way to Salisbury," Diaz said.
From 8 a.m. to 12:30 p.m., Espinal's family had no clue of his whereabouts. "We were about to do a report on a missing person because we didn't find out until almost 12:30," Diaz said.
Diaz said Espinal had no criminal record.
Since President Donald Trump took office in January, immigration arrests have doubled in the state of Maryland. More than 600 immigrants arrested during this time had no former criminal charges, according to the Deportation Data Project.
Espinal has three children and a large extended family that he cares for, Diaz said. Tred Avon Strategies principal Len Foxwell referred to him as a pillar of the community.
Earlier this month, Espinal spoke at Foxwell's son Darren's funeral. Diaz said Darren and her brother were best friends and his death has been hard on Espinal and the family.
Diaz said she has received over 10 character letters on her father's behalf since his arrest yesterday morning, including one from Foxwell.
"It wasn't until I got to know him, however, that I saw how he honors and embodies the values of Christ in every aspect of his life," Foxwell wrote in a letter to ICE.
Espinal's family has tried obtaining citizenship legally for years, but due to backlogs and expenses, Espinal remained undocumented, Diaz said.
"He's contributing to this country, and we're just trying to do it the right way," Diaz said. "You know, unfortunately, with everything going on, everyone's a criminal apparently, but we're just hoping for the best and just to get him out of there."
Diaz said each phone call Espinal makes from the detention center costs $50 for a 20-minute call and bond amounts for release currently range from $10,000 to $15,000.
"I've heard stories that people say, 'But why didn't you do it the legal way? Why aren't you doing it the legal way?' It's not easy," Diaz said. "You know, if you're not in that person's shoes, you shouldn't be judging, and you shouldn't be criticizing."
Espinal's family is relying on their faith and are hopeful that he will return home.
ICE could not be reached via phone to comment on this incident.

title: Cambridge parents plead guilty, sentenced for neglect of a minor
author: MAGGIE TROVATO mtrovato@chespub.com

Cambridge parents plead guilty, sentenced for neglect of a minor

 November 18, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: MAGGIE TROVATO mtrovato@chespub.com | Section: Crime 
 
 699
 Words

 CAMBRIDGE — Two Cambridge parents pleaded guilty to neglect of a minor Monday following the death of their 14-year-old daughter.David and Mandy Insley were each handed a sentence of five years of incarceration with all but 271 days of the incarceration suspended. Both have 271 days of credit for time served leading up to their plea hearing Monday.
Judge Karen Dean also sentenced David and Mandy Insley to five years of supervised probation. Conditions of probation include that they cannot bring pets into their home and that they both continue mental health treatment.
The parents were originally each charged with first-degree child abuse resulting in death, but the state entered into nolle prosequi on those counts, meaning the state will not prosecute for those charges.
As a part of a plea deal, Dorchester County State's Attorney Amanda Leonard recommended no more than an 18 month active sentence. She said no sentence is more difficult to go through than what David and Mandy Insley have to live with for the rest of their lives.
Leonard said that on June 26, 2023, police and emergency medical services responded to the Insley home in response to a 14-year-old girl suffering from a cardiac arrest. Paige Insley was found unresponsive in her bed and pronounced dead on the scene.
Leonard said the teen had been diagnosed at birth with a developmental disability that caused her to suffer from seizures. She said Mandy Insley indicated to police that she had forgotten to give her daughter medication for her seizures the night before but gave them to her in the morning.
An autopsy report found that Paige Insley most likely died of a seizure that was due to an underlying condition, Leonard said.
Leonard also spoke about the condition of the Insley home. She said police noted the house was dirty and cluttered. There was animal feces on the ground. Leonard said mice and mice excrement were found throughout the house.
Leonard said there were no findings of abuse to the child as a result of the conditions of the home, but she said there were findings that Paige Insley was neglected by parents who were responsible for her wellness, safety and living conditions.
Cambridge Code Enforcement and Dorchester County Animal Control were called to the house following Paige Insley's death, and, according to a news release from the Cambridge Police Department, Cambridge Code Enforcement condemned the house.
Both David and Mandy Insley spoke during the hearing Monday. Mandy Insley said she has been attending weekly appointments with a therapist and has started taking medication. David asked the judge that she allow him to rebuild with his wife. He said that leading up to Paige's death, the tapestry of his life had begun to unravel and they weren't able to get help with the house.
"We just want a chance to try and function again," he said through tears. "She was my best friend."
Mandy Insley's attorney Archibald McFadden said there was no causal link between the conditions of the house and Paige's death. He said the COVID-19 pandemic affected everyone, and the Inselys are one of example of that. The pandemic, he said, resulted in David Insley losing his job as a reporter at the Star Democrat. He said mental health issues exacerbated by isolation resulted in the family's poor living conditions.
McFadden said both David and Mandy Insley have gotten treatment and cleaned up their house.
David Insley's attorney Michelle Moodispaw from the Office of the Public Defender said David Insley has struggled with mental health challenges for most of his life and the pandemic and its effects led to a steep decline of mental health. She said letters submitted into evidence show who David Insley is as a father, particularly with Paige.
Leonard said she didn't think there was a lack of love or care of Paige from David and Mandy Insley, adding, "I can't explain what was going on in that home."
Before handing down the sentence, Judge Karen Dean said she was sorry for the Insleys' loss and called the situation "horrible." Dean said it was clear that neglect based on the state of the household and the death of the teen were two separate things. She said the death brought the neglect to light.

title: Cambridge sees reduction in crime in 2024 compared to previous year
author: Maggie Trovato
content:
Cambridge sees reduction in crime in 2024 compared to previous year

 January 31, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Maggie Trovato | Section: Crime 
 
 529
 Words 

 Read News Document

 CAMBRIDGE — The City of Cambridge saw a 14% reduction in crime in 2024.While presenting the Cambridge Police Department's 2024 year end report to the Cambridge City Council on Jan. 27, Police Chief Justin Todd called this accomplishment the "big one."
He said the department achieved many accomplishments in 2024.
"I have a lot of people to thank for that," he said. "Not only my officers and the staff, but also the city staff and the commissioners." Todd said it wouldn't have been possible without funding and the "numerous resources" the department was provided.
Along with reducing crime overall, Todd mentioned increasing the number of cameras around the city, creating better working relationships with the Dorchester County Board of Education and the Department of Juvenile Services and reaching a clearance rate of 69.6% in the department's Criminal Investigations Division.
Todd said the average clearance rate, which is the rate of crimes that are solved, is around 28% nationally. "So that just shows you what a good job they are doing," Todd said.
Todd also talked about the department's efforts to map crimes by where and when they occur. He said that informs how the department spends its time patrolling.
"We make sure that officers are in those areas as much as possible during that time," he said.
Todd listed the department's continued commitment to community-oriented policing as an accomplishment.
"These things, patrolling with purpose and community-oriented policing, will continue as we charge harder to fine-tune it and make it better," he said.
When it comes to specific crime stats for 2024, there were 30 aggravated assaults reported. Todd pointed out the "significant difference" from 2022 when there were 110 aggravated assaults reported in Cambridge. Compared to 2023, there was a 53% reduction in aggravated assaults in Cambridge in 2024.
According to the report, compared to 2023, burglaries and simple assaults were down 12% and 16%, respectively, in 2024.
Todd said that like 2023, there were two homicides in Cambridge in 2024. This number is a decrease from seven homicides in 2022.
Todd said one of the homicides in Cambridge this year was the result of gun violence and the other was a kidnapping in Easton that law enforcement officials believe resulted in a homicide in Cambridge.
The number of robberies as well as the number of rapes and sex offenses each increased by 12% in 2024 compared to the previous year. Todd said some of those rape and sex offenses investigations are still open.
RECRUITMENT AND RETENTIONDuring his presentation to the City Council, Todd also talked about the city's efforts to recruit and keep a full staff, which will continue into 2025.
"We're going to recruit, recruit, recruit good quality people that want to invest in the City of Cambridge and be here," he said.
Todd said the city has 36 sworn officers, including a civilian liaison officer. He said they were ready to put three people in the police academy but one didn't make the final interview and the other two determined it wasn't a good fit.
"So we're back at the drawing boards," he said.
Todd said the department has seven civilian employees.
"That has been significant in helping us do our daily work and customer service as we continue to move along," he said.

title: State's Attorney's Office won't prosecute Cambridge man for shooting incident
author: MAGGIE TROVATO mtrovato@chespub.com
content:
State's Attorney's Office won't prosecute Cambridge man for shooting incident

 August 21, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: MAGGIE TROVATO mtrovato@chespub.com | Section: Crime 
 
 327
 Words

 CAMBRIDGE — The Dorchester County State's Attorney's Office will not prosecute a Cambridge man for charges relating to an August 2023 shooting at Maces Lane and Bayly Road.Shallamar Robinson, 47, was arrested last August for attempted first- and second-degree murder, firearm use in a felony violent crime, first- and second-degree assault, reckless endangerment, reckless endangerment from a car, handgun on person, handgun in vehicle, loaded handgun on person and loaded handgun in vehicle.
The State's Attorney's Office will not prosecute Robinson for any of these 11 charges. Dorchester County State's Attorney Amanda Leonard said the state made this decision because it felt there was insufficient evidence to prove that Robinson is guilty of the charges beyond a reasonable doubt.
According to previous Star Democrat reporting, police said officers met with a victim at the Cambridge Police Department on Aug. 16 in reference to a shooting. The victim told police that as they came to the intersection, there was another vehicle there. As the victim passed by, the subject in the other vehicle fired multiple shots at the victim, who was not struck, police said.
Robinson was identified as the shooter by the victim, police said. When officers responded to Maces Lane and Bayly Road, where the shooting was alleged to have occurred, they located multiple rounds of spent .45 caliber ammunition as well as a live round of ammunition, police said.
Robinson was arrested two days later at the University of Maryland Shore Medical Center at Cambridge.
Robinson's attorney Brad MacFee said Robinson was "extremely relieved" and "beyond excited" when he learned the state would not be prosecuting the case. MacFee said Robinson had been dealing with this "nightmare" situation for about a year and had been concerned about potentially having to be away from his children.
MacFee said Leonard made the right decision. He said there would be credibility issues associated with the alleged victim and that, at the end of the day, there was not enough evidence to convict Robinson.

title: St. Michaels Police Chief says salaries need to be raised for officer recruitment, retention
author: AHMAD GARNETT agarnett@chespub.com
content:
St. Michaels Police Chief says salaries need to be raised for officer recruitment, retention

 September 26, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: AHMAD GARNETT agarnett@chespub.com | Section: News 
 
 424
 Words 

 Read News Document

 ST. MICHAELS — During the St. Michaels Commissioners meeting on Wednesday, St. Michaels Police Chief Jeffrey Oswald said the police department will lose an 18-year veteran officer to another municipality. The officer, he said, is leaving for better pay."I'm coming up on my 24th year here, three as chief, and during this time, I've seen 43 officers come and go in our agency," Oswald said. "Obviously, there are several factors that contribute to some of the turnover, but the prominent and consistent driver from the exit interviews has been paying upward mobility."
Starting on Thursday, the St. Michaels Police Department will be operating with only four officers, excluding Oswald.
Oswald mentioned one of the reasons that officers leave besides salary is opportunities larger departments can provide.
"They have criminal investigation divisions, they have training divisions dedicated solely to ensure officers meet certifications, qualifications and criminal updates… and remember, each of these on their own is a full-time specially trained position," Oswald said. "... Every St. Michaels Police Department (officer) must be able to perform every one of these rules at any given time, and therefore, after a few years, an officer builds a strong resume and they take it to another agency who's more than happy to pay them some extra money."
Oswald suggested potentially hiring a police recruiting firm and raising wages commensurate to officers' total years of service.
"We're a good place to have an opportunity to do a reset because there's only four of us remaining," Oswald said.
According to Town Manager Don Richardson, the police department has four openings with two each at the corporal and sergeant level.
With potential salary raises, the cost would be north of $200,000 for the town to properly recruit and retain officers, Richardson said.
Commissioner Alexis Roiter mentioned accommodation taxes, which are paid by tourists who stay at hotels or rental properties, as a potential revenue source for police department needs. Commissioner David Wojciechowski mentioned allocating funds from town events.
The commissioners agreed to draft legislation allowing for salary amendments so the St. Michaels Police Department can become competitive in hiring and retention. The measure would have to go through the town's typical legislative process, which would include public hearings, before it can be adopted.
"Thank you for supporting this important need for the town of St. Michaels and our community," Richardson said. "It will ultimately require some level of budgeting amendment that will absolutely go through a public comment period and a legislative ordinance."
The town encourages anyone interested in joining the St. Michaels Police Department to contact the town for further instruction.

 EASTON — Police have arrested two Cambridge men and an Easton woman in connection to a bank robbery earlier this month.On June 2, Easton police asked for assistance identifying a man suspected of robbing BayVanguard Bank on Idlewild Avenue. Police on Wednesday announced the arrest of 31-year-old Deondre Williams, of Cambridge, along with two others alleged to be involved — 21-year-old Makhyla Jenkins, of Easton, and 20-year-old Jeremiah Carter, of Cambridge.
All three are charged with first- and second-degree assault, armed robbery, firearm use in a violent crime, handgun on person, reckless endangerment, theft and conspiracy. Williams and Jenkins face handgun in vehicle charges, while Jenkins and Carter are charged with neglect of a minor.
Police say around 2:30 p.m. on June 2, officers reported to BayVanguard Bank for a robbery. According to a press release, employees provided police with a description of a man who investigators later identified as Williams.
Williams demanded money from a bank teller and brandished a firearm, police said. He allegedly took a sum of money then fled on foot toward Idlewild Park. No employees were injured.
Easton police worked with the FBI to gather surveillance footage that allegedly shows Jenkins, the Easton woman, driving the two Cambridge men to Idlewild Park. Police say Williams left the vehicle, later returned with the money and was driven by Jenkins to Kelley Gibson Street, where he and Carter exited the vehicle.
Investigators obtained a search warrant for a residence on Kelley Gibson Street they say is linked to the two Cambridge men. Police found "further evidence of their involvement in the bank robbery," a press release states.
Carter was apprehended on Monday in Easton after a foot chase, police said. Williams and Jenkins were arrested Wednesday in Cambridge and Easton, respectively.
All three were taken to the Talbot County Detention Center and are listed as being held without bond. Carter had a bond hearing Tuesday and has a preliminary hearing slated for July 7. Williams and Jenkins have bond hearings on Friday and preliminary hearings on July 14.

title: Be responsible on the water
author: Staff Writer
content:
Be responsible on the water

 May 10, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Staff Writer | Section: Editors Inbox 
 
 453
 Words 

 Read News Document

 Summer is a great time to enjoy local waters. Whether you're a boater, angler or water sports enthusiast on the Eastern Shore, please remember to be responsible around the water. May 17-23 is National Safe Boating Week. The Safe Boating Campaign, led by the National Safe Boating Council, offers these tips for practicing social distancing and safety while boating:Wear a life jacket. No matter what activity you have planned on the water, always remember to wear a life jacket every time you are on the water. Accidents on the water can happen much too fast to reach and put on a stowed life jacket.Make sure your life jacket is U.S. Coast Guard approved, appropriate for your water activity and fits properly. A life jacket that is too large or too small can cause different situational problems.Know state boating laws. Rules and laws can differ from state to state and violations can result in ticketing, fines or jail time.Take a boating safety course.Learn valuable tips that can help save your life in unexpected situations.Make sure your boat is prepared. There are many items that need to be checked and rechecked on any boat. Schedule a vessel safety check with your local U.S. Coast Guard Auxiliary or U.S. Power Squadrons before you hit the water. Every vessel safety check is conducted at no charge.Always file a float plan. File a float plan before you leave shore with someone you trust that includes details about the trip, boat, persons, towing or trailer vehicle, communication equipment, and emergency contacts.Check the weather, including the water temperature. Know the latest marine weather forecast prior to going out, and keep a regular check for changing conditions.Don't drink while you boat. Where the primary cause was known, alcohol was listed as a leading factor in boating-related deaths.Beware of carbon monoxide poisoning. Gasoline-powered engines on boats, including onboard generators, produce carbon monoxide (CO), a colorless and odorless gas that can poison or kill someone who breathes too much of it. Be sure to install and maintain a working CO detector, never block exhaust outlets, and always dock, beach or anchor at least 20 feet away from the nearest boat that is running a generator or engine.Keep in touch. Communication devices can be the most important piece of emergency equipment on board a vessel, especially in case of emergency. Be sure to have and know how to use at least two communication devices that work when wet, such as satellite phones, emergency position indicating radio beacons, VHF radios and personal locator beacons.
By following these tips, you can enjoy your boat, the water, sunshine and fresh air responsibly. For additional boating resources and tips, please visit SafeBoatingCampaign.com.
CAPT. BRETT M. SAUSE
USCG master licensed captain

title: Residents displaced in 2-house fire
author: WENDY WEITZEL wweitzel@chespub.com
content:
Residents displaced in 2-house fire

 February 4, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: WENDY WEITZEL wweitzel@chespub.com | Section: Local News 
 
 346
 Words 

 Read News Document

 Of all the things in her home that Leona Demdy, 87, lost to a fire Saturday afternoon, she said her photographs are what she will miss the most.A lifelong resident of Easton, Demdy had collected photos of friends, family and neighbors. She said the snapshots were proudly displayed on her walls.
"I cried, cried, cried," Demdy said as she watched firefighters extinguish the last remaining embers at 17 South Locust Lane, many of her belongings strewn across the front yard of the early 20th century house. "I had everybody's picture on the wall. My walls were just full of pictures."
Demdy's home of 27 years was one of two houses that caught fire a little before 3 p.m. Saturday. It was the second house fire that Demdy had experienced in her life. Her home a few streets over had been lost to a fire three decades prior.
Firefighters were dispatched to the blaze at 3:07 p.m., by which time, neighbors said, flames were spreading quickly between the two structures.
Both Demby, who lived alone, and the family who lived next door were able to make it out of the houses, and emergency officials on the scene said that no serious injuries were reported.
It took firefighters a little more than two hours to control the blaze. Responding fire departments began to gather their equipment and leave the scene a little before 5:30 p.m.
Seven local fire departments responded to the fire — the Easton Volunteer Fire Department, the Cordova Volunteer Fire Company, the St. Michaels Fire Department, the Preston Volunteer Fire Company, the Oxford Fire Company, the Queen Anne-Hillsboro Volunteer Fire Company and the Trappe Volunteer Fire Company, along with local EMS and law enforcement personnel.
The state fire marshal is conducting an investigation into the fire and its causes, the results of which will be available at a later date.
Though exact damages are yet to be determined by the fire marshal, both houses sustained significant damage, and all residents of the structures were displaced.
Demdy said she would be staying with a relative near Salisbury, and arrangements were made for her neighbors.

title: Commissioners approve extended MOU with sheriff's office for Ridgely policing
author: TOM MCCALL
content:
Commissioners approve extended MOU with sheriff's office for Ridgely policing

 May 8, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: TOM MCCALL | Section: Life 
 
 655
 Words 

 Read News Document

 DENTON — Building on a temporary agreement forged in the weeks following the March suspension of Ridgely's entire police force, the Town of Ridgely and the Caroline County Sheriff's Office have agreed to a more permanent plan for ensuring law enforcement coverage in the town.At their May 6 meeting, the Ridgely commissioners approved a memorandum of understanding for fiscal year 2025 that will ensure the sheriff's office provides law enforcement services to Ridgely in the absence of the Ridgely Police Department.
This is a longer term arrangement than originally conceived.
On March 13, the commissioners of Ridgely suspended the entire Ridgely police department with pay, effective immediately, pending an investigation by the Office of the Maryland State Prosecutor. No reason for the investigation has been indicated publicly.
"To guarantee uninterrupted public safety services, the Commissioners initiated a temporary agreement with the Caroline County Sheriff's Office," said Ridgely in a press release. "Now, building upon this temporary arrangement, Ridgely and the Caroline County Sheriff's Office have established a long-term partnership through an updated Memorandum of Understanding (MOU). This MOU will provide the Town of Ridgely with complete law enforcement coverage, by the Caroline County Sheriff's Office, for the fiscal year 2025, with the option to renew service annually. This agreement includes a provision for maintaining 480 hours of coverage per month."
According to the first amendment to agreement for law enforcement services, a document between the town of Ridgely, the Caroline County Commissioners and Caroline County Sheriff Donald L. Baker, the estimated annual cost of this service is $474,971.44.
According to two versions of the town's proposed FY2025 budget, one with the town's police department and the other with the sheriff's office providing policing, posted to the town website Tuesday, the MOU with the sheriff's office cheaper the cost of maintaining a town police force.
"This partnership underscores our shared commitment to safety and community well-being," Baker said in the press release. "By working closely with the Ridgely community, we aim to build trust and ensure seamless law enforcement services to all residents. The updated MOU will take effect July 1, 2024, with the current MOU remaining in effect until then."
This matter was also addressed during the May 7 Caroline County Commissioners meeting.
"At this point in time, I plan on signing it if the County Commissioners sign it, and the (Ridgely) commissioners signed it last night," Baker said about the agreement at that meeting. "Frank Bartz was there. There was a lot of heated discussion, but that is to be expected. I look forward to the continued efforts by the county, the town and the sheriff's office. So I think that only good things are on the horizon."
Many Ridgely residents, like Lakia Harris-Pierce, who went to the meeting, are concerned about what they feel is a lack of transparency. Harris-Pierce said she is still wondering who gave the orders to suspend the police force in the first place.
Commissioner Larry Porter said, "I know there has been a lot of social media discussion about this, but basically this is going to provide 120 hours per week."
Then he asked the sheriff, "Just for clarification, how much coverage was the Ridgely Police Department providing when they were there?"
Baker said originally they were supposed to cover the town 140 hours a week. Vacancies and sickness kept them from reaching that number. The sheriff's office will cover the town as much as the police department had under the new agreement.
"Just so everybody knows, the sheriff's department is constitutionally obligated to handle and provide law enforcement services in Caroline County," Baker said. "Even if we back up the towns of Federalsburg, Greensboro or Denton, who have their own police departments… we are obligated to go in there… I do that in cooperation with the commissioners and your staff."
Baker said he takes the responsibility seriously and that he wants to give the citizens of Ridgely some peace of mind.
The county commissioners' motion unanimously passed to approve the MOU.

title: Pull over! – The complex realities of traffic stops
author: MARTY MADDEN mmadden@somdnews.com
content:
Pull over! – The complex realities of traffic stops

 July 16, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: MARTY MADDEN mmadden@somdnews.com | Section: News 
 
 1336
 Words 

 Read News Document

 "To protect and to serve." It's a motto first used by the Los Angeles Police Department over 60 years ago that has been embraced by law enforcement agencies all over the world. Simple words, but in the real world the goal has often seemed problematic.A nationwide study shows police patrol officers all over America pull over more than 50,000 drivers on a typical day, more than 20 million a year.
In Calvert County alone, as the halfway point of 2025 is reached, sheriff's deputies have made over 10,050 traffic stops.
"There's no such thing as a routine traffic stop," Capt. Nathan Funchion, patrol bureau commander for the Calvert County Sheriff's Office, told Southern Maryland News during a recent telephone interview.
Debora Harris, president of Calvert's NAACP chapter, noted that over the years the local organization has frequently fielded calls from citizens, in particular African Americans, who have sensed they were being profiled by county law enforcement when driving. She said those number of calls have dwindled somewhat.
"We don't get complaints, not lately," Harris told Southern Maryland News.
Harris said it was Calvert's NAACP chapter that engaged the American Civil Liberties Union of Maryland in researching questionable encounters among local deputies and African Americans. While traffic stops are part of the study, a major focus is what the state union calls "invasive police searches," which occurred from 2020 through 2024.
The state union's request for documentation reached a stalemate when sheriff's officials insisted on remittance of a $12,000 in exchange for the requested records. The ACLU challenged the hefty charge, citing the Maryland Public Information Act, and prevailed in both circuit and appellate courts.
Southern Maryland News made calls and sent emails to the state ACLU seeking an update on their study, plus basic information on how citizens should, within their rights, interact with law enforcement. No response was received.
When things go wrongLast December, a Prince George's County man with ties to Calvert County reached out to Southern Maryland News to share his story of a bad encounter with a Calvert County deputy.
On Dec. 18 William Jacks, 41, of Clinton was traveling with his wife, Kimberly, in Prince Frederick. The couple was traveling in their 2013 Ford Edge and Kimberly was driving.
Around 9:30 a.m., the vehicle was pulled over in the area of Prince Frederick Boulevard and Chapline Place. The officer conducting the stop is identified in court documents as Deputy Gavin Shuart of the Calvert County Sheriff's Office.
In his lengthy statement recalling the incident, Jacks said he put his passenger side window down "about 3½ inches. Once the officer walked up on the passenger side, his first words were 'wind your window all the way down.'"
Jacks said he refused the deputy's order, telling him, "You can see me, you can see inside my car, you can hear me, I can hear you and if I need to pass you something or if I need to receive something from you we are able to."
Jacks claimed in his statement that the deputy threatened to break the window if it wasn't rolled all the way down. When, according to Jacks, the deputy "proceeded to reach his arm in from his forearm up to the mid-bicep through my window" a cup of hot coffee in the vehicle's middle console spilled out on the two men, who were in a struggle for the vehicle's door handle. After the deputy managed to gain entry into the vehicle, Jacks said he demanded to speak with the officer's supervisor, which he eventually did, followed by the filing of a complaint with Calvert's Police Accountability Board.
According to the board's complaint tracker, the complaint filed Dec. 19 alleging "abuse of authority" was investigated, with the probe being completed Feb. 13. The final result was no administrative charges for the deputy.
Kimberly Jacks, identified in court documents as Kimberly Pilkerton, 44, was cited for displaying an expired registration plate, driving a vehicle on a highway without current registration plates, failure to maintain and to provide on request required security, and knowingly driving an uninsured vehicle.
All of the traffic citations were placed on the district court stet docket after a February hearing presided over by Judge Robyn Riddle.
In a followup phone call last week, Jacks expressed doubts that the board investigators reviewed Shuart's body camera footage when weighing the merits of the complaint.
In his statement provided to Southern Maryland News, Jacks said, "I truly feel that this officer had broken entry into by vehicle" and "assaulted me fighting over a door handle."
In another matter, Harris shared with Southern Maryland News that the local NAACP chapter "received a complaint last year by an elderly woman" who claimed Calvert police pulled her over and "charged her with drunk driving, and took her license."
Harris said subsequent sobriety tests showed "she was not driving under the influence." However, the woman, according to Harris, has not been able to get her license back.
Recommendations made
Funchion told Southern Maryland News, "in this county in particular, most interactions are positive."
The Calvert sheriff's office captain's advice for motorists is if they see a flashing light behind you "turn on your turn signal to indicate you are going to pull over. Keeping hands in sight is highly recommended. It's highly recommended" that you "roll your window down."
Funchion said the officer will identify themselves and let you know they are wearing an activated body camera.
"Be polite and courteous, provide documents," Funchion said, adding that if the vehicle's registration is in the glove box, "let the officer know you want to retrieve it."
The captain said the information provided will be run through a computer the deputy has in his or her patrol vehicle.
A citation or a warning will be provided to the motorist, who then "may pull back onto the road."
Occasionally, law enforcement officers also issue repair orders to motorists, who may not be aware that a brake light or tag light is out. Calvert's sheriff's office, said Funchoin, on average only issues 50 to 60 repair orders annually to motorists.
The national NAACP advises motorists on their website that they "have the right not to consent to a search of your vehicle. If the police state they have probable cause, they may begin to search your car without your consent. Do not interfere but clearly state your lack of consent. If you are given a ticket, sign it. You can always fight the case in court later."
The latter advice is also recommended by the American Civil Liberties Union, which states on its national website that anyone stopped by the police has a right to ask, "'Am I being detained or am I free to go.' If you wish to remain silent, you should say, 'I don't want to talk to you without a lawyer.'"
The union also advised, "You have the right to refuse to consent to a search of yourself, your car or your home, with certain exceptions."
Driving forward
Overall, in 2024 the Calvert County Sheriff's Office received a total of 33 complaints, with five resulting in administrative charges, which mostly resulted in letters of reprimand and one with suspension and loss of leave.
So far in 2025, 10 complaints are currently under investigation by the county's Police Accountability Board and four have been completed, resulting in a letter of reprimand given to an officer.
Harris said the local NAACP chapter does receive complaints about the way the two panels — police accountability board and administrative charging committee — do business.
"It's very limited to what can happen," Harris said. "Police are really governing themselves."
As to the low number of complaints resulting in punitive action, Funchion said he believes the body cameras each deputy is equipped with are making a difference.
"We felt like we were disliked and getting a bad rap," Funchion said. "The perception has changed."
Funchion acknowledged the county has seen "an uptick" in "roadside interactions," which he said is part of a strategy implemented due to the county's higher number of road fatalities in 2024.
The captain explained motorists who see police interactions tend to drive slower, so the increased traffic stops, due to their visibility "slows traffic."

Fire causes $125,000 in damages to Greensboro home

 Author/Byline: Konner Metz | Section: Caroline 
 
 102

title: Mother charged in killing of daughter, 3, extradited back to Maryland
author: Carl Hamilton cahamilton@chespub.com
content:
Mother charged in killing of daughter, 3, extradited back to Maryland

 October 2, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Carl Hamilton cahamilton@chespub.com | Section: News 
 
 694
 Words 

 Read News Document

 A woman charged with murder in the beating death of her 3-year-old daughter inside their North East residence in June remained in the Cecil County Detention Center on Thursday, Sept. 25.— two days after her extradition from Delaware and hours after her bail review hearing.Cecil County Circuit Court Judge Robert Sentman concluded that the defendant — Darrian Lynnelle Randle, 31 — should be held without bond, as recommended by Assistant State's Attorney Gavin Patashnick during Thursday afternoon's proceeding. (From the county jail, Randle appeared in the courtroom on a closed-circuit television screen.)
"The state cannot think of any (allegations) more heinous . . ." Patashnick told the judge.
The prosecutor opined that Randle poses a flight risk because she has no ties to Cecil County, noting that her relatives reside in Indiana and that her boyfriend — Cedrick Antoine Britten, 44 — owns the home in which they were living at the time of killing.
Britten also remains in the county jail on no bond, charged with first-degree child abuse resulting in death of a child under 13 and 10 other offenses relating to his alleged role in the incident.
In addition, Patashnick emphasized that an agreement between the governors of Maryland and Delaware allowed for Randle's extradition to Cecil County from Delaware, where she had been jailed since June on making a false report, and that the State of Maryland must ensure that Randle will be returned to Delaware to face that felony charge.
After allegedly killing her daughter — Nola Dinkins — Randle purportedly reported to Delaware police that the girl had been kidnapped in an attempted carjacking near Newark, to explain why the youngster was missing.
The agreement between the two governors allows the Cecil County State's Attorney's Office to try Randle in the murder case first. And then, regardless of the outcome — even if Randle is acquitted of all charges — the agreement calls for her return to Delaware to be tried in the felony false report case.
"Both governors in Delaware and Maryland signed the agreement. She must go back to Delaware immediately (after the adjudication of her Cecil County murder case)," Patashnick told the judge.
Randle's defense lawyer, Michael Halter, had asked the judge to allow Randle to remain free on home-monitored release until her murder trial. Halter reported in the courtroom that Randle "vehemently denies the allegations" against her and the she "looks forward to her day in court."
On Wednesday, a Cecil County grand jury handed up an 11-count indictment against Randle, charging her with first-degree murder, first-degree child abuse resulting in death and nine related charges, according to court records.
Court records allege that Randle admitted that she beat Nola to death inside their shared bedroom of Britten's residence in the 300 block of Elk Nest Road during the daytime hours on June 9 and then made arrangements to get rid of the girl's body.
Randle told investigators that she struck Nola 15 to 20 times with a belt all over her body, causing the girl to collapse to the floor and to stop breathing — a confession given after she allegedly had falsely reported that her daughter had been kidnapped, triggering an Amber Alert, according to the original charging document.
In addition, Randle told detectives that she asked Britten to get rid of Nola's body, which they had placed inside a dark blue suitcase, police said. She also told investigators that Britten later sent her a photograph of a park, after driving away from the residence with the suitcase inside his car, police added.
Court records further allege that, during an interview at the Maryland State Police North East Barrack on June 11, Britten "produced a map of where he believed that Randle may have disposed of" Nola's body, a statement that appears to allege that Randle got rid of the body.
Based on that map, investigators found human remains "consistent with an emaciated child" inside a suitcase found in a vacant lot in the unit block of Dune Drive near North East, close to Britten's residence, court records show.
The remains were positively identified as those of Nola, based on an autopsy performed by the Maryland Office of the Chief Medical Examiner in Baltimore, police reported.

title: Easton High School graduate dies in car crash

Easton High School graduate dies in car crash

 Words

 EASTON — The Easton community is mourning the death of recent high school graduate Darren Foxwell.Foxwell, 18, died following injuries sustained as a passenger in a single-vehicle car crash just outside Trappe on Tuesday morning. He was transported to Shock Trauma in Baltimore for treatment of life-threatening injuries. He died on Wednesday afternoon, his family said on Facebook Thursday.
In a Facebook post on Wednesday, Darren's father, Len Foxwell, wrote that the family is "eternally grateful for everyone who has sent their love and support, for those who have stepped up with profound gestures of support, and for Darren's friends who drove here from Easton yesterday to say goodbye to their childhood buddy."
"Each of you have been a lifeline and have honored Darren in your own special way," Len Foxwell wrote.
His father added that the team at Shock Trauma in Baltimore "fought like a tiger to keep Darren comfortable, preserve his dignity and provide solace for a family that has been destroyed."
A member of Easton High School's wrestling and lacrosse teams, Foxwell graduated last month. He planned to attend Bethany College in West Virginia this fall and play lacrosse for the Bison.
Foxwell played the last two years for Easton as a backup defenseman. Easton High boys head lacrosse coach Dennis Keenan said he was popular among his teammates and had a "bright future."
"I think he was funnier than he actually thought he was," Keenan said. "The things he would say would just crack me up. He was getting better each day. You could see flashes of brilliance."
Foxwell wrestled for three years at Easton, including under head coach Jason Biringer during his senior year. Biringer said Foxwell had an "infectious" personality.
Early this past season, Foxwell stepped away from the wrestling team. But after speaking with his coach, he returned and started at the 167-pound weight class for the Warriors.
After returning to the team, Biringer made Foxwell a team captain because of Foxwell's work ethic and focus.
"The other wrestlers looked up to him," Biringer said. "He has such a good, gentle demeanor that he was just very well liked."
"He just had one of those infectious smiles that you're like, 'It's always good to see Darren,'" Biringer added.
Family said on Thursday that arrangements for funeral services and a celebration of life are being made and will be announced soon.
