title: Cambridge man found not guilty in murder trial
author: MAGGIE TROVATO mtrovato@chespub.com
content:
Cambridge man found not guilty in murder trial

 August 30, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: MAGGIE TROVATO mtrovato@chespub.com | Section: Crime 
 
 734
 Words 

 Read News Document

 CAMBRIDGE — A Cambridge man was acquitted of charges relating to the November 2021 fatal shooting of 16-year-old Ja'Len Woolford.Key'Marion Ennals, 19, was found not guilty on 12 charges — including first-degree murder, reckless endangerment charges and assault charges. Ennals' attorney Larry Greenberg said Ennals is relieved that justice was served.
On Nov. 18, 2021, Cambridge Police Department officers responded to the 900 block of Camelia Street shortly before 8:15 p.m. for a shooting involving multiple victims. Woolford was declared dead on the scene. Two others were shot, including a 14-year-old who was wounded under his right arm.
During the trial, witnesses testified to the scene being chaotic, with hundreds of people outside when paramedics and police arrived. One paramedic testified to observing fighting on the hood of the ambulance.
During closing arguments in Ennals' trial, prosecutor Jonathon Church, who is from the Prince George's County State's Attorney's Office, played the 911 call that 14-year-old Nasir Pope made after getting shot. In the audio recording, Pope says that he saw the two assailants, who were wearing all black, going down the street.
Church also played footage from the city's camera system with a spotlight on two people alleged to be Ennals and Daeveon Johnson, 19, who entered an Alford plea for first-degree murder in the death of Woolford in November 2022. Johnson was 17 at the time of the plea hearing. His sentencing hearing is set for Sept. 6.
In the footage, the firing of gunshots is heard and the suspects are seen running down Camelia Street, where Woolford was found dead.
Although Johnson — who testified during Ennals' trial — entered into a plea for Woolford's death, Church said it didn't matter whose aim was better. He said a person can be guilty of murder by being an accomplice.
Church said that the two got out of a car with firearms and ski masks, and Johnson asked Ennals, "Are you ready?"
"He was ready," Church said. "Guns out and blazing."
Greenberg, Ennals' attorney, reminded the jury during closing arguments that testimony revealed Maryland State Police's investigation into the shooting is still open, meaning that someone else could be charged with the murder of Woolford.
"It causes shivers down my spine," he said about finding that out earlier that day.
Greenberg also questioned the use of the city's video footage and Johnson's testimony as main evidence of Ennals' involvement in the shooting.
He said the video footage was "grainy" and he did not see the two people spotlighted in the video wearing all black. He cautioned the jury of considering Johnson's testimony because Johnson took a plea deal.
Greenberg said a case should rely on scientific evidence, not blurry videos, and he said there was zero credible evidence given in the trial.
In an interview with the Star Democrat, Greenberg and Brice Baker, both attorneys for Ennals, talked about concerns with how the case was handled leading up to and during the trial.
In September, the Dorchester County State's Attorney's Office was disqualified from prosecuting the case after Dorchester County State's Attorney Amanda Leonard told Greenberg she met with Johnson to prepare for the trial and learned that two other people were involved in the shooting, according to Greenberg and documented in court papers.
According to previous Star Democrat reporting, in a Sept. 27 hearing, Greenberg asserted that the information shared in the interview was exculpatory. Not disclosing exculpatory information to defense attorneys is a violation of the Brady rule, which requires prosecutors to turn over information that could exonerate a defendant.
Ennals' trial has been postponed five times in the past two years. In that time, Ennals' defense attorneys filed multiple motions to dismiss the case.
Greenberg said the defense learned things they hadn't known during the trial, including that the case is still open with MSP.
"It is such an abuse of the legal system," he said. "And that's why there are innocent people in jail."
Baker said she was thankful the jury made the decision that it did.
"This really could have been another Adnan Syed situation where there's evidence that we don't have (and) evidence that was (given) late," she said.
After the verdict was read, Church told the Star Democrat, "I just have to respect the jury's decision."
Greenberg said that Ennals — who he said has been shot at multiple times since being charged — has become "afraid" of the country's legal process.
"This was his first ever experience," Baker said. "He's had no priors, and his first experience is this."

title: Former Easton Police officer to serve 6 months after sexual conduct with teenagers
author: Maggie Trovato
content:
Former Easton Police officer to serve 6 months after sexual conduct with teenagers

 November 1, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Maggie Trovato | Section: Crime 
 
 711
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — During a hearing Friday morning, a former Easton Police officer was sentenced to four years of incarceration with all but six months suspended.In September, Jason Dyott, 38, was found guilty of misconduct in office for engaging in physical sexual conduct with two different teenage girls while on duty.
The former sergeant — who resigned from the police department Thursday — will also have to serve three years of supervised probation upon his release. Judge C. Carey Deeley Jr., who handed down the sentence, said conditions of probation include completing treatment and not having any contact with the victims.
During the hearing Friday, Deeley said Dyott had leveraged his position of trust as a police officer in order to cause young women to "come under his spell."
"It was heinous conduct," Deeley said.
On Sept. 10, Deeley found Dyott guilty on two counts of misconduct in office. The charges stem from allegations that Dyott used his departmental cell phone to communicate in a sexual manner with several teenagers and students at local high schools. Dyott met up with the students while on duty.
During the September trial, Senior Assistant State Prosecutor Mary Setzer said in the fall of 2022, Dyott engaged in physical acts with the two teenage girls in separate instances.
Deputy State Prosecutor Sarah David said at the trial that in the two incidents, Dyott acted in his official capacity. Not only was he on duty, she said, but he was presenting himself to the public and to the teenage girls as an officer.
At the hearing Friday, Dyott apologized to the court, the victims, the Town of Easton and his family. He said he was going through a separation at the time of the incidents and he "wasn't in (his) right mind." He said he should not have used his position of power and said what he did was morally and ethically wrong.
Dyott said he has sought treatment and hopes to continue it. According to Dyott's defense attorney, Shaun Owens, Dyott has been undergoing sex offender treatment.
Dyott's wife, Amber Dyott, said her husband has owned up to his mistakes and grown and learned from them. She said her husband has faced public punishment and asked that the court consider her family, including Jason Dyott's kids, while determining the sentence.
The defense requested Dyott be sentenced to three years of supervised probation with no incarceration. The Office of the State Prosecutor asked that Dyott be sentenced to four years of incarceration with all but six months suspended.
Although one of the victims who testified in the trial wrote a statement for the sentencing, it was not read aloud during the hearing.
Until Thursday, Dyott — who was named the Easton Police Department's officer of the year in 2014 — had been suspended with pay by the department. He was put on suspension in the beginning stages of the investigation in 2023.
In an interview with the Star Democrat, Easton Police Chief Alan Lowrey said the department sent a letter to Dyott that if he did not resign, he would be terminated following his sentencing. Lowrey said Dyott resigned from the department Thursday.
Lowrey said Dyott had been served with charges by the Talbot County Administrative Charging Committee and they held off on pursuing a trial in an effort to protect the victims. Lowrey said an additional trial with the Administrative Charging Committee would mean the victims would have to testify twice. He said he didn't want to do that to them and that is why it took as long as it did for the department to separate from Dyott.
Lowrey said he agreed with the court's decision. In a news release he said the department is happy it can continue to serve the community "without the weight of Mr. Dyott's immoral actions on our shoulders."
"Being a police officer is more than a job, it is an acceptance of a duty to uphold the laws of our country and a duty to the safety of the members of our community," Lowrey said. "It is also the acceptance of a duty to your fellow law enforcement officers. It is disappointing and maddening to our community, our officers and to me that Mr. Dyott chose to violate these duties and serve his own gratifications at the expense of young people in our community."

 EASTON - An Easton woman was given two years of unsupervised probation Wednesday, Nov. 22, after she was found guilty of tampering with evidence related to a fatal shooting in Easton.During a trial last week in Talbot County District Court, presiding District Judge Joseph Riley found Dana L. Wilson, 59, guilty of tampering with evidence connected to the man charged with murder in the shooting. She was given a one-year sentence, all of which was suspended, according to court documents.The charges against Wilson stemmed from her actions in the minutes following the fatal Aug. 7 shooting.Police responded to the area of 104 Blake Street around 7 p.m. that day for a report of a person who had been shot and was laying in the grass.Officers arriving on scene rendered aid to the man, later identified as 55-year-old Ty A. Brooks, until paramedics arrived. Brooks died from his injuries at the scene, police said.Police said earlier on Aug. 7, Brooks argued with individuals who were near and operating a Range Rover, which was parked in the 100 block of Blake Street.Brooks left the area and returned later, operating an ATV.Brooks confronted the same individuals with a shotgun, police said.Police said after the group exchanged words, a man seated in the driver's seat of the Range Rover fired shots through the front passenger seat window and struck Brooks' side, causing him to fall from the ATV.The man in the driver's seat was identified by police as Daseir Cornish, 22, of Denton. title: Cambridge man handed two life sentences without parole
author: MAGGIE TROVATO mtrovato@chespub.com
content:
Cambridge man handed two life sentences without parole

 March 6, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: MAGGIE TROVATO mtrovato@chespub.com | Section: Crime 
 
 648
 Words 

 Read News Document

 CAMBRIDGE — Tramelle Williams, 23, of Cambridge was handed two consecutive life sentences without the possibility of parole for the December 2022 murders of 24-year-old Taijay Daniels and 69-year-old Lory Fields.Before handing over the sentence on Monday, Dorchester County Administrative Judge William Jones called surveillance footage of Daniels' death "possibly in the top five, if not No. 2 most difficult thing I've had to see."
Williams also was handed a consecutive 20-year sentence for robbery charges and two additional consecutive 20-year sentences with mandatory minimums of five years for firearms charges.
Williams was tried separately for the murders of Daniels and Fields. He was found guilty on all counts — which included first- and second-degree murder, first- and second-degree assault, robbery and firearms charges — in both trials.
A motion for a new trial for the death of Fields, filed by Williams' defense in late January, was denied at the sentencing hearing Monday.
According to court documents, Williams' defense argued there was insufficient evidence to support that a robbery had occurred and that Williams had intended to kill or harm Fields. His defense included in the motion that evidence related to Daniels' death was "unintentionally admitted and sent back" to the jury in the trial for the death of Fields.
According to court documents, in response, the state said the motion for a new trial should be denied because the evidence "clearly supported a conviction on all counts," and said none of the jurors had knowledge of the Daniels case.
"'Taijay Daniels' would be nothing more than a 'John Doe' to the seated jurors," the state's response to the motion says.
At the sentencing hearing, Jones denied the request for a new trial. He said there was sufficient evidence to prove that Williams was responsible for the death of Fields.
Jones said there was an extensive voir dire to make sure no jurors in the Fields trial knew anything about the Daniels case. He said that when the document related to Daniels' death was given to the jury on the Fields case, the jury was told to disregard it.
"And they did," he said.
Before the sentencing was handed over on Monday, Williams was given the opportunity to speak. He said he was sorry to the families of Daniels and Fields, and maintained his innocence. Williams said he thought he could benefit from going to a psychiatric hospital.
The events that resulted in the deaths of Daniels and Fields took place on Dec. 8, 2022. That day, the Cambridge Police Department responded to two shootings in the span of a few hours.
During the trial for Daniels' death, Dorchester County State's Attorney Amanda Leonard said Daniels was found dead from multiple gunshot wounds on Pleasant Street, one of which was fired at close range.
Surveillance footage shown in court showed Daniels' last minutes walking past a corner market, followed by Williams shortly after. A video from an apartment complex on Pleasant Street showed a man identified as Williams approaching Daniels with a gun. Daniels dropped his phone as Williams extended his arm, shooting him in the back.
Then, Williams shot again, striking Daniels in the head twice before taking his belongings and leaving.
During the trial for Fields' death, Leonard said Cambridge police had found Fields lying in his front yard. He had been shot once in the head at close range and robbed of the keys to his Chrysler 300, she said.
Police testified that Fields' car keys and Daniels' phone were recovered from Williams the night he was arrested.
At the sentencing hearing, members of both Daniels' and Fields' families spoke.
Daniels' mother, Barbara Gabbin called her son a giver, adding that he was "full of love."
"Taijay was my world," she said.
Fields' daughter Lauren Davis wrote a letter to her deceased father, which she read at the sentencing.
"I have been so lost without you," she said, later adding that she would give anything for just one more day, one more second with him.

title: Cambridge man charged with kidnapping in connection to missing woman
author: Natalie Jones
content:
Cambridge man charged with kidnapping in connection to missing woman

 February 22, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Natalie Jones | Section: Crime 
 
 1018
 Words 

 Read News Document

 CAMBRIDGE — A Cambridge man was arrested Monday in the alleged kidnapping of a 31-year-old woman who was reported missing over a week ago. The woman has yet to be located.Kenneth Stefan Bradley, 41, is charged with kidnapping, assault and related charges in connection to Tiyavauna Britt's disappearance.
An arrest warrant indicated Bradley was arrested in Anne Arundel County on Monday, Feb. 19. He was ordered held without bond during a bail review in Glen Burnie District Court that day, according to court records.
Britt, who was first reported missing to the Easton Police Department on Tuesday, Feb. 13, remains "critically missing," according to charging documents authored by a Maryland State Police sergeant.
According to charging documents, Britt's mother told police she had attempted to contact her daughter several times between Jan. 31 and Feb. 13, but had not been able to reach her. Several other family members were unable to make contact with Britt, her mother told police.
Britt's mother also told police that the car typically driven by Britt was found unoccupied in the Dollar Tree parking lot in Easton.
The car was found unlocked with Britt's belongings inside, including her phone and wallet.
Britt's mother said she found a note in the driver's side door of the car that appeared to be "a list of couple goals," according to charging documents. Police wrote that the end of the letter said "No phones, no kids, just us."
It was not clear who authored the note.
According to charging documents, Britt's mother believed her daughter was with her ex-boyfriend, identified as Bradley. The mother feared for her daughter's safety, citing previous domestic violence history between the two.
Bradley is currently on probation for a previous assault conviction related to Britt in Talbot County.
In early September 2021, police responded to an alleyway in Easton, where they found Britt crying. According to charging documents in that case, Britt told police Bradley was chasing her in his truck after the two got into an argument.
Britt told police that Bradley pulled her hair, grabbed her by the throat and choked her. He also reportedly held a pillow over her face and mouth, threatening to kill her, and told her not to leave.
Britt was found to have abrasions on her neck consistent with being choked, along with abrasions on her wrist and redness to the back of her neck at her hairline, police wrote.
While that case was still pending, police were called to an apartment in Hurlock in April 2022 for another altercation between Bradley and Britt, though that case was later placed on the stet, or inactive, docket.
Bradley was convicted of second-degree assault in Talbot County Circuit Court in June 2022 and was sentenced to 10 years, with all but time already served suspended.
He was placed on three years of supervised probation and ordered to complete an abusers' intervention program, though a violation of probation report filed on Feb. 16 indicated he had not provided verification of completing the course.
In further investigating Britt's disappearance, police spoke with three other people who knew her, all of whom said they had last heard from or seen Britt on Wednesday, Feb. 7.
Britt's employer told police she was seen leaving work in Delaware around 3 p.m. Surveillance footage from her employer showed Britt wearing a black coat and black sweatpants, police said.
A woman who identified herself as Britt's cousin told police she was with Britt that afternoon and heard her and Bradley having a verbal argument on the phone before the couple planned to go to dinner at Portside in Cambridge.
The cousin told police Britt dropped her off in Hurlock around 6 p.m., according to charging documents. The two spoke on the phone for several minutes afterward.
Police said a man who identified himself as an acquaintance of Britt said he received a phone call from her shortly after 7:30 p.m. The man told police he briefly spoke with Britt before hearing a male voice, adding that he believed the man with her "started to assault" her before the call suddenly ended.
Detectives obtained cell tower records for Britt's phone, giving police a timeline of events leading to the last time her phone was active, according to charging documents. Police wrote that Britt was in downtown Cambridge and Great Marsh Park that evening.
The last known cell tower location placed Britt's phone at Great Marsh Park shortly before 8:30 p.m. Feb. 7, police wrote.
Police also obtained cell tower data for Bradley's phone number, which placed him in the same area and locations as Britt during that time frame.
Officers from the Cambridge Police Department reviewed surveillance footage between Portside and Great Marsh Park, which showed a dark-colored Chevrolet Suburban pulling into the park shortly before 7:30 p.m.
According to charging documents, a Black male was seen exiting the vehicle with a woman who appeared to have her hands bound. The man walked the woman to the rear of the vehicle, opening and closing the hatch, and walked her to the front of the vehicle — out of view of the camera, police noted.
Further review of the camera footage revealed audio of male and female voices. Police wrote that "sounds of loud thuds" also were heard, which "appear to be consistent with forceful strikes."
Police interviewed a man connected to Britt on Feb. 16, who identified the voices as Britt and Bradley.
Charging documents said a "dark object" was seen lying on the ground in front of the vehicle as it drove away shortly before 8 p.m. The same vehicle was seen returning about 25 minutes later.
Police wrote that the footage showed a male driver leaving the vehicle and walking toward the object. Within minutes, the man was seen "carrying and dragging" what appeared to be a "small statured, light skinned female" consistent with the woman observed in the videos.
The man later carried the woman's "limp body" to the rear cargo area of the vehicle, placing other unknown items there before leaving at 8:30 p.m.

title: Two plead guilty in Eastern Shore Hospital Center shooting and escape
author: MAGGIE TROVATO mtrovato@chespub.com
content:
Two plead guilty in Eastern Shore Hospital Center shooting and escape

 June 9, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: MAGGIE TROVATO mtrovato@chespub.com | Section: Crime 
 
 585
 Words 

 Read News Document

 CAMBRIDGE — Two men have pleaded guilty to charges related to an August 2023 escape from the Eastern Shore Hospital Center.Darrin Jeter, 20, of Rockville, was sentenced to 10 years in prison and five years of supervised probation for first-degree escape. With eight years of his prison sentence suspended, Jeter will have to serve two years in prison and will get credit for 310 days already served.
Israel Labastida Jr., 19, of Glen Burnie, pleaded guilty on Friday to one count of first-degree assault, use of a firearm during a felony or violent crime and first-degree conspiracy to escape. Maryland Circuit Court Judge Karen Dean granted Labastida's request to defer his sentencing approximately 90 days so that his family could be present.
At Labastida's hearing, Dorchester County State's Attorney Amanda Leonard said the state is recommending Labastida be handed a sentence of a five-year mandatory minimum without parole, followed by five years of probation. Leonard said the state also recommends Labastida be required to stay away from the Eastern Shore Hospital Center and the facility's staff.
Charges against Jeter and Labastida stem from Jeter's August 2023 escape from the Eastern Shore Hospital Center, a psychiatric facility located on Woods Road in Cambridge. At that time, Jeter, who has schizophrenia, had been committed to the hospital center.
At both the Thursday hearing for Jeter and the Friday hearing for Labastida, Leonard said that Labastida approached the facility on Aug. 1 and shot into a window several times. She said Labastida and Jeter kicked out the broken window so that Jeter could exit the building, and the two fled the area in a black vehicle.
Jeter was located by the Montgomery County Sheriff's Office the following day and has remained in custody since.
During Jeter's plea hearing, Leonard said that through an investigation, evidence of an escape plan between Jeter and Labastida was discovered. She said that if the case had gone to trial, the state would have presented evidence that proves Jeter knew where to go during the escape.
At Labastida's plea hearing, Leonard said Labastida was identified as a suspect through investigation, and she said Bay Bridge records show Labastida's car crossing the bridge to and from the Eastern Shore before and after the Aug. 1 incident.
Leonard said that through a search warrant, texts between Labastida and Jeter's girlfriend were discovered. Leonard said that in the text chain, Jeter's girlfriend told Labastida that Jeter had been apprehended, and Labastida replied that she should tell Jeter to keep quiet about him helping Jeter escape.
Leonard said a handgun was found in Labastida's bedroom. She said that ballistics testing found the spent shell casings discovered at the hospital center consistent with the handgun found in Labastida's room.
Jeter, who's sentence was handed down by Dorchester County Circuit Court Judge William Jones on Thursday, was ordered to seek substance abuse treatment, mental health treatment with medication compliance and not make contact with Labastida.
Before handing down the sentence, Jones called the set of facts presented during the hearing "very troubling." He said that the people working in the hospital center that day should not have had to experience that.
Jeter's attorney Archibald McFadden said Jeter has a detailed track record of mental health struggles. He said Jeter has had those struggles since childhood.
McFadden also said he has spoken with Jeter's father regularly since taking on the case, and Jeter has a supportive family behind him. McFadden said that if Jeter takes the steps to manage his mental health struggles now, it will benefit him as he gets older.

title: Why we cannot solve America's gun problem
author: LARRY PIFER
content:
Why we cannot solve America's gun problem

 February 25, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: LARRY PIFER | Section: Columns 
 
 614
 Words 

 Read News Document

 On Feb. 14 the shooting of at least 23 people in Kansas City abruptly halted the celebration of the Super Bowl win by the Kansas City Chiefs. At least one person is dead. At least half of the victims were under the age of 16 (one only 6). The state of Missouri has some of the most permissive gun safety laws in the country. There are no background checks required, no permit to carry a concealed gun, no restrictions on gun ownership by violent offenders, no requirement to lock up firearms and no restrictions on assault weapons. Two juveniles are charged for this slaughter.The United States has more guns than people. We have mass shootings on a weekly basis. Our laws regulating gun sales, ownership and use are some of the most lax in the world. The United States has a gun homicide rate 26 times that of other high-income countries. The second leading cause of death for children under 18 years-old is gun homicide (second only to automobile deaths). This is our shameful problem.
Most everyone wants to fix it. Polls show that as many as 97% of us support a universal criminal background check on all gun purchases. Much of the senseless killing and mass shooting is by assault style weapons developed for use in war. The Second Amendment to the Constitution grants us the right to bear arms, but not for the unconstrained use of weapons of war to murder our fellow citizens and children.
A large majority of us want to ban these weapons. So what prevents us from altering what we have done to ourselves? Why can't we do better in saving our children from gun violence?
Is the latest tragedy in Kansas City a possible turning point in this terrible tale? Could the gun protectors suddenly perceive an economic impact if families cannot safely attend large gatherings and so they think twice about attending sporting events, the Easter parade or other American celebrations? Gun protectors seem unmoved by school, church or grocery store shootings, but perhaps families and individuals who value their safety above their support for guns might shy away from attending large events, costing event-organizers real money.
People might be less willing to spend large sums to attend a football game with their family if they fear that others with concealed weapons might also attend.
I truly believe that the issue lies with one party of lawmakers and politicians who have made their pact with the National Rifle Association. The elected members in one party in both the Senate and the House have consistently fought against laws that would help solve this problem. They oppose universal background checks, a ban on assault-style weapons and red flag laws that identify people who should not have guns.
They have successfully subverted what the citizens in the United States want. I believe that the lawmakers in one party have done this as a political weapon and message. I think they believe they must run on this stance for political gain. What a horrible, horrible thing to do. But until this stance changes, or such lawmakers are defeated, this is what we citizens, the next victims, must live with. And the framers of our Constitution did not intend for us to arm ourselves with weapons of war to defend ourselves at a celebratory parade.
I appeal to all of you, for the sake of our children, our fellow citizens and ourselves — do not vote for any candidate who opposes an assault weapons ban, red flag laws or universal background checks on gun sales and ownership.
Our future and our lives depend on it.
Larry Pifer lives in Easton and is a member of the Talbot Democratic Forum.

title: Ridgley commissioners vote to continue MOU with Caroline County Sheriff's Office
author: AHMAD GARNETT agarnett@chespub.com
content:
Ridgley commissioners vote to continue MOU with Caroline County Sheriff's Office

 May 6, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: AHMAD GARNETT agarnett@chespub.com | Section: News 
 
 456
 Words 

 Read News Document

 RIDGELY — The Ridgely commissioners voted to continue the town's memorandum of understanding with the Caroline County Sheriff's Office at their monthly meeting Monday.Commissioner Brad Sears voted in favor of the MOU, but he said he plans to continue negotiation with the Sheriff's Office over details of the agreement.
"I think at this point we're to a point where we would entertain a motion to give the town authorization to meet with the county to negotiate any changes to the MOU and go from there," Sears said.
Ridgely has maintained a contract with the Caroline County Sheriff's Office to have assigned officers covering the town since last year. In March of 2024, the town suspended the entirety of its police department amid a state investigation.
On July 25, 2024, an investigation report by the Office of the State Prosecutor found no "sufficient evidence of criminal activity warranting further investigation or prosecution." By that time, the Ridgely officers had already been laid off.
Monday's decision came after a discussion at last month's commissioners meeting about three potential options to continue policing for the town.
"I know last month we talked about three options, one completely going back to the sheriff's department regular patrol pattern," Sears said. "Second was to attempt to re-establish an original police force, and even that price was conservatively estimated at $852,000 for the first year if we could find the police officer."
The third option was to continue the MOU with the county.
The cost for the services of the Caroline County Sheriff's Office would be $493,415 on the fiscal year 2026 budget.
The Sheriff advocated for his office to continue its agreement with the town.
"The sheriff's office is providing what is going to be a high quality of law enforcement in the town," Caroline County Sheriff Donald Baker said in an interview. "The town going with the MOU with the sheriff's office, they get everything the sheriff's office has to provide as far as criminal investigations handled by a investigator or detective, as well as the sheriff's office is a member of the Caroline County Drug Task Force and we have two deputies assigned to that."
Multiple questions were brought up by town residents regarding where the $493,415 would go. Baker clarified to residents and commissioners how the funds would be broken down.
"There was some confusion that this money is dumped right into the Sheriff's Office budget. That's not true," Baker said. "The county is billing the town based upon the usage. So, if we don't use something or there's money left over, the county does not bill it and it goes back to the town or the town keeps it and it's never filled."
The vote to continue the MOU was unanimous. Commissioner John Hurley was absent from the meeting.

 EASTON — Police have arrested two people for hindering a drug investigation in April, alleging they made a fake report to 911 that there was a shooting at the Easton Walmart.Elon Black, 38, of Easton, and Lacira Wilson, 39, of Worton, are both facing charges in connection to a drug investigation on April 4.
They were arrested on Sept. 18 and 19 for intent to distribute drugs, obstructing and hindering, and making false statements to police officers.
According to a press release from the Easton Police Department, officers stopped Black's vehicle in the area of U.S. Route 50 and Cecil Drive on April 4. A K-9 search discovered "suspected heroin/fentanyl mix," crack cocaine and ecstasy, police wrote.
During the stop, police said Black was on his phone. Investigators eventually determined that Black called Wilson during that time. Black had Wilson make a call to 911 and report a fake shooting at the Easton Walmart, police said.
Officers went to the Walmart but found no evidence of shots fired.
According to online court records, Black and Wilson both posted $10,000 unsecured personal bond since their arrests, meaning they will only have to pay the full amount if they fail to appear for a court date or break other conditions imposed by the court.
Wilson has a trial scheduled for Nov. 5 in Talbot County District Court. She faces four total charges: obstructing and hindering, making a false statement to officers, and two counts of possession with the intent to distribute a controlled dangerous substance.
Black's trial is scheduled for Nov. 3 in District Court. He faces the same four counts as Wilson.
Black, in a separate case in Talbot County Circuit Court, is also facing two felony, six misdemeanor and 11 traffic counts in connection to the same April 4 traffic stop. A jury trial for those charges is scheduled for Dec. 8.
In that case, he's charged with two felony counts of possession with the intent to distribute narcotics. Black posted $10,000 unsecured bond for those charges back in July.

 EASTON - The victim of the shooting near Unionville on Sunday was targeted over a dispute with a common girlfriend, police said Wednesday.Stewart Orlando Ray, 37, of Clinton, was located Tuesday afternoon in northern Virginia in connection to the shooting, which occurred Sunday evening. Police obtained an arrest warrant charging Ray with attempted murder, first-degree assault, reckless endangerment and use of a firearm in a violent crime or felony.Deputies from the Talbot County Sheriff's Office responded to the University of Maryland Shore Medical Center at Easton around 9 p.m. Sunday for a shooting victim. The victim, identified as Jahari De'Mon Cooper, 39, of Talbot County was driving near Unionville when Ray passed him and pulled off to the side.As Cooper passed Ray's vehicle, Ray shot at him multiple times, striking both him and his car. Cooper drove himself to the emergency room for treatment, police said.Police said Ray fled the area in his vehicle, failed to stop for a stop sign at the intersection of Unionville Road and Bruffs Island Road, left the roadway and struck several parked vehicles, disabling his own car.Ray then fled on foot into the nearby woods, prompting a 24-hour manhunt beginning in the early morning hours Monday. Numerous police vehicles from the multiple agencies involved in the suit lined Bruffs Island Road and other nearby streets. A helicopter was seen circling the search area early Monday afternoon.The search for Ray continued despite severe storms hitting the area Monday night into early Tuesday morning.Police said investigators uncovered information early Tuesday morning that Ray may have slipped through the search area during the storms and made his way toward the Washington, D.C., metro area. Talbot County Sheriff's Office investigators then contacted the U.S. Marshals Capitol Area Regional Fugitive Task Force with information on Ray's possible location.The U.S. Marshals task force located Ray in northern Virginia Tuesday afternoon.Around 12:46 p.m. Tuesday, the Alexandria Police Department responded to a shooting in the Potomac Yard Shopping Center, located in the 3600 block of Richmond Highway in the city. After arriving, officers learned that the U.S. Marshals task force had found a wanted fugitive, who was later identified as Ray.Ray was shot when the task force attempted to apprehend him, police said. He was taken to the hospital with life-threatening injuries.Detectives from the Alexandria Police Department are investigating the shooting and are communicating with the Talbot County Sheriff's Office, police said.Ray is on probation for a 2009 attempted second-degree murder conviction.Talbot County Sheriff Joe Gamble expressed his appreciation to the multiple agencies involved in the manhunt."I am incredibly grateful to the countless state, local and federal law enforcement officers on the Eastern Shore, CARTIF, and the Alexandria Police Department who willingly put themselves in harm's way to make our community safer during this manhunt," Gamble said in a statement.He added: "During these strange times, as the Maryland Legislature continues to make policing more difficult, it is inspiring to know that there are still selfless men and women who are willing to risk their lives daily for all of us, knowing that their every action will be scrutinized by people who have risked nothing and have never known real danger.I can't thank these public servants enough for their sacrifice and heroism."

 GREENSBORO — The Town of Greensboro announced on Feb. 12 that its police department hired Sgt. Jeff Adams as its newest member, ending a long stretch during which Police Chief Lenox Trams was the town's sole officer."Sgt. Adams brings 18 years of law enforcement experience and officially started on February 11," The Town of Greensboro said in a Facebook post. "He's currently completing his 80-hour FTO training, and we can't wait for you to meet him."
Trams has been the lone officer at Greensboro Police Department since September of 2024, and he is pleased to bring Adams on board.
"I've been there since March of 2023, and I've been trying to recruit only the highest best qualified officers, and it's been a struggle," Trams said. "So when I was down to myself I didn't give up, I kept recruiting and I actually had the applicant who kind of met our standards, so he applied, and then he went through the hiring process and a very extensive background investigation, and I just hired him."
Adams' 18 years of law enforcement experience was one of these reasons Trams hired him, the police chief said, but also Adams' 18 years of loyalty.
"Sergeant Adams has been at one agency for 18 years and that track record to me says a lot," Trams said. "He's very loyal to the agency, and he just doesn't bounce around. We also look at like other factors of his application, but I think off the face, just having him be loyal to his one agency for 18 years says a lot."
In September 2024, the town of Greensboro considered closing the police department because the public safety demands were too much for one officer to handle. The Caroline County Sheriff's Office would have taken over the policing duties for the town.
Trams believes with this hire the conversations of dissolving the police department have been "tabled." He hopes to continue to grow the staff at the Greensboro Police Department.
When Trams was by himself, Greensboro moved its offices into the police department's building, with the town's town hall experiencing maintenance concerns. But now there will be talks of moving the police department to another office since the plan will be to continue to grow the department, Trams said.
"I was by myself, so that was the best move at the time," Trams said. "But now that I'm going to build up the agency and hire quality officers, we all can't be in the same building, so there is some talking about putting the police department in another building."

 Local police and emergency medical professionals took part in a serious training of the utmost importance in Easton on Thursday.Active shooter situations in elementary and secondary schools caused 328 deaths from 2000 to 2022, according to the National Center for Education Statistics.
That's why before every school year, local first responders have made it a habit to complete active shooter trainings. This year's training brought Talbot and Caroline sheriff's deputies, Easton police, local EMTs and paramedics, and others to The Country School.

 CAMBRIDGE — An unsanctioned "Freaknik" event in the area of Greenwood Avenue and Cosby Avenue on May 25 resulted in eight arrests.According to a news release from the Cambridge Police Department, at least 400 people were estimated to have been a part of the gathering.
Cambridge Police said there was fighting at the Cambridge event on May 25, and attendees gathered in residential complexes that have "no trespassing" and "no loitering" signs posted. Police said there were also vehicles parked in "no parking" zones, which resulted in citations being issued and vehicles getting towed.
As officers tried to get the crowds to disperse, police said a majority of groups were "very defiant, belligerent and hostile towards law enforcement," which included the Cambridge Police Department, Maryland State Police and the Dorchester County Sheriff's Office.
Police said that bottles were thrown at officers "on several occasions." They said one glass bottle hit an MSP vehicle, causing damage to the vehicle.
Police said officers deployed oleoresin capsicum spray, or pepper spray, and departmental-issued tasers "to affect arrest and to keep hostile crowds back from officers." They said officers were assaulted by attendees.
Jymaree Meekins, who attended the event said that the event was good for the community. He said the promoters gave out free food and drinks and people had a good time.
"I don't think any of the people that got arrested really did anything to get arrested," he said. "I think the cops were really harassing them."
Meekins said he didn't think anyone got into altercations other than with the cops.
"When the cops went up to people, I wasn't really around," he said. "But from afar, I could see them just chasing innocent people. Pepper spraying them, tackling people that weren't really doing anything."
According to the news release, CPD was made aware of the event that took place in the 500 and 600 blocks of Greenwood Avenue and the 1000 block of Cosby Avenue through social media.
Police said that CPD officers were assigned to the Greenwood Avenue area that afternoon "to show a police presence" in an effort to stop potential violence or illegal activities.
The eight people arrested include:
A 17-year-old from Cambridge who was charged, via a juvenile referral, with disorderly conduct, failure to obey a lawful order and trespassing.Princess La'Niya Justine Demby, 20, of Cambridge, who was charged with disorderly conduct, failure to obey a lawful order and resisting arrest.Velouse Richele'ne Georges, 20, of Salisbury, who was charged with second-degree assault, trespassing, obstructing and hindering and resisting arrest.Shaqueelah Shante Smith, 32 years, of Cambridge, who was charged with disorderly conduct.Camren Dajour Lake, 22, of Cambridge, who was charged with trespassing, disorderly conduct and failure to obey a lawful order.Ronald George Ricketts III, 24, of Cambridge, who was charged with disorderly conduct.Ja'nya Amara Sherwood, 19, of Salisbury, who was charged with disorderly conduct and possession of a dangerous weapon with intent to injure.Tei'Sha Na'Sha Simms, 22, of Cambridge, who was charged with failure to obey a lawful order.
Police said that all of the adults arrested were released on personal recognizance or on criminal citation.
CPD's investigation is on-going. They said additional arrests could be made.
This article has been updated to include comments from Jymaree Meekins.

title: Town of Greensboro approves K-9 to start immediately
author: AHMAD GARNETT agarnett@chespub.com
content:
Town of Greensboro approves K-9 to start immediately

 493
 Words

 EASTON — At their April 17 meeting, Greensboro Town Council members approved police K-9 Mosley to start immediately."It feels quite amazing," Police Chief Lenox Trams said to The Star Democrat Friday. "She's has a very good career, and my vision was to have a police K-9 at the Greensboro Police Department to assists with the K-9 scans with the county and just be the resource. So it feels amazing to actually have it all approved."
Mosley is the K-9 of new Greensboro Police Department Sgt. Jeff Adams. Mosley has been with Adams since 2017.
Mosley has been experienced cancer, but Adams says she is still able to work as a K-9.
"She's done everything," Adams told The Star Democrat when he was hired in February. "She's already certified in tracking and narcotics. Now we took off the tracking because she lost her leg to cancer in Halloween of 2023. She went through chemo, radiation, and she's she's still working. She's did awesome with the training. She nailed it."
Mosley was retired after Adams left Federalsburg Police Department because Adams wanted to make sure he was able to keep Mosley.
The council members asked multiple questions about the lack of K-9s on the Mid-Shore. The concern the council members had deals with Mosley being called into other towns in Caroline County or other jurisdictions in the Mid-Shore.
"I understand the shortage of the dogs in the county, and I understand they're a great resource," said Pete Brelia, town council member. "But this is the Greensboro Police Department, and it serves the citizens of Greensboro, and I don't want to hire a dog and have Jeff and his dog called all over the state and the county to do the duty or the job of the dog at our expense.
"We're paying him his overtime, we're going to take care of the dog, assume all his responsibilities, and the officer is not going to be in town, which is where we're hiring him to be, so that's my issue with the dog."
While the concerns where heard by Trams, he assured the council members that he can set a mile radius on where Mosley and Adams could go.
"As the police chief, I have the authority to give a time frame or a mile radius of Adams and the police K-9 to respond," Trams said.
The council members also discussed whether to bring the K-9 on before this fiscal budget year ends or in July, when the new fiscal year begins. The cost for the K-9 is $2,000 for this fiscal year.
After discussion, the council members voted 3-1 in favor of hiring Mosley immediately. Brelia voted against hiring the dog.
"I would like to go ahead and make a motion to hire the dog for two months until the July budget for $2,000," Joe Moon, council member, said. "We have a drug problem, I don't think it makes a difference from now until July. After hearing the public I just like to make that motion."

 DENTON — A Greensboro man entered an Alford plea for sexual abuse of a minor and reckless endangerment at a pre-trial hearing last week in the Caroline County Circuit Court.On Oct. 23, Enemias Simeon Bautista Perez, 37, took the plea for two of 14 counts of criminal charges, which included first-degree rape and first-degree child abuse.
An Alford plea allows a person to maintain their innocence while acknowledging the state had enough evidence to obtain a conviction. The other 12 counts will not be prosecuted.
Perez's jury trial, which was scheduled to begin Oct. 28, is now canceled.
The counts that will not be prosecuted included first-degree rape of an 8-year-old child, along with incest, first-degree child abuse, first-degree assault and sexual solicitation of a minor, all allegedly occurring at his residence in Greensboro around March 30.
Originally, Perez faced up to 211 years in prison in Caroline County, along with life in prison for the first-degree rape charge. His guilty counts of sexual abuse of a minor and reckless endangerment carry maximum sentences of 30 and five years, respectively.
Perez's sentencing is scheduled for Dec. 13. Judge Sidney S. Campen requested a full pre-sentence investigation into Perez prior to that date.
Attorney Eduardo Gonzalez, who represents Perez, did not immediately respond to request for comment.
Charging documents indicated Perez as the 8-year-old child's parent. Since being charged, he's been held without bond at the Caroline County Detention Center.
Perez faces an addition 19 counts of criminal charges in Wicomico County, including first-degree rape, sexual abuse of a minor and second-degree assault. All 19 of those charges state the offenses occurred between August 2021 and April 2024 in Wicomico County, according to court records.
The Wicomico County charges total a potential 224 years in prison, along with life in prison for the first-degree rape charge.
A pre-trial conference for that case is scheduled for Nov. 25, with a potential jury trial set to begin Dec. 9 in Wicomico County.

 CENTREVILLE — In a Wednesday interview, Queen Anne's County Sheriff Gary Hofmann emphasized that the homicide investigation into the shooting death of 19-year-old Christopher Parsley remains the department's primary focus.Parsley was shot and killed on Sunday, June 1, near a residence on Centreville Road while attending a bonfire with friends.
"We're dealing with a homicide here, and that's going to take precedence," Hofmann said. He noted that many attendees at the party have not come forward, and some individuals may be hesitant to share information out of fear of legal consequences related to underage drinking or drug use. "Let us be clear: We are not seeking to prosecute anyone for those actions," he said.
Hofmann encouraged the public to provide any information, stressing that failing to do so could hinder the investigation. "This shouldn't happen here," Hofmann stressed, "We're not going tolerate this happening here."
Having information that could aid in the investigation and withholding it, is definitely not helpful to the family of individual that you were friends with, Hofmann reiterated. It is hope that the person/s involved in this incident will soon be held accountable.
The Sheriff also warned that social media platforms like Instagram and Snapchat have exacerbated the problem, with parties being posted online drawing unwanted attention.
In addition to the ongoing investigation, Metro Crime Stoppers of Maryland is offering a cash reward for information leading to the arrest of the person or persons responsible for Parsley's death. All tips submitted through Metro Crime Stoppers are anonymous and eligible for a reward. Anyone with information is encouraged to call 1-866-7LOCKUP or submit an anonymous tip online at www.metrocrimestoppers.org.
"Christopher wasn't just a 'good kid' — he was the best," said friends of the family. "He was the kind of young man who would drop everything to help a friend, offer a smile to a stranger, and light up every room he walked into." A GoFundMe page has been created to help with funeral expenses, help support his family during this tragic time, and to pay off his truck loan, a symbol of something Christopher was proud of.

Cambridge created the Traffic and Safety Committee in 2021, and the city ran its first traffic safety pilot program in 2022.
According to Roche, who is also a member of the Cambridge Traffic and Safety Committee, pedestrian crashes increased significantly in 2020 while people were staying home as a result of Covid-19.

After the city implemented its first traffic safety pilot program at the intersection of High and Church streets, external consultants verified that the program reduced speeding and other traffic concerns.

Between now and the next City Council meeting, commissioners will select one or two areas in their wards they would like to address. Then, city staff will begin implementing traffic safety measures.
Roche says he is anxious to get residents' feedback on this year's pilot programs and that he understands it will be a transition for some.

title: YMCA fire on Saturday intentionally set, fire marshal says
author: Konner Metz
content:
YMCA fire on Saturday intentionally set, fire marshal says

 January 13, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Konner Metz | Section: Local News 
 
 457

 EASTON — A fire at the YMCA on Peachblossom Road on Saturday was intentionally set, according to the Office of the State Fire Marshal.At around 12:30 p.m., Easton firefighters responded to a fire on the second floor, which took just under an hour to control, per the fire marshal. No injuries were reported.
A preliminary investigation ruled the cause as "incendiary." The fire marshal stated that "subject(s) ignited a small pile of party supplies located on the second floor rear storage hallway."
Normal operations at the Y resumed Sunday.
YMCA of the Chesapeake CEO Robbie Gill said, "it's disheartening to know that that can happen."
"The Y's been in this community 168 years," Gill said Monday. "It serves one in three people. It's kind of a third place where people go. It's a place where everyone is welcome."
The blaze around 12:30 p.m. was the first of two fires at the Y on Saturday. Around 5:30 p.m., firefighters were once again called to the Y, where an HVAC unit was on fire on the building's roof.
The cause of the HVAC fire was deemed to be a mechanical failure. The fire marshal ruled that second blaze as accidental and said it was unrelated to the incident earlier that day.
Both fires caused a combined $50,000 in estimated damages, according to the fire marshal's reports.
Gill said he's grateful the Easton Volunteer Fire Department responded so promptly and that there weren't extensive damages to the Y. Saturday's first fire was extinguished by the Y's sprinkler system before firefighters arrived at the scene.
Peter Hyman, president of the YMCA's board, was on his way to the Y around noon on Saturday when he learned of the first fire. He noticed community members and Y staff gathering.
"The staff was upset. It was an upsetting moment, and I just did what I could to help both in terms of the emotions of the folks as well as the physical reality of the situation," Hyman said Sunday morning.
"When something like this happens, it's offensive on a multiplicity of levels," Hyman added.
Gill said the Y is going to take a look at its procedures and protocols moving forward, as well as continuing to work with law enforcement in its investigation.
The fire marshal's office is asking anyone with information regarding the intentionally set fire to contact its Upper Eastern Regional Office at 410-819-3500.
Gill said the fact that someone tried to "impact the sanctity" of the Y as a community center is "always scary at the time and also sad."
"But if there's one thing about Talbot County and our community, it is a tight group of people," Gill said. "... Something like this isn't going to deter us from continuing to make a positive impact."

title: Motorists encouraged to watch for deer as breeding season approaches
author: Tom McCall
content:
Motorists encouraged to watch for deer as breeding season approaches

 September 21, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Tom McCall | Section: Local News 
 
 505
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — As deer breeding season nears, motorists are encouraged to keep their eyes peeled for white tails on the road.Local auto repair businesses say they are busier fixing collisions this time of year. Hitting a deer can cause thousands of dollars worth of damage, bending front fenders, crumpling hoods and cracking front windshields.
"It is about 20% to 30% more this time of year," said TJ Jefferson of Grants Automotive in Easton. "I get more calls early in the morning, 'Can you come get my car? I just struck a deer or a deer just struck me.'"
With increased volume during deer season, he says they just get it done with the available manpower that they have.
According to data from State Farm, "U.S. drivers had an estimated 1.8 million animal collision insurance claims in the U.S. between July 2022 and June 2023."
About 1.5 million deer-car accidents happen every year. More than $1 billion in annual insured losses are due to damages caused by deer-car accidents. According to State Farm, Maryland drivers have a one-in-116-vehicle likelihood risk for animal collisions. The highest risk state for deer-car collisions is West Virginia at one in 37 vehicles.
Deer breeding season begins in October and runs through mid-December. During these months, bucks become more active, seeking out female deer. The females move around more to avoid the bucks. All this motion means more deer are on the roads.
Deer are most active between the hours of 5 and 8 a.m. and again from 5 to 8 p.m., which are also hours that many drivers are on the road commuting to or from work.
Trooper Ian Rola of the Easton Barracks of the Maryland State Police said, "The incidents that rise this time of year are car accidents. (Deer) are in rut and are running all over and crossing the roadway. It is usually up this time of year — in the November time frame."
Rola and fellow law enforcement officers work to help keep roadways clear of hazards during these peak months.
"It is between law enforcement and SHA. We try to keep the roads clear. We rely on the public. If you see a carcass, give us a call, and we will come out. If it is a mess, we call SHA (State Highway Administration) to help," Rola said.
Rola emphasized the importance of drivers slowing down and wearing seat belts, especially as deer breeding season approaches.
"You have got to imagine, you hit a dear, you slam on the brakes and you are going forward at the same time. The seat belt will stop that forward momentum. This saves a lot of injuries from deer accidents," he said.
Representatives from the State Highway Administration encouraged drivers to avoid making sudden turns or movements to avoid hitting deer.
"Making sudden, sharp turns is dangerous as it could place the driver in the path of oncoming traffic or cause your vehicle to strike a fixed object such as a tree or utility pole," wrote Charlie Gischlar of the Maryland Department of Transportation State Highway Administration in an email.

title: Wind causes Grasonville house fire
author: STAFF REPORT

Wind causes Grasonville house fire

 April 8, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: STAFF REPORT | Section: News 
 
 236
 Words

 GRASONVILLE — A single-family home on Grasonville Cemetery Road was destroyed by fire Tuesday morning after wind knocked over a bucket containing wood stove embers.The fire occurred at approximately 8:21 a.m. on April 8 at a residence in the 300 block of Grasonville Cemetery Road. According to the Queen Anne's County Fire Marshal's report, the blaze caused an estimated $240,000 in structural damage and $100,000 in content loss.
The owner and sole occupant, Bert Olmstead, 73, told officials he had cleaned out his wood stove and placed the embers in a closed bucket on the front porch when wind blew it over. Olmstead was alerted by the smell of burning plastic and discovered the fire had already spread significantly before calling 911.
"And after that, the whole thing went up," Olmstead said. "I just got out as quickly as I could."
Olmstead reported losing "everything" in the fire, including his wallet and hearing aids. He is currently being assisted by family and friends while waiting to hear from his insurance company.
Forty-six firefighters from Grasonville Volunteer Fire Department and Kent Island Volunteer Fire Department responded to the one-alarm fire, which took one hour and 24 minutes to control. The fire originated on the front porch and has been ruled accidental due to the discarded wood stove ashes.
According to the Office of the State Fire Marshal, no injuries were reported and emergency responders cleared the scene by approximately 11 a.m.

title: Trappe woman found guilty of criminally negligent manslaughter by vehicle
author: Natalie Jones
content:
Trappe woman found guilty of criminally negligent manslaughter by vehicle

 January 31, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Natalie Jones | Section: Crime 
 
 787
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — A Trappe woman who fatally injured an 84-year-old woman in a crash at the intersection of U.S. Route 50 and the southern end of the Easton Parkway nearly three years ago was sentenced Monday to 45 days in jail.Brittnee Ewing, 24, pleaded guilty to one count of criminally negligent manslaughter by vehicle — a misdemeanor charge — in connection to the fatal Easton crash, which occurred in the afternoon hours of April 8, 2021.
"These are the hearings where I feel the most powerless," said Talbot County Circuit Judge Stephen Kehoe, who presided in court Monday.
Though no specific disposition was recommended by prosecutor Jennifer Wilson and defense attorney Stephanie Shipley advocated for a probation before judgment and no active incarceration, Kehoe handed Ewing a three-year sentence, suspending all but 45 days.
The case against Ewing stemmed from a multi-agency investigation into the crash.
Ewing, the driver of a Ford Escape, was traveling eastbound on Route 50 toward its intersection with the parkway at a high rate of speed — 85 mph prior to the crash, 79 mph at the time of the collision, Wilson said.
Vicki Harvey, 63, of Easton, was driving a Ford C-Max Hybrid that day. Jo Ann Wright, 84, of Easton, was her passenger.
Harvey and Wright were crossing over eastbound Route 50 from westbound Route 50 at the light to turn onto the parkway, traveling roughly 25 mph heading toward the parkway, when they were struck by Ewing's car.
Wright was seriously injured in the crash, Wilson said. She was flown to the University of Maryland Shock Trauma Center in Baltimore. Harvey was taken to the hospital in Easton with minor injuries.
Wright suffered "devastating trauma" to her head, along with multiple fractures and bruises all over her body, Wilson said. She died at the trauma center on April 9, 2021.
Wilson said Ewing's car was "completely destroyed" in the crash. Ewing, who was also seriously injured in the crash, was flown with her 1-year-old son to Johns Hopkins in Baltimore for treatment.
A witness who was driving westbound on Route 50 at the time of the crash told police that the C-Max Hybrid had a green light. According to the witness, Ewing did not slow or brake, Wilson said.
In a later interview with police, Ewing said she remembered picking up her son before the crash, though she said she wasn't in a hurry, Wilson said. She did not remember the crash.
Speaking in court, Wright's daughters, Julia George and Janine Conway, recounted the painful memories surrounding their mother's death.
Both women said Wright was internally decapitated, meaning her spinal cord separated from her skull. The family decided to remove her from life support.
George recalled how her mother would outstretch her arms when scared, voicing a fearful suspicion that her mother's broken wrists from the crash were from that movement.
"Her death was one of pain," George said, remembering Wright gasping for breath. A tear rolled down the side of her face around the time of her death.
Conway remembered rounding up her family together to take a photo with Wright on Easter, just days before the crash. She recalled urging her brother to get up for the photo, saying they wouldn't know if it would be the last picture they took with Wright.
"And it was," she said, her voice catching.
Conway and George asked the judge to hold Ewing responsible for her actions that day.
"The accident didn't kill my mother, the choices Ms. Ewing made killed my mother," Conway said.
Shipley acknowledged the family's pain and desire to hold Ewing responsible, saying Ewing did suffer physically and mentally from her split-second decision at that yellow light.
Ewing had undergone multiple surgeries following the crash, she said. The 24-year-old mother of one was unable to walk for months afterward.
The crash was out of character for Ewing, Shipley said — she had never even been pulled over before. Her life was one of service and hard work, she added.
"She lives with, every day, the thought that she killed someone else," Shipley said.
With tears in her eyes, Ewing apologized multiple times for her actions that day, saying she took full responsibility for the tragedy.
"I will carry this with me for the rest of my life, as I should," she said, looking back toward Wright's family members seated in the courtroom. "I am so sorry."
Kehoe said he truly believed her, but given what happened, consequences were still needed.
Despite Shipley's pleas for a delay in Ewing reporting to the county detention center to serve her term, Kehoe denied the requests. Ewing was taken into custody after the hearing.
Court records indicate Shipley filed a motion Tuesday afternoon requesting the court grant Ewing emergency release or home detention due to potentially life-threatening health issues. No decision was made as of press time.

title: Leaders emphasize need for unity during 9/11 Remembrance Ceremony
author: Konner Metz
content:
Leaders emphasize need for unity during 9/11 Remembrance Ceremony

 September 11, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Konner Metz | Section: Local News 
 
 450
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — On the 24th anniversary of the 9/11 attacks, Talbot County and Easton officials gathered to pay tribute to first responders who put their lives on the line on Sept. 11, 2001, and honor those who continue to serve today.The annual 9/11 Remembrance Ceremony brought first responders and residents to the corner of Dover and West streets for a solemn display of remembrance for those who lost their lives in the attacks.
Speakers at the ceremony emphasized a theme of unity. Talbot County Council Vice President Pete Lesher delivered opening remarks.
"We come together today with unity of purpose," Lesher said. "It is a unity we recall we had in those days and weeks following the tragic events those 24 years ago. When attacked, Americans pulled together. We gathered together in our churches. We gathered with our friends, with our colleagues at work."
Lesher recalled how the nation showed immense gratitude toward police officers, firefighters, medical personnel and others in the days and weeks after 9/11. That display of gratitude has continued, he said.
"Today, as we gather, we continue to salute those first responders in our own community," he said. "Thank you to all of you, our first responders, for your service."
Easton Mayor Megan Cook said the "importance of 9/11 cannot be understated." She encouraged residents to lift each other up as people around the nation did in the days following the terror attacks in New York.
"Every day offers us the chance to support, encourage and serve one another, making our towns, our communities and a country a better place," Cook said. "Our greatness as a nation has always come from unity, our ability to come together as a sum greater than our parts."
Thursday's ceremony included a presentation of a wreath honoring the victims of the 9/11 attacks. During a moment of silence, members of the Easton Volunteer Fire Department participated in the tolling of the bells.
St. Michaels High School senior Thalia Turner sang the national anthem and "This Is My Country." Sean Guschke of the St. Michaels Fire Department performed "Amazing Grace," and Talbot County Sheriff's Office Deputy John Coleman belted "God Bless America."
The Easton Middle School band performed as people filtered in and out of the ceremony.
Talbot County Council Member Dave Stepp reflected on the kindness that spread throughout the nation on Sept. 12, 2001, a day Americans were forced to come to grips with the reality of the tragic events the day prior.
He asked those in the crowd to carry that same kindness and unity as they go about their everyday lives.
"There's a lot of lessons we can take from that day," Stepp said.
"As we move forward, let's not only remember 9/11," he added. "Let's also remember 9/12."

title: Speed cameras coming to stretch of I-95 starting July 8
author: Josh Shannon jshannon@chespub.com
content:
Speed cameras coming to stretch of I-95 starting July 8

 June 21, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Josh Shannon jshannon@chespub.com | Section: News 
 
 567
 Words 

 Read News Document

 Starting July 8, police in Delaware will use electronic speed cameras to help enforce speed limits in the Interstate 95 construction zone near Del. 896 in Newark.The first three weeks will be a warning period. After the warning period, registered vehicle owners receiving a first offense will receive a base violation of $20, plus an additional amount for each mile per hour over the posted work zone speed limit of 55 mph.
For example, if the captured violation occurs at a speed of 66 mph, the speed violation is $20 plus an additional $11, which accounts for $1 for each mile per hour over the speed limit. Additional fees and court costs that are tacked on to all speeding tickets in Delaware will bring the total cost up to $118.
Second and subsequent offenses are higher. These violations are civil penalties only, and no points will be assessed to drivers' licenses.
State officials first announced the program in April, saying the cameras are an important tool to make work zones safer.
"Even though we've reduced the speed limits out here in the work zone, we're still seeing people speeding through there," Delaware Department of Transportation Secretary Nicole Majeski said at the time. "It is a tight configuration, so law enforcement has difficulty pulling people over. We've also seen a spike in crashes, so we're hoping the cameras will help."
Similar to the red light cameras common throughout the state, speed cameras will take pictures of violators' license plates, and those drivers will receive a ticket in the mail. The driver must exceed the speed limit by at least 11 mph in order to receive a ticket via a speed camera.
DelDOT first used speed cameras in 2022 when the state legislature authorized a pilot program focused on an I-95 project in Wilmington.
"We saw speeds reduced significantly, both northbound and southbound, and accidents were cut in half," Majeski said. "We saw as a direct result of having those cameras that people slow down, and it really paid off."
Last year, after lobbying from Newark officials and others, the legislature expanded the program to allow cameras in work zones and residential areas throughout the state. After developing regulations and choosing a vendor, DelDOT is ready to install the first new cameras in the work zone at the I-95/Del. 896 interchange, which is in the midst of a two-year reconstruction project.
Brandon Zerilla, who is leading the project for DelDOT contractor Wagman, said earlier this year that the cameras will be a welcomed safety tool for his workers.
"These cameras have proven to reduce the speeds in the work zone, reduce crashes and increase awareness in the work zone," Zerilla said, adding that far too many drivers do not slow down while passing through the I-95 construction site.
The interchange project, which is the largest work zone in Delaware, involves building new flyover ramps from southbound Del. 896 to northbound I-95 and from southbound I-95 to southbound Del. 896. The flyovers will increase the distance between exit and entrance ramps, reducing the traffic weaving that causes crashes at the current interchange.
The project also includes widening a one-mile stretch of the interstate to provide for longer acceleration and deceleration lanes, as well as upgraded lighting, rehabilitation of 10 existing bridges, the construction of six new bridges for the flyovers, and the construction of a walking and biking bridge over the interstate.
Work began last spring and will continue through fall 2025.

title: K-9 Murph adjusts to retirement after cannabis legalization
author: Konner Metz
content:
K-9 Murph adjusts to retirement after cannabis legalization

 May 25, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Konner Metz | Section: Local News 
 
 297
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — Cpl. Joseph Schinault still remembers the first time his K-9 partner Murph tracked down a suspect.The Belgian malinois and German shepherd mix located a residence in the Doverbrook Apartments an unarmed robbery suspect ran to with stolen items. It was the dog's first tracking mission and far from his last.
Starting in 2018, Murph served as an integral part of vehicle searches and the Easton Police Department's crisis response unit.
But Maryland's legalization of recreational cannabis use put an end to Murph's career in 2024, Schinault said. Two other Easton K-9s trained to detect marijuana also retired.
"It was a huge hit to our unit," Schinault said.
The police department is filling its K-9 spots with a new guard of police dogs. Meanwhile, Schinault has moved up the ranks and is no longer a K-9 handler. But he still looks fondly on his time working alongside Murph.
"It is truly an honor to work with them," Schinault said of the skilled dogs.
Murph, 7, still lives with Schinault and his family. He's become the "best of friends" with Schinault's son, who is just six months younger than Murph.
Schinault said it took a while for Murph to adapt to staying home instead of jumping in the police car when it started. "He lives to have a purpose," Schinault said.
Schinault's younger brother and fellow Easton police officer, Mark, is the handler of one of Easton's new K-9s, Knox. Joseph Schinault says it's amazing what K-9s can do, emphasizing the importance of police dogs in solving crime.
"Who's to say we (would've) ever solved that?" he said of Murph's first tracking.
For the Easton police officer, having a partner like Murph was a source of daily motivation.
"There's not a day that you bring a K-9 to work that they don't want to work," Schinault said.

title: 'It was all smiles': Cambridge National Night Out brings more than 800 to county pool
author: MAGGIE TROVATO mtrovato@chespub.com
content:
'It was all smiles': Cambridge National Night Out brings more than 800 to county pool

 August 14, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: MAGGIE TROVATO mtrovato@chespub.com | Section: Local News 
 
 582
 Words 

 Read News Document

 CAMBRIDGE — This year's National Night Out event in Cambridge brought more people, more hotdogs and more smiles."Like many other years, it was another successful year," Cambridge Police Chief Justin Todd said. "We had tons of kids and a lot of people and businesses and community leaders that came out and all took part. It was all smiles."
Between 800 and 900 people showed up to the Dorchester County Pool on Aug. 6 for National Night Out on, compared to around 600 people last year, Cambridge Police Captain Antoine Patton said.
Patton said all of the feedback he received about the evening was positive. He said multiple children came up to him to thank him and tell him they had a great time.
Todd said all of the positive feedback is why the police department continues to hold the event at the pool year after year.
"I think there's just something about being at the county pool and the kids being able to have the opportunity to swim for a couple hours, not worry about any prices or charges and just enjoy time with their friends and family," he said.
Attendees were able to talk with a variety of vendors, from the Dorchester County Health Department to the Department of Juvenile Services to the Boys and Girls Club. The different vendors offered pamphlets and information about the resources they have available to residents.
Similar to the number of attendees, Patton said there were more vendors at this year's event than in years past. Todd said that number has increased every year.
"And it's good because you get those necessary resources and information that people may not otherwise see or get," Todd said. "It actually gets handed to them. And they can talk to one another and start forming those bonds."
Along with swimming in the pool, listening to the music played by DJ Doc Lane and eating hotdogs courtesy of the police department, a handful of lucky attendees won prizes that had been donated by Paul Davis Restoration. Prizes ranged from a TV, to a Minnie Mouse kitchen set, to a gas grill, to baskets filled with household goods.
"The lady who won a TV actually cried," Patton said.
Not only did attendees get served the 700 hotdogs the police station cooked up, but MidShore Meals til Monday — a nonprofit that provides food for food-insecure children and families in Dorchester County — handed out bags of food, Patton said.
Todd said National Night Out represents what Cambridge police have been trying to do for the last two years: community-oriented policing.
"It's building relationships between the police and the community," he said. "But also (building) other relationships such as (with) Juvenile Services, the health department, the Dorchester County school system. ... Us all working together to build a stronger community for tomorrow."
According to National Night Out's website, the event was first held in 1984. It aims to promote partnerships between the police and community nationwide, as well as make neighborhoods safer. Patton said the event was created with the intention of having a night without crime in every community.
"And what it does is it brings community together and it gives them a live interaction with law enforcement officers to let the community know that we're working together and we support them just like they support us," he said about the event.
Patton thanked Dorchester County Recreation and Parks for allowing Cambridge police to hold the event at the county pool.
"It was a great event and we look forward to doing it again," he said.
