Students and staff were evacuated out of EHS on Monday afternoon after the threat was made just after 2 p.m. Police say a caller contacted the front desk and "advised that there was a bomb inside of the school and hung up."
"The caller re-contacted the front desk staff a few minutes later and asked when dismissal was," the Talbot County Sheriff's Office stated.
Police stated EHS staff immediately notified the school resource officer of the threat, leading to a quick evacuation from the building. The sheriff's office said all students and staff were safely evacuated as of Monday afternoon.
Deputies responded to the school, and bomb-detecting K-9 teams searched the building and surrounding property. Once cleared, staff returned to the school building.
"I am so grateful for the outstanding work our Talbot Deputies, Easton Police Officers, and our Talbot County Department of Emergency Services Dispatchers performed today to identify the caller of the bomb threat," Sheriff Joe Gamble said in a release.
"Within two hours the suspect was identified, located and charged," he said. "The teachers and staff at Easton High worked tirelessly with law enforcement to make sure everyone was safe. We are so fortunate to have such dedicated professionals in our community who work very hard to keep our children safe."
Deputies are working with the Talbot County State's Attorney's Office and "will be seeking additional charges if applicable," the sheriff's office said.
At Monday's Easton Town Council meeting, Ward 2 Councilmember Don Abbatiello thanked staff and first responders who handled the situation on Monday.
"I want to offer my sincere thanks to the teachers and the staff, and the first responders who attended the bomb threat today at Easton High School," Abbatiello said. "You all were professional in caring for our children and put them first. In this day and age, you cannot be too careful."
Anyone with information is asked to contact the Talbot County Sheriff's Office at 410-822-1020.

title: On NTSB recommendations, FAA closes helicopter route near DC airport weeks after tragedy
author: MENNATALLA IBRAHIM Capital News Service
content:
On NTSB recommendations, FAA closes helicopter route near DC airport weeks after tragedy

 March 11, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: MENNATALLA IBRAHIM Capital News Service | Section: News 
 
 601
 Words 

 Read News Document

 WASHINGTON — The National Transportation Safety Board issued urgent safety recommendations Tuesday, warning that helicopter flights near the Ronald Reagan Washington National Airport pose serious safety risks and one helicopter route should be closed during airport operations.Hours later, Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy accepted the recommendations on behalf of the Federal Aviation Administration, promising long-term changes.
"Urgent recommendations require immediate action to prevent similar accidents or incidents when we issue them," NTSB Chair Jennifer Homendy said at an NTSB media briefing Tuesday. "We believe a critical safety issue must be addressed without delay."
The recommendations were released alongside a preliminary investigative report on the Jan. 29 midair collision of an American Airlines jetliner and a military helicopter near Reagan National that killed 67 people.
The NTSB urged the FAA to ban helicopters from a four-mile stretch over the Potomac River when airport runway 15/33 is in use and to designate an alternative route when the area is closed, according to the published recommendations. The American jet was on final approach to runway 15/33 when the collision occurred.
Homendy said that there were warning signs before the January collision, citing data detailing more than 15,000 near-collisions between commercial aircraft and helicopters at Reagan National between October 2021 and December 2024. The majority occurred during plane landings and at night, according to the NTSB's report.
"We're in a situation where we're threading the needle, allowing helicopters to fly down the same airspace as landing aircraft," Duffy said. "And why this information wasn't studied and known before January 29 is an important question."
Following the crash, Duffy restricted helicopter traffic around the airport through the end of March. He said those restrictions will continue in accordance with NTSB recommendations. Duffy said he also spoke with Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth about alternative military flight routes, with exceptions for presidential travel, life-saving operations and law enforcement.
The preliminary report does not identify any probable causes of the collision, as the NTSB is still in "the fact-finding phase" of its investigation, according to Homendy.
"We still have a lot of work to do in this investigation, so the report contains only the facts that we're able to validate and release at this time," Homendy said. "The easiest and quickest part of the investigation is determining what happened. The part that takes longer is the how and why."
Tuesday's NTSB media briefing was the fifth of its kind since the collision.
At a Feb. 14 briefing, Homendy told reporters that investigators believe that the helicopter crew was wearing night vision goggles that would have limited their peripheral vision. She also said that cockpit conversations suggest that the helicopter crew may not have heard key instructions from air traffic controllers and had inaccurate altitude readings in the moments before the crash.
Duffy criticized the air traffic control system as outdated, relying on 25- to 30-year-old technology, including floppy disks and plug-in headphones, at a separate press conference Tuesday. He pledged to propose a plan in the coming weeks that would revolutionize the "antiquated" technology, seeking congressional approval and funding.
"We're at a point where we can do this fast—three and a half to four years for a brand new air traffic control system. Gold plated. Envy of the world," he said. "It will greatly improve our safety…but it's also going to improve the efficiency that we have in American air travel, which I think will mean less delays, less cancellations, and again, better safety."
Despite concerns, Homendy reassured travelers.
"I just flew with my daughter out of DCA…aviation is incredibly safe," she said. "However, there are safety issues and areas where we need to improve to make sure that we are at zero."

title: Guilty but not held criminally responsible - 'I love you,' dad says to son who tried to kill him
author: Natalie Jones; njones@chespub.com
content:
Guilty but not held criminally responsible - 'I love you,' dad says to son who tried to kill him

 September 29, 2023 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Natalie Jones; njones@chespub.com | Page: 1 | Section: News 
 
 997
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON - The Ridgely man who struck his own father with a car in Cordova last December was found guilty, but not criminally responsible, of assault and related charges.Frank Justin Ashe Jr., 20, who goes by Justin, entered pleas to first-degree assault, use of a firearm in the commission of a violent crime and reckless endangerment, but maintained that he was not criminally responsible by reason of insanity - an argument that Talbot County Circuit Judge Stephen H. Kehoe later agreed with.The case against Justin stemmed from a reported assault in the 11000 block of Three Bridge Branch Road in Cordova around 3:30 p.m. on Dec. 4, 2022.In the roughly 90-minute hearing Thursday, the prosecution and defense shared two sides of the same story, providing joint insight on the day's events and Justin's mental state at the time.According to Frank J. Ashe Sr., Justin's father, his son wasn't acting like himself that morning, said Talbot County State's Attorney Joseph Coale. And to defense attorney Kisha Petticolas, Justin's unusual behavior had started some time before then.By all accounts, Justin was a normal kid who had never had problems, Petticolas said. But at some point in his teen years, he became fixated on Freemasonry, going down a social media rabbit hole that led to him seeing symbols and signs of the organization.Justin believed he knew too much and people wanted him eliminated because he knew their secrets, Pettico-las said. The night before, his mother had considered taking him to the hospital. And that day, he woke up "completely and positively sure" that someone was going to kill him.According to Coale, Justin, then 19, was in an outbuilding the afternoon of Dec. 4 when his father came to check on him. When Ashe Sr. entered, he found his son standing by the windows, holding a firearm and saying that someone was coming to get him, Coale said.Justin believed that the man who looked like his father was a clone who came to kill him, and the teen had armed himself for protection, Petti-colas said.Ashe Sr. told Justin to put the gun down, but Justin aimed it at his father.Ashe Sr. knew he needed to get the gun out of his son's hands and attempted to distract Justin. Ashe Sr. grabbed the gun, fighting to pull it away from Justin. But as the two wrestled, the gun went off, firing a bullet through a wall, Coale said.Justin ran out the back door of the outbuilding while Ashe Sr. went out the front door. He saw Justin get into a car and begin driving away, Coale said.But Justin turned the car around and accelerated toward his father, striking him and knocking him unconscious for several minutes.The family's security camera footage, which both father and son declined to view in court Thursday, captured the strike and the moments after. According to Coale, the video showed Justin approaching his father, taking the gun and stepping on his father's stomach and checking it for an old scar before getting back in the car.After regaining consciousness, Ashe Sr. was able to get up and enter his home, Coale said.Ashe Sr. suffered a broken back, brain bleeds and other smaller injuries from being struck with the car, Coale said. He was flown to the University of Maryland Shock Trauma in Baltimore for treatment.Justin's grandfather, who was inside the house, heard the earlier argument between the two men. By now, Justin had walked back into the house and was tackled by his grandfather, who was trying to secure the gun. A second shot was fired accidentally during the scuffle, according to the grandfather, Coale said.Justin drove off after the scuffle. Coale said he was apprehended by police on Interstate 95 near Rocky Mount, North Carolina, around 11 p.m. that night.Petticolas said while Justin's memory of the day didn't match what Coale presented, she acknowledged that the prosecution would have been able to produce those facts had the case gone to trial.Prior to rendering a verdict and final decision on the case, the court heard additional information to determine Justin's criminal responsibility.In a report from the Maryland Department of Health, a doctor diagnosed the 20-year-old with schizoaffective disorder, bipolar type. The diagnosis, along with Justin's behavior, paranoia and delusions, led to identical recommendations from the prosecution and defense - both asked the judge to find Justin not criminally responsible and commit him to the department.Justin's father provided tearful testimony in support of the best outcome for his son.Choked up with emotion, Ashe Sr. said he couldn't ask for a better son. He knew the teen wasn't trying to kill him, he said."What happened that day (was) just not my son," he said, later adding: "I didn't raise my son that way.""I love you, son," Ashe Sr. said, stepping off the witness stand. Across the courtroom, Justin replied: "I love you."To Petticolas, Justin's not criminally responsible plea was the clearest cut case she'd seen, and one in which justice could be found through the commitment to the Maryland Department of Health. The prosecution not arguing differently "speaks volumes," she said.And the Ashe family is "irreparably scarred," and they too need to heal, she said.After listening to the volume of testimony, Kehoe determined that Justin's actions directly stemmed from the delusions."(It's) clear to me beyond any question that he is not criminally responsible for what he did that day," he said.While Justin was found guilty, the lack of criminal responsibility finding in the case means that he will be committed to a state health department psychiatric hospital indefinitely until it's determined that he is not a danger.Not criminally responsible pleas are "fairly uncommon," according to Coale.After the hearing, Petticolas reflected on the the collegial practice within the smaller jurisdiction, which allowed the prosecution and defense to come up with results that served the public good, she said."I think justice was served today," she said.

title: Republicans pledge to 'restore balance' with public safety agenda
author: Steph Quinn; Capital News Service
content:
Republicans pledge to 'restore balance' with public safety agenda

 November 15, 2023 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Steph Quinn; Capital News Service | Page: 5 | Section: News 
 
 642
 Words 

 Read News Document

 ANNAPOLIS - Senate and House Republicans vowed Tuesday to redress what House Minority Leader Jason Buckel (R-Allegany) called Maryland's "soft on crime policies" with a 2024 public safety agenda that would intensify punishment for adults accused of gun-related and violent crimes and reverse reforms to the youth legal system passed by the General Assembly in 2022."The crime we're seeing in our communities is not anecdotal, nor media manufactured," said Senate Minority Leader Stephen Hershey (R-Kent, Queen Anne's, Cecil and Caroline). "It is real. The violence is real. And we are pleading with our Democrat colleagues to join us in making it their priority as well." The package would increase penalties for gun theft and violent firearms offenses, authorize law enforcement to search vehicles based on the smell of cannabis alone and limit eligibility for bail or reduced sentences for those charged with or convicted of violent crimes.One proposal would make theft of a firearm a felony - a measure Republicans have sponsored without success since 2018.Another would increase prison time and maximum fines for crimes committed with illegal firearms and would remove the "drug dealer loophole" whereby drug dealers receive a lighter sentence for possessing weapons than others committing similarly weighted offenses.A measure would eliminate reduced prison time for good behavior for those convicted of first-or second-degree murder, cap such reductions for other crimes of violence and prohibit bail for those accused of a crime of violence while facing pending violent crime charges.House and Senate Democratic leaders could not be reached to comment on the likelihood that the proposals in the package will clear Democratic majorities in both chambers.The youth justice proposal would require under-13 youth to appear before a juvenile court upon arrest for crimes involving firearms and broaden the juvenile court's jurisdiction to include youth on their third arrest for nonviolent crimes, including auto thefts. It would also allow police to interrogate youth with parental consent alone, rather than requiring that a young person first consult with an attorney.The proposal would allow law enforcement to skirt the Child in Need of Supervision process, which provides a pathway for police or citizens to enlist help from the Department of Juvenile Services in connecting youth of any age with services.Del. Jesse Pippy (R-Frederick) said current law, including the CINS process, has neither held "offenders that happen to be juveniles" accountable nor connected them with services."The argument we're hearing from on the street is (that) law enforcement doesn't know what to do with these kids," Pippy said."So they're not going anywhere.They're not getting any services. No one's talking with them. No one's following up with them." DJS data shows that most CINS cases end in referrals to services rather than in court, but also that law enforcement are using the process infrequently in much of the state.Though Pippy said he's open to programs to educate police officers on the CINS process, which dates to 1969 in Maryland law, he and others said that CINS is not sufficient.Buckel said youth involved in escalating and violent crimes "need more than what theChild In Need of Supervision system can provide." Pointing to closures of DJS residential facilities in western Maryland, Buckel suggested committed placement in DJS residential facilities could give youth "opportunities to succeed." "They're not draconian prisons," he said. "They're getting classes.They're getting education." But advocates of youth legal reform have pointed to research showing that youth incarceration increases the likelihood of recidivism and called for long-term investment in resource-starved communities.Senate Minority Whip Justin Ready (R-Frederick and Carroll) stressed a need for balance in comments after the press conference, saying, "I think we need to provide more accountability and more services that are truly effective."

title: CPD juvenile crime report shows juvenile referrals, vehicle thefts are up
author: MAGGIE TROVATO mtrovato@chespub.com
content:
CPD juvenile crime report shows juvenile referrals, vehicle thefts are up

 March 6, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: MAGGIE TROVATO mtrovato@chespub.com | Section: Local News 
 
 631
 Words 

 Read News Document

 CAMBRIDGE — The number of juvenile referrals made by the Cambridge Police Department has increased since 2021, according to a CPD report that looks at juvenile crime from 2021 to 2023.Juvenile referrals are incident reports, written by the police department, that are sent to the Maryland Department of Juvenile Services. According to the report, CPD issued 114 juvenile referrals in 2023. The year before, in 2022, 111 juvenile referrals were issued.
In 2021, 63 juvenile referrals were issued.
Cambridge Police Chief Justin Todd said that with juvenile referrals, instead of arresting a child and bringing them back to the police department to be charged, the Department of Juvenile Services steps in.
"Say two children get involved in an assault," Todd said. "They fight each other, there's no serious injuries. We do juvenile referrals and send them to Juvenile Services so Juvenile Services can do their part by following up with the child and the parents, instead of (CPD) actually going through an arrest practice with them."
Todd said a change in juvenile laws has contributed to this rise in referrals.
Under the Maryland Juvenile Justice Reform Act of 2022, children under the age of 13 can only be charged with crimes of violence, which include murder, robbery, carjacking and first-degree assault, among other offenses considered violent.
In its report, CPD states that this act has also made it so that most children are released by police to a parent or guardian unless they are arrested on a warrant or writ issued by the court, or they have a violation involving a firearm or crime of violence.
"So instead of charging a child, we just send a report on over to the Juvenile Services and let it be handled at that level, since it's not a crime of violence," Todd said about the referrals.
The CPD report also shows that the number of juvenile warrant arrests recorded in Cambridge has decreased 80%, from 25 to five, between 2022 and 2023.
Todd noted this change is significant and said it could possibly be attributed to the change in laws as well.
"It's simply because we're not receiving the court orders or the warrants to go and file paperwork against juveniles," he said.
Other than the referrals, Todd said there isn't a huge difference in the data over three years. He said the area where CPD is seeing a big difference is stolen vehicle cases involving youth.
From 2021 to 2023, the number of motor vehicle thefts has gone up from 15 to 102. The CPD report states that for 15 reports of vehicle theft in 2021, 10 cases involved juvenile suspects.
For the 102 reports of vehicle theft in 2023, 29 cases involved juvenile suspects.
In the report, CPD said that in 2023, all of the juvenile offenders caught and charged with vehicle theft were immediately released due to changes in state law.
"Through investigation and statistical analysis, we have determined that the overwhelming suspect profiles for these crimes are male juveniles under the age of 16," the report said. "But we have detained suspects as young as 11 for stealing vehicles in Cambridge."
According to the report, there is one 12-year-old that has been arrested for vehicle theft 11 times in the past three years.
As the number of vehicle thefts have increased in Cambridge, Todd said the current juvenile laws have affected what police can do when the suspect is a child.
"We can't interview that juvenile after we arrested him because of the new juvenile laws," he said. "... We can't go and do an interrogation or anything without first asking — not even permission from the parents — we have to have (the child) obtain a lawyer."
Todd said it's unlikely a lawyer would have the child speak with the police in this instance.
"So that's where our juvenile laws really are starting to affect us," he said.

title: Ridgely police force saga is far from over
author: Konner Metz
content:
Ridgely police force saga is far from over

 Author/Byline: Konner Metz | Section: Headlines

 Though it hasn't been an active agency for nearly 18 months, the Ridgely Police Department is still making noise in Caroline County.Police officers and employees were suspended by town commissioners in March 2024 and later laid off, leaving the town with coverage through a contract with the Caroline County Sheriff's Office. But the matter is now being taken to federal court.
Former Police Chief Jeff Eckrich, six former officers and a former employee have filed a lawsuit, alleging that town officials and Caroline County Sheriff Donnie Baker formed a "coup" to disband RPD.
Among many claims, the lawsuit asserts that Baker and former Ridgely officer James Joles "devised a plan that would eliminate the RPD and allow the Sheriff's Office" to take over policing in the town."
Joles, who resigned in 2024 and provided documentation to town officials that led to a state investigation into Eckrich for alleged misconduct, spoke to The Star Democrat on Wednesday. He denied claims made in the lawsuit.
To learn more about Joles' comments and the lawsuit itself, read our story below.
Thanks for reading.

HOMICIDE: Fatal shooting under investigation in Queen Anne's

 June 1, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Staff Writer | Section: News 
 
 379
 Words 

 Read News Document

 QUEENSTOWN — Route 213 (Centerville Road) John Brown Road and Lloyds Meadow Lane has reopened following an ongoing fatal shooting investigation.At approximately 1:15 a.m. on June 1, deputies from the Queen Anne's County Office of the Sheriff responded to reports of gunfire in the 1500 block of Centreville Road. Prior to law enforcement arrival, a large party had been held at a residence in the area.
According to a statement released by the sheriff's office, witnesses reported that upon hearing gunshots, attendees fled the scene. Deputies located three individuals suffering from gunshot wounds. One victim was pronounced deceased, and the other two victims were transported to area hospitals, where they remain hospitalized.
Mid-day Sunday, police confirmed Christopher Parsley, 19, of Centreville is the deceased victim. Police said they would not release the names of the other two gunshot victims at this point in the investigation.
Through witness interviews, investigators believe the suspect or suspects were present at the party before the shooting occurred.
Dispatch reports indicated that at 1:19 a.m., emergency medical teams, including units from Talbot and Caroline counties and two Maryland State Police helicopters, were dispatched to the scene. At 1:35 a.m., EMS personnel advised a Mass Casualty Incident response. By 2:06 a.m., the incident was placed under control, with EMS and fire units clearing the scene shortly afterward.
Sheriff Gary Hofmann expressed his condolences: "Our thoughts and prayers are with the family of the victim whose life was tragically taken, as well as with those who were injured. This kind of violence has no place in our community. We are working diligently to identify and apprehend those responsible. I encourage anyone with information to come forward, your help could make all the difference in delivering justice for these families."
There is no suspect in custody at this time, Public Information Officer Kaitlyn Briselli said.
The Queen Anne's County Sheriff's Office is leading the investigation. Anyone with information related to this incident or the identity of those involved is urged to contact the Queen Anne's County Office of the Sheriff at Sheriff-Info@qac.org or by calling the Anonymous Tip Line at 410-758-6666.
Further updates will be provided when released by the investigating authorities.
This story was updated at 10:10 a.m., June 1. This story was updated again at 2:11 p.m. with the name of the deceased.

title: Maryland State Police investigating two late-night fatal crashes in Queen Anne’s, Kent counties
author: Staff Writer
content:
Maryland State Police investigating two late-night fatal crashes in Queen Anne’s, Kent counties

 September 21, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Staff Writer | Section: News 
 
 396
 Words 

 Read News Document

 CENTREVILLE — Maryland State Police are investigating two fatal crashes that occurred late Saturday in Queen Anne's and Kent counties, police said.Around 11:22 p.m. Saturday, troopers from the Maryland State Police Centreville Barrack responded to the area of northbound U.S. Route 301 at Hayden Clark Road in Centreville for a report of a two-vehicle crash involving a motorcycle, police said.
The operator of the motorcycle, identified as Marcus Dangerfield, 20, of Dover, Delaware, was pronounced dead at the scene, police said. The driver of a GMC Acadia, a 45-year-old man, was taken by ambulance to the R Adams Cowley Shock Trauma Center. A passenger in the SUV, a 38-year-old woman, was flown by Maryland State Police Aviation Command to the same hospital.
The preliminary investigation indicates the GMC was traveling east on Hayden Clark Road, attempting to cross northbound U.S. Route 301, when it was struck by the motorcycle for unknown reasons, police said.
U.S. Route 301 was closed for more than two hours for the crash investigation. Assistance at the scene was provided by the Church Hill Fire Department, Queen Anne's County emergency medical services and the Maryland Department of Transportation State Highway Administration.
Around 11:55 p.m. Saturday, troopers from the Centreville Barrack responded to Maryland Route 213 and Riley's Mill Road in Chestertown for a report of a single-vehicle crash, police said.
A passenger in a Ford Fusion, a 17-year-old boy, was pronounced dead at the scene, police said. The driver, a 19-year-old woman, was flown by Maryland State Police Aviation Command to the Shock Trauma Center for treatment of her injuries. Three other passengers — a 21-year-old woman, a 17-year-old boy and a 23-year-old woman — were transported by ambulance to University of Maryland Shore Medical Center at Chestertown, police said.
As of Sunday morning, police had not released the names of those involved in the Kent County crash.
The preliminary investigation indicates the Ford was traveling south when, for unknown reasons, it left the roadway onto the right shoulder, lost control, struck a telephone pole and overturned, police said. Investigators believe impairment may have been a factor.
Maryland Route 213 was closed for more than two hours. Assistance at the scene was provided by the Chestertown Fire Department, Kent County emergency medical services and the Maryland Department of Transportation State Highway Administration.
The Maryland State Police Crash Team is leading the active and ongoing investigations into both crashes, police said.
